Proprio is a free, open course that takes you from zero to expert in Physical AI and humanoid robotics, with 11 modules, 52 lessons and a lab in every one.
Build a voice-commanded robot assistant end to end, take it toward real hardware, understand safety and standards, and turn the course into a career.
Read the full specification for the capstone, plan your milestones, and know exactly how your finished robot will be graded.
documents.s: Capstone brief: a voice-commanded robot assistant

documents.t: Follow a week-by-week plan, with the package layout, node graph, interfaces, test plan and debugging checklists, to build the capstone.
documents.s: Capstone build guide: from empty workspace to working robot

documents.t: Pick a robotics role, turn this course into a portfolio hiring managers trust, and follow a concrete 90-day plan after you finish.
documents.s: Careers and portfolio in physical AI

documents.t: Move your stack from Gazebo to a physical robot using embedded compute, ros2_control, safety stops, calibration, logging and staged field tests.
documents.s: Deploying on hardware: from simulation to a real robot

documents.t: Apply a functional-safety mindset, run a simple risk assessment, and know which standards govern robots near people.
documents.s: Ethics, safety and standards for physical AI

documents.t: Use language, vision and action models to turn spoken instructions into safe robot behavior, and learn how to measure whether it works.
Measure a language-driven robot honestly with success rates and confidence intervals, test generalization, and add guardrails, oversight and failure recovery.
Turn a plain-language instruction into a validated plan of robot skills, and explain SayCan-style grounding, code as policies and tool calling.
documents.s: Large language models as robot planners

documents.t: Explain how VLA models turn images and instructions into actions, compare tokenized and diffusion or flow-based action heads, and outline how to fine-tune one.
Connect words to pixels and 3D points using CLIP-style embeddings, open-vocabulary detection and vision-language question answering.
documents.s: Vision-language grounding: finding what the words mean

documents.t: Design and build a pipeline that turns spoken commands into ROS 2 action goals, with speech recognition, intent parsing, safety words and spoken feedback.
documents.s: Voice-to-action: from speech to a ROS 2 action

documents.t: Learn the Python, math and tools that every robotics topic uses: NumPy, rotations and transforms, probability, optimization, Linux, Git and Docker.
Compute derivatives and gradients, check them numerically, and fit a model to noisy data with gradient descent and with least squares.
Use vectors, rotation matrices, homogeneous transforms and quaternions to describe where things are and to move a point between a camera, a robot and the world.
Work fluently in the Linux shell, version your code with Git, and run reproducible environments in Docker, including a ROS 2 Jazzy container.
Model noisy sensors with Gaussians, fuse two measurements, and use Bayes rule to update a belief, finishing with a small localizer that finds a robot in a corridor.
Use NumPy arrays, vectorised code, broadcasting and dataclasses to represent poses and trajectories, and simulate a differential-drive robot without a single slow loop.
Understand how two-legged robots stand, walk, use their whole body and handle objects, and build a push-recovery simulator.
Model a standing or walking robot as a linear inverted pendulum, compute its capture point and decide where to step to avoid a fall.
documents.s: Balance, the ZMP and the inverted pendulum

documents.t: Compare robot hand designs, explain how tactile sensors work, and describe how reinforcement learning produces in-hand manipulation.
Name the parts of a humanoid robot, count its degrees of freedom, and compare actuator choices using simple torque and inertia arithmetic.
documents.s: Humanoid anatomy: joints, actuators, sensors and compute

documents.t: Explain the gait cycle, how model-predictive control plans footsteps, and how reinforcement-learned walking policies are trained and moved to real robots.
documents.s: Locomotion: gaits, MPC walking and learned policies

documents.t: Combine many goals (balance, hand motion, posture, contact limits) into one controller using task-space control and prioritized quadratic programs.
Turn a goal into collision-free movement, for a wheeled robot with Nav2, for an arm with MoveIt 2, and for a gripper that has to pick something up.
Represent grasps, judge stability with antipodal and force-closure ideas, understand learned grasp detection, and design a full pick-and-place pipeline.
Plan and execute arm motions with MoveIt 2: the planning scene, move_group, collision objects, Cartesian paths and the Python and C++ interfaces.
Launch Nav2 with a simulated robot, understand costmaps, planners, controllers and behavior trees, and send navigation goals from Python.
Search a robot's configuration space with BFS, Dijkstra, A*, RRT and RRT*, then turn the resulting path into a smooth, timed trajectory.
Teach a robot to see and to know where it is: cameras, depth, deep learning, state estimation and SLAM.
Use the pinhole camera model to project and back-project points, calibrate a camera, and process images with OpenCV.
Run pretrained detectors and segmentation models on robot camera images and turn their outputs into 3D positions.
documents.s: Deep learning for detection and segmentation

documents.t: Turn depth images and lidar scans into 3D point clouds, then find the floor and separate objects with Open3D.
Build occupancy grids, align scans, localize with particle filters, and run slam_toolbox and AMCL on a ROS 2 robot.
Fuse noisy sensors into one reliable estimate with Bayes and Kalman filters, and configure robot_localization on a ROS 2 robot.
The physics and maths every robot shares: parts, frames, kinematics, dynamics and feedback control.
Name the four building blocks of any robot, trace how a signal travels from sensor to motor, and size a simple power and bandwidth budget.
Build a PID controller in Python, test it on a simulated motor, tune it, prevent integral windup, and see how cascaded and impedance control extend the idea.
Relate joint torques to motion with the manipulator equation, compute gravity and mass terms for a 2-link arm, and check torque limits.
Compute where a robot arm's hand is from its joint angles, and solve the reverse problem analytically and with damped least squares.
Describe where things are and how they are oriented using rotation matrices, homogeneous transforms and quaternions, and compose them correctly in NumPy.
Teach robots with data instead of hand-written rules: supervised learning, imitation learning, reinforcement learning, simulation at scale and the datasets behind it all.
Collect robot data through teleoperation, judge dataset quality, and understand how Open X-Embodiment and cross-embodiment learning change what robot models can do.
Teach a robot by showing it: behavior cloning, why it drifts, how DAgger fixes it, and how ACT and Diffusion Policy produce action sequences.
Review supervised learning, loss functions, gradient descent and overfitting, and write a complete PyTorch training loop on toy robot data.
documents.s: A machine learning refresher for robotics

documents.t: Learn MDPs, returns, value functions and policy gradients, build a REINFORCE agent that balances CartPole, and understand the intuition behind PPO.
See how thousands of simulated robots train in parallel, and design rewards, domain randomization and curricula that transfer to real hardware.
documents.s: Reinforcement learning in simulation with Isaac Lab

documents.t: Learn ROS 2 Jazzy hands-on: nodes, topics, services, actions, parameters, launch files, TF2, URDF, workspaces and bags.
Write an action server and client with feedback and cancellation, make nodes configurable with parameters, and start whole systems from one Python launch file.
Build a complete Python package with publishers, subscribers, a service server and client, and drive a simulated robot from your own node.
documents.s: Nodes, topics and services with rclpy

documents.t: Organise code in colcon workspaces, debug a live ROS 2 system with the CLI and rqt, and record and replay data with rosbag2.
Understand the ROS 2 graph, how DDS moves messages between processes, and choose QoS profiles and executors that fit your robot.
Keep track of every coordinate frame with TF2, describe a robot with URDF and xacro, and see it move in RViz using robot_state_publisher.
Build virtual worlds where robots can fail safely: Gazebo, simulated sensors, Isaac Sim and the sim-to-real gap.
Write an SDF world, spawn a URDF robot into Gazebo Harmonic, and drive it with a velocity command.
Understand how Isaac Sim is built (USD, Omniverse, PhysX, Replicator, the ROS 2 bridge) and when to choose it over Gazebo.
Explain why robots that work in simulation fail on hardware, and apply system identification and domain randomization to close the gap.
Add camera, depth, lidar and IMU sensors to a Gazebo robot, bridge their data to ROS 2, and see it in RViz.
documents.s: Simulated sensors and the ros_gz bridge

documents.t: Explain why robotics teams simulate first, how a physics engine steps time, and where its answers stop being trustworthy.
documents.s: Why simulate: physics engines and their limits

documents.t: Learn how the course works, set up an Ubuntu, ROS 2 and Gazebo workstation, and get a map of Physical AI before you write any robot code.
Set up a study routine and a project repository, and learn to use labs, exercises, quizzes, progress tracking and Rivet so the course actually sticks.
See the whole field at once: the sense, think, act loop, the stack from hardware to foundation models, where humanoids fit, and where each course module lives.
Install Ubuntu 24.04, ROS 2 Jazzy, Gazebo Harmonic, a Python virtual environment and VS Code, then prove it all works with a talker and listener.

Close your eyes and touch your nose. You did that without looking because your body knows where its own parts are. That sense is called proprioception, and it is the thing a robot has to learn before it can do anything useful. Proprio is a free, open course in Physical AI and humanoid robotics. It starts with a laptop and a terminal, and it ends with you building and demonstrating a robot system that sees, plans and acts. Every lesson has something you run, break and fix.

You are the right reader if you are curious about robots and willing to put in the hours. You do not need a robotics degree, and you do not need a robot. Complete beginners who can write a little code in any language and want a clear path into robotics. Software engineers who want to move into robotics, ROS 2, or AI that acts in the physical world. Students and researchers who know machine learning and need the robotics half: frames, control, perception, planning. Hobbyists who have built a robot arm or a rover and want to understand why it behaves the way it does. What you need A computer that can run Ubuntu 24.04 (natively, dual boot, or WSL2 on Windows), about 40 GB of free disk space, and 8 GB of RAM or more. A GPU helps in Modules 05, 07 and 09 but is not required to start. No hardware robot is needed: everything runs in simulation, and Module 10 shows you how to move to real hardware.

By the final module you can: Explain how a robot senses, thinks and acts, and where each part of the stack lives. Build, debug and launch multi-node systems in ROS 2 Jazzy. Model a robot, simulate it in Gazebo Harmonic, and understand the sim-to-real gap. Turn camera, depth and lidar data into maps, poses and object detections. Plan paths, navigate with Nav2, and pick and place with MoveIt 2. Train policies with imitation learning and reinforcement learning, and judge when they are ready. Describe how a humanoid balances, walks and uses its hands. Connect language and vision-language-action models to a robot, safely and with measurement. Ship a capstone project that you can show to an employer or a research group. The Proprio promise You learn by doing. Each module ends in something that runs on your machine, and each lesson builds one small, working piece of it. If you finish a lesson and cannot show something that works, the lesson has failed you, not the other way round.

documents.t: The order matters. Each module uses the tools from the one before it. If you already know a topic, skim its lesson, do the exercises as a test, and move on. Module What you learn What you build 00 · Start here How the course works, your workstation, the map of Physical AI A working Ubuntu, ROS 2 and Gazebo install 01 · Foundations Python and NumPy, linear algebra, probability, optimization, Linux and Git A small transform and sensor-fusion toolkit 02 · Robot fundamentals Robot anatomy, frames, kinematics, dynamics, PID control A two-link arm with kinematics and a tuned controller 03 · ROS 2 DDS, nodes, topics, services, actions, tf2, URDF, bags A multi-node ROS 2 package with launch files 04 · Simulation Gazebo worlds, simulated sensors, Isaac Sim, the sim-to-real gap A simulated mobile robot streaming sensor data 05 · Perception Cameras, depth, lidar, detection, Kalman filters, SLAM A pipeline that detects objects and localizes the robot 06 · Motion Path planning, Nav2, MoveIt 2, grasping A robot that navigates a room and picks an object 07 · Robot learning Imitation learning, reinforcement learning, Isaac Lab, datasets A trained policy running in simulation 08 · Humanoids Humanoid anatomy, balance and ZMP, locomotion, whole-body control, hands A balance and walking study on a simulated humanoid 09 · Foundation models LLM planners, grounding, VLA models, voice, evaluation and safety A voice-to-action pipeline with safety checks 10 · Capstone and career Capstone design, hardware deployment, ethics and standards, portfolio Your capstone project and a portfolio page

Every lesson follows the same shape, so you always know where you are. A hook. A real robot problem that needs the lesson. Objectives. Three to five things you will be able to do. Teaching. Intuition first, then the precise version, with diagrams, math and code. Hands-on lab. A small build with a clear check that tells you it worked. Exercises. Two or three tasks, each with a hidden solution. Try before you peek. Quiz. Four questions. They are there to help you remember, not to grade you. Takeaways and Go deeper. A summary, plus links to the official docs and papers. Read the lesson with a terminal open beside it. Type the code yourself instead of pasting it. It is slower, and you will remember more. Do the lab before the exercises. Take the quiz without scrolling back up. Mark the lesson complete. Your progress is saved in your browser and shown as ticks in the sidebar. Keep a lab journal Make one git repository for your work (Module 00 shows how) and commit after every lab. By Module 10 you will have a history of everything you built, which is also your portfolio.

Rivet is the course assistant. Find it at the bottom-right of any page. It reads the course, knows which lesson you are on, and answers with links back to the relevant sections. Good questions to ask: "Explain the difference between a topic and a service, with a robot example." "My ros2 run says package not found. What should I check?" "Give me one more exercise like this one, but harder." Rivet is a helper, not an oracle. It can be wrong, especially about versions and error messages, so check commands against the official docs linked in each lesson. Try the problem for ten minutes before you ask. You will learn more from the struggle.
documents.s: Ask Rivet when you are stuck

documents.t: At about 8 to 10 hours a week this fits a semester. Go faster if you have the time, and slower if you do not. There is no deadline. Weeks Modules Focus 1 to 2 00 and 01 Start here and Foundations: setup, the big picture, Python, math and tools 3 to 4 02 Robot fundamentals: anatomy, kinematics, control 5 to 6 03 ROS 2 in depth 7 04 Simulation 8 to 9 05 Perception and state estimation 10 06 Motion: navigation and manipulation 11 to 12 07 Robot learning 13 08 Humanoids 14 09 Foundation models for robots 15 to 16 10 Capstone and career: project, deployment, portfolio Note Each lesson is 25 to 45 minutes of reading plus a lab of similar length. Labs are where most of the learning happens, so budget for them.

Begin with Module 00 · Start here. In about three lessons you will know how the course works, have a complete robotics workstation, and have a mental map of the whole field. Next: How this course works

This is where everything comes together. Across the earlier modules you learned each piece on its own: how robots move, how ROS 2 connects software, how to simulate, perceive, plan and learn, and how foundation models can turn language into action. In this module you combine those pieces into one working system, a voice-commanded robot assistant that hears a request, plans, drives, finds an object and picks it up. The module also looks past the screen. A system that works in simulation is only half of the story. You will learn what changes on real hardware, how to think about safety and standards before a robot ever goes near people, and how to present your work so that others can see what you can do.

Specify, plan and build a complete robot system with measurable requirements. Structure a multi-package ROS 2 workspace with clear interfaces and tests. Evaluate a robot with logged trials and fix the biggest failure first. Describe how to move from Gazebo to real hardware using ros2_control, safety stops and calibration. Run a simple risk assessment and name the main robot-safety standards. Present a portfolio and follow a 90-day plan toward your first robotics role.

The module project is the capstone itself: a voice-commanded robot assistant in simulation. A mobile manipulator in Gazebo Harmonic hears a spoken request such as "bring the red cup to the table", plans with an LLM, navigates with Nav2, perceives with a detector and picks and places with MoveIt 2. You finish with a repository that builds and runs from one command, an evaluation of at least 20 logged trials with a failure breakdown, a short demo video and a written safety summary. Choose one stretch goal, such as a humanoid variant or a reduced run on real hardware, if you want to go further. Stuck at any point? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

Advanced40 minBefore this:Modules 03 to 09 (or the lessons you plan to lean on) · A working ROS 2 Jazzy and Gazebo Harmonic setup You are standing in a simulated apartment. You say, "Bring the red cup to the table." A mobile robot hears you, works out what you mean, drives to the counter, spots the red cup among three other objects, grasps it, carries it across the room and sets it down on the table. Nobody touches a keyboard. That one sentence touches nearly everything you have learned: speech, language models, navigation, perception, manipulation and the glue that holds them together. This lesson is the contract for building it. You will be able to Describe the capstone system end to end and name the subsystem that owns each step. Turn the requirements into a milestone plan you can actually finish. Predict how your project will be graded, using the rubric, and design your evidence to match. Choose a stretch goal that fits your time and ambition.
documents.s: Capstone brief: a voice-commanded robot assistant

documents.t: The capstone is a voice-commanded robot assistant in simulation. The robot is a mobile manipulatorA robot with a wheeled or tracked base that can drive around, plus one or more arms that can grasp and move objects.: a base that drives plus an arm with a gripper. It lives in Gazebo Harmonic, talks to ROS 2 Jazzy through ros_gz, and must complete spoken fetch-and-carry requests with no human help after the command. Here is the whole loop at a glance. Every box maps to a lesson you have already read. The planner comes from LLMs as robot planners, the full chain from Voice to action, navigation from Navigation with Nav2, and manipulation from Manipulation with MoveIt 2. Integration is the hard part Each subsystem on its own is a solved exercise from an earlier module. The capstone is difficult because they must work together: timing, frames, failure handling and shared state. A robot that does four things 90 percent of the time finishes the whole task only about two thirds of the time. Plan for the seams.

You choose your robot model, but it must meet these minimums. A differential-drive or omnidirectional base with odometry. A 2D lidar (or a depth camera usable for navigation) for localization and obstacle avoidance. An arm with at least 5 degrees of freedom and a parallel-jaw gripper. An RGB-D camera that can see the workspace in front of the arm. A way to receive audio. In simulation this can be your computer microphone, or recorded .wav files played into the pipeline. The world is an apartment-style environment you build in Gazebo: at least two rooms, a counter, a table, and four to six household objects. The objects include a red cup, a blue cup and a green box, plus one or two distractors. Object positions on the counter are randomized for each trial. Fixed positions are not allowed, because they let you skip perception.

Requirements are numbered so your write-up and the grading can refer to them. ID Requirement Must or should R1 Accept a spoken English request and convert it to text Must R2 Use an LLM to produce a structured plan from the text Must R3 Validate every plan against an allowlist of actions and known places before any motion Must R4 Navigate between rooms with Nav2, avoiding a moving or unexpected obstacle Must R5 Detect and localize the target object from camera data, not from ground truth Must R6 Pick the object and place it on a named surface with MoveIt 2 Must R7 Report progress and failures back to the user in text (speech output is a stretch goal) Must R8 Recover from at least two failure types without human help (for example a failed grasp or a blocked path) Must R9 Provide a one-command bring-up and a one-command evaluation run Must R10 Stop motion within one second when a stop command is published Should R3 and R10 are not decoration. A language model can emit a confident, wrong plan, and your robot has to survive that. You will meet this idea again in Evaluation and safety and in Ethics, safety and standards. Ground truth is a cheat Gazebo can tell you exactly where every object is. Using that for R5 will make the demo easy and the grade low. Use it only to score your trials, never to drive the robot.

Eight weeks is a comfortable pace if you work a few evenings each week. Cut it shorter if you are already strong in some areas, but keep the order, because later milestones depend on earlier ones. Milestone Week Done means M1: Robot and world 1 The robot spawns, drives with teleop, and publishes sensors into ROS 2 M2: Navigation 2 to 3 The robot reaches named places in the map reliably, 9 of 10 times M3: Perception 3 to 4 The detector returns the target object pose in the map frame with a measured error M4: Manipulation 4 to 5 The arm picks and places a known object at a known spot, scripted M5: Language and voice 6 Spoken text becomes a validated plan, tested on 20 phrasings M6: Integration 7 The full request works end to end, with recovery behaviors M7: Evaluation and demo 8 Trial results, a demo video and a written report The detailed week-by-week instructions, package layout and node graph are in the Capstone build guide.

Your work is scored out of 100. Whether you are submitting to an instructor, a study group or just yourself, grade honestly against this table. Criterion Weight Full marks look like Functionality 30 The end-to-end request succeeds on most trials with randomized object placement Evaluation and robustness 20 At least 20 logged trials, a success rate, a failure breakdown by stage, and fixes driven by that breakdown Architecture and code quality 15 Clear packages, typed interfaces, launch files, parameters in YAML, a few real tests Safety and failure handling 15 Plan validation, stop command, timeouts, and recovery behaviors you can demonstrate Documentation and reproducibility 10 A stranger can clone, build and run in under 30 minutes using your README Demo and write-up 10 A clear 3-minute video and a short report with honest limitations Measure, then fix The strongest submissions are not the ones that work first time. They are the ones that log every trial, find that, say, 60 percent of failures happen at the grasp, and then improve the grasp. A failure breakdown table is worth more than a polished video.

A trial is one spoken request, from the moment the command is accepted to the moment the robot reports done or gives up. Success means the correct object rests on the correct surface, within 10 cm of the target spot, and nothing was knocked over. Record each trial as one line of JSON. eval/scenario.yaml name: bring_red_cup_to_table trials: 20 randomize: red_cup_on_counter: {x_range: [-0.3, 0.3], y_range: [-0.2, 0.2]} distractors: [blue_cup, green_box] command: "Bring the red cup to the table." success: object: red_cup surface: table max_distance_m: 0.10 timeout_s: 240 Your evaluation script then turns the log into the numbers the rubric asks for. eval/summarize.py import json import statistics import sys from collections import Counter from pathlib import Path def load(path): lines = Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines() return [json.loads(line) for line in lines if line.strip()] def summarize(trials): wins = [t for t in trials if t["success"]] print(f"trials: {len(trials)}") print(f"success rate: {len(wins) / len(trials):.0%}") if wins: median = statistics.median(t["duration_s"] for t in wins) print(f"median time of successful trials: {median:.0f} s") failures = Counter(t["failure_stage"] for t in trials if not t["success"]) for stage, count in failures.most_common(): print(f" failed at {stage}: {count}") if __name__ == "__main__": summarize(load(sys.argv[1])) Each line in trials.jsonl looks like {"success": false, "duration_s": 212.4, "failure_stage": "grasp"}. For successful trials, set failure_stage to null.

Do the required work first. Then pick one stretch goal, not three. Depth beats breadth. Speech out. Add text-to-speech so the robot says what it is doing and asks a clarifying question when the request is ambiguous ("I see two cups. Which one?"). Multi-step requests. "Put the blue cup on the counter, then bring me the green box." Your plan validator needs to handle ordering and shared state. Humanoid variant. Swap the wheeled base for a humanoid in simulation and have it walk or be carried between rooms by a locomotion policy. Pair this with Locomotion and Whole-body control. Expect this to take several extra weeks. Learned grasping or a VLA. Replace the scripted grasp with a learned policy, as in Vision-language-action models, and compare success rates against your classical baseline. Real hardware. Run a reduced version on a physical robot, following Deploying on hardware. A low-cost wheeled base with a small arm is enough.

Set up the project skeleton and the evaluation harness before you write any robot code. It is the cheapest way to make the rest of the project measurable. Create a repository named proprio-capstone with a README.md that states the project goal, the requirements table (R1 to R10) and your milestone dates. Copy scenario.yaml and summarize.py from this lesson into an eval/ folder. Change the command and objects to match your own world. Write a tiny eval/fake_trials.jsonl with ten invented trials (a mix of successes and failures at different stages) and run python eval/summarize.py eval/fake_trials.jsonl. You should see a success rate and a failure breakdown. In your README, add a one-paragraph risk list: the three things most likely to go wrong and your plan for each. Commit with a message such as "Add capstone skeleton and eval harness", and tag it m0. You know it worked when the summary script prints sensible numbers from your fake data and someone else could read your README and tell what "done" means. Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

Compose the probabilityIntermediate Suppose your system has four stages with independent success rates: speech 0.95, planning 0.95, navigation 0.9 and manipulation 0.8. What is the expected end-to-end success rate, and which stage should you improve first if you can raise only one stage by 0.05? Show solutionHide solution Multiply the stages: 0.95 × 0.95 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.65, about 65 percent. Raising manipulation from 0.8 to 0.85 gives 0.69. Raising navigation from 0.9 to 0.95 gives 0.69 too, while raising speech or planning to 1.0 would give about 0.68. In practice, improve the stage with the lowest rate that is cheapest to fix, and always confirm with measured failure data, since the independence assumption is rarely true. Write an ambiguity ruleBeginner The user says, "Bring me the cup." There are two cups in the scene. Write the behavior your robot should show, in two or three sentences, and say which requirement it relates to. Show solutionHide solution The robot should not guess. It should report that it sees two cups (red and blue) and ask which one to fetch, then wait for a reply or time out safely. This relates to R3 (validating the plan before motion, since the plan is underspecified) and R7 (reporting back to the user). A stretch goal would speak the question aloud. Pick your stretch goalAdvanced Choose one stretch goal and write a half-page plan: what you will build, how you will measure it against the baseline, and what you will cut if you fall behind. Show solutionHide solution A good answer names a measurable outcome ("learned grasp reaches at least the scripted grasp success rate over 20 trials"), a comparison against the required baseline, a date, and an explicit fallback ("if the learned policy is not working by week 7, report what I tried and ship the scripted grasp"). Plans that name a fallback are more likely to finish.

1Why is using Gazebo ground truth for object locations not allowed for driving the robot? AIt runs too slowly in simulationBIt skips perception, which the capstone is meant to exerciseCROS 2 does not publish ground truthDIt breaks the Nav2 costmap 2Which requirement protects the robot from a confident but wrong LLM plan? AR1, speech to textBR3, validating every plan against an allowlist before motionCR6, pick and place with MoveIt 2DR9, one-command bring-up 3What does the grading rubric reward most directly for improving a project over time? AA longer demo videoBMore packages in the repositoryCLogged trials with a failure breakdown that drives fixesDUsing the newest language model 4Why does a chain of four 90 percent subsystems finish the whole task only about two thirds of the time? ASuccess probabilities multiply across stagesBROS 2 adds latency at each hopCLanguage models are unreliableDGazebo randomizes failures 0 of 4 answered Takeaways The capstone is a voice-commanded mobile manipulator in Gazebo Harmonic that hears, plans, navigates, perceives and picks and places. Requirements R1 to R10 define done; R3 (plan validation) and R10 (stop command) are the safety backbone. Integration, not any single subsystem, is where most of the difficulty lives. You are graded on measured evidence: logged trials, failure breakdowns, reproducibility and an honest write-up. Never drive the robot with simulator ground truth; use it only to score trials. Choose one stretch goal and plan a fallback before you start.

Gazebo documentation for worlds, models and the ros_gz bridge. Nav2 documentation for the navigation stack you will configure. MoveIt 2 documentation for planning and pick-and-place tutorials. ROS 2 Jazzy documentation for everything underneath. Next: Capstone build guide

Expert45 minBefore this:Capstone brief · ROS 2 actions, launch files and tf2 · Nav2 and MoveIt 2 basics Week three of the build. The robot drives beautifully on its own, the arm picks beautifully on its own, and when you wire them together the arm waves at an empty counter because the camera frame was never connected to the map. Every capstone hits a moment like this. The fix is rarely clever; it is a clear structure that makes the problem easy to find. This guide gives you that structure: how to lay out your packages, how the nodes talk, what to build each week and how to test and debug it. You will be able to Lay out a ROS 2 workspace for a multi-subsystem robot with clean package boundaries. Define the topics and actions that connect the subsystems, including one custom action. Build the system in the right order, testing each layer before the next. Apply a debugging checklist to find which layer a failure lives in.
documents.s: Capstone build guide: from empty workspace to working robot

documents.t: Split the project by responsibility, not by language. Each package has one job and a short list of dependencies. This keeps builds fast and lets you test each piece alone. proprio_ws/src/ proprio_interfaces/ custom msg and action definitions (CMake package) proprio_description/ URDF/xacro, meshes, ros2_control tags proprio_sim/ Gazebo worlds, ros_gz bridge config, spawn launch proprio_navigation/ Nav2 params, maps, localization launch proprio_perception/ detector node, pose estimation, camera config proprio_manipulation/ MoveIt 2 config, pick_place action server proprio_voice/ audio capture, speech-to-text node proprio_planner/ LLM client, prompt, plan validator proprio_mission/ orchestrator (state machine over actions) proprio_bringup/ top-level launch files and parameter YAML proprio_eval/ trial runner, scoring, scenario files Keep every tunable value (frame names, object names, timeouts, model names) in YAML under proprio_bringup/config/. Never hard-code them in nodes. This is the habit from Actions, parameters and launch files.
Here is how the nodes talk at runtime. Solid arrows are topics; the orchestrator calls actions on Nav2 and on your pick-and-place server.

Agree on interfaces first. If the contracts are stable, you can build and test the pieces in any order. Interface Type Direction Purpose /audio/utterance audio_common_msgs or a file path in std_msgs/String mic to ASR One recorded utterance (your choice, document it) /speech/text std_msgs/String ASR to planner Transcript of the request /mission/plan std_msgs/String (JSON list) planner to orchestrator A validated list of steps /mission/status std_msgs/String orchestrator to user Progress and failures navigate_to_pose nav2_msgs/action/NavigateToPose orchestrator to Nav2 Drive to a named place pick_place proprio_interfaces/action/PickPlace orchestrator to manipulation Pick or place /perception/objects vision_msgs/Detection3DArray detector to manipulation Detected objects with map-frame poses /emergency_stop std_msgs/Bool anyone to all movers Latched stop request Only one interface is custom. Define it once in proprio_interfaces. proprio_interfaces/action/PickPlace.action # mode is "pick" or "place" string mode # object to pick, or surface to place on string name --- bool success string message --- string phase The plan itself is a short JSON list with an allowlist of three actions. example plan [ {"action": "navigate_to", "target": "counter"}, {"action": "pick", "object": "red_cup"}, {"action": "navigate_to", "target": "table"}, {"action": "place", "target": "table"} ] The orchestrator is a small, boring state machine Resist putting intelligence in the glue. The LLM decides what to do; the orchestrator only runs validated steps one at a time, checks each result and aborts cleanly on failure. A short, deterministic orchestrator is easy to test and easy to trust.

This node validates the plan, then executes steps in order. Notice that it rejects bad plans before anything moves. proprio_mission/orchestrator.py import json import math import rclpy from action_msgs.msg import GoalStatus from geometry_msgs.msg import PoseStamped from nav2_msgs.action import NavigateToPose from proprio_interfaces.action import PickPlace from rclpy.action import ActionClient from rclpy.node import Node from std_msgs.msg import String # (x, y, yaw) in the map frame; load these from YAML in your real project PLACES = {"table": (2.0, 0.5, 0.0), "counter": (-1.0, 2.0, 1.57)} ALLOWED = {"navigate_to": "target", "pick": "object", "place": "target"} def validate(plan): if not isinstance(plan, list) or not plan: raise ValueError("plan must be a non-empty list") for step in plan: if not isinstance(step, dict) or step.get("action") not in ALLOWED: raise ValueError(f"unknown step: {step!r}") field = ALLOWED[step["action"]] if set(step) != {"action", field}: raise ValueError(f"bad fields for {step['action']}: {sorted(step)}") if field == "target" and step["target"] not in PLACES: raise ValueError(f"unknown place: {step['target']!r}") return plan def pose_for(name, stamp): x, y, yaw = PLACES[name] pose = PoseStamped() pose.header.frame_id = "map" pose.header.stamp = stamp pose.pose.position.x = x pose.pose.position.y = y pose.pose.orientation.z = math.sin(yaw / 2) pose.pose.orientation.w = math.cos(yaw / 2) return pose class Orchestrator(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__("orchestrator") self.nav = ActionClient(self, NavigateToPose, "navigate_to_pose") self.manip = ActionClient(self, PickPlace, "pick_place") self.status_pub = self.create_publisher(String, "/mission/status", 10) self.create_subscription(String, "/mission/plan", self.on_plan, 10) self.steps = [] self.busy = False def say(self, text): self.get_logger().info(text) self.status_pub.publish(String(data=text)) def on_plan(self, msg): if self.busy: self.say("busy: plan ignored") return try: self.steps = validate(json.loads(msg.data)) except ValueError as err: self.say(f"rejected plan: {err}") return self.busy = True self.next_step() def next_step(self): if not self.steps: self.busy = False self.say("done") return step = self.steps.pop(0) self.say(f"step: {step}") if step["action"] == "navigate_to": goal = NavigateToPose.Goal() goal.pose = pose_for(step["target"], self.get_clock().now().to_msg()) self.send(self.nav, goal) elif step["action"] == "pick": self.send(self.manip, PickPlace.Goal(mode="pick", name=step["object"])) else: self.send(self.manip, PickPlace.Goal(mode="place", name=step["target"])) def send(self, client, goal): if not client.server_is_ready(): self.abort("action server not available") return client.send_goal_async(goal).add_done_callback(self.on_accepted) def on_accepted(self, future): handle = future.result() if not handle.accepted: self.abort("goal rejected") return handle.get_result_async().add_done_callback(self.on_result) def on_result(self, future): wrapped = future.result() ok = wrapped.status == GoalStatus.STATUS_SUCCEEDED if ok and hasattr(wrapped.result, "success"): ok = wrapped.result.success if ok: self.next_step() else: self.abort(f"step failed (status {wrapped.status})") def abort(self, why): self.steps.clear() self.busy = False self.say(f"aborted: {why}") def main(): rclpy.init() rclpy.spin(Orchestrator()) if __name__ == "__main__": main() For recovery (requirement R8), extend on_result: when a pick fails once, re-run the detector and retry; when navigation fails, call Nav2’s clear-costmap service and retry. Keep the retry count small and logged.

Week 1: robot and world. Build the world and the robot description. Bridge the sensors with ros_gz. Drive with keyboard teleop and confirm /tf, /scan, /odom and camera topics appear. Lesson links: Gazebo worlds and robots, Simulated sensors and ros_gz, TF2 and URDF. Weeks 2 to 3: navigation. Build a map with SLAM, then localize and navigate with Nav2. Define the named places. Test 10 runs between each pair. See Navigation with Nav2 and SLAM and localization. Weeks 3 to 4: perception. Detect the objects, back-project the detection with the depth image, and transform the result into the map frame with tf2. Measure position error against ground truth, using ground truth only for scoring. See Deep learning for detection and segmentation and Depth, point clouds and lidar. Weeks 4 to 5: manipulation. Configure MoveIt 2 for your arm, add the table and counter as collision objects, and write the pick_place server: approach, grasp, lift, carry pose, place, retreat. See Manipulation with MoveIt 2 and Grasping. Week 6: language and voice. Build speech-to-text, the LLM planner with a system prompt that lists only the allowed actions and places, and test 20 different phrasings. See LLMs as robot planners and Voice to action. Week 7: integration. Run the orchestrator with the real subsystems. Add the stop topic, timeouts and the two recovery behaviors. Week 8: evaluation and demo. Run 20 or more trials, fix the biggest failure stage, record the demo and write the report.

Test at three levels, and run the cheaper tests more often. Level What it checks Example Unit Pure functions with no ROS validate() accepts the example plan and rejects an unknown place, a missing field and an empty list Subsystem One package with the others faked Publish a fake plan and confirm the orchestrator calls the right action servers in order System The whole chain in simulation The 20-trial evaluation from the brief A unit test for the validator takes five minutes and catches the most dangerous class of bug: proprio_mission/test/test_validate.py import pytest from proprio_mission.orchestrator import validate def test_accepts_good_plan(): plan = [{"action": "navigate_to", "target": "table"}] assert validate(plan) == plan @pytest.mark.parametrize("bad", [ [], [{"action": "fly", "target": "table"}], [{"action": "navigate_to", "target": "moon"}], [{"action": "pick"}], ]) def test_rejects_bad_plans(bad): with pytest.raises(ValueError): validate(bad)

When something fails, work down the stack. Do not guess. Nothing moves. Is the simulation running and unpaused? Check ros2 topic hz /clock. Is the bridge up? ros2 topic list should show your sensor topics. Did the orchestrator accept the plan? Read /mission/status. Is the action server visible? ros2 action list. Robot drives to the wrong place. Is the map frame correct? View in RViz with the fixed frame set to map. Is localization converged? Check the particle cloud or pose covariance. Do named places match the map you are actually using? Arm misses the object. Print the detected pose in the camera frame, then in the map frame. Does it match what you see? Check the TF tree with ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames. A missing or stale camera frame is the usual culprit. Check clock use: all nodes must use simulated time (use_sim_time: true). LLM plan is rejected or odd. Print the raw model output and the prompt. Is the allowlist in the prompt? Lower the temperature and ask for JSON only. Add the failing phrasing to your 20-phrase test set. Pro tip Record a bag of every failed trial with ros2 bag record -a in a short window. A failure you can replay is a failure you can fix. More on this in Packages, debugging and bags.

Build the spine of the system first, using fakes for the hard parts. Create proprio_interfaces with PickPlace.action and build it with colcon build --packages-select proprio_interfaces. Add proprio_mission/orchestrator.py and the test_validate.py unit test. Run pytest and make all tests pass. Write a fake pick_place action server that sleeps one second and returns success=True. Launch Nav2 in simulation, or a fake navigate_to_pose server if Nav2 is not ready yet. Publish a plan: ros2 topic pub --once /mission/plan std_msgs/msg/String "{data: '[{\"action\": \"navigate_to\", \"target\": \"table\"}]'}". Watch ros2 topic echo /mission/status. You should see the step, then done. Publish a bad plan with an unknown place and confirm you see rejected plan. You know it worked when good plans run to done, bad plans are rejected with a reason, and no robot ever moved for a bad plan.

Add a stopIntermediate Add a subscription to /emergency_stop (std_msgs/Bool) in the orchestrator. When it receives True, it should clear remaining steps, cancel the active goal and publish aborted: stop requested. What do you need to store to cancel the active goal? Show solutionHide solution Store the goal handle from on_accepted (for example self.active = handle). On stop, call self.active.cancel_goal_async() if it exists, then call self.abort("stop requested"). Also keep a flag so a stale result callback does not start the next step after the stop. Find the layerIntermediate The arm reaches 15 cm to the left of the cup on every trial, always by roughly the same amount. Which layer most likely has the bug, and how would you confirm it? Show solutionHide solution A consistent offset points to a calibration or frame problem, not noise: likely the camera extrinsics in the URDF or the transform from camera to map. Confirm by placing the object at a known pose, printing the detected pose in the map frame and comparing it with ground truth. Random errors would instead suggest the detector or depth noise.

1Why does the orchestrator validate the plan before executing any step? ATo make the JSON smallerBSo a wrong or hallucinated plan is rejected before anything movesCBecause Nav2 requires itDTo speed up the LLM 2Which is the best first test for the plan validator? AA full 20-trial simulationBA unit test with good and bad plans, no ROS neededCA hardware testDA demo video 3The arm is always 15 cm off in the same direction. The most likely cause is: ARandom sensor noiseBA calibration or frame transform errorCA slow LLMDToo many trials 4Where should values like frame names and timeouts live? AHard-coded in each nodeBIn YAML parameter files loaded at launchCIn the LLM promptDIn the URDF only 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Split the workspace by responsibility, and put every tunable value in YAML. Fix the interfaces first; only one custom action, PickPlace, is needed. The orchestrator is a short, deterministic state machine over validated steps. Build in order: world, navigation, perception, manipulation, language, integration, evaluation. Test at three levels: unit, subsystem with fakes, and full system trials. Debug top-down through the layers and use bags to replay failures.

Beginner35 minBefore this:Finished or planned capstone You have spent weeks building things that move. Now someone asks, "So what do you do?" and the honest answer is a pile of repositories, half-remembered debugging stories and a robot that once fetched a red cup. This lesson turns that pile into a story a hiring manager, a lab or a collaborator can understand in two minutes. You will be able to Describe the main roles in robotics and which skills each one leans on. Turn the capstone and lab work into a portfolio with repositories, videos and write-ups. Start contributing to open-source robotics projects. Prepare for robotics interviews and follow a 90-day plan after the course.
documents.s: Careers and portfolio in physical AI

documents.t: "Robotics engineer" covers very different jobs. Titles vary by company, but most work falls into a few families. Robotics software engineer. Builds the system that runs on the robot: ROS 2 nodes, state machines, drivers, tooling, tests, deployment. The most common entry point. Perception engineer. Turns sensor data into understanding: detection, segmentation, depth, tracking, SLAM, calibration. Controls engineer. Makes the robot move accurately and stably: kinematics, dynamics, feedback control, trajectory generation, whole-body control for legged machines. Machine learning and robot learning engineer. Trains policies and models: imitation learning, reinforcement learning, datasets, evaluation, foundation models for robots. Simulation engineer. Builds simulated worlds, sensors and tools for testing and training: Gazebo, Isaac Sim, synthetic data and continuous integration. Field and applications engineer. Deploys robots with customers, tunes them in real environments, and brings back what breaks. Other doors exist: mechanical and electrical design, hardware bring-up, safety and test engineering, product and program roles. Even if you do not choose them, working alongside them is part of every robotics job. Be T-shaped Go deep in one area and be able to work across the stack. A perception specialist who can launch a ROS 2 system, read a transform tree and deploy to hardware is far more useful than one who cannot. The capstone gave you the breadth; your portfolio should show one place where you went deep.

The table shows how much each skill matters for each role: Core means you will use it daily, Strong means you need it comfortably, Useful means it helps. It is a guide, not a rule. Skill Software Perception Controls ML / learning Simulation Field Python and C++ Core Core Strong Core (Python) Strong Strong ROS 2, tf2, launch Core Strong Strong Strong Strong Core Linear algebra, transforms Strong Core Core Strong Strong Useful Probability, state estimation Useful Core Strong Strong Useful Useful Control theory, dynamics Useful Useful Core Strong Strong Useful Deep learning (PyTorch) Useful Strong Useful Core Useful Useful Computer vision (OpenCV, 3D) Useful Core Useful Strong Useful Useful Simulation (Gazebo, Isaac) Strong Strong Strong Core Core Useful Linux, Git, CI, containers Core Strong Strong Strong Strong Core Hardware, electronics, debugging Strong Useful Strong Useful Useful Core Communication and write-ups Strong Strong Strong Strong Strong Core Use it to find gaps. If you want to be a controls engineer and the "Control theory, dynamics" row is shaky, revisit Dynamics essentials and Control and PID before your next project.
A portfolio is evidence. It answers: can this person build something real, explain it and finish it? Aim for three to five strong pieces rather than twenty weak ones.

This is your flagship. Make the repository excellent: A README that says what the project does in the first two sentences, shows a GIF or screenshot, lists requirements and gives a one-command quick start. A short architecture diagram (reuse the node graph). Your evaluation results: success rate, failure breakdown and what you improved because of it. Clean commit history, tests that pass and a license.

Three minutes maximum. Show the robot doing the task, then show one failure and how you handled it. Failures shown honestly build more trust than polished perfection. Put a caption on every scene so it works without sound.
One page or a blog post about a hard problem you solved: what failed, how you diagnosed it, what you changed and what you measured. This is the artifact that interviewers actually discuss.

Choose the area you want to be hired for and build something focused. Examples: a better detector for transparent cups with a measured improvement; a Kalman filter comparison on real recorded data; a reproducible imitation learning pipeline with a small dataset and clear evaluation; a Nav2 plugin or custom behavior tree node; a simulation environment others can reuse.

Even a small robot kit, a servo arm or a rover with a camera. Real hardware shows you can handle the mess that simulation hides. See Deploying on hardware. Here is a README skeleton that works well. README.md # Project name: one sentence of what it does ![demo](docs/demo.gif) ## What it does Two or three sentences in plain words. ## Results | Metric | Value | |---|---| | Success rate (20 trials) | 70% | | Median task time | 94 s | | Biggest failure stage | grasp (40% of failures) | ## Architecture Link to a node graph image and a short description of each package. ## Quick start git clone ... ./scripts/bringup.sh ./scripts/evaluate.sh ## Limitations and next steps What does not work yet, and what you would do next. Quote only numbers your logs support. Hiring managers read hundreds of project pages and a made-up metric is easy to spot in a conversation.

Robotics is built on open source: ROS 2, Nav2, MoveIt 2, Gazebo and countless drivers and tools. Contributing is one of the best ways to learn and to be seen. Start with documentation and small fixes. A typo, an unclear tutorial step or a broken link is a real contribution and teaches you the review process. Reproduce and report bugs well. A bug report with a minimal example and your versions is valuable. Maintainers are often short of exactly this. Pick up labelled beginner issues. Many projects tag issues for newcomers. Read the contributing guide first, then comment that you are working on it. Add tests or examples. Projects almost always welcome better tests and runnable examples. Share your own work. A well-documented package for a sensor or a robot that others use is a contribution by itself. Be patient and polite. Reviews take time, and feedback is a gift. A single merged pull request in a well-known project is a strong line on a resume.

Robotics interviews usually mix several kinds of questions. Prepare for each. Coding. Standard data structures and algorithms in Python or C++, since many roles ask for them. Practice writing clean code under time pressure. Math and fundamentals. Rotation matrices and quaternions, composing transforms, forward and inverse kinematics, Bayes rule and a Kalman filter step, PID tuning, the Jacobian. Revisit Frames and rigid transforms and Probability for robots. System design. "Design a pick-and-place system for a warehouse" or "How would you add voice control to a mobile robot?" Practice drawing blocks, naming interfaces, discussing failure modes and how you would test. Debugging scenarios. "The robot drifts left. Walk me through your investigation." Your checklist from the build guide is the answer pattern: start from the lowest layer you can check and work upward. Project deep dive. Be ready to explain every decision in your capstone, including what you would change. This is often the longest part. Behavioral questions. A time you were stuck, a time you disagreed, a time something broke in front of other people. Prepare real stories with a clear outcome. Practice out loud Explain a technical topic from this course to a friend or a rubber duck in five minutes, without notes. The spots where you stumble are the spots to study. Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

Momentum matters. Without a plan, the weeks after a course tend to evaporate. Here is a plan; adjust the pace to your life. Days 1 to 30: polish and publish. Finish the capstone README, results and demo video. Write one technical write-up and publish it on a blog or your repository. Fix gaps found in the skills matrix by reviewing the relevant lessons. Set up a profile page that links to your three best projects. Days 31 to 60: go deep and go public. Start the depth project in your chosen area, with a measurable goal. Make your first open-source contribution (documentation or a small fix). Join a robotics community, a local group or an online forum, and answer one question per week. Practice interview fundamentals for 30 minutes a day. Days 61 to 90: apply and iterate. Finish the depth project and write it up. Apply to roles, internships, research groups or open-source programs. Tailor each application to the role family it targets. Do mock interviews with a friend and review your project deep dive. Review progress: what worked, what did not, and plan the next 90 days.

Build your portfolio page and your first contribution. Open your capstone repository and rewrite the README using the skeleton in this lesson. Include real results from your evaluation log. Record a three-minute demo with one honest failure, add captions and link it from the README. Create a skills matrix for yourself: copy the table, mark your current level for the role you want and list three gaps. Find one open-source robotics repository you used in the capstone, read its contributing guide and find one documentation or beginner-labelled issue you can address. Write your 90-day plan with dates and one measurable deliverable per month. You know it worked when a stranger can open your README, understand the project in under two minutes and see real results.

Write the resume bulletBeginner Turn this into a strong resume bullet: "Built a robot that fetches things when you talk to it." Use a verb, the technologies and a measured result. Show solutionHide solution Example: "Built a voice-commanded mobile manipulator in Gazebo Harmonic using ROS 2 Jazzy, Nav2 and MoveIt 2 with an LLM task planner and plan validator; achieved a 75 percent end-to-end success rate over 20 randomized trials and cut grasp failures by half by recalibrating camera extrinsics." Replace the numbers with your own measured ones. Answer the debugging questionIntermediate An interviewer asks: "Your mobile robot arrives 30 cm from the target on every run." Describe how you would investigate in five steps. Show solutionHide solution A good answer is systematic: (1) note that the error is consistent, which suggests a systematic cause, not noise; (2) check the frames: is the goal in the right frame and is the map frame aligned with where the robot thinks it is; (3) check localization quality and odometry calibration (wheel radius, track width); (4) test with a simple scripted motion to separate planning from execution; (5) verify the goal tolerance parameters, since a loose tolerance can stop the robot early. State what you would measure at each step. Choose your laneBeginner Pick the role you would most like in a year. List the three rows in the skills matrix where you are weakest for that role and one project that would fix each. Show solutionHide solution Answers will vary. A strong answer picks a role, names three honest gaps from its column (for example "Core: control theory"), and ties each to a small, concrete project with a deliverable, such as "implement and tune a joint-space PID on the simulated arm and plot step responses".

AAs many repositories as possibleBA few finished projects with real results and honest limitationsCOnly theory notesDScreenshots with no code 2Which is a good first open-source contribution? ARewriting the whole navigation stackBA documentation fix or a well-reproduced bug reportCRenaming every variableDOpening many pull requests with no description 3For a perception engineer, which skill in the matrix is Core? AComputer vision and state estimationBField service routesCMechanical CAD onlyDMarketing 4Why should you show a failure in your demo video? ATo make the video longerBHonest failures and recoveries build trust and show engineering judgmentCTo hide the real success rateDVideos need exactly one failure 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Robotics roles include software, perception, controls, robot learning, simulation and field engineering. Be deep in one and broad across the rest. Use the skills matrix to find and close gaps for your chosen role. A portfolio of three to five finished projects with real results beats many half-done ones. Document honestly: demo video, results table, limitations. Contribute to open source starting with documentation, bug reports and small fixes. Prepare for coding, fundamentals, system design, debugging and project deep-dive questions, and follow a 90-day plan.

Expert45 minBefore this:Capstone build guide · ros2_control basics · Sim-to-real gap In simulation, a bug costs you a restart. On a real robot, the same bug can cost a motor, a table lamp or a finger. The robot you built drives straight in Gazebo; on the floor it drifts left, because one wheel is a fraction of a millimetre smaller than the other. The code is the same. The world is not. This lesson is the checklist for crossing that gap carefully: what hardware runs your software, how to keep the timing honest, how to talk to motors, how to stop safely and how to test without hurting anything. You will be able to Choose and set up embedded compute for a robot, and explain the trade-offs. Explain what real-time means for a robot and which parts of the stack need it. Use ros2_control to run the same controllers in simulation and on hardware. Add layered safety stops, calibrate sensors and log every run. Plan a staged field test that reveals problems at low risk.
documents.s: Deploying on hardware: from simulation to a real robot

documents.t: Everything you have built assumed things that real hardware does not give you for free. Time is messy. In simulation, the clock is yours. On hardware, sensors arrive late, jitter and drop. Physics is not exact. Friction, backlash, battery sag and wheel slip all exist. Failure is physical. A crash is not a restart; it is a repair. Resources are limited. Your laptop GPU is not on the robot. Power, heat and weight are budgets. The sim-to-real gapThe difference in behavior between a simulated robot and the real one, caused by modelling errors, sensor noise, delays and unmodelled physics. from The sim-to-real gap is not a research curiosity here; it is the thing you manage every day. Keep one software stack for both worlds Design so that moving from sim to hardware means swapping the lowest layer (the hardware interface) and some YAML, not rewriting your nodes. Same topics, same controllers, same launch structure. Every difference you leave in is a new bug.

A robot carries its own computer. Many teams choose a single-board computer with an integrated GPU, such as the NVIDIA Jetson class of boards, because running neural networks for detection and speech on the robot saves network latency and works without Wi-Fi. Other options are small x86 mini PCs, or a split design where a microcontroller handles motors and sensors in tight loops while a bigger computer handles perception and planning. Things to weigh: Compute and memory. Can the board run your detector at the frame rate you need? Optimized inference engines (for example TensorRT on NVIDIA hardware) often make the difference between 5 and 30 frames per second. Power and heat. Boards have power modes. A board that runs fine on the bench can throttle inside a closed chassis. Measure temperature during a long run. Operating system match. The reference stack in this course is Ubuntu 24.04 with ROS 2 Jazzy. Vendor images may ship a different Ubuntu release. Check what your board supports; if it differs, run ROS 2 in a container so the software environment matches what you tested. Storage and I/O. Logging at full rate needs fast storage. Check the ports for cameras, lidar and CAN or serial buses. A common split is: microcontroller for motor loops at 1 kHz or more, onboard computer for ROS 2 nodes, and an optional operator laptop for visualization over the network.

A real-timeA system where the correctness of a result depends on delivering it before a deadline, not only on its value. system is not one that is fast. It is one that is predictable: a control loop meant to run every 5 ms must run every 5 ms, every time. A late motor command is a wrong motor command. Standard Linux is a general-purpose scheduler and can delay your process for many milliseconds at an unlucky moment. For a slow mobile base at 20 to 50 Hz that is usually acceptable. For fast arm control or balancing a legged robot, it is not. Practical advice, from cheapest to hardest: Put the hard real-time loop on a microcontroller or the motor drive itself. Let the onboard computer send setpoints at a modest rate. Use a real-time kernel (a PREEMPT_RT kernel) on the computer if it must close fast loops itself. Keep the control loop clean. No memory allocation, no logging to disk, no blocking calls inside the loop. Pre-allocate and lock memory, and give the control thread a real-time scheduling priority. Keep clocks in sync across computers with a network time service such as chrony, or your timestamps and tf lookups will fail in strange ways. Choose DDS settings and QoS deliberately. Sensor streams usually want best-effort, shallow queues; commands and maps want reliable delivery. Measure instead of hoping. Log the actual period of your control loop and plot the worst case, not the average.

ros2_controlA ROS 2 framework that separates controllers (what to compute) from hardware interfaces (how to talk to a specific device). is built for exactly this goal. A controller, such as a joint trajectory controller, reads joint states and writes commands through named interfaces. A hardware interfaceA plugin that reads sensor values from a device and writes commands to it, exposing them to controllers as named state and command interfaces. plugin turns those names into real bus traffic. In simulation, a Gazebo plugin plays that role instead. You describe the hardware in the URDF with a ros2_control tag. The only thing that changes between sim and real is the plugin name and its parameters. proprio_description/urdf/arm.ros2_control.xacro <ros2_control name="ArmSystem" type="system"> <hardware> <!-- simulation: --> <plugin>gz_ros2_control/GazeboSimSystem</plugin> <!-- real robot: replace with your own plugin and add its parameters <plugin>proprio_hardware/ArmSystemHardware</plugin> <param name="serial_port">/dev/ttyUSB0</param> --> </hardware> <joint name="shoulder_joint"> <command_interface name="position"/> <state_interface name="position"/> <state_interface name="velocity"/> </joint> </ros2_control> The controller configuration is plain YAML and is identical in both worlds. proprio_bringup/config/controllers.yaml controller_manager: ros__parameters: update_rate: 100 joint_state_broadcaster: type: joint_state_broadcaster/JointStateBroadcaster arm_controller: type: joint_trajectory_controller/JointTrajectoryController arm_controller: ros__parameters: joints: - shoulder_joint command_interfaces: - position state_interfaces: - position - velocity Writing a real hardware interface means implementing a C++ class derived from the ros2_control system interface. At minimum it declares its joints, exports state and command interfaces, and implements read (device to interface) and write (interface to device), plus lifecycle steps such as configure and activate. The exact method signatures change between ROS 2 releases, so follow the ros2_control documentation for Jazzy and start from its example hardware interfaces. Keep read and write fast and non-blocking. Note Start with the bus driver as a standalone library you can test with a script. Wrap it in the hardware interface only when it already works. Debugging a driver and a plugin at once is twice as hard.

Never rely on a single mechanism to stop a robot. Stack independent layers, so a failure in one still leaves another. Hardware emergency stop. A physical button that cuts motor power through a circuit, not through software. This is your last line of defense and must work when the computer is frozen. Drive-level limits. Current, torque, speed and position limits configured in the motor drives themselves. Watchdogs. If commands stop arriving, the robot stops. A dead-man timer is simple and very effective. Software limits and state machine. Speed caps near people, joint limits, workspace boundaries, and a state machine that refuses motion when in a fault state. Operator procedure. Spotter within reach of the e-stop, clear test area, written checklist. Here is a command watchdog you can put between any planner and the base. It forwards velocity commands only while they are fresh and publishes zero velocity otherwise. proprio_bringup/cmd_vel_watchdog.py import rclpy from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist from rclpy.node import Node class CmdVelWatchdog(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__("cmd_vel_watchdog") self.declare_parameter("timeout_s", 0.5) self.timeout = self.get_parameter("timeout_s").value self.last_cmd = Twist() self.last_time = self.get_clock().now() self.create_subscription(Twist, "cmd_vel_raw", self.on_cmd, 10) self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, "cmd_vel", 10) self.create_timer(0.05, self.tick) # 20 Hz def on_cmd(self, msg): self.last_cmd = msg self.last_time = self.get_clock().now() def tick(self): age = (self.get_clock().now() - self.last_time).nanoseconds * 1e-9 self.pub.publish(self.last_cmd if age < self.timeout else Twist()) def main(): rclpy.init() rclpy.spin(CmdVelWatchdog()) if __name__ == "__main__": main() Check which velocity message type your base controller expects in your ROS 2 version and match it. The idea is the same either way. A software stop is not an emergency stop A ROS topic that says "stop" depends on the computer, the network, the middleware and your code all working. Treat it as a convenience layer. The hardware e-stop must not depend on any of them.

Simulation gave you perfect numbers. Reality needs measurement. Camera intrinsics. Focal length, optical center, distortion. Use a checkerboard and the ROS camera calibration tools. Camera extrinsics and hand-eye calibration. Where the camera sits relative to the robot base or the gripper. A few millimetres of error here becomes centimetres at the gripper. The "arm misses by a constant offset" symptom from the previous lesson usually lives here. Joint zero offsets. The angle your encoder reads when the arm is at its model-defined zero. Mark a physical reference pose and verify it. Wheel odometry. Measure the true wheel radius and track width by driving a marked distance and a full rotation, then correct the parameters. IMU bias. Record a few seconds at rest to estimate gyroscope bias. Store calibration values in version-controlled YAML, with the date and the method. A calibration you cannot reproduce is a calibration you cannot trust.

Log every run. Record sensors, transforms, commands, states and your own mission status. terminal ros2 bag record -s mcap -o run_$(date +%F_%H%M) \ /tf /tf_static /odom /scan /joint_states /cmd_vel /mission/status Check the storage plugins available on your install, and watch disk usage, since camera images are large. Add the software version (git rev-parse HEAD) and the parameter files to your run folder so any run can be reproduced. Test in stages, and do not skip rungs. Bench, wheels or arm unloaded. Motors respond in the right direction and the e-stop cuts power. Tethered or wheels lifted. Full stack running, robot cannot move away. Low speed, open space. Speed capped to a fraction of normal, a spotter holding the e-stop. Realistic environment, no people. Run the capstone scenario. Realistic environment, supervised. Only after the previous stages pass repeatedly. After every stage, review the logs. Anything surprising is a reason to stay at the current stage. Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

You will add a watchdog to your simulated robot and prove it works, which is the same process you would follow on hardware. Save cmd_vel_watchdog.py from this lesson into a package, add it as an entry point, and build. Remap your teleop or Nav2 output to cmd_vel_raw, and run the watchdog so cmd_vel drives the simulated base. Drive the robot with a teleop node, then stop the teleop process with Ctrl+C while the robot is moving. Confirm with ros2 topic echo /cmd_vel that zero velocity appears within about half a second, and that the robot stops in Gazebo. Start ros2 bag record -s mcap /tf /odom /cmd_vel_raw /cmd_vel, repeat the test, and replay the bag with ros2 bag play to check the timing. You know it worked when the robot stops by itself after the command stream ends, and the bag shows the zero command arriving on time.

Layer the stopsBeginner List the five safety layers for your capstone robot, and for each say what failure it protects against that the others do not. Show solutionHide solution Hardware e-stop: protects against frozen software or network loss. Drive limits: protect against a bad command that exceeds current or speed. Watchdog: protects against a crashed or disconnected planner. Software limits: protect against planned motion into a forbidden zone. Operator procedure: protects against conditions nobody modelled, such as a person walking in. Each layer covers a case where the layers below it may fail. Budget the loopAdvanced Your arm controller needs a 200 Hz loop. What is the period, and why would logging to disk inside the loop be a problem? Show solutionHide solution The period is 1 / 200 = 5 ms. Disk writes can block for many milliseconds at unpredictable times, which would cause deadline misses and jerky or unsafe motion. Move logging to a separate low-priority thread or process, and pass data through a lock-free buffer or use ros2 bag outside the loop. Plan a staged testIntermediate Write a five-line test plan for the first time your robot carries a cup, one line per stage in the ladder, with a pass condition for each. Show solutionHide solution Example: (1) Bench: gripper opens and closes without a cup, e-stop cuts power. (2) Tethered: arm completes the pick motion with a cup in a fixture, no base motion. (3) Low speed: base drives 2 m with the cup held, at one quarter speed. (4) Full scenario, no people: 10 trials, no drops. (5) Supervised: demo with a spotter, only if stage 4 had zero safety events.

1What does ros2_control let you keep identical between simulation and a real robot? AThe physicsBThe controllers and their YAML configurationCThe sensor noiseDThe battery 2Which stop is the last line of defense and must not depend on software? AA watchdog timer nodeBA speed limit in the plannerCA hardware emergency stop that cuts motor powerDA ROS topic called /stop 3What does real-time mean for a control loop? AIt runs as fast as possibleBIt meets its deadline predictably every cycleCIt uses a GPUDIt runs on a cloud server 4A robot always reaches 15 cm off target on hardware but not in simulation. What should you check first? ACalibration, especially camera extrinsics and joint offsetsBThe color of the objectCThe length of the demo videoDThe Wi-Fi password 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Design so that only the hardware interface and some YAML change between sim and real. Pick embedded compute by inference speed, power, heat and operating system fit, and use containers when versions differ. Real-time means predictable timing; keep tight loops on microcontrollers or a real-time kernel and measure the worst case. ros2_control keeps controllers identical while hardware plugins vary. Stack independent safety layers, with a hardware e-stop at the bottom. Calibrate, log every run, and test in stages from bench to supervised field trial.
