You will extend the simulator from lesson 2 into a small push-recovery demo. A point-mass biped stands still. A random shove arrives, the controller computes the capture point, picks a foot placement within a step-length limit, and takes as many steps as it needs. You then plot how recovery success changes as the push gets bigger. It runs in pure Python in a few seconds, and it is the same idea real humanoids use when someone bumps into them. Before you start You should be comfortable with rigid-body frames and forward kinematics (Module 02) and with the basic idea of reinforcement learning (Module 07). If a formula looks unfamiliar, the lesson links back to the right place. Stuck at any point? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

Intermediate40 minBefore this:Dynamics essentials · Control and PID · Python basics Someone bumps a standing humanoid from behind. In the first tenth of a second the robot has already been pushed off balance, and what it does next decides whether it stays up. Move the feet? Lean? Swing the arms? To answer that, we need a model simple enough to reason about in real time and good enough to predict a fall. That model is a stick with a weight on top. You will be able to Explain the support polygon and the center of mass, and why a robot can be statically stable. Define the zero moment point (ZMP) and say when it leaves the support polygon. Write and solve the linear inverted pendulum model (LIPM). Compute the capture point and use it to choose a recovery step. Simulate a push and recovery in a short Python program.
documents.s: Balance, the ZMP and the inverted pendulum

documents.t: The center of massThe point where the total mass of the robot can be treated as concentrated. For balance we usually care about where it is, projected straight down onto the floor. (CoM) is the average position of all the robot’s mass. The support polygonThe smallest convex shape that contains all the points where the feet touch the ground. is the shape on the floor spanned by the contact points. With two feet planted, it covers both soles and the gap between them. If the CoM projected onto the floor stays inside the support polygon and the robot moves slowly, it is statically stableStable without needing to move: gravity alone cannot tip it over.. A table works this way. But walking is not static: at some moments the CoM is outside the support polygon, and the robot is, briefly, falling forward and catching itself. We need a criterion that works for motion.

When a robot accelerates, the ground pushes back with a force that is spread over the sole of the foot. Add up that distributed force and you get one equivalent force acting at one point. The zero moment pointZero moment point: the point on the ground where the horizontal components of the total moment from gravity and inertia cancel. On flat ground with the feet in contact, it equals the center of pressure. (ZMP) is the point where the ground-reaction moments about the horizontal axes sum to zero. The rule is short: The ZMP must stay inside the support polygon As long as the ZMP is inside the support polygon, the foot sits flat and the robot does not tip over its edge. When the ZMP reaches the edge, the foot starts to roll. The robot can no longer control its tilt with that foot, and it is falling unless something else (another step, a swung arm, a grab) takes over. Think of standing on one foot and leaning. You push your toes down to stop yourself tipping forward. Your center of pressure moves toward your toes. When it hits the toe edge, you have run out of control authority and must step.

A real humanoid has dozens of links. For balance, we compress it into three assumptions: All the mass sits at one point, the CoM. The CoM moves at a constant height zcz_czc​. The legs are massless; the only thing the ground does is push at the ZMP, which we call ppp. Take moments about the ZMP in one horizontal direction xxx. Gravity tries to tip the mass over with moment mg(x−p)m g (x - p)mg(x−p), and the acceleration of the mass resists with mzcx¨m z_c \ddot{x}mzc​x¨. Setting them equal gives the linear inverted pendulum modelLinear inverted pendulum model: a point mass held at constant height above a pivot that can move along the ground.: x¨=gzc (x−p)=ω2(x−p),ω=gzc\ddot{x} = \frac{g}{z_c}\,(x - p) = \omega^2 (x - p), \qquad \omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{z_c}}x¨=zc​g​(x−p)=ω2(x−p),ω=zc​g​​ Rearranged, the ZMP follows from the CoM motion alone: p=x−zcg x¨p = x - \frac{z_c}{g}\,\ddot{x}p=x−gzc​​x¨ Read the first equation with care. If the CoM is ahead of the foot (x>px > px>p), acceleration points further ahead: the error grows. That is an inverted pendulum: left alone it falls exponentially, at rate ω\omegaω. For a leg-height of about 0.85 m, ω≈3.4 s−1\omega \approx 3.4\ \text{s}^{-1}ω≈3.4 s−1, so a small error doubles in roughly 0.2 s. With ppp constant, the solution is exact: x(t)=(x0−p)cosh⁡(ωt)+x˙0ωsinh⁡(ωt)+px(t) = (x_0 - p)\cosh(\omega t) + \frac{\dot{x}_0}{\omega}\sinh(\omega t) + px(t)=(x0​−p)cosh(ωt)+ωx˙0​​sinh(ωt)+p The model is linear because zcz_czc​ is fixed, which turns a hard nonlinear problem into one you can solve in closed form and optimize quickly. It ignores angular momentum, leg mass and height changes, and that is why real controllers add corrections on top. Note Everything above is written for one direction, xxx (forward). Sideways, yyy, follows the same equation with its own pyp_ypy​. In the LIPM the two directions are independent.

How hard a push can the robot absorb without stepping? Ask the opposite question: if the robot could put its foot (and therefore the ZMP) at any point ppp, where must it be so that the CoM comes to rest above it? Define the capture pointThe point on the ground where the robot must place its foot so that the pendulum comes to a stop over it. (sometimes called the divergent component of motion): ξ=x+x˙ω\xi = x + \frac{\dot{x}}{\omega}ξ=x+ωx˙​ Differentiate and use the LIPM equation: ξ˙=x˙+x¨ω=ω(ξ−p)\dot{\xi} = \dot{x} + \frac{\ddot{x}}{\omega} = \omega (\xi - p)ξ˙​=x˙+ωx¨​=ω(ξ−p) Two things follow. If you place the foot exactly at p=ξp = \xip=ξ, then ξ˙=0\dot{\xi} = 0ξ˙​=0: the capture point stops moving, and the CoM converges smoothly to rest above the foot. If ppp is anywhere else, ξ\xiξ diverges away from ppp exponentially. The CoM itself obeys x˙=ω(ξ−x)\dot{x} = \omega(\xi - x)x˙=ω(ξ−x), so it is pulled toward ξ\xiξ on its own. That makes ξ\xiξ the only part of the motion you actually have to control. Step where you would otherwise fall The capture point is where the robot will end up if it stops pushing. To stop, put the foot there. The distance from the current foot to the capture point is the step you need; if it is more than the longest step the legs can take, one step is not enough.

lipm_push.py import math G, ZC = 9.81, 0.85 W = math.sqrt(G / ZC) # natural frequency, 1/s def lipm(x0, v0, p, t): """Exact LIPM motion for a fixed ZMP p after t seconds.""" c, s = math.cosh(W * t), math.sinh(W * t) x = (x0 - p) * c + (v0 / W) * s + p v = (x0 - p) * W * s + v0 * c return x, v def capture_point(x, v): return x + v / W def recover(x, v, foot, max_step=0.30, step_time=0.35, max_steps=6): """Step to the capture point each time, limited by leg reach.""" for k in range(1, max_steps + 1): xi = capture_point(x, v) want = xi - foot step = max(-max_step, min(max_step, want)) foot += step x, v = lipm(x, v, foot, step_time) print(f" step {k}: foot={foot:6.3f} m x={x:6.3f} m v={v:6.3f} m/s") if abs(v) < 0.05 and abs(x - foot) < 0.05: return True return False print("omega =", round(W, 3), "1/s") for push in (0.3, 0.8, 1.6): print(f"push gives v = {push} m/s, capture point = {capture_point(0.0, push):.3f} m") print(" stays up:", recover(0.0, push, foot=0.0)) print("never step, v0 = 0.3 m/s:") for t in (0.2, 0.4, 0.8): x, v = lipm(0.0, 0.3, 0.0, t) print(f" t={t:.1f} s x={x:6.3f} m v={v:6.3f} m/s") Run it. For the two smaller pushes the capture point lies within one step of the foot, so the robot places its foot there and the speed dies away over the next few updates (each printed line is one more step decision; when the foot is already at the capture point it simply stays). The 1.6 m/s push needs a step of 0.47 m, which is beyond the 0.30 m limit. The robot steps as far as it can, the capture point keeps running away from it, and recover reports failure. The last block shows what happens if the robot never steps: position and speed grow exponentially. This is a toy: it places the foot instantly, ignores that stepping takes time during which the pendulum keeps falling, and assumes the foot can go anywhere. Real controllers add step timing, swing-leg dynamics and the option to shift the CoM or use the arms, but the core move (step to the capture point) is exactly what many humanoid push-recovery controllers do.

The LIPM assumes you control ppp freely inside the foot. When ppp hits the edge, you have other tools: Ankle strategy: shift the ZMP within the foot. Good for small pushes. Hip strategy: swing the upper body to create angular momentum and a restoring moment. Stepping strategy: move the support polygon under the capture point. Best for large pushes. Arm swing and grabbing: more angular momentum, or a new contact. Humans blend them naturally. Robot controllers choose between them based on the size of the capture-point error.
documents.s: What if the ZMP is not enough?

documents.t: Save lipm_push.py and run it. Record, for each push, whether the robot recovers and how many steps it takes. Change max_step to 0.15. Which of the three pushes can the robot still recover from? Change ZC to 1.2 (a taller robot). Does the natural frequency go up or down? Is the capture point for a 0.8 m/s push closer or further away? Set step_time=0.6 and see whether a slower step helps or hurts the 0.8 m/s push. Why? Done when you can predict, before running, whether a push of a given size will be recovered.

Compute omegaBeginner A robot’s CoM is 0.9 m above the ground. Compute ω\omegaω and the capture-point offset for a CoM velocity of 0.5 m/s. Show solutionHide solution ω=9.81/0.9≈3.30 s−1\omega = \sqrt{9.81 / 0.9} \approx 3.30\ \text{s}^{-1}ω=9.81/0.9​≈3.30 s−1. The offset is x˙/ω=0.5/3.30≈0.15\dot{x}/\omega = 0.5/3.30 \approx 0.15x˙/ω=0.5/3.30≈0.15 m, so the capture point is about 15 cm ahead of the CoM. Why a taller robot is easierIntermediate Using the LIPM, explain why taller robots (larger zcz_czc​) have more time to react than short ones. Show solutionHide solution ω=g/zc\omega = \sqrt{g/z_c}ω=g/zc​​ falls as zcz_czc​ grows, so the exponential divergence is slower: the time constant 1/ω1/\omega1/ω is longer. A tall pendulum falls more slowly than a short one, just as a long broom is easier to balance on a fingertip than a pencil. One step is not enoughIntermediate A robot can step at most 0.25 m. Its capture point is 0.40 m from the support foot. What does it do, and does the capture point move while it steps? Show solutionHide solution It cannot reach the capture point, so it steps as far as it can (0.25 m) and takes another step soon after. Meanwhile ξ˙=ω(ξ−p)\dot{\xi} = \omega(\xi - p)ξ˙​=ω(ξ−p) is positive because the foot is behind the capture point, so ξ\xiξ keeps moving away, and the second step may need to be larger. If it grows beyond the limit, the robot falls unless another strategy (hip, arms) helps.

1What does the ZMP tell you? AThe robot’s total energyBWhere the ground-reaction moments cancel, which must stay inside the support polygon for a flat footCThe CoM heightDThe battery level 2In the LIPM, what happens if the CoM is ahead of the ZMP? AIt decelerates back to the ZMPBIt accelerates further ahead, so the error grows exponentiallyCNothingDIt oscillates forever at constant amplitude 3Where should the foot go to bring the pendulum to rest over it? ADirectly under the CoMBAt the capture point, x plus velocity over omegaCBehind the CoMDAs far away as possible 4Which statement about the LIPM is true? AIt includes angular momentumBIt assumes constant CoM height and massless legsCIt only works for wheeled robotsDIt models every joint separately 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Static balance means the CoM projection stays inside the support polygon; walking breaks that rule on purpose. The ZMP must stay inside the support polygon for the foot to stay flat. The LIPM gives x¨=ω2(x−p)\ddot{x} = \omega^2 (x - p)x¨=ω2(x−p) with ω=g/zc\omega = \sqrt{g/z_c}ω=g/zc​​, and an exact solution with cosh and sinh. The capture point ξ=x+x˙/ω\xi = x + \dot{x}/\omegaξ=x+x˙/ω is where to step to stop. Beyond the ankle strategy there are hip, stepping and arm strategies; controllers choose by how big the error is. Simple models are valuable because you can optimize over them in milliseconds.

Pinocchio documentation for computing center of mass and centroidal quantities of full models. Drake documentation for multibody dynamics and optimization-based control tools. MuJoCo documentation to try push recovery on a full humanoid model. Next: Locomotion

Advanced35 minBefore this:Grasping · Reinforcement learning basics · Python basics A humanoid can walk to the table, reach out, and then drop the cup. The arm was fine; the hand was the problem. A hand has to be gentle with an egg, firm with a hammer, and quick enough to catch a pen that starts to slip. For most robots, the hand is still the weakest part of the body, and the biggest opportunity. You will be able to Compare parallel grippers, underactuated hands and fully actuated dexterous hands. Explain how resistive, capacitive, magnetic and optical tactile sensors work. Write a simple slip detector and a grip-force reflex. Describe how RL produced in-hand manipulation, and why sim-to-real is hard for touch.

A human hand has roughly twenty degrees of freedom, driven by muscles mostly in the forearm and connected by tendons. Copying all of that is expensive, so robot hands sit on a spectrum. Design Idea Strengths Weaknesses Parallel-jaw gripper Two fingers that close on each other Cheap, robust, easy to control; fine for boxes and bins Cannot re-orient objects, little shape adaptation Underactuated adaptive hand Fewer motors than joints; linkages or tendons let the fingers wrap around the object Conforms to shape without sensing, simple control Limited fine control, hard to do in-hand motion Fully actuated dexterous hand Roughly one actuator per joint, an opposable thumb Can re-orient and manipulate tools Many actuators and wires, expensive, fragile, hard to control Soft or compliant hand Flexible fingers, pneumatic or elastic bodies Safe, gentle, tolerant of error Imprecise, hard to model, limited force An underactuatedA mechanism with fewer actuators than joints, so some joints move passively, driven by contact and springs. finger is a clever trick: one motor pulls a tendon, and springs and geometry make the finger wrap around whatever is in the way. Many commercial arms ship with simple grippers for this reason: they work. The opposable thumb matters most. A hand without a thumb that can oppose the other fingers cannot make a precision pinch or a stable power grasp, which is why dexterous hands spend a large share of their design effort on the thumb. Where the motors live is another design choice. Motors in the palm and fingers give compact, quick hands with limited torque. Motors in the forearm pulling tendons down to the fingers give strength and low finger weight, at the price of tendon friction, stretch and maintenance. Humanoid designs often mix both. Note Choosing the hand is choosing the task. A warehouse humanoid that moves totes needs two sturdy pads. A humanoid that assembles electronics needs fine fingers. Do not buy dexterity you cannot control.

Vision tells you what the object looks like. It cannot tell you how hard you are squeezing, whether the object is slipping, or where the contact is once your own fingers hide it from the camera. That is the job of touch. Common tactile sensorA sensor that measures contact: where, how hard, and sometimes the direction of sliding. technologies: Resistive and capacitive arrays. A grid of small pads (taxels), each changing resistance or capacitance as it is pressed. Thin, cheap and easy to put on fingertips, but with limited range and drift over time. Piezoelectric sensors. They produce a voltage when force changes, so they are excellent at detecting the vibration of a starting slip, and poor at measuring steady force. Magnetic sensors. A small magnet embedded in soft rubber moves when the rubber is pressed or sheared, and Hall-effect chips measure the field. Compact and robust, with force in more than one direction. Optical, vision-based sensors. A small camera looks at the back of a soft gel pad. The gel deforms around the contact, and the camera sees the shape, even fine texture. Sensors in this family (GelSight is the best-known name) give very high-resolution contact images, and can estimate shear from the movement of dots printed on the gel. They are bulkier and need processing, but are rich. What you can estimate: whether there is contact, where, how hard, how the force is directed, whether the object is sliding, and sometimes the object’s shape and texture. Touch closes the loop where vision cannot During a grasp, your hand blocks the camera. Tactile sensing keeps working exactly then. It lets a robot react in milliseconds to slip or to a load change, a loop that is much faster than anything vision can close.

When an object begins to slip, the contact patch on a sensor moves, even though the total force stays about the same. A very simple detector watches for that. In the demo below, a synthetic 8 by 8 sensor holds an object that starts to slide because the grip is too small. Each time slip is detected, the controller squeezes 30 percent harder, up to a safe limit. tactile_slip.py import numpy as np def make_frame(cx, cy, force, size=8, width=1.5): """Synthetic 8x8 taxel pressure image: a Gaussian blob centred at (cx, cy).""" ys, xs = np.indices((size, size)) blob = np.exp(-((xs - cx) ** 2 + (ys - cy) ** 2) / (2 * width ** 2)) return force * blob / blob.sum() def centroid(frame): total = frame.sum() ys, xs = np.indices(frame.shape) return np.array([(xs * frame).sum() / total, (ys * frame).sum() / total]) def slipping(prev, curr, max_shift=0.25, force_tol=0.35): """Slip if the contact patch moves although the total force barely changed.""" shift = np.linalg.norm(centroid(curr) - centroid(prev)) steady = abs(curr.sum() - prev.sum()) <= force_tol * prev.sum() return bool(shift > max_shift and steady) grip, grip_max = 2.0, 10.0 # commanded grip force in newtons needed = 5.0 # grip the object really needs so it does not slide cx = 3.5 # where the contact patch sits, in taxel units prev = make_frame(cx, 3.5, grip) for t in range(12): if grip < needed: cx += 0.4 # too little grip: the object slides and drags the patch curr = make_frame(cx, 3.5, grip) slip = slipping(prev, curr) if slip: grip = min(grip * 1.3, grip_max) # squeeze a little harder print(f"t={t:2d} grip={grip:5.2f} N patch x={cx:4.1f} slip={slip}") prev = curr Run it. Slip is detected four times in a row, the grip climbs from 2 N to about 5.7 N, which is above what the object needs, and then the sliding stops and the reflex goes quiet. Real hands do the same with higher-rate signals and more careful filters, and they also release the grip again once the load is safe so they do not crush what they hold.

In-hand manipulation means moving an object around inside the hand without putting it down: rotating a pen, turning a cube to show a different face, switching a screwdriver from a lifting grip to a turning grip. It is hard because fingers must make and break contact in just the right order, while keeping the object from falling. Writing the contact model and planner by hand is difficult, and small errors in friction cause a drop. Reinforcement learning changed this. In a well-known project, OpenAI trained a policy entirely in simulation to reorient a block with an anthropomorphic research hand, then ran it on the real hand, and later solved a Rubik’s cube with the same hand. The ingredients are worth remembering because they appear again and again: A simulator with many parallel copies. The policy practices for the equivalent of years of hand time. A reward for progress toward a goal orientation, with a penalty for dropping. Heavy domain randomization. Friction, object size and mass, finger gains, delays and sensor noise all change from episode to episode. A later version increased the randomization automatically as the policy got better. Observations from sensors the real robot has. Joint angles, plus the object pose estimated by cameras (or in newer work, by touch). Privileged information for the critic, and sometimes a teacher-student setup: a teacher policy that knows the true friction and mass is distilled into a student that must infer them from its recent history. The remaining gap is touch. Vision-based tactile sensors give rich data but are costly to simulate faithfully, so many learned policies still run blind to contact, or use simple force estimates. Teleoperation with a glove or a camera-tracked hand, combined with imitation learning, is a practical alternative for collecting dexterous data, and is a very active area. The field moves quickly; check the current literature for the latest hand hardware and learned skills. Safety near fingers Dexterous hands are fast and strong for their size. Use current and torque limits on every finger during development, and never test with a hand near your own.

Save tactile_slip.py and run it. Confirm slip is detected for the first few steps and then stops. Lower max_shift to 0.1 and raise it to 0.6. How does the number of detected slips and the final grip change? What does that tell you about sensitivity versus false alarms? Add a release rule: once there has been no slip for 5 steps, reduce grip by 5 percent each step, but never below the last value that stopped the slip. Add random noise (for example np.random.normal(0, 0.01, frame.shape)) to each frame. Does the detector still work? What would you add to cope? Done when you can describe the trade-off between reacting quickly and reacting to noise.

Pick a handBeginner A robot must move boxes and plastic totes between conveyor belts all day. Which hand design would you choose, and why? Show solutionHide solution A parallel-jaw gripper or a simple suction/pad gripper. The objects are regular, force and speed matter more than dexterity, and a simple hand is cheap, robust and easy to control. A dexterous hand adds cost and failure modes for no benefit here. Why a slip is visibleIntermediate Explain why a slip shows up as a moving contact patch with roughly constant total force, and why a sensor that only measures total force would miss it. Show solutionHide solution When an object slides, the fingertip keeps pressing about as hard (the normal force is about unchanged), but the point of contact moves across the pad. A sensor that reports only a single total force sees no change, so it cannot tell sliding from holding. An array or camera that sees where the pressure is can see the patch move. Design the randomizationAdvanced You are training an in-hand cube-rotation policy in simulation. List four physical parameters you would randomize and what failure each one prevents on the real hand. Show solutionHide solution Friction coefficient between finger and object: prevents a policy that works only on a perfectly grippy surface. Object mass and size: prevents overfitting to one cube. Joint controller gains or motor strength: covers differences between simulated and real actuators. Observation noise and delay: covers imperfect sensing, so the policy does not depend on exact, instant measurements. (Other good answers: gravity direction offsets, finger link masses, camera pose error.)

1What is an underactuated hand? AA hand with no motorsBA hand with fewer actuators than joints, using passive mechanics to adapt to the objectCA hand that is brokenDA hand with extra actuators for redundancy 2Why can tactile sensing help when vision cannot? AIt works in the dark onlyBThe robot’s own hand blocks the camera during a grasp, but touch still works and is fastCIt is cheaper than a cameraDIt needs no processing 3In optical tactile sensors of the GelSight type, what does the camera look at? AThe outside worldBThe back of a soft gel that deforms around the contactCThe robot’s faceDA laser grid on the floor 4Why is domain randomization central to learned in-hand manipulation? AIt makes the simulator fasterBIt prepares the policy for the differences between simulated and real friction, mass, delays and noiseCIt removes the need for a rewardDIt lets the hand work without joints 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Hand designs trade simplicity and robustness against dexterity: parallel grippers, underactuated, fully actuated and soft hands. The opposable thumb is the key to precision grasps. Touch works where vision cannot, and enables fast reflexes like slip response. Sensor technologies include resistive and capacitive arrays, piezoelectric, magnetic and optical gel sensors. RL learns in-hand manipulation in simulation using massive parallelism, domain randomization and privileged teacher information. Simulating touch faithfully is still an open problem, so check the current literature for progress.

Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation, the OpenAI paper on block reorientation with RL and domain randomization. Solving Rubik’s Cube with a Robot Hand, which adds automatic domain randomization. Intermediate30 minBefore this:Anatomy of a robot · Frames and rigid transforms · Python basics Picture a humanoid carrying a box up a flight of stairs. Its knee has to deliver a burst of torque on every step, its ankle has to feel the floor within a few milliseconds, its hip must not shake itself apart, and the whole machine must carry its own battery and computer. Every one of those requirements is a design choice made months earlier, when someone picked an actuator, a sensor or a processor. This lesson is a tour of those choices. You will be able to Count the degrees of freedom of a humanoid and explain where they go. Compare quasi-direct-drive, series elastic and hydraulic actuators. Use gear ratio to compute output torque and reflected inertia. List the sensors and compute layers a humanoid needs, and what each one is for. Argue honestly for and against the human form.
documents.s: Humanoid anatomy: joints, actuators, sensors and compute

documents.t: A degree of freedomA single independent way a body can move. A hinge joint adds one; a ball joint adds three. (DoF) is one independent way the robot can move. A hinge (like your elbow) gives one. A ball-and-socket joint (like your shoulder) gives three. Most humanoids build a ball joint from three hinge axes that meet at a point. A typical humanoid layout looks like this: Part Typical DoF Why Each leg 6 3 at the hip, 1 at the knee, 2 at the ankle: enough to place a foot anywhere in space with any orientation Each arm 6 or 7 3 at the shoulder, 1 at the elbow, 2 or 3 at the wrist; a 7th lets the elbow swing while the hand stays put Waist or torso 0 to 3 Extends reach and helps balance Neck and head 1 to 3 Points the cameras Each hand 1 to 20 or more From a simple two-finger gripper to a dexterous hand Add it up and an ordinary full-size humanoid has somewhere between 25 and 50 actuated joints, plus the hands. The exact number depends on the design, so treat the table as a rule of thumb, not a spec for any particular robot. There is one more number that matters. A humanoid is a floating-baseA robot whose base is not bolted to the world. Its body can translate and rotate freely, which adds 6 unactuated degrees of freedom. system: nothing fixes the pelvis to the world, so the robot has 6 extra DoF (position and orientation of the body) that no motor controls directly. The robot can only change them by pushing on the ground through its feet. That single fact is why balance (the next lesson) is hard. joint_budget.py from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class Joint: name: str dof: int peak_torque_nm: float # round, made-up numbers for practice; not any real robot leg = [Joint("hip", 3, 150.0), Joint("knee", 1, 200.0), Joint("ankle", 2, 80.0)] arm = [Joint("shoulder", 3, 60.0), Joint("elbow", 1, 40.0), Joint("wrist", 3, 15.0)] neck = [Joint("neck", 2, 10.0)] waist = [Joint("waist", 1, 120.0)] def dof(chain): return sum(j.dof for j in chain) body = {"left leg": leg, "right leg": leg, "left arm": arm, "right arm": arm, "neck": neck, "waist": waist} total = 0 for name, chain in body.items(): print(f"{name:10s} {dof(chain)} DoF") total += dof(chain) print("actuated body DoF (no hands):", total) print("floating-base DoF (unactuated):", 6) print("configuration size:", total + 6) Run it and you get 6 per leg, 7 per arm, 2 for the neck, 1 for the waist: 29 actuated DoF without hands, 35 numbers in the full configuration. Notice that the legs hold the biggest torques. They carry the whole weight and must catch it on every step.
An actuatorThe motor, gearbox and drive electronics that together move one joint. is more than a motor. The gearbox decides how the motor feels to the rest of the robot. Three families dominate.
documents.s: Actuators: where the muscle comes from

documents.t: A small, fast motor is cheap and light but weak. A gearbox with ratio NNN trades speed for torque: τout=η N τmotor,Jreflected=N2Jrotor\tau_{\text{out}} = \eta \, N \, \tau_{\text{motor}}, \qquad J_{\text{reflected}} = N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}τout​=ηNτmotor​,Jreflected​=N2Jrotor​ Here η\etaη is efficiency (always below 1) and JrotorJ_{\text{rotor}}Jrotor​ is the rotor’s inertia. The second equation is the surprise. Torque grows with NNN, but the inertia the joint feels grows with N2N^2N2. A high gear ratio makes the joint strong, slow to accelerate, and hard to move by hand. Friction in the gearbox also gets multiplied, so you cannot feel the outside world through the motor current. actuator_tradeoff.py def joint_from_motor(tau_motor, j_rotor, n, efficiency=0.9): """Return (output torque in Nm, reflected inertia in kg m^2).""" return tau_motor * n * efficiency, j_rotor * n ** 2 print(" N output torque reflected inertia") for n in (6, 9, 30, 100): tau, j = joint_from_motor(tau_motor=1.5, j_rotor=2.0e-4, n=n) print(f"{n:3d} {tau:8.1f} Nm {j:12.4f} kg m^2") Going from N=9N=9N=9 to N=100N=100N=100 multiplies torque by about 11 but reflected inertia by about 123. That is the heart of the next design choice.

Quasi-direct-driveAn actuator with a large, torque-dense motor and a low gear ratio, typically around 6 to 10, so that it stays backdrivable. actuators use a large-diameter, high-torque motor and a small gear ratio. Because NNN is low, the joint is backdrivableAble to be moved from the output side. A backdrivable joint gives way when something pushes on it.: a push on the leg turns the motor, and the motor current tells you how hard you were pushed. That gives free proprioceptive force sensingEstimating the force a joint exerts or feels from motor current alone, with no force sensor. and makes impacts (a foot hitting the floor) much gentler on the gearbox. The price is a bigger, heavier, hotter motor for the same torque. This design became popular in legged robots over the last decade.

A series elastic actuatorAn actuator with a spring placed between the motor and the load. Measuring the spring’s stretch measures the force. puts a deliberate spring between the gearbox and the link. Measure how far the spring stretches and you know the torque, with a cheap encoder and excellent accuracy. The spring also absorbs shocks and can store energy between steps. The cost is bandwidth: the spring limits how fast the force can change, and the control loop has to handle one more resonance.

Hydraulic actuators push fluid through cylinders. They have very high power density and can deliver huge forces from a small package, which is why some pioneering humanoids used them for jumping and flips. They also need a pump, hoses, a reservoir and careful sealing, run hot and noisy, and can leak. Electric actuators are quieter, cleaner, more efficient and simpler to control, and as motors and batteries have improved, most new humanoids have moved to electric. A well-known hydraulic research humanoid was later followed by an electric version from the same maker. Linear actuators Legs also use linear actuators (such as roller-screw designs) that push a knee or ankle through a short linkage. They give high force in a compact line and are common at the knee and ankle of larger robots. Gear ratio is a trade, not a free lunch More gearing buys torque and costs speed, backdrivability and force sensing. Legged robots that must absorb impacts and react to pushes usually want low gear ratios (QDD) or a spring (SEA). Slow, strong, precise joints can afford more gearing.

The word proprioception means sensing your own body. A humanoid needs it in layers: Joint encoders measure every joint angle, usually at the motor and often again at the output. Velocity comes from differencing. An IMU (inertial measurement unit: gyroscope plus accelerometer) sits in the pelvis or torso and reports body orientation and angular velocity. It is the most important balance sensor. Force/torque sensors in the ankles (and sometimes wrists) measure the ground reaction. They tell the controller where the pressure is under the foot, which is exactly the quantity the next lesson needs. Cameras, depth sensors and LiDAR in the head see the world: stairs, doors, objects. Tactile sensors in the fingertips feel contact; see Hands and dexterity. State estimation fuses these into one estimate of where the body is and how fast it is moving. That uses the filters from State estimation and Kalman filters.
documents.s: Sensors: how the robot knows itself

documents.t: Think in layers, each running at its own rate: The joint-level loops live in the motor drives and talk over a real-time bus such as EtherCAT or CAN. A control computer runs the motion layer with hard real-time deadlines. A separate, more powerful computer (usually with a GPU or AI accelerator) runs perception and learned models, because those can take tens of milliseconds and must never block the balance loop. Keeping the layers apart is how a robot can think slowly and still not fall over.

Humanoid robots are not the best shape for every job. A wheeled base with two arms is cheaper, more stable and often fine. The argument for two legs and two arms is practical: The world is built for humans: stairs, door handles, shelves, tools, vehicles. A humanoid fits without changing the building. Human demonstrations transfer: a person can teleoperate the robot, and video of people doing tasks maps naturally onto a body of the same shape. One general body, many tasks, which makes large data collection and large models worthwhile. The arguments against are just as real. Two legs are unstable, expensive, energy-hungry and slow to commercialise. Every joint is a possible failure. Be skeptical of claims that a humanoid is always the right answer; pick the body that fits the task. Don’t trust spec sheets blindly Payload, runtime and speed figures for commercial humanoids change quickly and are often best-case numbers. Treat any figure you read as marketing until you find the test conditions.

Save joint_budget.py and run it. Confirm you get 29 actuated DoF and a configuration of size 35. Add a hand chain of your choice (for example 6 DoF) to each arm and re-run. How does the count change? Save actuator_tradeoff.py, run it, then change j_rotor to double. Which column changes, and by how much? Add a column for the time to reach a target angular acceleration, assuming a load inertia of 0.5 kg m^2 plus the reflected inertia. Which gear ratio is best now? You are done when you can explain, in two sentences, why a 100:1 joint is poor at absorbing a footstrike.

Count the jointsBeginner A humanoid has 6-DoF legs, 7-DoF arms, a 3-DoF waist and a 2-DoF neck. How many actuated DoF does it have, and how large is its full configuration vector? Show solutionHide solution Legs: 2 × 6 = 12. Arms: 2 × 7 = 14. Waist 3, neck 2. Total actuated: 12 + 14 + 3 + 2 = 31. Add 6 for the floating base: the configuration has 37 values. Pick a gear ratioIntermediate A motor gives 2 N·m and has rotor inertia 3×10−43\times10^{-4}3×10−4 kg m². With efficiency 0.9, compute output torque and reflected inertia for N=8N = 8N=8 and N=50N = 50N=50. Which would you choose for a hip that must react to pushes, and why? Show solutionHide solution For N=8N=8N=8: torque =0.9×8×2=14.4= 0.9 \times 8 \times 2 = 14.4=0.9×8×2=14.4 N·m; reflected inertia =3×10−4×64=0.0192= 3\times10^{-4} \times 64 = 0.0192=3×10−4×64=0.0192 kg m². For N=50N=50N=50: torque =90= 90=90 N·m; inertia =3×10−4×2500=0.75= 3\times10^{-4} \times 2500 = 0.75=3×10−4×2500=0.75 kg m². The hip that reacts to pushes should favour N=8N=8N=8 (backdrivable, low reflected inertia, can sense force through current), provided the motor can be made strong enough. N=50N=50N=50 gives more torque but the joint is stiff and slow to respond. Layers of computeIntermediate Why should a large vision model not run in the same loop as the balance controller? Show solutionHide solution Balance needs a deadline met every cycle, within a few milliseconds. A large model has variable, much longer latency and could occasionally miss its deadline, leaving the robot without a command while it is unstable. Running perception on a separate computer or process, and handing the controller its latest result asynchronously, keeps balance safe.

1What makes a humanoid a floating-base system? AIt has no legsBIts body is not fixed to the world, so 6 body degrees of freedom are not directly actuatedCIt floats in waterDIt uses a spring in every joint 2If you double the gear ratio of a joint, what happens to reflected inertia? AIt doublesBIt halvesCIt grows by four timesDIt stays the same 3Why do many legged robots prefer low-gear-ratio actuators? AThey are cheaper in every caseBThey are backdrivable, absorb impacts better and allow force sensing from motor currentCThey never overheatDThey run without batteries 4Which sensor is the most important for balance? AAn IMU in the pelvis or torsoBA microphoneCA thermometerDA GPS receiver 0 of 4 answered Takeaways A typical humanoid has roughly 25 to 50 actuated joints plus 6 unactuated floating-base DoF. Gear ratio trades torque against speed and backdrivability; reflected inertia grows with the square of the ratio. QDD actuators favour impact tolerance and force sensing; SEAs measure force with a spring; hydraulics offer power density at the cost of complexity. Sensing comes in layers: encoders, IMU, foot force, vision, touch. Compute is layered by rate, so slow AI never blocks fast balance. The human form is a practical bet about environments and data, not a law of nature.

Advanced40 minBefore this:Balance and the ZMP · Reinforcement learning basics · Python basics A humanoid has been standing nicely for ten minutes. Now you say "walk to the door" and everything gets harder: the feet leave the ground one at a time, the robot is falling forward on purpose and catching itself, the floor might be uneven, and a person might step in the way. Walking is not one skill. It is a rhythm, a model, and a lot of small corrections. This lesson shows the two big families of walking controllers and what each one needs. You will be able to Describe the phases of the human gait cycle and map them onto a robot. Explain how model predictive control (MPC) generates footsteps and a CoM path from the pendulum model. Describe how a reinforcement-learned walking policy is built: observations, actions, rewards, randomization. Compare the two approaches and name the sim-to-real steps each one needs. Write a gait clock and a simple walking reward in Python.
documents.s: Locomotion: gaits, MPC walking and learned policies

documents.t: Walking repeats the same pattern. Follow one foot: Stance: the foot is on the ground and carries weight. In ordinary human walking it lasts roughly 60 percent of the cycle. Swing: the foot is in the air, moving forward to its next landing spot, roughly the other 40 percent. Double support: both feet are down. It happens twice per cycle, once at each handover, and usually accounts for around 20 percent of the total time. When the robot speeds up, double support shrinks. At a run it disappears and a flight phase appears, where neither foot touches the ground. For most humanoid walking you can assume stance on one foot, double support, stance on the other, and repeat. Two other terms are useful. A strideOne full left-right sequence of steps; the time it takes for one foot to go from landing to the next landing. is two steps; the duty factorThe fraction of the gait cycle a foot spends on the ground. is the share of each cycle the foot is in stance. gait_clock.py def gait_phase(t, period=0.8, duty=0.6): """Return (phase, left_in_stance, right_in_stance). The right foot runs half a cycle behind.""" phase = (t / period) % 1.0 left = phase < duty right = ((phase + 0.5) % 1.0) < duty return phase, left, right def label(left, right): if left and right: return "double support" if left: return "left stance, right swing" if right: return "right stance, left swing" return "flight" for i in range(0, 17): t = i * 0.05 phase, left, right = gait_phase(t) print(f"t={t:4.2f} phase={phase:4.2f} {label(left, right)}") samples = 1000 double = sum(1 for k in range(samples) if all(gait_phase(0.8 * k / samples)[1:])) print("double support share of the cycle:", double / samples) Running it prints a repeating sequence of left stance, double support, right stance, double support, and finally reports 0.2 for the double-support share. That clock is more than a toy. Many walking controllers, learned or planned, are driven by exactly this kind of phase signal.

In Balance and the ZMP you saw that the capture point tells you where to step. Walking is that idea repeated: at every step, place the foot so that the pendulum keeps moving in the direction you want, rather than stopping. Instead of stopping at the capture point, the robot picks a footstep so that the capture point lands where it wants next time. With ξ˙=ω(ξ−p)\dot{\xi} = \omega(\xi - p)ξ˙​=ω(ξ−p), a foot placed behind ξ\xiξ lets ξ\xiξ run forward, and the robot speeds up; a foot placed ahead of it slows it down. How far behind or ahead you place it, together with the step timing, sets how quickly the robot speeds up or slows down. Doing this by hand works for a clean flat floor. Planning many steps ahead, with limits on step length, foot rotation and contact timing, is a job for optimization.
documents.s: Walking with a model: capture point and MPC

documents.t: Model predictive controlModel predictive control: at every control cycle, solve an optimization over a short future horizon using a model, apply only the first control, then repeat. (MPC) does this. At each cycle the controller: Takes the current estimated state (CoM position and velocity, foot positions). Predicts the next NNN steps (or the next second or so) with a model, usually the LIPM or a richer centroidal model. Chooses the ZMP positions or foot placements pkp_kpk​ that make the CoM follow the desired velocity while respecting limits. Applies only the first command, then re-solves at the next cycle with fresh sensor data. A discretized LIPM gives the prediction: sk+1=Ask+Bpks_{k+1} = A s_k + B p_ksk+1​=Ask​+Bpk​ with s=(x,x˙)s = (x, \dot{x})s=(x,x˙). Stacking NNN steps turns the problem into a quadratic program: min⁡p0,…,pN−1 ∑k=1N∥x˙k−x˙ref∥2+α∑k=0N−1∥pk−pkref∥2s.t. pkmin⁡≤pk≤pkmax⁡\min_{p_0,\dots,p_{N-1}} \;\sum_{k=1}^{N} \left\| \dot{x}_k - \dot{x}^{\text{ref}} \right\|^2 + \alpha \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \left\| p_k - p^{\text{ref}}_k \right\|^2 \quad \text{s.t. } p^{\min}_k \le p_k \le p^{\max}_kp0​,…,pN−1​min​k=1∑N​​x˙k​−x˙ref​2+αk=0∑N−1​​pk​−pkref​​2s.t. pkmin​≤pk​≤pkmax​ The bounds are the support polygon (ZMP stays in the foot) and the reachable foot positions. A QP solver finds the answer in a millisecond or less, so the whole thing runs at 100 Hz or faster. An earlier classic, preview control of the ZMP, tracks a planned future ZMP reference with a feedback law, and is the ancestor of this approach. The planned CoM and foot trajectories are then handed to a whole-body controller (next lesson), which turns them into joint torques. MPC trades computation for foresight A model-based walker looks ahead. That makes it excellent at planned, constrained motion: stepping onto stones, turning in place, stopping exactly. It is limited by its model. A single point mass cannot capture swinging arms or a heavy payload, so richer models and good state estimation matter.

The other approach throws away the hand-written model. A neural network observes the robot and outputs actions, and training on millions of simulated steps teaches it to walk. You met the basics in Reinforcement learning and the training setup in RL in simulation with Isaac Lab. For walking, the standard recipe looks like this: Observations (what the policy sees): body angular velocity and orientation from the IMU (often as the gravity vector expressed in the body frame), joint positions and velocities, the previous action, a velocity command from the user, and often the gait phase from the clock above. Actions: target joint angles. A fast PD controller on the drive turns them into torque. The policy runs at around 50 Hz while the PD loop runs far faster. Reward: a weighted sum that says what good walking is: reward matching the commanded forward and turning speed, reward the feet for being on the ground when the gait clock says stance, penalize torque (energy), jerky action changes, and feet that slide on the floor, end the episode and penalize if the robot falls. walking_reward.py import math def tracking(err, sigma): """1.0 when the error is zero, decaying smoothly as it grows.""" return math.exp(-(err * err) / sigma) def walking_reward(cmd, state, action, last_action, torques, contacts, contact_target): r = 1.0 * tracking(cmd["vx"] - state["vx"], 0.25) r += 0.5 * tracking(cmd["yaw"] - state["yaw"], 0.25) match = sum(1 for c, t in zip(contacts, contact_target) if c == t) r += 0.3 * match / len(contacts) r -= 2e-4 * sum(tq * tq for tq in torques) r -= 0.05 * sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(action, last_action)) if state["fell"]: r -= 1.0 return r cmd = {"vx": 0.5, "yaw": 0.0} good = walking_reward(cmd, {"vx": 0.48, "yaw": 0.02, "fell": False}, [0.1, 0.2], [0.1, 0.19], [20.0, 25.0, 18.0], [True, False], [True, False]) bad = walking_reward(cmd, {"vx": 0.05, "yaw": 0.4, "fell": True}, [0.9, -0.8], [0.0, 0.0], [90.0, 95.0, 80.0], [False, True], [True, False]) print("good step reward:", round(good, 3)) print("bad step reward: ", round(bad, 3)) Run it and the good step scores about 1.5 while the bad step is strongly negative. Real training uses a dozen or more reward terms, and tuning their weights is a large part of the craft. Training runs thousands of simulated robots in parallel on a GPU, so a policy can accumulate years of walking experience in hours. A terrain curriculumGradually making the training environment harder, for example by increasing slope or roughness as the policy improves. starts on flat ground and moves on to slopes, stairs and rough surfaces as the policy improves.
documents.s: Walking with a policy: reinforcement learning

documents.t: A policy that walks in simulation will often fall on hardware, because simulation is never exact. The tools are the ones from The sim-to-real gap: Domain randomization: each training episode changes friction, link masses, motor strength, sensor noise, delays and random shoves. The policy learns to cope with a whole family of robots, one of which resembles the real one. Actuator modelling: fit a model of the real motor and drive (including torque limits, friction and latency) and use it in the simulator. This closes a surprisingly large part of the gap. Asymmetric actor-critic: the critic gets privileged information (true friction, terrain height) that the real robot does not have, which speeds up learning while the actor only uses sensors the robot actually has. Safe deployment: start with the robot hanging from a gantry, clip the actions, set torque and joint limits on the drives, and keep an emergency stop in reach.

MPC and model-based RL policy Needs Good model, state estimator, solver Simulator, reward, compute Strength Constraints, precision, explainable, works the first time on flat ground Rough terrain, recovery, natural motion, handles unmodelled effects Weakness Fails when the model is wrong; hard to tune for new tasks Reward tuning, sim-to-real work, hard to guarantee behavior Debugging Inspect the plan and the constraints Inspect rewards and randomization In practice they mix. A common pattern is an RL policy for robust low-level walking, with a model-based planner choosing footsteps or velocity commands above it, or an MPC that uses a learned value function. Which one wins depends on the task, the terrain, and how much simulation you can afford. Check the current literature for the latest results; this area changes quickly. Falls are real A full-size humanoid that falls can damage itself and hurt people. Always test new walking controllers in simulation first, then on a gantry or with a safety line, and never inside the reach of an untrained bystander.

Save gait_clock.py and run it. Confirm you see two double-support intervals per cycle and that the share is 0.2. Change duty to 0.5. What does the double-support share become? Try 0.45. What does the robot do now? Save walking_reward.py and run it. Make a third scenario, a robot walking at the right speed but sliding its feet, and add a foot-slip penalty term. Experiment: change the weight of the action-rate penalty from 0.05 to 1.0. Which behaviour does it discourage, and what might the downside be on a real robot? You are done when you can explain how each reward term maps to a visible walking behaviour.

Double supportBeginner A gait has period 1.0 s and duty factor 0.55. What fraction of the cycle is double support, and how long is each double-support interval? Show solutionHide solution With two feet half a cycle apart, each foot spends 0.55−0.5=0.050.55 - 0.5 = 0.050.55−0.5=0.05 of the cycle overlapping at each handover. There are two handovers, so double support is 2×0.05=0.102 \times 0.05 = 0.102×0.05=0.10 of the cycle, or 0.1 s per cycle, and each interval lasts 0.05 s. Where to stepIntermediate A robot walks with CoM velocity 0.6 m/s and a LIPM with ω=3.4 s−1\omega = 3.4\ \text{s}^{-1}ω=3.4 s−1. Its capture point is how far ahead of the CoM? If it places the foot exactly there, what happens? Show solutionHide solution The offset is x˙/ω=0.6/3.4≈0.18\dot{x}/\omega = 0.6/3.4 \approx 0.18x˙/ω=0.6/3.4≈0.18 m. Placing the foot at the capture point makes ξ˙=0\dot{\xi} = 0ξ˙​=0, so the robot comes to rest over the foot. To keep walking, it must place the foot somewhat behind the capture point, so the capture point keeps moving forward. Design a rewardAdvanced Your RL walker moves quickly but its feet shuffle on the ground and it vibrates. Name two reward terms you could add or change, and say why. Show solutionHide solution Add a foot-air-time reward (paid when a foot spends a reasonable time in the air per step), which discourages shuffling. Increase the penalty on action rate or joint acceleration, which discourages vibration. You could also add a penalty on foot velocity while in contact. Check each change in simulation first to confirm it does not make the robot stand still instead.

1In normal walking, what is double support? ABoth feet in the airBBoth feet on the ground, at each handover between stepsCUsing both arms for balanceDTwo controllers running at once 2What does MPC do at each control cycle? APlays back a fixed trajectoryBSolves an optimization over a short future horizon, applies the first command, then repeatsCTrains a neural network from scratchDOnly measures the state 3Why use domain randomization when training a walking policy? ATo make training slowerBSo the policy copes with a range of physics and is more likely to work on the real robotCTo avoid using a simulatorDTo reduce the number of joints 4What is an asymmetric actor-critic? AA critic with privileged simulator information, and an actor that uses only real sensorsBA critic that is bigger than the actorCAn actor trained on one leg onlyDA policy with two reward functions 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Walking alternates stance and swing; double support is the short overlap when both feet are down. Model-based walkers step relative to the capture point; MPC solves for ZMP or footstep sequences with a QP, many times per second. RL walkers map observations to joint targets, trained with a shaped reward on thousands of simulated robots. Sim-to-real work (randomization, actuator models, careful deployment) is what makes learned walking reach hardware. MPC excels at constraints and precision; RL excels at robustness and rough terrain; real systems often combine them. Test on a gantry first.

Learning agile and dynamic motor skills for legged robots, an early demonstration of sim-to-real legged RL with actuator modelling. Advanced40 minBefore this:Forward and inverse kinematics · Dynamics essentials · Locomotion Your humanoid has to pick a box off a shelf. The hands need to reach it. The feet must stay planted without slipping. The body must not fall over as the arms move forward. The elbows must stay clear of the torso, and no joint may exceed its limit. Each of those is a goal, and they all compete for the same few dozen joints. A whole-body controller is the piece of software that settles the argument, hundreds of times a second. You will be able to Write a task in task space and compute a joint motion that achieves it. Use null-space projection to run a lower-priority task without disturbing a higher one. Explain how a hierarchical quadratic program (HQP) organizes tasks and constraints. Describe the floating-base dynamics and contact constraints inside a whole-body controller. Explain why loco-manipulation is harder than walking or reaching alone.

A taskA desired behavior written as a quantity the robot should control, such as a hand pose, the center-of-mass position or a foot height. is something you want, expressed in the space where it makes sense. A hand task lives in 3D space, not in joint angles. You already know the link between the two spaces, the Jacobian JJJ from Forward and inverse kinematics: x˙=J(q) q˙\dot{x} = J(q)\,\dot{q}x˙=J(q)q˙​ To move the hand with velocity x˙des\dot{x}^{\text{des}}x˙des, invert the relation using the pseudo-inverse J+J^{+}J+: q˙=J+ x˙des,x˙des=K (xtarget−x)\dot{q} = J^{+}\,\dot{x}^{\text{des}}, \qquad \dot{x}^{\text{des}} = K\,(x^{\text{target}} - x)q˙​=J+x˙des,x˙des=K(xtarget−x) When there are more joints than task dimensions the robot is redundantHaving more degrees of freedom than the task needs, so many joint motions achieve the same task., and infinitely many joint motions give the same hand motion. The pseudo-inverse picks the smallest one. The extra freedom is not wasted. It is exactly the room we use for secondary goals.

The set of joint motions that do not move the hand at all is called the null spaceThe set of joint velocities that produce zero task velocity. Moving inside it changes the robot’s posture without disturbing the task. of JJJ. The projector onto it is N=I−J+JN = I - J^{+} JN=I−J+J Any motion of the form NzN zNz leaves the first task untouched. So a second, less important task can use it. With task 1 (hand) and task 2 (stay near a comfortable posture), the prioritized solution is: q˙=J1+x˙1+N1 (J2N1)+(x˙2−J2J1+x˙1)\dot{q} = J_1^{+}\dot{x}_1 + N_1\, (J_2 N_1)^{+}\left(\dot{x}_2 - J_2 J_1^{+}\dot{x}_1\right)q˙​=J1+​x˙1​+N1​(J2​N1​)+(x˙2​−J2​J1+​x˙1​) You do not need to memorize it. Read it as: do task 1 as well as possible; then do as much of task 2 as you can inside what task 1 does not care about. prioritized_ik.py import numpy as np LINKS = np.array([0.40, 0.30, 0.20]) # link lengths in metres def fk(q): """End-effector (x, y) of a planar 3-link arm.""" a = np.cumsum(q) return np.array([np.sum(LINKS * np.cos(a)), np.sum(LINKS * np.sin(a))]) def jacobian(q): a = np.cumsum(q) J = np.zeros((2, 3)) for i in range(3): J[0, i] = -np.sum(LINKS[i:] * np.sin(a[i:])) J[1, i] = np.sum(LINKS[i:] * np.cos(a[i:])) return J def pinv(A, damping=1e-6): """Damped pseudo-inverse: safe near singularities.""" return A.T @ np.linalg.inv(A @ A.T + damping * np.eye(A.shape[0])) def prioritized_step(q, target, q_rest, gain=0.5): """Task 1 (strict priority): hand position. Task 2: stay near q_rest.""" J1 = jacobian(q) e1 = gain * (target - fk(q)) J1p = pinv(J1) N1 = np.eye(3) - J1p @ J1 # motions that do not disturb task 1 J2 = np.eye(3) e2 = gain * (q_rest - q) dq1 = J1p @ e1 dq2 = pinv(J2 @ N1) @ (e2 - J2 @ dq1) return dq1 + N1 @ dq2 q = np.array([0.3, 0.4, 0.3]) q_rest = np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]) target = np.array([0.55, 0.35]) for it in range(200): q = q + prioritized_step(q, target, q_rest) print("with posture task: hand error", np.linalg.norm(target - fk(q)).round(5), " posture error", np.linalg.norm(q_rest - q).round(3)) # compare: task 1 only (no posture task in the null space) q3 = np.array([0.3, 0.4, 0.3]) for it in range(200): q3 = q3 + pinv(jacobian(q3)) @ (0.5 * (target - fk(q3))) print("task 1 only: hand error", np.linalg.norm(target - fk(q3)).round(5), " posture error", np.linalg.norm(q_rest - q3).round(3)) Both runs put the hand on the target. The first run finishes slightly closer to the rest posture, because it used the leftover freedom. With a three-joint arm and a two-dimensional task, there is only one direction of freedom to spare, so the gain is modest. A humanoid has dozens of spare directions. Priorities are strict, not weighted In a prioritized controller, a lower task can never hurt a higher one. That is different from adding up weighted costs, where a big enough weight on the posture could pull the hand off target. Strict priority is how you tell the robot "never drop the balance task, even if the hand has to give up."

A walking humanoid cannot be controlled with velocities alone. It must manage forces on the ground. Whole-body controllers use the full dynamics of a floating-base robot: M(q) v˙+h(q,v)=S⊤τ+Jc⊤fM(q)\,\dot{v} + h(q, v) = S^{\top}\tau + J_c^{\top} fM(q)v˙+h(q,v)=S⊤τ+Jc⊤​f Here vvv is the generalized velocity (including the 6 floating-base entries), MMM is the mass matrix, hhh gathers gravity, Coriolis and centrifugal terms, τ\tauτ are joint torques, and fff are the contact forces at the feet or hands. The matrix SSS selects the actuated joints: the first 6 rows have no motors, which is the floating-base problem from Humanoid anatomy. The body only moves because the contact forces fff push on it. Contact adds more rules: A foot that is planted does not move: Jcv˙+J˙cv=0J_c \dot{v} + \dot{J}_c v = 0Jc​v˙+J˙c​v=0. The ground can only push, never pull: the normal force fz≥0f_z \ge 0fz​≥0. The foot must not slip: the sideways force stays inside the friction coneThe set of contact forces that friction can supply without sliding, shaped like a cone around the contact normal., fx2+fy2≤μfz\sqrt{f_x^2 + f_y^2} \le \mu f_zfx2​+fy2​​≤μfz​. Controllers replace the cone with a pyramid of linear inequalities so it fits in a QP. Joint torques and angles stay within their limits.

Now put it all together. The unknowns are the accelerations v˙\dot{v}v˙, torques τ\tauτ and contact forces fff. Stack them as uuu. Every task becomes a linear equation in uuu. A task on a point with Jacobian JiJ_iJi​ says Jiv˙+J˙iv=x¨idesJ_i \dot{v} + \dot{J}_i v = \ddot{x}_i^{\text{des}}Ji​v˙+J˙i​v=x¨ides​, with the desired acceleration from a spring-damper law: x¨ides=x¨iref+Kd(x˙iref−x˙i)+Kp(xiref−xi)\ddot{x}_i^{\text{des}} = \ddot{x}^{\text{ref}}_i + K_d(\dot{x}^{\text{ref}}_i - \dot{x}_i) + K_p(x^{\text{ref}}_i - x_i)x¨ides​=x¨iref​+Kd​(x˙iref​−x˙i​)+Kp​(xiref​−xi​) Physical laws (the dynamics, the contact, friction and limits) are hard constraintsA requirement that must be satisfied exactly, as opposed to a task, which is only satisfied as well as possible.. Tasks are soft: satisfied as well as possible. There are two common ways to combine the tasks. Weighted QP. One optimization with all tasks summed and a weight wiw_iwi​ on each: min⁡u ∑iwi ∥Aiu−bi∥2s.t. Cu≤d, Eu=e\min_{u}\; \sum_i w_i\,\| A_i u - b_i \|^2 \quad \text{s.t. } C u \le d,\; Eu = eumin​i∑​wi​∥Ai​u−bi​∥2s.t. Cu≤d,Eu=e This is simple and fast but priorities are only "soft"; with the wrong weights tasks interfere. Hierarchical QP (HQP). Solve the tasks in order of priority, one QP per level. At level kkk: min⁡u, wk ∥wk∥2s.t. Aku−bk=wk, Aiu−bi=wi∗ (i<k), Cu≤d\min_{u,\,w_k}\; \| w_k \|^2 \quad \text{s.t. } A_k u - b_k = w_k,\; A_i u - b_i = w_i^{*}\;(i < k),\; Cu \le du,wk​min​∥wk​∥2s.t. Ak​u−bk​=wk​,Ai​u−bi​=wi∗​(i<k),Cu≤d Here wkw_kwk​ is the residual (error) of task kkk. The constraint Aiu−bi=wi∗A_i u - b_i = w_i^{*}Ai​u−bi​=wi∗​ says that earlier tasks keep exactly the error they already achieved. So level kkk can only use freedom that the higher levels left behind: the same idea as the null-space formula, now with inequalities added. A typical priority list from top to bottom: physics and contact constraints; balance (momentum or CoM); foot placement and swing-foot trajectory; hand tasks; torso orientation; posture; minimize torque. If the robot is pushed hard, the hand tasks quietly degrade while balance stays satisfied. In practice you rarely write this solver yourself. Libraries such as Pinocchio provide the dynamics terms, and open-source task-space controllers (the tsid library, for example) and QP solvers handle the rest. The skill to learn is shaping tasks, priorities and constraints, not coding the solver.

Loco-manipulation is moving and manipulating at the same time: walking while carrying a box, pushing a cart, opening a door with a hand while stepping through. It is hard because the arms and legs are coupled through the floating base. Swinging an arm shifts the center of mass and creates angular momentum. A heavy payload moves the CoM forward and changes how much force the feet must supply. A door push comes back as a force on the body. Three approaches are common: Treat the arms as a disturbance. The leg controller keeps balance, estimates the extra forces from the arms and compensates. Simple, and robust for light loads. Optimize jointly. Plan the CoM, momentum and arm motion together (whole-body MPC, centroidal momentum control). More capable, more compute and more model accuracy needed. Learn it. Train a whole-body RL policy that receives upper-body commands (from a planner or from human teleoperation) and learns to keep balance while following them. This is an active research direction, and results change fast, so check the current literature. Many real systems use a hybrid: a learned or model-based lower body for balance, and a task-space controller for the arms, connected by a shared state estimate. Pro tip When a whole-body controller misbehaves, print the active constraints. Nine times out of ten the QP is infeasible or a friction cone is saturated, and that tells you which task to relax.

Save prioritized_ik.py and run it. Both lines should show a hand error near zero. Move target to np.array([0.8, 0.2]). Is it reachable? What do you see if you ask for [1.2, 0.0] (beyond the arm length of 0.9 m)? Change q_rest to [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]. Does the hand still reach the target? Does the posture error grow? Swap the priorities: make posture task 1 and the hand task 2. What happens to the hand error? Done when you can say which task is allowed to fail, and why.

Spot the null spaceIntermediate A 7-joint arm controls only the 3D position of the hand. How many dimensions does its null space have, and what is the physical meaning of moving in it? Show solutionHide solution There are 7 joint velocities and 3 task constraints, so the null space has 7−3=47 - 3 = 47−3=4 dimensions (assuming a non-singular configuration). Moving in it changes the arm’s posture (for example swinging the elbow) while the hand stays exactly where it is. Weights versus prioritiesAdvanced A weighted QP has a balance task with weight 100 and a hand task with weight 1. Describe a situation where the hand task still ends up disturbing balance, and how strict priorities fix it. Show solutionHide solution If the hand is asked to move very far or very fast, its error term can become large enough that 1×error21 \times \text{error}^21×error2 exceeds the (small) balance error that results from shifting the weight. The optimizer then trades a little balance for hand accuracy. With strict priorities, the hand task is only solved in what is left after balance is satisfied as well as possible, so it cannot degrade balance at all. FeasibilityIntermediate A foot is on ice with friction coefficient μ=0.1\mu = 0.1μ=0.1 and carries a normal force of 300 N. What is the largest sideways force the foot can resist? Show solutionHide solution ft≤μfz=0.1×300=30f_t \le \mu f_z = 0.1 \times 300 = 30ft​≤μfz​=0.1×300=30 N. Any whole-body plan that asks for more horizontal force at that foot is infeasible, and the QP will either fail or move the demand to the other foot.

1What is the null space of a task Jacobian? AJoint motions that do not change the task, so they can be used for lower-priority goalsBThe motions that break the robotCThe empty list of tasksDThe set of unreachable points 2What does it mean that priorities in a hierarchical QP are strict? AAll tasks are weighted equallyBA lower-priority task may not worsen the result of a higher-priority oneCOnly one task runsDPriorities change randomly 3Why is S in the floating-base dynamics equation needed? AThe first six degrees of freedom of the body have no motors, so torque only enters through the actuated jointsBIt scales the gravityCIt selects the cameraDIt removes friction 4Why is loco-manipulation harder than walking alone? AArms are heavyBThe arms and legs are coupled through the body, so arm motion and loads disturb balanceCWalking is not allowed with handsDThere is no model 0 of 4 answered Takeaways A task is a goal in the space where it makes sense; the Jacobian maps it to joint motion. Redundancy gives a null space where lower-priority tasks can work without disturbing higher ones. A floating-base controller must respect dynamics, contact, friction cones and limits. A hierarchical QP solves tasks level by level and keeps earlier results fixed, giving strict priorities. Loco-manipulation couples arms and legs through the body; approaches range from disturbance rejection to joint optimization to learned policies. Debug by checking which constraints are active.

Pinocchio documentation for the dynamics terms (mass matrix, Jacobians) used above. Drake documentation for optimization-based control examples. Isaac Lab documentation: check the current release for whole-body and humanoid environments. Next: Hands and dexterity

Perception tells a robot what is around it. Motion decides what to do about it. Given a goal ("get to the kitchen", "put the cup on the shelf"), a robot has to find a path through a world full of obstacles, turn that path into movement that its motors can actually follow, and keep checking that nothing went wrong along the way. This module has one idea at three scales. First you learn the planning algorithms themselves, on a grid you can read with your own eyes. Then you meet the two big ROS 2 frameworks that package those algorithms for real robots: Nav2 for mobile bases and MoveIt 2 for arms. Finally you zoom in on the last few centimetres of manipulation, grasping, where geometry, friction and learning meet.

Describe a robot's configuration space and explain why planning there is easier than planning in the real world. Implement breadth-first search, Dijkstra and A* on a grid, and explain RRT and RRT* well enough to know when to pick which. Bring up Nav2 with a simulated robot, tune its costmaps, and send navigation goals from Python. Use MoveIt 2 to plan, add collision objects to the planning scene, and follow a Cartesian path with an arm. Reason about what makes a grasp stable and sketch a complete pick-and-place pipeline.
