Fetch it. In simulation, make a mobile robot drive to a table (Nav2), then make an arm pick a block off that table and put it on a tray (MoveIt 2 and your grasp logic). You do not need one robot that does both yet; two simulations and a short script that glues the steps together is a fine result. Write down every point where the pipeline failed and what you changed. Those notes are the real deliverable.

Advanced35 minBefore this:Manipulation with MoveIt 2 · Depth, point clouds and lidar · Deep learning for detection and segmentation Getting the arm to a pose is the easy half of picking something up. The hard half is the last few centimetres: where exactly should the fingers touch, how hard should they squeeze, and what happens when the object is a slippery, transparent bottle you have never seen before? Grasping is where geometry, friction, sensing and learning all collide, and it is still one of the open problems in robotics. You will be able to Describe common grasp representations, from planar four-degree-of-freedom grasps to full six-degree-of-freedom poses. Explain the antipodal condition and the intuition behind force closure using friction cones. Describe how learned grasp detectors work and where they fail. Lay out a complete pick-and-place pipeline and say what can go wrong at each step.

A graspA hand pose and finger configuration that lets the hand hold an object securely is an answer to: where do I put the hand, how wide do I open it, and from which direction do I approach? In code, a grasp is usually a small data structure. Planar (4-DoF) grasp: for a camera looking straight down at a table. The grasp is a point (x,y)(x, y)(x,y), a rotation angle in the image plane, and a gripper width. The gripper always approaches from above. This is simple and surprisingly effective for bin picking. 6-DoF grasp: a full pose in 3D (position and orientation) plus a width. It lets the hand approach from the side or at an angle, which is needed for cluttered shelves and awkward objects. Multi-finger grasps: for a dexterous hand, a grasp also includes all the finger joint angles. You meet those in the humanoids module. Most representations also carry a quality score, a number that says how likely the grasp is to succeed. Planners and learned models rank candidates by it.

Think about pinching a pencil between two fingers. If you squeeze at the middle, it holds. If you push the fingers against the pencil at an angle, it squirts out. Physics explains why. At each contact, the finger can push along the surface normal and also pull sideways through friction. The Coulomb friction model says the sideways force can be at most μ\muμ times the normal force: ∥ft∥≤μ fn\|f_t\| \le \mu \, f_n∥ft​∥≤μfn​ That limit defines a friction cone around the contact normal, with half-angle α=arctan⁡(μ)\alpha = \arctan(\mu)α=arctan(μ). Any force within the cone can be applied without slipping. Beyond it, the finger slides. For a two-finger grasp, the antipodal condition says: the straight line joining the two contact points must lie inside the friction cone at both contacts. When it does, the two fingers can push directly against each other, and the line of force passes through both cones, so the object does not slip. Antipodal means the squeeze line stays inside both friction cones If the line between your two fingertips tilts more than the friction angle away from either surface normal, the object will slide out. Flat, parallel faces (a box) are easy. Smooth, slippery curved objects have wide cones only when friction is high, which is why rubber fingertips help so much. A grasp has force closure when the contacts can resist any external force and torque (any "wrench") by adjusting contact forces, within the friction cones. For a planar object held with two frictional point contacts, the antipodal condition is enough for force closure. In 3D, with point contacts and friction, you need contact forces that can balance disturbances in all six directions, which can take three or more contacts, or a contact with torsional friction (a soft fingertip). You do not have to prove this by hand for every grasp, but the intuition guides everything: contacts opposite each other, on surfaces with grip, near the object’s centre of mass so gravity does not rotate the object out of the fingers.
documents.s: Why a grasp holds: friction and force closure

documents.t: antipodal.py import math import numpy as np def antipodal(p1, n1, p2, n2, mu=0.5): """Two-finger frictional point contacts. p1, p2 are contact points; n1, n2 are unit surface normals pointing OUT of the object.""" alpha = math.atan(mu) # half-angle of the friction cone line = p2 - p1 line = line / np.linalg.norm(line) # direction from contact 1 to contact 2 a1 = math.acos(np.clip(np.dot(line, -n1), -1, 1)) # angle between squeeze line and inward normal 1 a2 = math.acos(np.clip(np.dot(-line, -n2), -1, 1)) # same at contact 2 return a1 <= alpha and a2 <= alpha # a 4 cm wide box, fingers on opposite faces left_p, left_n = np.array([-0.02, 0.0]), np.array([-1.0, 0.0]) right_p, right_n = np.array([0.02, 0.0]), np.array([1.0, 0.0]) print(antipodal(left_p, left_n, right_p, right_n)) # True # the right finger is 3 cm higher, so the squeeze line tilts right_p2 = np.array([0.02, 0.03]) print(antipodal(left_p, left_n, right_p2, right_n, mu=0.5)) # False print(antipodal(left_p, left_n, right_p2, right_n, mu=1.0)) # True (grippier fingers) Notice how raising friction from 0.5 to 1.0 rescues the second grasp. The same geometry holds or slips depending only on the contact material.

Analytic and model-based methods need a 3D model of the object. They sample candidate contact pairs on the surface and score them with measures like the antipodal check above or the size of the largest disturbance wrench the grasp can resist. They work well for known objects and fail when the model is wrong or missing. Learned grasp detection skips the model. A neural network looks at a depth image or point cloud and directly proposes grasps with quality scores. Training data comes from simulation (where physics can test millions of grasps), from real trial and error, or from human labels. Dex-Net 2.0 (Mahler et al., arxiv.org/abs/1703.09312) trained a network on synthetic point clouds scored by analytic grasp quality, then ranked planar grasps at test time. GG-CNN (Morrison, Corke, Leitner) predicts a grasp quality, angle and width for every pixel, fast enough for closed-loop control. Contact-GraspNet (Sundermeyer et al., arxiv.org/abs/2103.14127) proposes 6-DoF grasps directly from a point cloud of a cluttered scene. These methods work well on household objects with good depth data. They get into trouble with transparent or very shiny objects (depth sensors fail), heavily occluded objects and objects far from the training distribution. Plan for those failures: a grasp detector is a good source of candidates, not a guarantee. Note Newer foundation-model approaches and large pretrained grasp models are improving fast. Check current releases rather than relying on a specific model, and always measure on your own objects.

A working pick-and-place is a chain, and every link can break. Perceive. Detect and segment the target, then get its 3D shape or a point cloud. Calibration between camera and robot (hand-eye calibration) must be good, since a 1 cm error in the camera-to-base transform is a 1 cm miss. Generate grasps. Use a model-based sampler or a learned detector. Filter. Throw away candidates the arm cannot reach (IK fails), that collide with the table or neighbours, or whose approach direction is blocked. Rank the survivors by quality. Pre-grasp. Plan a free-space motion to a pose a few centimetres back along the approach direction, with the gripper open. Approach. Move in a straight line (Cartesian path) to the grasp pose. Slow down near the object. Close and check. Close the gripper and confirm you are holding something: finger width at stop, motor current or a tactile sensor. Attach and lift. Attach the object to the hand in the planning scene so planning accounts for it, then lift straight up. Place. Plan to a pre-place pose, lower and release. Retreat. Open and back away in a straight line so you do not knock what you just placed. The MoveIt Task Constructor, mentioned in the previous lesson, lets you describe these stages as one task and plans them together so that, for example, a grasp chosen in step 2 is guaranteed to allow the lift in step 7. Warning Always verify the grasp before moving at full speed. A failed grasp that is not detected sends the arm through a place motion with nothing in the gripper, or worse, an object loosely held.

Open-loop pipelines (look once, then move) fail when the object shifts as the fingers close. Better systems re-observe during the approach, retry with the next-best candidate after a failed grasp and track success rates. Treat grasp success as a statistic: log every attempt, and a pipeline with a 90% success rate over hundreds of trials tells you far more than a single working demo.

Save antipodal.py and run it. Confirm the three outputs match the comments. Add a third test: two contacts on a circle of radius 2 cm at angles 0 and 170 degrees (surface normals pointing radially outwards). Find the smallest friction coefficient for which the grasp passes the antipodal test. Write the pipeline above as a Python function skeleton, with one empty function per step. For each, write one sentence on what failure looks like and how you would detect it. Optional: in the MoveIt Panda demo from the previous lesson, add a box as a collision object and use the MotionPlanning panel to plan a pre-grasp pose above it and then a straight-line approach.

Friction angleBeginner A rubber fingertip on a plastic bottle has μ=0.8\mu = 0.8μ=0.8. What is the half-angle of the friction cone, and is a grasp whose squeeze line is 35 degrees away from the contact normal antipodal? Show solutionHide solution α=arctan⁡(0.8)≈38.7∘\alpha = \arctan(0.8) \approx 38.7^\circα=arctan(0.8)≈38.7∘. A squeeze line 35 degrees off the normal lies within the cone, so (if the same is true at the other contact) the grasp satisfies the antipodal condition. With a slippery plastic finger and μ=0.3\mu = 0.3μ=0.3, α≈16.7∘\alpha \approx 16.7^\circα≈16.7∘ and the same grasp would slip. Where do learned detectors break?Intermediate Name two kinds of object that commonly cause trouble for depth-based learned grasp detectors, and one fix for each. Show solutionHide solution Transparent objects (glass, clear plastic) return missing or wrong depth. Fixes include using a depth-completion model, using RGB-based or multi-view methods, or placing objects in view of a sensor that handles them. Heavily cluttered or occluded objects produce incomplete point clouds. Fixes include viewing from several angles, re-sensing after each pick, or pushing items apart first. Design the verificationIntermediate Your gripper has no tactile sensors. How can you tell whether a grasp succeeded before lifting? Show solutionHide solution Check the gripper width after closing: if it closed fully (or to a width much smaller than the object), you grasped nothing. Check motor current or effort: holding an object produces a stall at a width close to the object’s size. You can also lift a few centimetres and re-check width and current, which catches objects that slip during lift.

1What does the antipodal condition require for a two-finger grasp? AFingers must be the same sizeBThe line between the contacts lies inside the friction cone at both contactsCThe object must be symmetricDThe gripper must be open fully 2The friction cone half-angle for friction coefficient mu is: AmuBarctan(mu)Carcsin(mu)D1/mu 3Why use a pre-grasp pose and a straight-line approach? AIt is fasterBIt lets the gripper approach along a safe direction without sweeping into the object or its neighboursCIt avoids needing IKDIt improves friction 4A learned grasp detector gives you a top-scoring grasp. What should the pipeline still do? AExecute it immediatelyBFilter it for reachability and collisions, then verify the grasp after closingCRetrain the modelDSkip planning 0 of 4 answered Takeaways A grasp is a hand pose plus gripper settings, often with a quality score. Planar 4-DoF grasps are simple and effective, 6-DoF grasps are more general. Friction cones explain why grasps hold. The antipodal condition means the squeeze line stays inside both cones. Force closure means the contacts can resist any external wrench. Intuition: opposed contacts, good friction, near the centre of mass. Learned detectors propose grasps from depth data without a model, and fail on transparent, shiny and occluded objects. Pick-and-place is a pipeline: perceive, generate, filter, pre-grasp, approach, close and verify, attach, lift, place, retreat. Measure success over many trials.

Murray, Li and Sastry, A Mathematical Introduction to Robotic Manipulation, the classic text on grasp analysis (free from the authors’ site). Mahler et al., "Dex-Net 2.0" (arxiv.org/abs/1703.09312). Sundermeyer et al., "Contact-GraspNet" (arxiv.org/abs/2103.14127). The MoveIt documentation at moveit.picknik.ai, including the MoveIt Task Constructor pick-and-place tutorial. Intermediate45 minBefore this:Path planning algorithms · Forward and inverse kinematics · ROS 2 actions, parameters and launch · TF2 and URDF A robot arm sits next to a table with a mug on it. You want the gripper above the mug, without the elbow knocking over the lamp. Writing that planner from scratch means kinematics, collision checking, a sampling planner, time parameterization and controller hand-off. MoveIt 2 is the ROS 2 framework that bundles all of it, and it is the standard starting point for arm manipulation. You will be able to Describe the roles of move_group, the planning scene and the planning pipeline. Add and remove collision objects so plans avoid real obstacles. Plan to a joint goal and a pose goal, and follow a straight-line Cartesian path. Choose between the MoveItPy Python API, the C++ interface and ROS messages for your project.

MoveIt does not move motors. It computes trajectories and hands them to your ROS 2 controllers. The pieces you need to know: move_group: the central node. It owns the robot model, the planning scene, the planners and the kinematics solvers, and exposes them as ROS 2 actions, services and topics. Robot model: read from your robot’s URDF and a companion SRDF, which adds SRDFSemantic Robot Description Format: names planning groups, named poses and which link pairs may safely touch information such as the planning group panda_arm (which joints plan together), named poses like ready, and collision pairs that can be ignored. Planning scene: MoveIt’s picture of the world: the robot’s current state plus obstacles, attached objects and the occupancy map from your sensors. Planning pipeline: a chain of a planner (OMPL by default, or Pilz industrial motion planner, CHOMP, STOMP) plus request adapters that pre- and post-process, for instance by time-parameterizing the result. Kinematics plugin: solves inverse kinematics (KDL by default, with alternatives such as TRAC-IK and the analytical IKFast). Controller interface: sends the trajectory to a FollowJointTrajectory controller, normally from ros2_control. MoveIt plans against a model of the world, not the world Plans are only as safe as the planning scene. If a box exists on the table but not in the scene, MoveIt will happily plan straight through it. Keeping the scene in sync with reality, through collision objects you add or an occupancy map from a depth camera, is the heart of using MoveIt well.

Install MoveIt 2 and a ready-made Panda arm configuration on ROS 2 Jazzy: terminal sudo apt install ros-jazzy-moveit ros-jazzy-moveit-resources-panda-moveit-config ros2 launch moveit_resources_panda_moveit_config demo.launch.py RViz opens with a MotionPlanning panel. Drag the orange interactive marker on the end effector to a new pose, press Plan to see the trajectory preview, then Execute. With fake controllers, the arm moves in RViz only. Try dragging the goal into the table and notice that the planner either refuses or finds a way around. For your own arm, the MoveIt Setup Assistant (ros2 launch moveit_setup_assistant setup_assistant.launch.py) generates the config package from your URDF: planning groups, named poses, controllers and collision matrix.

You have three main ways to command MoveIt, and they differ in language and level. MoveItPy is the Python binding to the C++ planning stack. It runs the planning components inside your own process, so you do not need a separate move_group node for the plan itself. You configure it with MoveIt parameter files from a launch file. A plan to a named pose looks like this: plan_to_named_pose.py import rclpy from moveit.planning import MoveItPy def main(): rclpy.init() robot = MoveItPy(node_name="moveit_py") arm = robot.get_planning_component("panda_arm") arm.set_start_state_to_current_state() arm.set_goal_state(configuration_name="ready") # named pose from the SRDF result = arm.plan() if result: robot.execute(result.trajectory, controllers=[]) else: print("Planning failed") rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == "__main__": main() This must be launched with the robot description, SRDF, kinematics and planning parameters passed to the node, which the MoveIt tutorials show in a launch file. A bare python3 plan_to_named_pose.py will not find them. The C++ MoveGroupInterface is the long-standing, most complete interface. It talks to a running move_group node. It offers pose targets, joint targets, computeCartesianPath, scene manipulation and more, and most official tutorials use it. If you need a feature and MoveItPy lacks it, this is the fallback. Raw ROS interfaces work from any language. move_group exposes the MoveGroup action (plan and execute), services such as /compute_cartesian_path and /apply_planning_scene, and the /planning_scene topic. Python nodes that only need to modify the scene or request a Cartesian path often use these directly. Info MoveItPy has been developed alongside MoveIt 2 and its coverage is smaller than the C++ interface. Check the MoveIt documentation for your release for the up-to-date list of what is supported, rather than assuming a C++ method has a Python twin.

A joint goal says exactly which angles you want. It is unambiguous. A pose goal says where the end effector should be (position and orientation) and leaves IK to find joint values. That may fail for several reasons: the pose is out of reach, IK finds no solution that is collision-free, or the planner times out. When it fails, ask which stage failed rather than assuming the planner is broken.

To keep the arm away from the table, tell MoveIt about it. A moveit_msgs/CollisionObject describes a shape (box, sphere, cylinder, mesh), its pose and the operation (add, remove, move). You can publish it as a diff to the planning scene: add_table.py import time import rclpy from geometry_msgs.msg import Pose from moveit_msgs.msg import CollisionObject, PlanningScene from rclpy.node import Node from shape_msgs.msg import SolidPrimitive class SceneAdder(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__("scene_adder") self.pub = self.create_publisher(PlanningScene, "/planning_scene", 10) def add_table(self): box = SolidPrimitive() box.type = SolidPrimitive.BOX box.dimensions = [0.8, 1.2, 0.04] # x, y, z in metres pose = Pose() pose.position.x = 0.6 pose.position.z = 0.3 pose.orientation.w = 1.0 obj = CollisionObject() obj.header.frame_id = "panda_link0" # the robot base frame obj.id = "table" obj.primitives = [box] obj.primitive_poses = [pose] obj.operation = CollisionObject.ADD scene = PlanningScene() scene.is_diff = True # only the changes, not the whole scene scene.world.collision_objects = [obj] self.pub.publish(scene) def main(): rclpy.init() node = SceneAdder() time.sleep(1.0) # give the publisher time to connect node.add_table() rclpy.spin_once(node, timeout_sec=0.5) rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == "__main__": main() Run it while the Panda demo is up and the table appears in RViz. Plans now avoid it. Use CollisionObject.REMOVE with the same id to delete it.
documents.s: Collision objects and the planning scene

documents.t: When the gripper holds a cup, the cup is part of the robot for collision purposes: it moves with the hand, and it must not hit the world. MoveIt models this with an attached collision object, which you attach to a link (usually the hand). You also list links the object may touch, such as the finger links, so the gripper holding it does not count as a collision. Forgetting to attach an object after a grasp is a classic reason an arm sweeps a held object through obstacles.

MoveIt can also build an occupancy map from point clouds or depth images using its octomap support. That keeps the scene honest without you describing every object. It trades convenience for noise and compute, so many teams model the key fixtures by hand and use the octomap for unknowns.

Sometimes you want the hand to move in a straight line: lowering a gripper onto an object, wiping a table, inserting a plug. A normal planner is free to choose any joint-space route, and the hand traces a curve. Cartesian planning instead interpolates poses along a line (or through waypoints) and solves IK at each step. You send MoveIt a list of waypoints, a maximum step size in metres and whether to avoid collisions. It returns a trajectory and a fraction between 0.0 and 1.0 telling you how much of the path was achievable before IK failed or a collision appeared. Always check it: cartesian_service.py (the key part) from moveit_msgs.srv import GetCartesianPath req = GetCartesianPath.Request() req.group_name = "panda_arm" req.header.frame_id = "panda_link0" req.waypoints = waypoints # a list of geometry_msgs/Pose req.max_step = 0.01 # metres between interpolated poses req.avoid_collisions = True future = client.call_async(req) # client for the /compute_cartesian_path service # ... after it completes: response = future.result() if response.fraction < 0.99: print(f"Only {response.fraction:.0%} of the path is reachable") The C++ computeCartesianPath call has the same behaviour. A fraction below 1.0 means partial success. Executing it blindly is how arms stop halfway down a pick. If you want industrial-style linear and circular moves with predictable timing, the Pilz industrial motion planner provides PTP, LIN and CIRC motion types as a planning pipeline.

Real tasks are sequences: approach, grasp, lift, move, place, retreat. MoveIt Task Constructor lets you compose such stages and plans the whole chain consistently, so the grasp pose you pick also allows the lift. It is the usual tool for pick-and-place. You will use these ideas in the next lesson. Pro tip Start by checking everything on the planning scene in RViz. When planning fails, the reason is almost always visible there: a missing object, a start state already in collision, or a goal pose just outside the workspace.

Install MoveIt 2 and the Panda configuration, then launch demo.launch.py from moveit_resources_panda_moveit_config. In the MotionPlanning panel, plan and execute to the ready named pose, then to a random valid goal. Run add_table.py and confirm a box appears in RViz. Plan a goal that would pass through it and observe the planner detour or fail. Use the panel’s Scene Objects tab to add a second obstacle by hand. Plan again. Write a short script that calls /compute_cartesian_path with two waypoints 10 cm apart. Print the fraction. Success: a fraction of 1.0 for a reachable line and a lower value when you aim into the table.

Why did it plan through my box?Beginner You can see a box on the table through the camera, but the arm plans straight through the space. What is the most likely cause? Show solutionHide solution The box is not in the planning scene. MoveIt only avoids what it has been told about. Add a collision object for the box, or enable an occupancy map from the depth camera so the scene tracks it. Reading the fractionIntermediate A Cartesian path request returns fraction = 0.6. List two causes and what you would try for each. Show solutionHide solution (1) The path leaves the arm’s reachable workspace, or IK hits a joint limit or singularity. Try moving the object or the base, a different start configuration or a different orientation along the path. (2) A collision appears partway along the line. Check the scene in RViz, reduce the path’s length, or add an intermediate waypoint that detours. Do not execute a trajectory with a low fraction as if it were complete. Holding a cupAdvanced After closing the gripper on a cup, your arm plans a motion that sweeps the cup into a shelf. What step did you forget, and what must you configure with it? Show solutionHide solution Attach the cup to the hand link as an attached collision object, so MoveIt treats it as part of the robot and checks it for collisions. List the finger and hand links as touch links so the gripper holding the cup is not considered a collision. Remove the attachment when you place it down.

It does not drive motors. move_group ties together the robot model, planning scene, planning pipeline, IK and execution. Plans are only as safe as the planning scene. Add collision objects or an occupancy map, and attach held objects. Cartesian paths give straight-line hand motion and return a fraction. Always check it. Pick the interface by need: MoveItPy for Python scripts, the C++ interface for the full feature set, or raw ROS actions and services for anything else.

Intermediate45 minBefore this:ROS 2 nodes, topics and services · ROS 2 actions and launch files · Gazebo basics · SLAM and localization Your delivery robot has a map of the building and knows where it is. Someone taps "go to room 214". Between that tap and the robot rolling down the corridor, a lot has to happen: plan a route, follow it while a person steps into the way, slow down near walls, and recover if it gets stuck. Nav2 is the open-source ROS 2 stack that does all of that, and you rarely have to write any of it yourself. You will be able to Name the main Nav2 servers and what each one does. Explain how costmaps represent obstacles and how inflation shapes the robot’s paths. Choose between common planner and controller plugins for a given robot. Launch Nav2 with a simulated robot and send goals from a Python script with the simple commander API.

Nav2 is not one program. It is a set of cooperating ROS 2 nodes, most of them lifecycle nodes (nodes with managed start-up states) that a manager brings up in the right order. The core nodes are: Node Job planner_server Computes a global path from the robot to the goal controller_server Follows that path locally, publishing velocity commands smoother_server Smooths a path after planning behavior_server Recovery actions such as spin, back up and wait bt_navigator Runs the behavior tree that decides which of the above to call, and when map_server and amcl Provide a saved map and localize the robot on it lifecycle_manager Starts and stops the lifecycle nodes in order The robot itself must provide a few things: a transform tree with map, odom and base_link frames, an odometry source, and a sensor that sees obstacles (a 2D lidar or depth camera). If you have done the SLAM and tf2 lessons, you already know where these come from.

Planners do not look at raw sensor data. They look at a costmap, a 2D grid where each cell holds a cost from 0 (free) up to 254 (lethal, an obstacle). Cell value 255 means unknown. Nav2 keeps two: The global costmap covers the whole map and is used for long-range planning. The local costmap is a small window that moves with the robot and is used by the controller to dodge things the map did not know about. Each costmap is built from stacked layers: Static layer: the saved map. Obstacle or voxel layer: live sensor readings (lidar hits, depth points). Inflation layer: spreads a decaying cost around every obstacle. Inflation is the clever part. It reuses the configuration-space idea from the previous lesson: a cell within the robot’s radius of an obstacle is marked as "inscribed", so the robot’s centre can never enter it. Cells farther out get a cost that falls off with distance, so the planner prefers staying in the middle of corridors without being forbidden from going near walls. nav2_params.yaml (excerpt) local_costmap: local_costmap: ros__parameters: update_frequency: 5.0 rolling_window: true width: 3 height: 3 resolution: 0.05 robot_radius: 0.22 plugins: ["voxel_layer", "inflation_layer"] inflation_layer: plugin: "nav2_costmap_2d::InflationLayer" inflation_radius: 0.7 cost_scaling_factor: 3.0 Costmaps turn the world into numbers a planner can compare Everything Nav2 plans or avoids goes through the costmap. If the robot clips corners, drives too close to walls or refuses to enter a doorway, look at robot_radius (or the footprint), inflation_radius and cost_scaling_factor first. Most "navigation bugs" are costmap settings.
documents.s: Costmaps: how Nav2 sees the world

documents.t: Nav2 is plugin-based. Planners, controllers, costmap layers and behaviors are all plugins named in a YAML file, so you can swap algorithms without changing code. Planners (global, run on demand): NavFn is a classic Dijkstra or A* planner on the costmap. Simple and fast, good for round robots that can turn on the spot. Smac Planner is a family: 2D (grid A*), Hybrid-A* (respects a car-like turning radius) and State Lattice (uses a library of feasible motions). Choose Hybrid-A* or Lattice for robots that cannot rotate in place. Theta* produces any-angle paths with fewer jagged turns on open ground. Controllers (local, run at about 20 Hz): DWB samples velocity commands and scores their short trajectories against critics (stay near the path, avoid obstacles, reach the goal). Regulated Pure Pursuit follows a lookahead point on the path and slows down near obstacles and sharp turns. Predictable and a common choice for differential-drive robots. MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) samples many random trajectories and picks a weighted blend. Flexible and handles tight spaces well, at higher compute cost. The split mirrors a human driver: the planner picks the route on the map, the controller steers along it and reacts to what is right in front.

The bt_navigator decides what to do next with a behavior tree (BT), a tree of small tasks that returns success, failure or running. Nav2 uses the BehaviorTree.CPP library and ships ready-made trees as XML files. Here is the idea as an outline of a simplified tree (each line is one XML element): simplified navigation tree (outline of the XML) RecoveryNode (retry up to 3 times) ├── PipelineSequence "NavigateWithReplanning" │ ├── RateController (1 Hz) │ │ └── ComputePathToPose -> writes {path} │ └── FollowPath -> reads {path} └── Sequence "Recovery" ├── ClearEntireCostmap (local) ├── Spin (1.57 rad) └── Wait (2 s) Read it like a recipe: plan once a second while following the path. If something fails, run the recovery sequence (clear the local costmap, spin, wait), then try again up to three times. Because the logic lives in XML, you can change how a robot behaves, say "never spin in a crowded hallway", without rebuilding C++. Note The tree above is a teaching simplification, with the XML attributes left out. The real default trees in the nav2_bt_navigator package are longer, with more recovery options. Open them to see how they work.

Install Nav2 and its bringup package on ROS 2 Jazzy: terminal sudo apt install ros-jazzy-navigation2 ros-jazzy-nav2-bringup The Nav2 bringup package includes a launch file that starts Gazebo with a TurtleBot 3 world, the Nav2 stack and RViz together. The exact environment variables and extra simulation packages have changed between releases, so follow the current "Getting Started" page at navigation.ros.org for Jazzy, then launch: terminal export TURTLEBOT3_MODEL=waffle ros2 launch nav2_bringup tb3_simulation_launch.py headless:=False In RViz, use 2D Pose Estimate to tell the robot where it starts (this seeds localization), wait for the costmaps to appear, then use Nav2 Goal to click a destination. Watch the global path (the planner’s idea) and the local path (what the controller is doing).
documents.s: Running Nav2 with a simulated robot

documents.t: Clicking in RViz is fine for a demo. Real applications send goals from code. Nav2 exposes a NavigateToPose action, and the nav2_simple_commander package wraps it in a friendly Python class, BasicNavigator. terminal sudo apt install ros-jazzy-nav2-simple-commander go_to_pose.py import math import rclpy from geometry_msgs.msg import PoseStamped from nav2_simple_commander.robot_navigator import BasicNavigator, TaskResult def make_pose(navigator, x, y, yaw): pose = PoseStamped() pose.header.frame_id = "map" pose.header.stamp = navigator.get_clock().now().to_msg() pose.pose.position.x = x pose.pose.position.y = y pose.pose.orientation.z = math.sin(yaw / 2.0) pose.pose.orientation.w = math.cos(yaw / 2.0) return pose def main(): rclpy.init() navigator = BasicNavigator() navigator.setInitialPose(make_pose(navigator, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) navigator.waitUntilNav2Active() goal = make_pose(navigator, 1.5, 0.5, math.pi / 2) navigator.goToPose(goal) while not navigator.isTaskComplete(): feedback = navigator.getFeedback() if feedback: print(f"distance remaining: {feedback.distance_remaining:.2f} m") result = navigator.getResult() if result == TaskResult.SUCCEEDED: print("Arrived.") elif result == TaskResult.CANCELED: print("Goal was canceled.") else: print("Navigation failed.") navigator.lifecycleShutdown() rclpy.shutdown() if __name__ == "__main__": main() A few things worth noticing. Poses are stamped in the map frame, and orientation is a quaternion, so a heading angle ψ\psiψ becomes z=sin⁡(ψ/2)z = \sin(\psi/2)z=sin(ψ/2), w=cos⁡(ψ/2)w = \cos(\psi/2)w=cos(ψ/2). goToPose is non-blocking: it starts the action and returns, so you poll isTaskComplete() and can cancel with navigator.cancelTask(). The same class also offers followWaypoints for a list of poses and goThroughPoses for passing through poses along one route. Note that lifecycleShutdown() shuts the whole Nav2 stack down, so skip it if you want Nav2 to keep running after your script ends. Warning Choose goals in free space. A goal inside an inflated obstacle will be rejected or fail repeatedly, and it looks like Nav2 is broken when the real cause is the goal.

Install Nav2, the bringup package and the simple commander, then launch the TurtleBot 3 simulation as shown above. In RViz, set the initial pose, then send one goal with the Nav2 Goal tool. Confirm the robot arrives. Enable the Global Costmap and Local Costmap displays in RViz and identify the inflated area around the walls. Run go_to_pose.py in a second terminal (with your ROS 2 environment sourced). Adjust the coordinates to a free point in your map. Success: it prints decreasing distances and then "Arrived." Copy the default parameters, increase inflation_radius, and relaunch with your params. Describe how the robot’s paths change.

Fix the doorwayBeginner The robot refuses to drive through a 0.8 m door. Its radius is 0.30 m and the inflation radius is 0.9 m. What do you change and why? Show solutionHide solution With a 0.9 m inflation radius, the cost zone from each side of the door overlaps in the middle and the whole doorway is expensive. Reduce inflation_radius (for example to about 0.5 m) or raise cost_scaling_factor so costs decay faster. The robot can physically fit (0.6 m diameter in 0.8 m), but the planner thinks the door is too costly. Pick the pluginsIntermediate You are building a car-like robot with a minimum turning radius of 1 m. Which planner and which controller families would you try first, and why? Show solutionHide solution A planner that respects turning radius: Smac Hybrid-A* or the State Lattice planner. NavFn and 2D planners would produce paths with sharp turns the robot cannot follow. For the controller, Regulated Pure Pursuit or MPPI, since both can work with car-like motion, while DWB assumes a velocity-sampling model that suits differential drive better. Patrol scriptIntermediate Use BasicNavigator to make the robot visit three waypoints in order and print the result. Which method do you use? Show solutionHide solution Build a list of three PoseStamped messages and call navigator.followWaypoints(waypoints). Then poll isTaskComplete() as before and check getResult(). Use goThroughPoses instead if you want a single smooth route through the poses rather than stopping at each one.

1What does the inflation layer of a costmap do? AMakes the map largerBAdds costs around obstacles so paths keep a safe distanceCStores the saved mapDSmooths the path 2Which Nav2 node runs the behavior tree? Aplanner_serverBcontroller_serverCbt_navigatorDmap_server 3Which of these is a local controller plugin? ANavFnBSmac PlannerCRegulated Pure PursuitDAMCL 4What does navigator.goToPose(goal) do? ABlocks until the robot arrivesBStarts a NavigateToPose action and returns, so you poll isTaskComplete()CTeleports the robotDOnly works in simulation 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Nav2 is a set of lifecycle nodes: planner, controller, smoother, behavior server and a behavior-tree navigator. Costmaps (global and local, built from layers) are how Nav2 sees the world. Inflation settings shape the paths. Planners and controllers are plugins. Pick them to match your robot’s motion model. Behavior trees express "plan, follow, recover" logic in XML you can edit without recompiling. BasicNavigator lets you set the initial pose, send goals and waypoints, and read results from Python.

The Nav2 documentation at navigation.ros.org, especially Getting Started, Configuration Guide and Behavior Trees. The nav2_simple_commander examples in the Nav2 GitHub repository. Macenski et al., "The Marathon 2: A Navigation System" (arxiv.org/abs/2003.00368), the paper behind Nav2’s design. BehaviorTree.CPP documentation at behaviortree.dev. Intermediate40 minBefore this:Python basics · Forward and inverse kinematics · Frames and transforms A warehouse robot has to cross a floor full of shelves. A robot arm has to reach into a bin without clipping its edge. In both cases someone has to answer the same question: out of the infinite ways to move, which one gets there without hitting anything? That is motion planning, and almost every robot you will build relies on it. You will be able to Describe a robot's configuration space and explain why obstacles become regions in it. Implement breadth-first search, Dijkstra and A* on a grid and explain how they differ. Explain how RRT and RRT* explore high-dimensional spaces and what "asymptotically optimal" means. Turn a jagged path into a smooth trajectory with timing, using shortcutting and a velocity profile.

A robot is not a point. A two-link arm is a long shape that sweeps through the room. Checking "does the arm hit the box?" for every candidate motion is awkward. The trick is to change the question so the robot becomes a single point. Configuration spaceThe set of all possible poses of the robot, described by one number per degree of freedom (often written C-space, with points called qqq) does exactly that. A planar two-link arm has two joint angles, so its C-space is a 2D plane with axes θ1\theta_1θ1​ and θ2\theta_2θ2​. Every point in that plane is one full arm pose. A mobile robot driving on a floor has a C-space of (x,y,θ)(x, y, \theta)(x,y,θ). Now obstacles transform too. A configuration is in the obstacle region CobsC_{obs}Cobs​ if the robot, placed in that pose, overlaps anything in the world. Everything else is free space CfreeC_{free}Cfree​. Planning becomes: find a continuous curve q(t)q(t)q(t) from qstartq_{start}qstart​ to qgoalq_{goal}qgoal​ that stays inside CfreeC_{free}Cfree​. Plan for a point, not a body Configuration space folds the robot's shape into the obstacles. The robot becomes a single point and the world becomes a set of forbidden regions. The cost is dimension: a 7-joint arm lives in a 7D space, which you cannot draw or enumerate. Choosing an algorithm is mostly about how well it copes as dimension grows. For a small mobile robot you can often cheat: inflate every obstacle by the robot's radius and treat the robot as a point on a 2D map. That is what costmaps do in Nav2, which you meet in the next lesson.

The simplest planner chops the free space into a grid. Each cell is a node, and edges connect neighbouring cells. Planning is now a graph-search problem, and three classic algorithms solve it with the same skeleton: keep a frontier of cells to explore, pull one out, add its neighbours, repeat. Breadth-first search (BFS) pulls cells in the order they were discovered (a queue). It finds the path with the fewest steps, but treats every step as equal cost. Dijkstra's algorithm pulls the cell with the lowest cost-so-far g(n)g(n)g(n) (a priority queue). It finds the cheapest path when moves have different costs, for example a step through a risky area costs more. A* (pronounced "A-star") also uses a heuristic h(n)h(n)h(n), an optimistic guess of the remaining cost. It pulls the cell with the lowest f(n)=g(n)+h(n)f(n) = g(n) + h(n)f(n)=g(n)+h(n) If hhh never overestimates the true remaining cost (it is admissible), A* still returns an optimal path, but it usually explores far fewer cells than Dijkstra because it leans towards the goal. On a 4-connected grid, Manhattan distance is a good admissible heuristic. Here is a complete, runnable implementation. Setting the heuristic to zero turns A* into Dijkstra, which makes the comparison honest. astar_grid.py import heapq MAP = [ "S...#.....", ".##.#.###.", ".#......#.", ".#.####.#.", "...#.....G", ] def parse(rows): walls, start, goal = set(), None, None for r, row in enumerate(rows): for c, ch in enumerate(row): if ch == "#": walls.add((r, c)) elif ch == "S": start = (r, c) elif ch == "G": goal = (r, c) return walls, start, goal, len(rows), len(rows[0]) def manhattan(a, b): return abs(a[0] - b[0]) + abs(a[1] - b[1]) def search(rows, use_heuristic=True): """Dijkstra when use_heuristic is False, A* when True. Returns (path, expanded).""" walls, start, goal, h, w = parse(rows) frontier = [(0, start)] # (priority, cell) cost = {start: 0} # best known cost-to-come g(n) parent = {start: None} expanded = 0 while frontier: _, cell = heapq.heappop(frontier) expanded += 1 if cell == goal: path = [] while cell is not None: path.append(cell) cell = parent[cell] return path[::-1], expanded r, c = cell for nxt in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)): nr, nc = nxt if not (0 <= nr < h and 0 <= nc < w) or nxt in walls: continue new_cost = cost[cell] + 1 if nxt not in cost or new_cost < cost[nxt]: cost[nxt] = new_cost parent[nxt] = cell priority = new_cost + (manhattan(nxt, goal) if use_heuristic else 0) heapq.heappush(frontier, (priority, nxt)) return None, expanded if __name__ == "__main__": for name, flag in (("Dijkstra", False), ("A*", True)): path, n = search(MAP, flag) print(f"{name:9s} path length {len(path) - 1}, cells expanded {n}") path, _ = search(MAP) canvas = [list(row) for row in MAP] for r, c in path[1:-1]: canvas[r][c] = "*" print("\n".join("".join(row) for row in canvas)) Run it and you should see both algorithms report a path of length 13, with A* expanding 20 cells to Dijkstra's 30. Same answer, less work. On a big open map the gap is dramatic. Note Grid search gives paths made of grid moves, which look blocky and ignore the robot's real motion. Planners such as Hybrid A* and lattice planners fix this by searching over motions the robot can actually perform. Nav2 ships planners of both kinds.

A grid with kkk cells per axis in ddd dimensions has kdk^dkd cells. A 7-joint arm with 100 cells per joint would need 101410^{14}1014 cells. Grid search is dead on arrival. Sampling-based planners give up on covering the space. Instead they sample random configurations, test whether they are collision-free, and connect good ones. Collision checking is the only thing they need from the world, which is why they work with any obstacle shape.

A Rapidly-exploring Random TreeRapidly-exploring Random Tree: grows a tree from the start by repeatedly stepping towards random samples (RRT) grows a tree outward from the start: Sample a random configuration qrandq_{rand}qrand​ (now and then, sample the goal itself: a goal bias). Find the tree node qnearq_{near}qnear​ closest to it. Take a small step from qnearq_{near}qnear​ towards qrandq_{rand}qrand​ to get qnewq_{new}qnew​. If the segment is collision-free, add qnewq_{new}qnew​ to the tree. Stop when a node is close enough to the goal and the last segment is free. The random samples pull the tree towards big unexplored regions, so it spreads quickly. RRT is probabilistically complete: if a path exists, the chance of finding it approaches 1 as you add samples. It is not optimal, though. RRT paths wander. rrt_2d.py import math import random random.seed(3) OBSTACLES = [(5.0, 5.0, 1.5), (3.0, 7.5, 1.0), (7.5, 2.5, 1.2)] # (x, y, radius) START, GOAL = (1.0, 1.0), (9.0, 9.0) STEP, GOAL_BIAS, MAX_ITERS = 0.5, 0.05, 5000 def collision_free(p, q, samples=10): for i in range(samples + 1): t = i / samples x = p[0] + t * (q[0] - p[0]) y = p[1] + t * (q[1] - p[1]) if any(math.hypot(x - ox, y - oy) <= r for ox, oy, r in OBSTACLES): return False return True def rrt(): nodes, parent = [START], {0: None} for _ in range(MAX_ITERS): target = GOAL if random.random() < GOAL_BIAS else (random.uniform(0, 10), random.uniform(0, 10)) i = min(range(len(nodes)), key=lambda k: math.dist(nodes[k], target)) near = nodes[i] d = math.dist(near, target) if d == 0: continue s = min(STEP, d) / d new = (near[0] + s * (target[0] - near[0]), near[1] + s * (target[1] - near[1])) if not collision_free(near, new): continue nodes.append(new) parent[len(nodes) - 1] = i if math.dist(new, GOAL) < STEP and collision_free(new, GOAL): nodes.append(GOAL) parent[len(nodes) - 1] = len(nodes) - 2 path, k = [], len(nodes) - 1 while k is not None: path.append(nodes[k]) k = parent[k] return path[::-1], len(nodes) return None, len(nodes) def length(path): return sum(math.dist(a, b) for a, b in zip(path, path[1:])) if __name__ == "__main__": path, n = rrt() print(f"tree nodes: {n}") print(f"path: {len(path)} waypoints, length {length(path):.2f}")

RRT* adds two small steps that change the guarantee. When a new node is added, it looks at nearby nodes and picks the parent that gives the lowest cost-from-start (choose parent). Then it checks whether routing existing neighbours through the new node would make them cheaper, and if so rewires them (rewire). The result is asymptotically optimal: as the number of samples grows, the path cost converges to the best possible one. The price is more computation per sample. In practice RRT is fine when you need any feasible path fast, and RRT* (or variants such as Informed RRT*) when path quality matters and you have time. For arms, MoveIt's default OMPL library offers both families, plus bidirectional versions (RRT-Connect), which are often the fastest.

A path is only geometry: a list of configurations. A robot needs a trajectory: positions that change with time, within velocity and acceleration limits. Two steps get you there. Shortcutting. Sampling planners leave kinks. Pick two random points on the path and, if the straight segment between them is collision-free, replace everything in between. Repeat a few hundred times. Add this to the end of the previous script: shortcut.py def shortcut(path, tries=200): path = list(path) for _ in range(tries): if len(path) < 3: break i, j = sorted(random.sample(range(len(path)), 2)) if j - i > 1 and collision_free(path[i], path[j]): path = path[: i + 1] + path[j:] return path Time parameterization. Now decide how fast to move along the path. The simplest profile is a trapezoid: accelerate at amaxa_{max}amax​ up to vmaxv_{max}vmax​, cruise, then decelerate. If the path is short, you never reach vmaxv_{max}vmax​ and the profile is a triangle. trapezoid.py def trapezoid(distance, v_max, a_max): """Rest-to-rest move along a path of the given length. Returns (t_accel, t_cruise, t_total).""" t_acc = v_max / a_max d_acc = 0.5 * a_max * t_acc ** 2 if 2 * d_acc > distance: # never reaches v_max: triangular profile t_acc = (distance / a_max) ** 0.5 return t_acc, 0.0, 2 * t_acc t_cruise = (distance - 2 * d_acc) / v_max return t_acc, t_cruise, 2 * t_acc + t_cruise print(trapezoid(2.0, 1.0, 0.5)) # (2.0, 0.0, 4.0) print(trapezoid(0.2, 1.0, 0.5)) # triangular: never reaches v_max Real systems do this per joint, along a multi-waypoint path, with limits on every joint at once. MoveIt 2 ships time-parameterization routines for that (including time-optimal trajectory generation), and libraries such as Ruckig generate jerk-limited motions, which are gentler on hardware. Jerk, the rate of change of acceleration, is what makes a motion feel jolting. Pro tip When a plan "works in the planner but shakes the real robot", look at time parameterization before you blame the planner. Overly aggressive limits and sharp corners in the path are the usual causes.

Save the A* script as astar_grid.py and run it. Confirm the path length is 13 and that A* expands fewer cells than Dijkstra. Change the map: add walls so the only route is long and winding. Re-run and compare the expanded-cell counts again. Replace manhattan with a heuristic that returns 10 * manhattan(a, b). It is no longer admissible. Does the path stay optimal? Does it expand fewer cells? Save the RRT script as rrt_2d.py. Run it with three different seeds and record the tree size and path length each time. Add the shortcut function and print the path length before and after. Success looks like a path with a handful of waypoints that is clearly shorter.

Admissible or not?Beginner A robot moves on an 8-connected grid (diagonal moves allowed, each diagonal costs 1.41 and each straight move 1). Is Manhattan distance an admissible heuristic? Suggest a better one. Show solutionHide solution No. Manhattan distance can overestimate: going diagonally by one cell costs 1.41, but Manhattan distance says 2. An overestimate can make A* return a non-optimal path. Use octile distance (move diagonally as far as possible, then straight) or plain Euclidean distance, both of which never overestimate. Why not just use a grid for the arm?Intermediate Estimate how many grid cells you need for a 6-joint arm if each joint is divided into 50 values. Explain what a sampling-based planner does differently. Show solutionHide solution 506≈1.6×101050^6 \approx 1.6 \times 10^{10}506≈1.6×1010 cells, far too many to store or search comfortably. A sampling-based planner never builds the whole grid. It only generates configurations it chooses to test, so its cost depends on how hard the obstacles make the problem, not on the volume of the space. Make RRT optimal-ishAdvanced Sketch what you would change in rrt_2d.py to get RRT*. Name the two operations and the extra data you need to store per node. Show solutionHide solution Store the cost-from-start for every node. When adding a new node, (1) examine all nodes within a radius and choose as parent the one that gives the lowest total cost through a collision-free edge, then (2) for each of those neighbours, check whether going through the new node is cheaper, and if so make the new node its parent and update the costs of its descendants. The search radius normally shrinks slowly as the tree grows.

1What does configuration space let a planner do? AIgnore obstacles entirelyBTreat the robot as a single point and obstacles as forbidden regionsCReplace collision checking with a lookup tableDPlan only in 2D 2Which statement about A* is correct? AIt always explores more cells than DijkstraBIt uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n) and stays optimal if h never overestimatesCIt requires a random samplerDIt only works on 3D maps 3What makes RRT* different from RRT? AIt samples the goal more oftenBIt chooses the best parent and rewires neighbours, so its paths converge to optimalCIt does not need collision checkingDIt plans in joint space only 4Why do we time-parameterize a path? ATo make it shorterBTo add collision checksCTo decide how fast to move along it within velocity and acceleration limitsDTo convert it to a grid 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Configuration space turns "a body moving among obstacles" into "a point moving among forbidden regions", with one dimension per degree of freedom. BFS, Dijkstra and A* are one algorithm with different priorities. A* adds an admissible heuristic to explore less. Grids explode in high dimensions. Sampling-based planners (RRT, RRT*) avoid that by only collision-checking what they sample. RRT is probabilistically complete. RRT* is also asymptotically optimal, at higher cost. A path is geometry. Shortcutting and time parameterization turn it into a smooth trajectory the robot can follow.

Steven LaValle, Planning Algorithms (free online book, lavalle.pl/planning) for the full theory. The OMPL project (ompl.kavrakilab.org), the library behind MoveIt's default planners. Karaman and Frazzoli, "Sampling-based algorithms for optimal motion planning" (arxiv.org/abs/1105.1186), the paper that introduced RRT*. The Nav2 documentation (navigation.ros.org) for planners you can use on a real mobile robot. Next: Navigation with Nav2

A robot without perception is a very expensive remote-control car. Perception is the whole pipeline that turns raw numbers from sensors, such as pixel intensities, laser ranges and gyro rates, into things a robot can act on: "that is a cup, 40 centimetres ahead", "I am in the kitchen, facing the door". It has two halves. Seeing means extracting meaning from a single moment of sensor data. Estimating means combining many noisy moments into one belief about the world and about the robot itself. This module walks through both halves in the order you will meet them in practice. You will start with the camera model and OpenCV, move to depth cameras, point clouds and lidar, then use pretrained deep networks for detection and segmentation. After that comes the mathematical heart of robotics, Bayesian state estimation and the Kalman filter, and finally SLAM, where a robot builds a map and locates itself in it at the same time.

Project 3D points into an image with the pinhole model and calibrate a real camera. Process images and point clouds with OpenCV and Open3D. Run pretrained detection and segmentation models and read their outputs correctly. Implement a Kalman filter in NumPy and configure robot_localization for a real robot. Build a map with slam_toolbox and localize in it with AMCL.

Intermediate40 minBefore this:Python and NumPy · Frames and rigid transforms · Matrix multiplication Your robot sees an orange cone in the camera image at pixel (470, 240). Is the cone 1 metre away or 10? Is it to the left or right of the robot’s centre line? A pixel on its own tells you almost nothing. To turn pixels into directions, and directions into positions, you need a model of how the camera turns the 3D world into a flat picture. This lesson gives you that model, shows you how to measure it for a real camera, and then teaches the first image-processing tools every robot vision pipeline uses. You will be able to Project 3D points into pixels, and pixels back into rays, using the pinhole model. Distinguish intrinsic parameters from extrinsic parameters and say what each one means. Calibrate a real camera with a chessboard and read the result. Use OpenCV to convert colour spaces, filter noise, find edges and match features.

Imagine a dark box with a tiny hole in one side. Light from each point in the scene travels in a straight line through the hole and lands on the back wall, making an upside-down picture. A real camera has a lens instead of a hole, but the maths is the same, and it is called the pinhole modelA simplified camera model in which every 3D point is projected onto the image plane along a straight line through a single point, the optical centre. Place a coordinate frame at the hole. The optical frame convention used by ROS and OpenCV is: xxx to the right in the image, yyy downward, zzz straight ahead out of the lens. A 3D point (X,Y,Z)(X, Y, Z)(X,Y,Z) in this frame lands on the image at pixel (u,v)(u, v)(u,v) given by similar triangles: u=fxXZ+cx,v=fyYZ+cy.u = f_x \frac{X}{Z} + c_x, \qquad v = f_y \frac{Y}{Z} + c_y .u=fx​ZX​+cx​,v=fy​ZY​+cy​. Here fxf_xfx​ and fyf_yfy​ are the focal lengths measured in pixels, and (cx,cy)(c_x, c_y)(cx​,cy​) is the principal point, roughly the image centre. Notice the division by ZZZ: far-away things get smaller. That one division is the reason a single image cannot tell you depth. Written with matrices, using homogeneous coordinates: s[uv1]=[fx0cx0fycy001]⏟K[XYZ],s=Z.s \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} f_x & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{K} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix}, \qquad s = Z .s​uv1​​=K​fx​00​0fy​0​cx​cy​1​​​​​XYZ​​,s=Z. The matrix KKK holds the intrinsic parametersCamera parameters that describe the internal geometry: focal lengths, principal point, and lens distortion. They belong to the camera and its lens, and do not change when the robot moves. A pixel is a ray, not a point Given pixel (u,v)(u, v)(u,v) you can compute the direction of the ray it came from, K−1[u,v,1]TK^{-1}[u, v, 1]^TK−1[u,v,1]T. But every point along that ray lands on the same pixel. To pin down a 3D point you need one more piece of information: depth from a depth camera, a second camera (stereo), motion, or a known object size.

The point PwP_wPw​ may be known in the world or robot frame rather than the camera frame. The extrinsic parametersCamera parameters describing its pose in the world: a rotation R and a translation t, a rotation RRR and translation ttt, convert between them: Pc=RPw+tP_c = R P_w + tPc​=RPw​+t. This is exactly the rigid transform from Frames and rigid transforms. In ROS the extrinsics are TF transforms, for example base_link to camera_optical_frame. The full projection is therefore s p~=K [R∣t] P~ws\,\tilde{p} = K\,[R \mid t]\,\tilde{P}_wsp~​=K[R∣t]P~w​.

Real lenses bend straight lines. The usual correction models radial distortion with coefficients k1,k2,k3k_1, k_2, k_3k1​,k2​,k3​, where a normalised point (x,y)=(X/Z,Y/Z)(x, y) = (X/Z, Y/Z)(x,y)=(X/Z,Y/Z) is moved outward or inward by xd=x (1+k1r2+k2r4+k3r6),r2=x2+y2,x_d = x\,(1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4 + k_3 r^6), \quad r^2 = x^2 + y^2,xd​=x(1+k1​r2+k2​r4+k3​r6),r2=x2+y2, and the same for yyy, plus a small tangential term p1,p2p_1, p_2p1​,p2​. Wide-angle lenses have strong distortion; a k1k_1k1​ of a few tenths is common. OpenCV and ROS store all of these in a distortion vector DDD.

pinhole.py import numpy as np fx = fy = 600.0 cx, cy = 320.0, 240.0 K = np.array([[fx, 0.0, cx], [0.0, fy, cy], [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]]) def project(points_cam: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """Project Nx3 points in the camera frame (x right, y down, z forward) to Nx2 pixels.""" uvw = (K @ points_cam.T).T return uvw[:, :2] / uvw[:, 2:3] def unproject(pixels: np.ndarray, depth: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """Turn Nx2 pixels plus Nx depths (metres along z) into Nx3 camera-frame points.""" ones = np.ones((len(pixels), 1)) rays = (np.linalg.inv(K) @ np.hstack([pixels, ones]).T).T return rays * depth[:, None] def world_to_camera(points_world, R, t): """Extrinsics: a point in the world frame to the camera frame, p_c = R p_w + t.""" return (R @ points_world.T).T + t # A point 2 m ahead and 0.5 m to the right of the camera: P = np.array([[0.5, 0.0, 2.0]]) uv = project(P) print("pixel:", uv) # [[470. 240.]] print("back :", unproject(uv, np.array([2.0]))) # The same point seen through extrinsics: the world origin is 1 m to the camera's right R = np.eye(3) t = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) P_world = np.array([[-0.5, 0.0, 2.0]]) print("via extrinsics:", project(world_to_camera(P_world, R, t))) Run it. The first answer is pixel (470, 240), exactly the cone from the hook: 0.5 m to the right at 2 m range is 600⋅0.5/2=150600 \cdot 0.5 / 2 = 150600⋅0.5/2=150 pixels right of centre. unproject recovers the point only because we supplied the depth, which is the lesson of the key idea above. The same functions work for a whole point cloud at once because they are vectorised.

Datasheets give you the focal length in millimetres, not pixels, and say nothing about distortion. Camera calibrationEstimating a camera’s intrinsic parameters and distortion by observing a known pattern from many viewpoints measures them. The standard recipe: print a chessboard of known square size, take 15 to 30 pictures of it from many angles and distances, detect the inner corners in each, and let an optimiser find the KKK and DDD that make the known 3D corner grid project onto the detected pixels with the smallest error. calibrate.py import glob import cv2 import numpy as np COLS, ROWS = 8, 6 # inner corners per row and column (a 9x7-square board) SQUARE = 0.025 # square size in metres grid = np.zeros((ROWS * COLS, 3), np.float32) grid[:, :2] = np.mgrid[0:COLS, 0:ROWS].T.reshape(-1, 2) * SQUARE object_points, image_points = [], [] size = None for path in sorted(glob.glob("calib/*.png")): gray = cv2.imread(path, cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE) size = gray.shape[::-1] # (width, height) found, corners = cv2.findChessboardCorners(gray, (COLS, ROWS)) if not found: print("no board in", path) continue criteria = (cv2.TERM_CRITERIA_EPS + cv2.TERM_CRITERIA_MAX_ITER, 30, 0.001) corners = cv2.cornerSubPix(gray, corners, (11, 11), (-1, -1), criteria) object_points.append(grid) image_points.append(corners) rms, K, D, rvecs, tvecs = cv2.calibrateCamera(object_points, image_points, size, None, None) print("reprojection error (px):", round(rms, 3)) print("K =\n", K) print("D =", D.ravel()) Put your photos in a calib/ folder and run it. A reprojection error below about 0.5 pixels is good; above 1 pixel means something is wrong (blurry images, a board that is not flat, or too few viewpoints). Vary the board’s tilt and position, and cover the corners of the image where distortion is strongest. If your camera is already a ROS 2 camera, the camera_calibration package does the same through a GUI: terminal ros2 run camera_calibration cameracalibrator --size 8x6 --square 0.025 \ --ros-args -r image:=/camera/image_raw -r camera:=/camera The result becomes a CameraInfo message, whose k field is your KKK and d your DDD. In simulation, CameraInfo comes straight from the sensor definition (the field of view and resolution), with zero distortion.

OpenCVOpen Source Computer Vision Library: the standard toolkit for classical image processing in Python and C++ (pip install opencv-python) represents an image as a NumPy array of shape (height, width, channels). Two traps catch every beginner. First, OpenCV orders colour channels BGR, not RGB. Second, the origin is the top-left corner, with yyy increasing downward, matching the camera frame above. This script makes its own test image, so it runs with no files: cv_basics.py import cv2 import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(0) # 1. A test picture: grey floor, a blue box, a red ball (BGR order!) img = np.full((240, 320, 3), 200, np.uint8) cv2.rectangle(img, (40, 60), (140, 160), (255, 0, 0), -1) cv2.circle(img, (220, 120), 40, (0, 0, 255), -1) noisy = np.clip(img.astype(np.int16) + rng.normal(0, 15, img.shape), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8) # 2. Filtering: a Gaussian blur averages away noise blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(noisy, (5, 5), 0) # 3. Colour spaces: in HSV, "find red things" is a range test (red wraps around hue 0) hsv = cv2.cvtColor(blur, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV) mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, (0, 120, 70), (10, 255, 255)) | cv2.inRange(hsv, (170, 120, 70), (180, 255, 255)) mask = cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, np.ones((5, 5), np.uint8)) contours, _ = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE) for c in contours: if cv2.contourArea(c) < 200: continue m = cv2.moments(c) print("red blob centre: (%.0f, %.0f), area %.0f px" % (m["m10"] / m["m00"], m["m01"] / m["m00"], cv2.contourArea(c))) # 4. Edges gray = cv2.cvtColor(blur, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY) edges = cv2.Canny(gray, 50, 150) print("edge pixels:", int(np.count_nonzero(edges))) # 5. Features: ORB keypoints matched between two views of a textured scene scene = np.full((300, 400), 128, np.uint8) for _ in range(120): x, y = rng.integers(10, 390), rng.integers(10, 290) cv2.circle(scene, (int(x), int(y)), int(rng.integers(3, 12)), int(rng.integers(0, 255)), -1) shift = np.float32([[1, 0, 25], [0, 1, 10]]) moved = cv2.warpAffine(scene, shift, (400, 300)) orb = cv2.ORB_create(nfeatures=500) k1, d1 = orb.detectAndCompute(scene, None) k2, d2 = orb.detectAndCompute(moved, None) matches = cv2.BFMatcher(cv2.NORM_HAMMING, crossCheck=True).match(d1, d2) dx = np.median([k2[m.trainIdx].pt[0] - k1[m.queryIdx].pt[0] for m in matches]) dy = np.median([k2[m.trainIdx].pt[1] - k1[m.queryIdx].pt[1] for m in matches]) print(f"{len(matches)} matches, median shift = ({dx:.0f}, {dy:.0f}) px (true: 25, 10)") cv2.imwrite("edges.png", edges) cv2.imwrite("mask.png", mask) Open edges.png and mask.png to see what each step did. Here is what the tools are for: Colour spaces. RGB mixes colour and brightness together, so a red ball in shadow has very different RGB values. HSV separates hue (the colour), saturation and value (brightness), so thresholding on hue survives lighting changes. Filtering. A Gaussian blur replaces each pixel by a weighted average of its neighbours, removing noise but also softening edges. A median blur is better against salt-and-pepper noise. Always blur before taking edges. Edges. An edge is a place where brightness changes quickly. Canny finds the gradient, thins it to one-pixel lines, and keeps strong edges and the weak ones connected to them (two thresholds, here 50 and 150). Features. A featureA distinctive image location, such as a corner or blob, described by a vector so the same point can be recognised in another image is a point that looks distinctive enough to find again. ORB detects corners and describes each with a 256-bit string; matching compares strings by Hamming distance. Matched features between two images give you motion estimation, visual odometry and image-based SLAM. Reading ROS images in Python goes through cv_bridge: image_listener.py import cv2 import rclpy from cv_bridge import CvBridge from rclpy.node import Node from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data from sensor_msgs.msg import Image class Listener(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__("image_listener") self.bridge = CvBridge() self.create_subscription(Image, "/camera/image_raw", self.on_image, qos_profile_sensor_data) def on_image(self, msg: Image): frame = self.bridge.imgmsg_to_cv2(msg, "bgr8") # numpy array, BGR edges = cv2.Canny(cv2.GaussianBlur(frame, (5, 5), 0), 50, 150) self.get_logger().info(f"{frame.shape}, {int(edges.sum() / 255)} edge pixels") def main(): rclpy.init() rclpy.spin(Listener()) if __name__ == "__main__": main() Common mistake Using cv2.imshow inside a ROS callback often freezes or crashes on remote or headless machines. Publish the processed image on a topic and view it in RViz or rqt_image_view instead.

Run pinhole.py. Change fx to 300 and predict the new pixel before running. (Hint: the offset from centre halves.) Run cv_basics.py. Open the two PNGs. Increase the noise standard deviation to 40 and see which step breaks first. Print a chessboard (search for "OpenCV calibration pattern"), take about 20 photos with your phone or webcam from different angles, put them in calib/, and run calibrate.py. Record the reprojection error. Check your answer: does the cx,cyc_x, c_ycx​,cy​ you found land near half the image width and height, and is fxf_xfx​ close to fyf_yfy​? Both should be true for a normal camera. It worked if your reprojection error is below about 0.5 to 1.0 pixels and the principal point is near the image centre.

How far to the right?Beginner A camera has fx=500f_x = 500fx​=500 and cx=320c_x = 320cx​=320. A point at X=1.0X = 1.0X=1.0 m and Z=4.0Z = 4.0Z=4.0 m is visible. At which pixel column does it appear? Show solutionHide solution u=500⋅1.0/4.0+320=125+320=445u = 500 \cdot 1.0 / 4.0 + 320 = 125 + 320 = 445u=500⋅1.0/4.0+320=125+320=445. Find the cone’s positionIntermediate A depth camera with fx=fy=600f_x = f_y = 600fx​=fy​=600 and (cx,cy)=(320,240)(c_x, c_y) = (320, 240)(cx​,cy​)=(320,240) reports depth Z=3Z = 3Z=3 m at pixel (500,300)(500, 300)(500,300). What is the 3D point in the camera frame? Show solutionHide solution X=(500−320)⋅3/600=0.9X = (500 - 320) \cdot 3 / 600 = 0.9X=(500−320)⋅3/600=0.9 m, Y=(300−240)⋅3/600=0.3Y = (300 - 240) \cdot 3 / 600 = 0.3Y=(300−240)⋅3/600=0.3 m, Z=3Z = 3Z=3 m. So the point is (0.9, 0.3, 3.0): to the right, slightly below the optical axis (positive yyy is down), 3 m ahead. Why is my calibration bad?Intermediate You calibrate with 12 photos, all taken from the front with the board filling the centre of the image. The error is low, but undistorting real images leaves curved lines near the edges. Why, and what do you do? Show solutionHide solution The data never constrained distortion near the image edges, and the board was almost always parallel to the camera, which makes focal length and distance ambiguous. Retake 20 or more photos with the board tilted in different directions, at different distances, and covering the corners of the frame.

AThe camera’s position on the robotBFocal lengths, principal point and distortionCThe robot’s wheel radiusDThe image file format 2Why can a single pixel not give you a 3D position? AThe time to load the imageBThe pixel distance between detected corners and where the model projects themCThe distance between two camerasDThe error in the chessboard print size 0 of 4 answered Takeaways The pinhole model maps (X,Y,Z)(X, Y, Z)(X,Y,Z) to u=fxX/Z+cxu = f_x X / Z + c_xu=fx​X/Z+cx​ and v=fyY/Z+cyv = f_y Y / Z + c_yv=fy​Y/Z+cy​; the division by ZZZ discards depth. Intrinsics (KKK, distortion) belong to the camera; extrinsics (RRR, ttt) say where it is, and in ROS they are TF. A pixel is a ray; you need depth, stereo or motion to get a 3D point. Calibrate with a chessboard from many viewpoints and aim for a reprojection error well under one pixel. OpenCV uses BGR and a top-left origin; HSV thresholding, blur, Canny and ORB cover a large share of classical vision tasks. Do image work in callbacks that publish results, not in ones that open windows.

OpenCV documentation and tutorials: docs.opencv.org OpenCV camera calibration tutorial: docs.opencv.org/4.x/dc/dbb/tutorial_py_calibration.html ROS 2 camera_calibration and image_pipeline packages: docs.ros.org Zhang, "A Flexible New Technique for Camera Calibration": the paper behind chessboard calibration, widely available online.
