Intermediate40 minBefore this:Cameras and image processing · Python and NumPy · Basic idea of a neural network Colour thresholding found the red ball in the last lesson, but real robots must find mugs, people, doors and pallets, in every kind of light and from every angle. No hand-written rule covers that. This is where deep learning changed robotics: a neural network trained on millions of labelled images can look at a photo and say "a mug here, a person there", and today you can use such a network in ten lines of Python without training anything. You will be able to Explain in plain words what a convolutional neural network (CNN) computes, and why it suits images. Distinguish classification, detection, semantic segmentation and instance segmentation. Run a pretrained detector and a segmentation model with torchvision, and a YOLO-style detector with ultralytics. Measure detections with IoU, apply non-maximum suppression, and convert a detection plus depth into a 3D position.
documents.s: Deep learning for detection and segmentation

documents.t: An image is a grid of numbers. A convolutional neural networkConvolutional neural network: a network built from small learned filters slid across the image, so the same pattern detector is applied at every location processes it with filters: tiny grids (say 3 by 3) that slide across the image, computing a weighted sum at each position. You already know one filter: the Sobel kernel that finds vertical edges. In a CNN, the filter weights are learned from data rather than written by hand. conv_demo.py import numpy as np def conv2d(image, kernel): """Valid cross-correlation of a 2D image with a small kernel (what CNN layers compute).""" kh, kw = kernel.shape h, w = image.shape out = np.zeros((h - kh + 1, w - kw + 1)) for i in range(out.shape[0]): for j in range(out.shape[1]): out[i, j] = np.sum(image[i:i + kh, j:j + kw] * kernel) return out image = np.zeros((8, 8)) image[:, 4:] = 1.0 # dark left half, bright right half sobel_x = np.array([[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]], float) print(conv2d(image, sobel_x)[0]) # [0. 0. 4. 4. 0. 0.]: it fires at the edge Stack many layers and something remarkable happens. The first layers learn edges and colour blobs. Middle layers combine them into corners, textures and parts (a wheel, an eye). Late layers recognise whole objects. Between layers, pooling or strided convolutions shrink the image so that later filters "see" larger regions: the receptive fieldThe region of the input image that can influence one value inside the network grows with depth. Features are learned, not designed Classical vision (the last lesson) asks you to choose the features: edges, colour ranges, corners. A deep network learns the features that best solve the task from labelled examples. That is why it can handle variety that no hand-written rule can, and also why it can fail in surprising ways on images unlike its training data.

Classification: "this is a kitchen". Rarely enough for a robot. Detection: boxes with class labels and confidence scores. The workhorse for finding things to avoid or grasp. Semantic segmentation: every pixel gets a class (floor, wall, person), but two people merge into one blob. Good for "where can I drive?". Instance segmentation: a separate mask per object. Good for grasping, since the mask outlines the object.

Two-stage detectors (the R-CNN family such as Faster R-CNN, 2015) first propose regions that might hold objects, then classify and refine each one. Accurate, slower. One-stage detectors (the YOLO family, "You Only Look Once", and SSD) predict boxes and classes for all locations in a single pass. Fast enough for real time on a robot, and the usual first choice. Transformer-based detectors treat detection as set prediction and are strong but often heavier. Check the current documentation for the latest model names and speed-accuracy numbers; they change every few months.

A detector often fires several overlapping boxes on the same object. Two tools clean this up. IoUIntersection over union: the area where two boxes overlap divided by the area they cover together, from 0 (disjoint) to 1 (identical) measures how much two boxes overlap, and non-maximum suppression (NMS)Non-maximum suppression: keep the highest-scoring box and discard other boxes that overlap it strongly keeps the best box and drops its near-duplicates. IoU(A,B)=∣A∩B∣∣A∪B∣.\text{IoU}(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}.IoU(A,B)=∣A∪B∣∣A∩B∣​. iou_nms.py import numpy as np def iou(a, b): """Boxes are [x1, y1, x2, y2] in pixels.""" x1, y1 = max(a[0], b[0]), max(a[1], b[1]) x2, y2 = min(a[2], b[2]), min(a[3], b[3]) inter = max(0.0, x2 - x1) * max(0.0, y2 - y1) area = lambda r: (r[2] - r[0]) * (r[3] - r[1]) return inter / (area(a) + area(b) - inter) def nms(boxes, scores, iou_threshold=0.5): order = np.argsort(scores)[::-1] # best first keep = [] while len(order): i = order[0] keep.append(int(i)) order = np.array([j for j in order[1:] if iou(boxes[i], boxes[j]) < iou_threshold], dtype=int) return keep boxes = np.array([[10, 10, 110, 110], [12, 14, 112, 108], [200, 200, 260, 280]], float) scores = np.array([0.90, 0.80, 0.70]) print("IoU of first two:", round(iou(boxes[0], boxes[1]), 3)) # 0.904 print("kept:", nms(boxes, scores)) # [0, 2] IoU is also how detectors are scored. A prediction counts as correct if its IoU with a true box exceeds a threshold, and the standard metric mAP (mean average precision) summarises precision and recall over all classes. For a robot, also measure what matters in your task: how often a grasp target is missed, and how often it hallucinates an obstacle that is not there.

Training from scratch needs huge data. Instead you start from a model trained on a large dataset (COCO, with 80 everyday object classes) and use it directly or fine-tune it. Install the libraries with pip install torch torchvision. detect_torchvision.py import torch from torchvision.io import read_image, write_png from torchvision.models.detection import FasterRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights, fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn from torchvision.utils import draw_bounding_boxes weights = FasterRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights.DEFAULT model = fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn(weights=weights, box_score_thresh=0.6).eval() preprocess = weights.transforms() categories = weights.meta["categories"] image = read_image("street.jpg") # uint8 tensor, shape [3, H, W], RGB with torch.no_grad(): pred = model([preprocess(image)])[0] # a list of images in, a list of dicts out labels = [f"{categories[int(i)]} {float(s):.2f}" for i, s in zip(pred["labels"], pred["scores"])] for lab, box in zip(labels, pred["boxes"].tolist()): print(lab, [round(v) for v in box]) annotated = draw_bounding_boxes(image, pred["boxes"], labels, colors="red", width=3) write_png(annotated, "street_detected.png") Use any photo of a street or room as street.jpg. The first run downloads the weights. Things to notice: the model takes a list of images; weights.transforms() applies the exact preprocessing the model was trained with (skipping it is a classic source of bad results); and box_score_thresh hides low-confidence boxes. Runs on CPU, slowly; add .to("cuda") on the model and input tensors if you have a GPU.

For real-time work, a one-stage detector is the usual choice. The ultralytics package wraps the YOLO family with a very short interface (pip install ultralytics): detect_yolo.py from ultralytics import YOLO model = YOLO("yolo11n.pt") # small pretrained model, downloaded on first use results = model("street.jpg", conf=0.4) # run inference for box in results[0].boxes: cls_id = int(box.cls[0]) x1, y1, x2, y2 = box.xyxy[0].tolist() print(f"{model.names[cls_id]:<12} {float(box.conf[0]):.2f} " f"({x1:.0f}, {y1:.0f}) to ({x2:.0f}, {y2:.0f})") results[0].save(filename="street_yolo.jpg") # draws the boxes Model names, sizes and speeds change with releases, so check the ultralytics documentation for the current ones. The small "n" models run on modest hardware, and larger ones are more accurate. The same API gives you instance segmentation (use a -seg checkpoint) and, with model.train(data="mydata.yaml", epochs=50), fine-tuning on your own labelled images. Pro tip Fine-tuning a pretrained model on 200 to 500 images of your objects in your lighting usually beats a bigger generic model. Generating those images in simulation, as in the Isaac Sim lesson, is a good way to bootstrap, but always mix in real photos.

A segmentation network outputs, for every pixel, a score for each class. Take the highest per pixel and you have a label map. segment_torchvision.py import torch from torchvision.io import read_image from torchvision.models.segmentation import DeepLabV3_ResNet50_Weights, deeplabv3_resnet50 weights = DeepLabV3_ResNet50_Weights.DEFAULT model = deeplabv3_resnet50(weights=weights).eval() preprocess = weights.transforms() categories = weights.meta["categories"] image = read_image("street.jpg") batch = preprocess(image).unsqueeze(0) # [1, 3, H', W'] with torch.no_grad(): scores = model(batch)["out"][0] # [num_classes, H', W'] labels = scores.argmax(dim=0) # [H', W'] class id per pixel total = labels.numel() for class_id in labels.unique(): share = float((labels == class_id).sum()) / total print(f"{categories[int(class_id)]:<12} {share:5.1%}") This prints the fraction of the image covered by each class (this particular model uses a small set of 21 classes, including person and car, plus background). For driving or floor-finding you would use a model trained on classes such as road, sidewalk and obstacle. Foundation models such as Segment Anything (arXiv 2304.02643) can segment objects from simple prompts like a clicked point or a box, which is useful for labelling and for grasp targeting.

A detection is a box in the image. The robot needs a position in 3D. Combine what you have learned: take the box centre, read the depth there (the median of a small patch, which resists holes), and unproject with the camera intrinsics. box_to_3d.py import numpy as np def box_to_point(box, depth_m, K): """box = [x1, y1, x2, y2] pixels; depth_m = HxW depth in metres; K = 3x3 intrinsics.""" u = int((box[0] + box[2]) / 2) v = int((box[1] + box[3]) / 2) patch = depth_m[max(v - 2, 0):v + 3, max(u - 2, 0):u + 3] z = float(np.nanmedian(patch[patch > 0.1])) x = (u - K[0, 2]) * z / K[0, 0] y = (v - K[1, 2]) * z / K[1, 1] return np.array([x, y, z]) K = np.array([[600.0, 0, 320], [0, 600.0, 240], [0, 0, 1]]) depth = np.full((480, 640), 2.0) print(box_to_point([400, 200, 500, 300], depth, K)) # about [0.433 0.033 2.0] Then use TF to transform that point from the camera frame into base_link or map, as you learned in the ROS 2 module. Better still, use the segmentation mask instead of the box centre: take the median over the mask’s pixels, which is not fooled by background showing inside the box.

Latency. A detector at 5 frames per second means decisions on stale data. Measure end-to-end latency, and use smaller models, lower resolution, half precision or GPU inference runtimes when needed. Distribution shift. Models fail on lighting, camera angles or object types unlike their training data. Test on images from your robot early. Confidence is not truth. Scores are often over-confident. Track detections over time, and require a few consecutive frames before acting. Safety. Never let a detector be the only thing that stops a robot from hitting a person. Use it alongside lidar-based obstacle avoidance and hardware limits.

Run conv_demo.py and iou_nms.py to see the building blocks work on tiny examples. Take three photos with your phone (a desk, a street, a room). Run detect_torchvision.py on each. Note what it finds and what it misses. Install ultralytics and run detect_yolo.py on the same photos. Compare the time taken and the boxes found with the torchvision model. Run segment_torchvision.py on the street photo and print the class shares. Using a depth camera in your Gazebo world (or a made-up depth image), run box_to_3d.py on a detection and check that the answer is plausible. It worked if both detectors label the obvious objects and your 3D point is in front of the camera at a believable distance.

Compute an IoUBeginner Box A is [0, 0, 10, 10] and box B is [5, 0, 15, 10]. What is their IoU? Show solutionHide solution The overlap is x from 5 to 10 and y from 0 to 10: area 50. Each box has area 100, so the union is 100 + 100 - 50 = 150. IoU = 50 / 150 = 1/3, about 0.33. Tune the thresholdIntermediate Your detector keeps producing two boxes on every large object. Which parameter do you adjust, and in which direction? What goes wrong if you overdo it? Show solutionHide solution Lower the NMS IoU threshold (for example from 0.7 to 0.5) so overlapping boxes are suppressed more aggressively. If you overdo it, two genuinely different objects that overlap in the image, such as two people standing close together, get merged into one detection. Pick the taskIntermediate For each robot job, choose detection, semantic segmentation or instance segmentation: (a) deciding where a wheelchair-sized robot can drive, (b) counting boxes on a pallet, (c) picking one specific bolt out of a bin of identical bolts. Show solutionHide solution (a) Semantic segmentation of the drivable floor. (b) Detection or instance segmentation; detection is enough to count. (c) Instance segmentation, because you need the outline of the individual bolt to plan a grasp.

1What does a CNN filter do? AIt deletes pixels at randomBIt slides over the image computing weighted sums, with weights learned from dataCIt converts images to textDIt stores the image on disk 2What is the purpose of non-maximum suppression? ATo increase image resolutionBTo remove duplicate overlapping boxes for the same objectCTo compute depthDTo train the network faster 3Which task gives a separate mask for each individual object? AClassificationBSemantic segmentationCInstance segmentationDCalibration 4Why use the median depth of a patch rather than one pixel? AIt is required by PyTorchBSingle pixels can be holes or noise in depth imagesCPatches are always larger objectsDThe median is faster than reading one pixel 0 of 4 answered Takeaways CNNs learn their own filters; early layers find edges, later layers find parts and objects. Detection gives boxes and labels, semantic segmentation labels pixels, instance segmentation separates objects. Pretrained models from torchvision or ultralytics work in a few lines; always use the matching preprocessing. IoU measures box overlap, NMS removes duplicates, and mAP is the standard accuracy score. Combine a detection with depth and intrinsics to get a 3D position, then use TF to move it into a useful frame. Check latency, test on your own camera images, and never rely on a detector alone for safety.

Intermediate45 minBefore this:Cameras and image processing · NumPy · Frames and rigid transforms A camera image tells your robot what things look like. To pick up a mug, or to avoid walking into a table, it also needs to know how far away things are, and where they sit in three dimensions. This is the job of depth sensors and lidar. They give you a point cloud: thousands of 3D points on the surfaces around the robot. In this lesson you will build a point cloud, find the floor in it, and pull out the objects standing on it. You will be able to Explain how stereo cameras, structured light or time-of-flight cameras, and lidar measure distance. Convert a depth image or a laser scan to 3D points with NumPy. Downsample, clean and estimate normals for a point cloud with Open3D. Find a ground plane with RANSAC and separate objects with clustering.

Stereo. Two cameras a distance BBB apart (the baseline) see the same point at slightly different columns. The difference is the disparityThe horizontal pixel offset of the same scene point between the left and right images of a stereo pair; larger disparity means closer d=uL−uRd = u_L - u_Rd=uL​−uR​. Similar triangles give Z=f Bd.Z = \frac{f\,B}{d}.Z=dfB​. Near things have a large disparity, far things a small one. Differentiating shows the catch: a depth error of δZ≈Z2 δd/(fB)\delta Z \approx Z^2\,\delta d / (f B)δZ≈Z2δd/(fB), so stereo accuracy degrades with the square of distance. Stereo needs texture to match points, so blank white walls are a problem. Structured light and time-of-flight (ToF) cameras. These are active: the camera projects a known infrared pattern, or pulses of light, and works out distance from the pattern’s distortion or the light’s travel time. They work on blank walls but struggle in strong sunlight and on shiny or transparent surfaces. Lidar. A lidarLight detection and ranging: measures distance by timing the return of laser pulses spins a laser and measures the return time of each pulse. A 2D lidar scans one plane and returns a ring of ranges, which is perfect for navigation on flat floors. A 3D lidar has many beams stacked vertically and returns a full cloud, common on outdoor robots and cars. Learned depth. Neural networks can estimate depth from a single image. The result is plausible but not metrically reliable, so treat it as a hint rather than a measurement. Sensor Range Strengths Weak spots Stereo a few metres Cheap, works outdoors Needs texture, error grows with distance squared Structured light / ToF 0.3 to ~8 m Dense depth, indoors Sunlight, glass, black or shiny surfaces 2D lidar 10 m and up Accurate, fast, simple Only one plane 3D lidar tens to hundreds of m Full 3D, long range Cost, sparse data

A depth image stores, for each pixel, the distance ZZZ along the optical axis. In ROS, depth is either 32FC1 in metres or 16UC1 in millimetres (check the encoding). Reusing the pinhole model from the last lesson, a pixel (u,v)(u, v)(u,v) with depth ZZZ becomes X=(u−cx) Zfx,Y=(v−cy) Zfy.X = \frac{(u - c_x)\,Z}{f_x}, \quad Y = \frac{(v - c_y)\,Z}{f_y}.X=fx​(u−cx​)Z​,Y=fy​(v−cy​)Z​. depth_to_points.py import numpy as np def depth_to_points(depth_m: np.ndarray, fx, fy, cx, cy) -> np.ndarray: """HxW depth image in metres -> Nx3 points in the camera optical frame.""" h, w = depth_m.shape u, v = np.meshgrid(np.arange(w), np.arange(h)) z = depth_m valid = np.isfinite(z) & (z > 0.1) # drop NaN, zero and too-close values x = (u - cx) * z / fx y = (v - cy) * z / fy return np.column_stack([x[valid], y[valid], z[valid]]) # A flat wall 2 m in front of a 640x480 camera: depth = np.full((480, 640), 2.0) pts = depth_to_points(depth, fx=600, fy=600, cx=320, cy=240) print(pts.shape, pts[:, 2].min(), pts[:, 2].max()) # (307200, 3) 2.0 2.0 A 2D lidar is even simpler. A LaserScan message gives you a list of ranges rir_iri​ at angles θi=θmin+i Δθ\theta_i = \theta_\text{min} + i\,\Delta\thetaθi​=θmin​+iΔθ, and the points are xi=ricos⁡θi,yi=risin⁡θi.x_i = r_i \cos\theta_i, \qquad y_i = r_i \sin\theta_i .xi​=ri​cosθi​,yi​=ri​sinθi​. scan_to_points.py import numpy as np def scan_to_points(ranges, angle_min, angle_increment, range_min, range_max) -> np.ndarray: """Convert LaserScan fields to Nx2 points in the sensor frame, dropping invalid returns.""" r = np.asarray(ranges, dtype=float) theta = angle_min + angle_increment * np.arange(len(r)) ok = np.isfinite(r) & (r >= range_min) & (r <= range_max) return np.column_stack([r[ok] * np.cos(theta[ok]), r[ok] * np.sin(theta[ok])]) # A fake scan of a circular room of radius 3 m: angles = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 360, endpoint=False) pts = scan_to_points([3.0] * 360, -np.pi, angles[1] - angles[0], 0.12, 10.0) print(pts.shape, np.round(np.hypot(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1]).mean(), 3)) # (360, 2) 3.0 In ROS 2 a 3D cloud arrives as sensor_msgs/msg/PointCloud2, a packed binary buffer. The helper in sensor_msgs_py unpacks it: cloud_listener.py import numpy as np import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data from sensor_msgs.msg import PointCloud2 from sensor_msgs_py import point_cloud2 class CloudListener(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__("cloud_listener") self.create_subscription(PointCloud2, "/depth_camera/points", self.on_cloud, qos_profile_sensor_data) def on_cloud(self, msg: PointCloud2): pts = point_cloud2.read_points(msg, field_names=("x", "y", "z"), skip_nans=True) xyz = np.column_stack([pts["x"], pts["y"], pts["z"]]) self.get_logger().info(f"{len(xyz)} points, nearest {np.linalg.norm(xyz, axis=1).min():.2f} m") def main(): rclpy.init() rclpy.spin(CloudListener()) if __name__ == "__main__": main() Note Every cloud lives in a frame, given by msg.header.frame_id. Before you combine clouds from two sensors, or combine one with a map, transform them into a common frame using TF. Mixing frames is the most common point-cloud bug.

documents.t: If you have two rectified images (left and right, same row alignment), OpenCV can compute disparity, and you apply Z=fB/dZ = fB/dZ=fB/d: stereo.py import cv2 import numpy as np left = cv2.imread("left.png", cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE) right = cv2.imread("right.png", cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE) matcher = cv2.StereoSGBM_create(minDisparity=0, numDisparities=64, blockSize=5) disparity = matcher.compute(left, right).astype(np.float32) / 16.0 # SGBM returns fixed point x16 FOCAL_PX, BASELINE_M = 600.0, 0.12 # from your calibration with np.errstate(divide="ignore"): depth = np.where(disparity > 0, FOCAL_PX * BASELINE_M / disparity, np.nan) print("median depth:", np.nanmedian(depth), "m") "Rectified" means calibration has removed distortion and aligned the two image planes so that matching points lie on the same row. Calibrate a stereo pair with cv2.stereoCalibrate and cv2.stereoRectify, or use a camera that ships with factory calibration.

Open3DAn open-source library for 3D data processing, with point cloud, mesh and registration tools in Python and C++ (pip install open3d; check that your Python version is supported by the current release) gives you fast, simple tools. The workflow almost every perception pipeline follows is: Each step earns its place: Outlier removal. Stray points from reflections or noise confuse everything after. A statistical filter drops points whose neighbours are unusually far away. Voxel downsampling. Divide space into small cubes (voxels) and keep one point per cube. Clouds of a million points become tens of thousands, and density becomes even. Normals. The surface normalA unit vector perpendicular to a surface at a point; estimated from the neighbours of each point at each point tells you which way the surface faces. Normals help segment surfaces, align clouds and plan grasps. RANSAC plane fit. Find the biggest flat thing, usually the floor. Clustering. Group the remaining points into separate objects. RANSAC: guess, check, repeat RANSACRandom Sample Consensus: repeatedly fit a model to a tiny random subset of the data and keep the model that most of the data agrees with is the standard way to fit a model to data that contains many outliers. To find a plane: pick 3 random points, compute the plane through them, count how many points lie within a small distance of it, and repeat. Keep the plane with the most inliers. Least squares would be pulled off by the boxes; RANSAC ignores them. Here is RANSAC from scratch in NumPy so you can see the idea. It makes its own data: a flat floor plus a box. ransac_plane.py import numpy as np def ransac_plane(points, threshold=0.02, iterations=200, seed=0): """Fit a plane n.x + d = 0 to Nx3 points. Returns (normal, d, inlier_mask).""" rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) best_mask, best_model = None, None for _ in range(iterations): a, b, c = points[rng.choice(len(points), 3, replace=False)] n = np.cross(b - a, c - a) norm = np.linalg.norm(n) if norm < 1e-9: # the three points were collinear continue n /= norm d = -n @ a mask = np.abs(points @ n + d) < threshold if best_mask is None or mask.sum() > best_mask.sum(): best_mask, best_model = mask, (n, d) return best_model[0], best_model[1], best_mask rng = np.random.default_rng(0) floor = np.column_stack([rng.uniform(-3, 3, (6000, 2)), rng.normal(0, 0.005, 6000)]) box = rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, (800, 3)) * [0.4, 0.4, 0.5] + [1.0, 0.5, 0.25] cloud = np.vstack([floor, box]) n, d, inliers = ransac_plane(cloud) print("normal:", np.round(n, 3), "d:", round(d, 3), "inliers:", inliers.sum(), "of", len(cloud)) The printed normal is close to (0,0,±1)(0, 0, \pm 1)(0,0,±1) and ddd close to 0: the floor, found even though the box sits on it. (The sign of a plane normal is arbitrary.) The number of iterations needed is N≈log⁡(1−p)/log⁡(1−w3)N \approx \log(1-p)/\log(1-w^3)N≈log(1−p)/log(1−w3), where www is the fraction of inliers and ppp the desired confidence; with 88% inliers, 200 iterations is far more than enough. Now the full pipeline in Open3D, on a similar synthetic scene: pipeline.py import numpy as np import open3d as o3d rng = np.random.default_rng(0) floor = np.column_stack([rng.uniform(-3, 3, (6000, 2)), rng.normal(0, 0.005, 6000)]) box1 = rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, (1500, 3)) * [0.4, 0.4, 0.5] + [1.0, 0.5, 0.25] box2 = rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, (700, 3)) * [0.3, 0.3, 0.3] + [-1.0, -1.0, 0.15] stray = rng.uniform(-3, 3, (40, 3)) * [1, 1, 0.5] + [0, 0, 0.8] # flying outliers pcd = o3d.geometry.PointCloud() pcd.points = o3d.utility.Vector3dVector(np.vstack([floor, box1, box2, stray])) print("raw points:", len(pcd.points)) # 1. Remove outliers: drop points far from their 20 nearest neighbours pcd, _ = pcd.remove_statistical_outlier(nb_neighbors=20, std_ratio=2.0) # 2. Voxel downsample to 3 cm pcd = pcd.voxel_down_sample(voxel_size=0.03) print("after filtering:", len(pcd.points)) # 3. Normals from the 30 nearest neighbours within 10 cm pcd.estimate_normals(search_param=o3d.geometry.KDTreeSearchParamHybrid(radius=0.1, max_nn=30)) # 4. RANSAC: the biggest plane is the floor (a, b, c, d), floor_idx = pcd.segment_plane(distance_threshold=0.02, ransac_n=3, num_iterations=1000) print(f"floor plane: {a:.2f}x + {b:.2f}y + {c:.2f}z + {d:.2f} = 0, {len(floor_idx)} points") # 5. Keep everything that is not floor, then cluster with DBSCAN objects = pcd.select_by_index(floor_idx, invert=True) labels = np.array(objects.cluster_dbscan(eps=0.1, min_points=10)) pts = np.asarray(objects.points) for k in range(labels.max() + 1): cluster = pts[labels == k] print(f"object {k}: {len(cluster)} points, centre {np.round(cluster.mean(axis=0), 2)}, " f"size {np.round(np.ptp(cluster, axis=0), 2)}") Run it and you should see two objects, near (1.0, 0.5, 0.25) and (-1.0, -1.0, 0.15), with sizes close to the boxes’ dimensions. (Points with label -1 are noise.) Add o3d.visualization.draw_geometries([objects]) to view them in 3D, if you have a display. DBSCAN grows a cluster from any point that has at least min_points neighbours within distance eps. Choose eps a little bigger than the point spacing on an object, and smaller than the gap between objects.

documents.t: Run depth_to_points.py and scan_to_points.py. Confirm the printed shapes and values. Run ransac_plane.py. Change threshold to 0.2 and see how many points become inliers, then change it to 0.001 and see what happens. Install Open3D and run pipeline.py. Verify that you get two clusters with centres near the boxes. In your Gazebo world from the simulation module, run cloud_listener.py on /depth_camera/points and check that the nearest-point distance matches the distance you see in the simulator. Optional: save one cloud to a .npy file and run the Open3D pipeline on it. It worked if the pipeline finds exactly the number of objects you placed, and the floor plane normal is vertical.

Stereo depthBeginner A stereo camera has f=700f = 700f=700 px and baseline B=0.10B = 0.10B=0.10 m. A point has disparity 14 px. How far away is it, and how much does the depth change if the disparity is off by 1 px? Show solutionHide solution Z=fB/d=700⋅0.10/14=5Z = fB/d = 700 \cdot 0.10 / 14 = 5Z=fB/d=700⋅0.10/14=5 m. With d=13d = 13d=13, Z=70/13≈5.38Z = 70/13 \approx 5.38Z=70/13≈5.38 m, an error of about 0.38 m. With d=15d = 15d=15, Z≈4.67Z \approx 4.67Z≈4.67 m. This is why stereo at long range is imprecise. Lidar to a wallIntermediate A 2D lidar reports a range of 2.0 m at angle 30 degrees to the left of straight ahead (take the sensor’s x axis forward and y to the left). Where is that point in the sensor frame? Show solutionHide solution x=2.0cos⁡30∘≈1.73x = 2.0\cos 30^\circ \approx 1.73x=2.0cos30∘≈1.73 m and y=2.0sin⁡30∘=1.0y = 2.0 \sin 30^\circ = 1.0y=2.0sin30∘=1.0 m. So the point is 1.73 m ahead and 1.0 m to the left. Choosing the voxel sizeIntermediate Your cloud has a 5 mm spacing, the smallest object you care about is a 4 cm cube, and you need real-time speed. Suggest a voxel size and explain the trade-off. Show solutionHide solution Something like 1 cm to 2 cm. It reduces the point count by roughly 4x to 16x per axis-pair (fewer points), while a 4 cm cube still keeps several points per side. A 10 cm voxel would erase the cube’s shape; a 5 mm voxel would barely downsample at all.

1How does stereo depth error change with distance? AIt is constantBIt grows roughly with the square of the distanceCIt shrinks with distanceDIt depends only on the colour of objects 2Why use RANSAC instead of ordinary least squares to find the floor? AIt is always fasterBIt ignores the many points that are not on the floorCIt needs no dataDIt guarantees an exact fit 3What does voxel downsampling do? AColours the cloudBKeeps roughly one point per small cube, reducing and evening out densityCRotates the cloudDRemoves the floor 4A LaserScan range of inf means what? AA very close objectBNo return within range, so it must be filtered outCA sensor fault that crashes ROSDAn object exactly at the maximum range 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Depth comes from stereo, active infrared sensors, lidar or learned estimates, each with different strengths and failure cases. A depth pixel becomes a 3D point with X=(u−cx)Z/fxX = (u-c_x)Z/f_xX=(u−cx​)Z/fx​ and Y=(v−cy)Z/fyY = (v-c_y)Z/f_yY=(v−cy​)Z/fy​; a laser scan becomes points with cosine and sine. Stereo depth error grows with Z2Z^2Z2; lidar and active depth are better at range, at a cost. Standard pipeline: remove outliers, voxel downsample, estimate normals, RANSAC the floor, cluster the rest. Always know which frame a cloud is in, and transform with TF before combining sensors. Filter invalid ranges and NaNs before doing any maths.

Advanced45 minBefore this:State estimation and Kalman filters · Depth, point clouds and lidar · TF2 and URDF · NumPy You drop a robot into a building it has never seen and ask it to fetch something from the kitchen. It has no map. To build a map it needs to know where it has been; to know where it has been, it needs a map. This chicken-and-egg puzzle is called SLAM, simultaneous localization and mapping, and solving it is what lets a vacuum cleaner remember your living room and a warehouse robot find its shelf. You will be able to Explain the difference between mapping, localization and SLAM, and why drift makes SLAM hard. Build an occupancy grid from lidar scans using log-odds, and align two scans with ICP. Localize with a particle filter and explain how AMCL works. Describe graph SLAM and loop closure, and run slam_toolbox and AMCL in ROS 2.

Mapping: the robot’s pose is known, build the map. Easy. Localization: the map is known, find the robot’s pose. Done with a particle filter or EKF. SLAM: neither is known; estimate both at once. Hard, because errors in one corrupt the other. Every robot has odometry: an estimate of motion from wheel encoders or an IMU. It is smooth and quick but drifts, because small errors add up without bound. Drive around a room and come back, and the odometry says you are 40 cm from where you started. The map built from drifting poses would show a double wall. SLAM uses what the sensors see (the walls themselves) to correct the drift.

The most common map for a ground robot is an occupancy gridA map that divides space into a grid of cells, each holding the probability that the cell is occupied by an obstacle. Each cell holds a probability of being occupied. Unknown cells start at 0.5. When a lidar beam travels from the robot to a hit point, every cell the beam passes through is probably free, and the end cell is probably occupied. Rather than multiply probabilities, we add log-odds, l=log⁡p1−pl = \log\frac{p}{1-p}l=log1−pp​, which turns the Bayes update into a sum: lt(cell)=lt−1(cell)+lsensor,p=1−11+el.l_t(\text{cell}) = l_{t-1}(\text{cell}) + l_\text{sensor}, \qquad p = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + e^{l}} .lt​(cell)=lt−1​(cell)+lsensor​,p=1−1+el1​. A hit adds a positive number, a pass-through adds a negative number, and cells that are repeatedly observed become confident. The code below ray-marches a simulated lidar in an 8 m room with a box, and builds a grid from five scans taken at known poses. occupancy_grid.py import numpy as np # ---------- a tiny world: an 8 m x 8 m room with a box obstacle ---------- def is_occupied(p): x, y = p outside = not (0.0 < x < 8.0 and 0.0 < y < 8.0) in_box = 5.0 < x < 6.0 and 2.0 < y < 4.0 return outside or in_box def true_scan(pose, angles, max_range=10.0, step=0.02): """Ray-march a simulated lidar from pose = (x, y, theta).""" ranges = np.full(len(angles), max_range) for i, a in enumerate(angles): d = np.array([np.cos(pose[2] + a), np.sin(pose[2] + a)]) for r in np.arange(step, max_range, step): if is_occupied(pose[:2] + r * d): ranges[i] = r break return ranges # ---------- occupancy grid with log-odds ---------- class OccupancyGrid: def __init__(self, size_m=8.0, resolution=0.2): self.res = resolution n = int(size_m / resolution) self.logodds = np.zeros((n, n)) # 0 = unknown (p = 0.5) self.L_OCC, self.L_FREE = 0.85, -0.40 # evidence per hit / pass-through def cell(self, x, y): return int(y / self.res), int(x / self.res) # (row, col) def _line(self, r0, c0, r1, c1): """Bresenham: all cells on the line from (r0, c0) to (r1, c1).""" cells = [] dr, dc = abs(r1 - r0), abs(c1 - c0) sr, sc = (1 if r1 > r0 else -1), (1 if c1 > c0 else -1) err = dc - dr while True: cells.append((r0, c0)) if (r0, c0) == (r1, c1): return cells e2 = 2 * err if e2 > -dr: err -= dr c0 += sc if e2 < dc: err += dc r0 += sr def integrate_scan(self, pose, angles, ranges, max_range=10.0): r0, c0 = self.cell(pose[0], pose[1]) n = self.logodds.shape[0] for a, r in zip(angles, ranges): hit = r < max_range ex = pose[0] + r * np.cos(pose[2] + a) ey = pose[1] + r * np.sin(pose[2] + a) r1, c1 = self.cell(ex, ey) r1, c1 = min(max(r1, 0), n - 1), min(max(c1, 0), n - 1) ray = self._line(r0, c0, r1, c1) for (rr, cc) in ray[:-1]: self.logodds[rr, cc] += self.L_FREE # the beam passed through: free if hit: self.logodds[r1, c1] += self.L_OCC # the beam ended here: occupied def probability(self): return 1.0 - 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(self.logodds)) grid = OccupancyGrid() angles = np.radians(np.arange(-180, 180, 2)) for pose in [(2.0, 2.0, 0.0), (2.0, 6.0, 1.0), (4.0, 4.0, 2.0), (6.5, 6.0, -1.0), (6.5, 1.0, 3.0)]: pose = np.array(pose) grid.integrate_scan(pose, angles, true_scan(pose, angles)) p = grid.probability() for row in range(p.shape[0] - 1, -1, -2): # north at the top print("".join("#" if p[row, c] > 0.65 else ("." if p[row, c] < 0.35 else " ") for c in range(p.shape[1]))) The printed map shows # for occupied, . for free and a space for unknown. You will see the room outline and the box’s visible sides; the inside of the box stays unknown because no beam ever got there. This is exactly what the /map topic (nav_msgs/msg/OccupancyGrid) contains, as integers from 0 to 100 with -1 for unknown.

The code above assumed known poses. In real SLAM you estimate the pose change between two consecutive scans by scan matching: find the rotation RRR and translation ttt that best lay one scan on top of the other. The classic method is ICPIterative Closest Point: repeatedly match each point to its nearest neighbour in the other cloud, solve for the best rigid transform, apply it, and repeat. Given matched pairs pi↔qip_i \leftrightarrow q_ipi​↔qi​, it minimises min⁡R,t∑i∥R pi+t−qi∥2,\min_{R, t} \sum_i \left\| R\,p_i + t - q_i \right\|^2 ,R,tmin​i∑​∥Rpi​+t−qi​∥2, which has a closed-form solution through the singular value decomposition: subtract the centroids, build H=∑(pi−pˉ)(qi−qˉ)TH = \sum (p_i - \bar{p})(q_i - \bar{q})^TH=∑(pi​−pˉ​)(qi​−qˉ​)T, take H=UΣVTH = U \Sigma V^TH=UΣVT, and then R=VUTR = V U^TR=VUT and t=qˉ−Rpˉt = \bar{q} - R\bar{p}t=qˉ​−Rpˉ​. icp.py import numpy as np def icp_2d(source, target, iterations=30): """Align Nx2 `source` points to `target` points. Returns R (2x2), t (2,).""" R_total, t_total = np.eye(2), np.zeros(2) current = source.copy() for _ in range(iterations): # 1. match every source point to its nearest target point (brute force) d2 = ((current[:, None, :] - target[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2) matched = target[d2.argmin(axis=1)] # 2. best rigid transform for these matches (Kabsch / SVD) mu_s, mu_t = current.mean(axis=0), matched.mean(axis=0) H = (current - mu_s).T @ (matched - mu_t) U, _, Vt = np.linalg.svd(H) R = Vt.T @ U.T if np.linalg.det(R) < 0: # avoid a reflection Vt[-1] *= -1 R = Vt.T @ U.T t = mu_t - R @ mu_s # 3. apply and accumulate current = current @ R.T + t R_total, t_total = R @ R_total, R @ t_total + t return R_total, t_total def rot(a): return np.array([[np.cos(a), -np.sin(a)], [np.sin(a), np.cos(a)]]) # A scan of an L-shaped corridor, then the same scan after the robot moved rng = np.random.default_rng(0) wall1 = np.column_stack([np.linspace(0, 4, 80), np.zeros(80)]) wall2 = np.column_stack([np.zeros(60), np.linspace(0, 3, 60)]) wall3 = np.column_stack([np.linspace(0, 2, 40), np.full(40, 3.0)]) scan_a = np.vstack([wall1, wall2, wall3]) + rng.normal(0, 0.005, (180, 2)) true_R, true_t = rot(np.radians(8)), np.array([0.15, -0.10]) scan_b = scan_a @ true_R.T + true_t + rng.normal(0, 0.005, scan_a.shape) # Find the transform that maps scan_b back onto scan_a R, t = icp_2d(scan_b, scan_a) print("recovered rotation: %.2f deg (the scan was rotated by +8, so we expect -8)" % np.degrees(np.arctan2(R[1, 0], R[0, 0]))) print("recovered translation:", np.round(t, 3)) print("mean alignment error after ICP: %.4f m" % np.mean(np.linalg.norm(scan_b @ R.T + t - scan_a, axis=1))) The recovered motion is the inverse of the one we applied, and the residual error drops to a few millimetres. ICP has a weakness: it needs a decent starting guess (odometry provides one), and it can slide along a featureless corridor because every position looks the same along its length. Production systems use faster variants (correlative scan matching, NDT) but the idea is identical. The long-corridor problem In a long straight corridor with smooth walls, scan matching cannot tell how far you moved along the corridor, because the scans look identical. Fusing wheel odometry or an IMU (previous lesson) is what keeps SLAM from getting stuck there.

Chaining scan matches gives smooth local motion but still accumulates error. The cure is loop closure: when the robot returns to a place it has seen before, it recognises it, and adds a constraint that pulls the trajectory back into agreement. Graph SLAMA SLAM formulation where robot poses are nodes and measurements (odometry, scan matches, loop closures) are edges, and the best set of poses is found by least squares represents this cleanly. Each robot pose is a node. Each measurement of relative motion between two poses is an edge, a constraint of the form "pose jjj should be at TijT_{ij}Tij​ relative to pose iii". Because measurements are noisy, the constraints disagree slightly, and we look for the poses that disagree least: min⁡x1,…,xn∑(i,j)eij(xi,xj)T Ωij eij(xi,xj),\min_{x_1, \dots, x_n} \sum_{(i,j)} e_{ij}(x_i, x_j)^T \, \Omega_{ij} \, e_{ij}(x_i, x_j),x1​,…,xn​min​(i,j)∑​eij​(xi​,xj​)TΩij​eij​(xi​,xj​), where eije_{ij}eij​ is the mismatch between predicted and measured relative pose, and Ωij\Omega_{ij}Ωij​ (the information matrix) says how much to trust that edge. Think of the graph as springs. Odometry edges are soft springs, and the loop-closure edge is a spring that yanks pose 6 back to pose 1; the optimiser relaxes all the springs together, spreading the error evenly along the loop. The part that finds scan matches and detects loops is called the front end; the optimiser is the back end. slam_toolbox uses a sparse solver (Ceres) for the back end.

documents.t: When you already have a map, localization is a Bayes filter again, but with strongly non-Gaussian beliefs (a robot in a long hallway of identical doors could be in many places). A particle filterA Bayes filter that represents the belief by many weighted random samples of the state, called particles keeps hundreds of guesses ("particles"), each a full pose. Every step: Move each particle with the motion model plus random noise. Weight each particle by how well the real scan matches the map as seen from that pose. Resample: copy likely particles, drop unlikely ones. This is Monte Carlo localization. The code below localizes a robot from range readings to three known landmarks, starting with particles spread over the whole room (global localization): particle_filter.py import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(4) LANDMARKS = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [7.0, 1.5], [4.0, 7.0]]) # known map, 8 m x 8 m room N = 1000 SIGMA_RANGE = 0.3 def motion(poses, v, w, dt, noise=(0.15, 0.1)): """Move Nx3 poses (x, y, theta) with noisy unicycle motion.""" v_n = v + rng.normal(0, noise[0], len(poses)) w_n = w + rng.normal(0, noise[1], len(poses)) poses[:, 0] += v_n * np.cos(poses[:, 2]) * dt poses[:, 1] += v_n * np.sin(poses[:, 2]) * dt poses[:, 2] += w_n * dt return poses def ranges_to_landmarks(pose): return np.linalg.norm(LANDMARKS - pose[:2], axis=1) def systematic_resample(weights): positions = (rng.random() + np.arange(len(weights))) / len(weights) return np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(weights), positions) # Global localization: start with particles spread over the whole room particles = np.column_stack([rng.uniform(0, 8, N), rng.uniform(0, 8, N), rng.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi, N)]) truth = np.array([4.0, 3.0, 0.0]) dt = 0.1 for step in range(100): v, w = 0.8, 0.4 truth = motion(truth[None, :].copy(), v, w, dt, noise=(0, 0))[0] particles = motion(particles, v, w, dt) z = ranges_to_landmarks(truth) + rng.normal(0, SIGMA_RANGE, len(LANDMARKS)) expected = np.linalg.norm(particles[:, None, :2] - LANDMARKS[None, :, :], axis=2) # N x 3 log_w = -0.5 * (((expected - z) / SIGMA_RANGE) ** 2).sum(axis=1) weights = np.exp(log_w - log_w.max()) weights /= weights.sum() particles = particles[systematic_resample(weights)] particles += rng.normal(0, [0.03, 0.03, 0.02], particles.shape) # roughening keeps diversity if step % 20 == 0 or step == 99: est = particles[:, :2].mean(axis=0) print(f"step {step:3d}: estimate ({est[0]:.2f}, {est[1]:.2f}), " f"spread {particles[:, :2].std(axis=0).mean():.2f} m, " f"error {np.linalg.norm(est - truth[:2]):.2f} m") Run it. The particle cloud collapses onto the true position within a handful of steps (three ranges pin down a position quickly) and then tracks it with an error of a few centimetres. Heading is not measured directly here; the filter learns it from how the position changes as the robot moves. Remove the "roughening" line to see a classic failure, particle depletion, where all particles collapse onto one wrong guess and never recover. Why particles beat a single Gaussian for global localization A Kalman filter holds one bump. If the robot could be in either of two identical corridors, one bump cannot represent that. A particle filter happily holds two clusters until the evidence favours one. That is why the standard ROS 2 localizer, AMCL (adaptive Monte Carlo localization), is a particle filter. "Adaptive" means it uses more particles when it is confused and fewer when it is confident.
The two standard packages are slam_toolbox for mapping and AMCL (from Nav2) for localization.

The robot’s pose in the world is split in two on purpose. odom to base_link is smooth and continuous but drifts (from wheel odometry or your EKF). map to odom is published by SLAM or AMCL and holds the correction; it may jump when the estimate is corrected. Navigation uses the smooth one for control and the corrected one for goals.

terminal sudo apt install ros-jazzy-slam-toolbox ros-jazzy-nav2-map-server ros2 launch slam_toolbox online_async_launch.py use_sim_time:=true With your Gazebo robot running (lidar bridged as /scan, TF from odom to base_link), slam_toolbox publishes /map and the map to odom transform. Add a Map display in RViz and drive around with teleop_twist_keyboard: the map grows as you move. "Online" means it processes live data, and "async" means it processes scans as fast as it can rather than every one. Its behaviour is set through a YAML file passed as slam_params_file:=my_slam.yaml. The important settings: my_slam.yaml (excerpt) slam_toolbox: ros__parameters: use_sim_time: true odom_frame: odom map_frame: map base_frame: base_link scan_topic: /scan mode: mapping # or: localization resolution: 0.05 # map cell size in metres max_laser_range: 10.0 minimum_travel_distance: 0.3 minimum_travel_heading: 0.3 do_loop_closing: true Drive slowly and make loops: revisit the start so a loop closure can fire. When the map looks good, save it: terminal ros2 run nav2_map_server map_saver_cli -f my_map This writes my_map.pgm (the image) and my_map.yaml (resolution, origin, thresholds).

terminal ros2 launch nav2_bringup localization_launch.py map:=my_map.yaml use_sim_time:=true In RViz set the Fixed Frame to map, add the Map display on /map and a PoseArray on /particle_cloud, then use the 2D Pose Estimate tool to click an approximate starting pose and drag the arrow in the heading direction. You will see the particle cloud appear around that pose. Drive the robot and watch the cloud tighten as the lidar matches the map. If you give a wildly wrong initial pose, the cloud will not recover, which is the kidnapped robot problemThe failure case where a robot is moved or starts with a completely wrong pose estimate, and must re-localize from scratch; AMCL can also be asked to spread particles globally for this case. Pro tip Most "my SLAM is bad" problems are not SLAM problems. Check, in order: is use_sim_time consistent everywhere, is the TF tree complete and does ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames show one tree, are the lidar frame and its mounting height correct, and is the odometry reasonably smooth? Fix those before touching any SLAM parameter.

Cameras can do SLAM too, by tracking features (like the ORB features from lesson one) across frames. Visual and visual-inertial SLAM systems exist in open source, and NVIDIA publishes GPU-accelerated versions in Isaac ROS. They need good lighting and texture, and monocular systems cannot recover true scale without extra information such as an IMU. Check the current documentation of whichever system you adopt.

Run occupancy_grid.py and icp.py. Change the ICP starting offset to 30 degrees and see whether it still converges. Where does it break down? Run particle_filter.py. Reduce N to 50 and then comment out the roughening line. Describe what changes. In your Gazebo world, start the simulation, the bridge and slam_toolbox. Drive around the box and back to the start. Save the map with map_saver_cli. Stop SLAM. Launch localization_launch.py with your saved map, set a deliberately slightly wrong initial pose in RViz, drive forward and watch the particle cloud converge. Record a bag during step 4 with ros2 bag record /scan /odom /tf /particle_cloud for the module project. It worked if the saved map has straight walls (no ghost or doubled walls) and AMCL’s particles tighten around the robot within a few metres of driving.

Log-odds updateBeginner A cell has log-odds 0 (unknown). Three beams end in it (hits, each +0.85). One beam then passes through it (free, -0.40). What is its log-odds and its probability of being occupied? Show solutionHide solution Log-odds =3⋅0.85−0.40=2.15= 3 \cdot 0.85 - 0.40 = 2.15=3⋅0.85−0.40=2.15. Probability =1−1/(1+e2.15)≈1−1/9.59≈0.90= 1 - 1/(1 + e^{2.15}) \approx 1 - 1/9.59 \approx 0.90=1−1/(1+e2.15)≈1−1/9.59≈0.90. The cell is quite confidently occupied. Why did the map double?Intermediate You map a square room, return to the start, and the walls appear twice, offset by 30 cm. Name the cause and two ways to improve it. Show solutionHide solution Accumulated drift with no loop closure, so the second pass was placed using drifted poses. Improve it by making sure loop closure is enabled and that the robot revisits the start before finishing, by driving more slowly and smoothly, and by improving odometry (fuse an IMU with an EKF). Particles or Kalman?Advanced A warehouse has many identical aisles. A robot is switched on at an unknown position. Would you use an EKF or a particle filter for the initial localization, and what would you use once it is confident? Show solutionHide solution A particle filter such as AMCL for global localization, because the belief is multimodal (many identical aisles). Once the particles have converged to one cluster, the posterior is close to Gaussian, so an EKF fusing odometry, IMU and the AMCL pose gives smooth, low-latency tracking.

1Why are log-odds used for occupancy grids? AThey make cells biggerBBayes updates become simple additionsCThey avoid needing a lidarDThey compress the map to fewer bytes 2What does loop closure do? ACloses the lidar shutterBAdds a constraint when the robot revisits a place, reducing accumulated driftCStops the robot at the end of a loopDDoubles the map resolution 3Which transform does SLAM or AMCL publish in ROS 2? Aodom to base_linkBmap to odomCbase_link to lidar_linkDworld to map 4Why is a particle filter good for global localization? AIt needs no mapBIt can represent several hypotheses at onceCIt is exactDIt ignores sensor noise 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Mapping needs poses, localization needs a map, SLAM estimates both and fights odometry drift. Occupancy grids store cell probabilities as log-odds, updated by adding evidence along each beam. Scan matching (ICP and relatives) estimates motion between scans; it needs a good initial guess and can fail in featureless corridors. Graph SLAM treats poses as nodes and measurements as edges, and loop closures remove accumulated drift. Particle filters (AMCL) hold multiple hypotheses and are the standard way to localize in a known map. In ROS 2: slam_toolbox to map, map_saver_cli to save, Nav2 AMCL to localize; check TF, time and odometry before tuning.

slam_toolbox repository and documentation: github.com/SteveMacenski/slam_toolbox Nav2 documentation on AMCL and map management: navigation.ros.org Grisetti et al., "A Tutorial on Graph-Based SLAM": widely available online and a clear introduction to the back end. Besl and McKay, "A Method for Registration of 3-D Shapes" (1992), the original ICP paper. Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right. Next: Path planning algorithms

Advanced45 minBefore this:Probability for robots · Linear algebra and transforms · Python and NumPy · ROS 2 topics and parameters Your robot has wheel encoders that say it moved 1.00 m, an IMU that says it turned 3 degrees, and a lidar that says the wall is 2.31 m away. None of them agrees exactly with the others, and none is the truth. Wheels slip, gyros drift, lidars have noise. The robot still has to decide, many times a second, "where am I and how fast am I going?". The tool for this is state estimation, and its most famous member is the Kalman filter, which flew astronauts to the Moon and now runs inside almost every robot. You will be able to Explain the Bayes filter as a loop of predict and update, and run a simple discrete version. Derive the intuition behind the Kalman gain and write predict and update steps in NumPy. Implement a 2D Kalman filter and an extended Kalman filter (EKF) for a robot with range and bearing measurements. Fuse an IMU with an absolute heading, and configure robot_localization for wheel odometry plus IMU in ROS 2.

The stateThe set of numbers that describes everything about the robot you need to predict its future, such as position, heading and velocity xtx_txt​ is what you want to know: for a ground robot, maybe (x,y,θ)(x, y, \theta)(x,y,θ). You never see it directly. You see measurements ztz_tzt​ (sensor readings) and you know the controls utu_tut​ (what you commanded). So instead of one answer you keep a beliefA probability distribution over the possible states, given everything the robot has measured and commanded so far: a probability distribution over where the robot could be. Every estimator you will meet repeats two steps. Predict. Use the motion model to push the belief forward in time. Because motion is noisy, the belief gets wider (more uncertain). Update. A measurement arrives. Multiply the belief by how likely that measurement would be in each possible state, and normalise. The belief gets narrower. In symbols, with η\etaη a normalising constant: bel‾(xt)=∫p(xt∣xt−1,ut) bel(xt−1) dxt−1,bel(xt)=η p(zt∣xt) bel‾(xt).\overline{bel}(x_t) = \int p(x_t \mid x_{t-1}, u_t)\, bel(x_{t-1})\, dx_{t-1}, \qquad bel(x_t) = \eta\, p(z_t \mid x_t)\, \overline{bel}(x_t).bel(xt​)=∫p(xt​∣xt−1​,ut​)bel(xt−1​)dxt−1​,bel(xt​)=ηp(zt​∣xt​)bel(xt​). You can run this loop on a tiny problem. A robot is in a corridor of 10 cells with doors (D) and walls (W). It can only sense "door" or "wall", with an 80% accurate sensor, and its moves sometimes slip. histogram_filter.py import numpy as np # A 1D corridor of 10 cells. D = door, W = wall. world = np.array(list("WDWWDWWWDW")) belief = np.full(len(world), 1.0 / len(world)) # start: no idea where we are P_HIT, P_MISS = 0.8, 0.2 # sensor is right 80% of the time def sense(belief, reading): likelihood = np.where(world == reading, P_HIT, P_MISS) posterior = belief * likelihood # Bayes: prior x likelihood return posterior / posterior.sum() # normalise def move(belief, steps): moved = np.roll(belief, steps) # shift right (the corridor wraps) return 0.8 * moved + 0.1 * np.roll(moved, 1) + 0.1 * np.roll(moved, -1) # slip blur for reading, step in [("D", 1), ("W", 1), ("W", 1), ("W", 1), ("D", 0)]: belief = sense(belief, reading) print("sense", reading, "->", np.round(belief, 2)) belief = move(belief, step) print("most likely cell now:", int(np.argmax(belief))) # 8 Watch the belief. After the first "door" it has three bumps (one per door). Each further reading kills the bumps that do not fit, until one remains. That is localization in a nutshell, and it is exactly what AMCL does with particles in the next lesson. Every filter is predict, then update Prediction spends information (uncertainty grows because the world is noisy). Measurement buys it back (uncertainty shrinks). A good estimator is one that trusts each source exactly as much as its accuracy deserves.
documents.s: State, belief and the Bayes filter

documents.t: The histogram filter stores a number per cell, which explodes in many dimensions. The Kalman filterAn optimal recursive estimator for linear systems with Gaussian noise; it tracks a mean and a covariance instead of a full distribution makes a bargain: assume everything is a Gaussian and the models are linear. Then the belief is described by just two things: a mean x^\hat{x}x^ (best guess) and a covariance PPP (how unsure, and how the errors in different variables relate).

Say your prediction of a position is μ1\mu_1μ1​ with variance σ12\sigma_1^2σ12​, and a sensor says μ2\mu_2μ2​ with variance σ22\sigma_2^2σ22​. The fused estimate is a weighted average, weighted by confidence: μ=μ1+K(μ2−μ1),K=σ12σ12+σ22,σ2=(1−K) σ12.\mu = \mu_1 + K(\mu_2 - \mu_1), \quad K = \frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}, \quad \sigma^2 = (1-K)\,\sigma_1^2 .μ=μ1​+K(μ2​−μ1​),K=σ12​+σ22​σ12​​,σ2=(1−K)σ12​. Read KKK as "how much do I trust the new measurement?". If the sensor is very precise (σ22→0\sigma_2^2 \to 0σ22​→0), K→1K \to 1K→1 and you jump to its value. If the sensor is junk (σ22→∞\sigma_2^2 \to \inftyσ22​→∞), K→0K \to 0K→0 and you ignore it. The fused variance is always smaller than either input: combining two imperfect sources beats both.

Now use vectors. The model is xk=Fxk−1+wk,wk∼N(0,Q),zk=Hxk+vk,vk∼N(0,R).x_k = F x_{k-1} + w_k, \quad w_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q), \qquad z_k = H x_k + v_k, \quad v_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R).xk​=Fxk−1​+wk​,wk​∼N(0,Q),zk​=Hxk​+vk​,vk​∼N(0,R). FFF is how the state evolves (for example, position gains velocity times Δt\Delta tΔt), HHH picks out what the sensor measures, QQQ is process noise (how much you distrust your motion model) and RRR is measurement noise (how much you distrust the sensor; usually from the datasheet). The filter is: Step Equation Predict state x^−=Fx^\hat{x}^- = F \hat{x}x^−=Fx^ Predict covariance P−=FPFT+QP^- = F P F^T + QP−=FPFT+Q Innovation y=z−Hx^−y = z - H\hat{x}^-y=z−Hx^− Innovation covariance S=HP−HT+RS = H P^- H^T + RS=HP−HT+R Kalman gain K=P−HTS−1K = P^- H^T S^{-1}K=P−HTS−1 Update state x^=x^−+Ky\hat{x} = \hat{x}^- + K yx^=x^−+Ky Update covariance P=(I−KH) P−P = (I - KH)\,P^-P=(I−KH)P− The matrix gain is the 1D weighting in disguise: P−HTP^- H^TP−HT is "how uncertain the prediction is in the measured directions" and S−1S^{-1}S−1 divides by total uncertainty. The innovation yyy is the surprise: how far the measurement is from what you predicted. Large surprises are also a diagnostic for sensor faults.

State [x,y,vx,vy][x, y, v_x, v_y][x,y,vx​,vy​], and a sensor that reports only noisy position. The filter has to infer velocity, which it never sees directly. kalman_filter.py import numpy as np class KalmanFilter: """Linear Kalman filter: x_k = F x_{k-1} + w (cov Q), z_k = H x_k + v (cov R).""" def __init__(self, F, H, Q, R, x0, P0): self.F, self.H, self.Q, self.R = F, H, Q, R self.x, self.P = x0.astype(float), P0.astype(float) def predict(self): self.x = self.F @ self.x self.P = self.F @ self.P @ self.F.T + self.Q def update(self, z): y = z - self.H @ self.x # innovation S = self.H @ self.P @ self.H.T + self.R # innovation covariance K = self.P @ self.H.T @ np.linalg.inv(S) # Kalman gain self.x = self.x + K @ y I_KH = np.eye(len(self.x)) - K @ self.H self.P = I_KH @ self.P @ I_KH.T + K @ self.R @ K.T # Joseph form: stays symmetric return K rng = np.random.default_rng(1) dt = 0.1 F = np.array([[1, 0, dt, 0], [0, 1, 0, dt], [0, 0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0, 1]], float) H = np.array([[1, 0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0, 0]], float) Q = np.diag([1e-4, 1e-4, 1e-2, 1e-2]) R = np.eye(2) * 0.5**2 kf = KalmanFilter(F, H, Q, R, x0=np.zeros(4), P0=np.eye(4) * 10.0) truth = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.5]) meas_err, est_err = [], [] for _ in range(200): truth = F @ truth z = H @ truth + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 2) kf.predict() kf.update(z) meas_err.append(np.linalg.norm(z - truth[:2])) est_err.append(np.linalg.norm(kf.x[:2] - truth[:2])) print("RMS position error, raw measurement: %.3f m" % np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(meas_err)))) print("RMS position error, Kalman filter : %.3f m" % np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(est_err)))) print("estimated velocity: %.2f, %.2f (true 1.00, 0.50)" % tuple(kf.x[2:])) Run it: the filter’s position error is about a third of the raw sensor’s, and it recovers the velocity (to within a bit of lag) from positions alone. The initial covariance P0=10IP_0 = 10 IP0​=10I says "I know nothing", so the first few measurements dominate. Pro tip: tuning Q and R RRR comes from the sensor’s spec or from measuring it at rest. QQQ is the knob you tune. Too small and the filter becomes stubborn and lags behind real manoeuvres; too large and it just copies the noisy measurements. Plot the innovations: if they look like zero-mean noise with the spread the filter predicts (SSS), you are close.

Robots are not linear. A wheeled robot moves along x=vcos⁡θx = v\cos\thetax=vcosθ, and a range-bearing sensor involves square roots and arctangents. The EKFExtended Kalman filter: a Kalman filter that handles nonlinear models by linearising them around the current estimate with Jacobians keeps the same steps but replaces FFF and HHH by the Jacobians (matrices of partial derivatives) of the nonlinear functions fff and hhh, evaluated at the current estimate: x^−=f(x^,u),P−=FJPFJT+Q,y=z−h(x^−),HJ=∂h∂x∣x^−.\hat{x}^- = f(\hat{x}, u), \quad P^- = F_J P F_J^T + Q, \qquad y = z - h(\hat{x}^-), \quad H_J = \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\Big|_{\hat{x}^-} .x^−=f(x^,u),P−=FJ​PFJT​+Q,y=z−h(x^−),HJ​=∂x∂h​​x^−​. For a unicycle robot with state (x,y,θ)(x, y, \theta)(x,y,θ), speed vvv and turn rate ω\omegaω: f=[x+vcos⁡θ Δty+vsin⁡θ Δtθ+ω Δt],FJ=[10−vsin⁡θ Δt01vcos⁡θ Δt001].f = \begin{bmatrix} x + v\cos\theta\,\Delta t \\ y + v\sin\theta\,\Delta t \\ \theta + \omega\,\Delta t \end{bmatrix}, \qquad F_J = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -v\sin\theta\,\Delta t \\ 0 & 1 & v\cos\theta\,\Delta t \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.f=​x+vcosθΔty+vsinθΔtθ+ωΔt​​,FJ​=​100​010​−vsinθΔtvcosθΔt1​​. The sensor measures range rrr and bearing φ\varphiφ to a landmark at a known position (lx,ly)(l_x, l_y)(lx​,ly​). With dx=lx−xd_x = l_x - xdx​=lx​−x and dy=ly−yd_y = l_y - ydy​=ly​−y: h=[dx2+dy2atan2⁡(dy,dx)−θ],HJ=[−dx/r−dy/r0dy/r2−dx/r2−1].h = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{d_x^2 + d_y^2} \\ \operatorname{atan2}(d_y, d_x) - \theta \end{bmatrix}, \qquad H_J = \begin{bmatrix} -d_x/r & -d_y/r & 0 \\ d_y/r^2 & -d_x/r^2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}.h=[dx2​+dy2​​atan2(dy​,dx​)−θ​],HJ​=[−dx​/rdy​/r2​−dy​/r−dx​/r2​0−1​]. ekf_landmarks.py import numpy as np LANDMARKS = [np.array([5.0, 3.0]), np.array([-2.0, 4.0])] def wrap(a): """Wrap an angle to (-pi, pi].""" return (a + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi def motion(x, u, dt): """Unicycle model: state (x, y, theta), control (v, omega).""" v, w = u return np.array([x[0] + v * np.cos(x[2]) * dt, x[1] + v * np.sin(x[2]) * dt, wrap(x[2] + w * dt)]) def motion_jacobian(x, u, dt): v, _ = u return np.array([[1, 0, -v * np.sin(x[2]) * dt], [0, 1, v * np.cos(x[2]) * dt], [0, 0, 1]]) def measure(x, lm): """Range and bearing from the robot to a landmark at a known position.""" dx, dy = lm - x[:2] return np.array([np.hypot(dx, dy), wrap(np.arctan2(dy, dx) - x[2])]) def measure_jacobian(x, lm): dx, dy = lm - x[:2] r2 = dx**2 + dy**2 r = np.sqrt(r2) return np.array([[-dx / r, -dy / r, 0.0], [dy / r2, -dx / r2, -1.0]]) rng = np.random.default_rng(3) dt = 0.1 Q = np.diag([0.02, 0.02, 0.01]) ** 2 # process noise added per step R = np.diag([0.2, np.radians(3)]) ** 2 # range (m) and bearing (rad) noise truth = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) x = np.array([0.5, -0.5, 0.2]) # deliberately wrong initial guess P = np.diag([1.0, 1.0, 0.3]) dead = x.copy() # same odometry, no landmark corrections err_ekf, err_dead = [], [] for k in range(300): u = np.array([1.0, 0.3]) # true command: drive in a circle truth = motion(truth, u, dt) u_odom = u + rng.normal(0, [0.05, 0.02]) # what the wheels report (noisy) F = motion_jacobian(x, u_odom, dt) # predict x = motion(x, u_odom, dt) P = F @ P @ F.T + Q dead = motion(dead, u_odom, dt) if k % 2 == 0: # update with every landmark we can see for lm in LANDMARKS: z = measure(truth, lm) + rng.normal(0, [0.2, np.radians(3)]) H = measure_jacobian(x, lm) S = H @ P @ H.T + R K = P @ H.T @ np.linalg.inv(S) innovation = z - measure(x, lm) innovation[1] = wrap(innovation[1]) x = x + K @ innovation x[2] = wrap(x[2]) P = (np.eye(3) - K @ H) @ P err_ekf.append(np.linalg.norm(x[:2] - truth[:2])) err_dead.append(np.linalg.norm(dead[:2] - truth[:2])) print("final position error, dead reckoning: %.2f m" % err_dead[-1]) print("final position error, EKF : %.2f m" % err_ekf[-1]) print("mean position error over the run : %.2f m (EKF) vs %.2f m (dead reckoning)" % (np.mean(err_ekf), np.mean(err_dead))) Run it. The EKF starts with a wrong guess and recovers within a few updates, then stays within centimetres of the truth, while pure odometry ("dead reckoning") wanders away. Two details are easy to forget and cause real bugs: angles must be wrapped (the innovation between 179 degrees and -179 degrees is 2 degrees, not 358), and the Jacobians are evaluated at the current estimate, not the truth. The EKF is only as good as its linearisation. When the estimate is far off or the models are very curved, it can become overconfident and diverge. Alternatives include the unscented Kalman filter and particle filters, which you meet next lesson.

A gyroscope measures turn rate. Integrating it gives heading, but a small constant biasA slowly varying offset in a sensor’s output that persists even when the true quantity is zero accumulates into a large drift. A heading from another source (wheel odometry, a compass, scan matching) has no drift but is noisy or occasionally wrong. Together they are far better than either. The trick is to put the bias in the state, so the filter learns it: yaw_fusion.py import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(0) dt = 0.01 true_rate = 0.2 # rad/s, the robot turns slowly gyro_bias = 0.05 # rad/s of constant gyro bias gyro_noise, heading_noise = 0.01, 0.1 # State: [yaw, gyro bias]. The gyro is the control input; an absolute heading # (e.g. wheel odometry, a compass, or scan matching) is the measurement. F = np.array([[1.0, -dt], [0.0, 1.0]]) B = np.array([dt, 0.0]) H = np.array([[1.0, 0.0]]) Q = np.diag([1e-6, 1e-8]) R = np.array([[heading_noise**2]]) x = np.zeros(2) P = np.diag([1.0, 0.1]) yaw_true = 0.0 yaw_gyro_only = 0.0 for k in range(6000): # 60 seconds yaw_true += true_rate * dt gyro = true_rate + gyro_bias + rng.normal(0, gyro_noise) yaw_gyro_only += gyro * dt x = F @ x + B * gyro P = F @ P @ F.T + Q if k % 10 == 0: # heading arrives at 10 Hz z = yaw_true + rng.normal(0, heading_noise) S = H @ P @ H.T + R K = P @ H.T / S x = x + (K * (z - H @ x)).ravel() P = (np.eye(2) - K @ H) @ P print("yaw error, gyro integration only: %.3f rad" % abs(yaw_gyro_only - yaw_true)) print("yaw error, fused with heading : %.3f rad" % abs(x[0] - yaw_true)) print("estimated gyro bias: %.3f rad/s (true %.3f)" % (x[1], gyro_bias)) After 60 seconds the gyro-only yaw is about 3 radians off, while the fused estimate is within a hundredth of a radian and has discovered the bias. This idea (put slowly varying errors in the state) is the heart of every serious IMU fusion system.
documents.s: Fusing an IMU with another sensor

documents.t: You rarely write your own filter for a real robot. The robot_localization package provides ekf_node (and ukf_node), which fuses any mix of odometry, IMU and pose sources according to a YAML file. The key is the 15-element boolean list per sensor, in this order: position x,y,zx, y, zx,y,z; orientation roll, pitch, yaw; linear velocity x,y,zx, y, zx,y,z; angular velocity roll, pitch, yaw; linear acceleration x,y,zx, y, zx,y,z. true means "use this value from this sensor". ekf.yaml ekf_filter_node: ros__parameters: use_sim_time: true frequency: 30.0 two_d_mode: true # planar robot: ignore z, roll, pitch publish_tf: true map_frame: map odom_frame: odom base_link_frame: base_link world_frame: odom # this filter produces the odom -> base_link transform odom0: /odom # wheel odometry odom0_config: [false, false, false, false, false, false, true, true, false, # use vx, vy false, false, true, # use yaw rate false, false, false] odom0_differential: false imu0: /imu imu0_config: [false, false, false, false, false, false, false, false, false, false, false, true, # use yaw rate from the gyro true, false, false] # use forward acceleration imu0_differential: false imu0_remove_gravitational_acceleration: true terminal ros2 run robot_localization ekf_node --ros-args --params-file ekf.yaml \ -r odometry/filtered:=/odom/filtered Warning In the simulator from the previous module, the DiffDrive plugin already publishes an odom to base_link transform. If ekf_node publishes the same transform, two sources fight and RViz flickers. Either do not bridge the simulator’s /tf, or set publish_tf: false on the EKF and keep its output topic only. Common settings that matter: give each sensor a proper covariance in its message (the filter trusts the numbers it is given, so a message with all-zero covariance is trusted absolutely), use _differential: true to fuse a pose sensor as velocity changes if it jumps, and set world_frame: map in a second filter instance that also fuses GPS or localization pose.

Run histogram_filter.py. Change the sensor accuracy P_HIT to 0.6 and see how many steps it takes before one cell clearly wins. Run kalman_filter.py. Increase the measurement noise in the simulation (the 0.5 inside rng.normal) but leave R unchanged, and watch the filter become over-confident. Then fix R to match. Run ekf_landmarks.py. Remove the second landmark and compare the error. Then remove all updates after step 100 (set LANDMARKS = []) and watch the error grow again. Run yaw_fusion.py. Set gyro_bias to 0.2 and confirm the filter still learns it. In your Gazebo world, start ekf_node with ekf.yaml, drive the robot with the keyboard, and compare /odom with /odom/filtered in RViz or with ros2 topic echo. It worked if fused estimates are visibly steadier than any single sensor and you can explain which of Q and R you changed and why.

Scalar Kalman gainBeginner Your prediction says the robot is at 10.0 m with variance 4.0. A sensor reads 12.0 m with variance 1.0. What are the fused estimate and its variance? Show solutionHide solution K=4/(4+1)=0.8K = 4 / (4 + 1) = 0.8K=4/(4+1)=0.8. Estimate =10+0.8(12−10)=11.6= 10 + 0.8(12 - 10) = 11.6=10+0.8(12−10)=11.6 m. Variance =(1−0.8)⋅4=0.8= (1 - 0.8) \cdot 4 = 0.8=(1−0.8)⋅4=0.8, smaller than both inputs. Debug a stubborn filterIntermediate Your filter follows the robot smoothly but takes several seconds to notice that the robot turned sharply. Which matrix is probably too small, and what would you change? Show solutionHide solution The process noise QQQ is too small, so the filter overtrusts its smooth motion model and under-weights the measurements. Increase QQQ (especially for the velocity terms). Check by plotting innovations: they would show a long run of the same sign during the turn. Pick the configAdvanced A robot has wheel odometry (reliable velocities, slow drift in heading when wheels slip) and an IMU with a gyro. In robot_localization, which yaw-related inputs would you use from each, and why not use absolute yaw from both? Show solutionHide solution Use yaw rate from the gyro (smooth and responsive) and the linear velocities from odometry; take yaw rate from odometry only if its covariance is honest. Fusing absolute yaw from both can make the filter trust drifting heading twice; if the IMU provides a calibrated absolute orientation (with a magnetometer), use that for yaw. Always check the covariances in each message.

1In the Kalman filter, what does the process noise Q represent? ASensor inaccuracyBHow much you distrust the motion model between stepsCThe size of the mapDThe loop frequency 2What happens to uncertainty during the predict step and the update step? AGrows in predict, shrinks in updateBShrinks in predict, grows in updateCStays constant in bothDGrows in both 3Why does the EKF use Jacobians? ATo make code shorterBTo linearise nonlinear motion and measurement models around the current estimateCTo remove the need for noise modelsDTo speed up the camera 4Why include gyro bias in the state of an IMU fusion filter? ABecause bias is random each stepBSo the filter can estimate and cancel the slowly drifting offsetCTo make the state vector largerDBecause bias equals yaw 0 of 4 answered Takeaways State estimation keeps a belief about the state and repeats predict (uncertainty grows) and update (uncertainty shrinks). The Kalman gain weights prediction and measurement by their confidence; the fused variance is lower than either source. QQQ encodes distrust of the model, RRR distrust of the sensor; tune QQQ, measure RRR. The EKF linearises nonlinear models with Jacobians; wrap angles and expect trouble if the estimate is far off. Put slowly varying errors, such as gyro bias, in the state so the filter learns them. In ROS 2, robot_localization fuses odometry and IMU from a YAML file; avoid two nodes publishing the same TF.

Every robot, from a vacuum cleaner to a humanoid, is built from the same few ideas. It has parts that sense, think and move. Those parts live in different places and point in different directions, so the robot needs a clean way to describe where things are. It has to turn desired motions into joint angles and joint angles into forces, and it has to keep correcting itself because the world never behaves exactly as predicted. This module teaches those ideas in the order you will use them: anatomy, frames, kinematics, dynamics, control. The maths is real but always tied to code you can run in NumPy, so you can poke at every formula. Nothing here needs a robot. By the end you will have a tiny virtual arm and a tuned motor controller of your own.

Name the subsystems of a robot and estimate its power and data budget. Describe poses with rotation matrices, homogeneous transforms and quaternions, and compose them without ordering mistakes. Compute forward kinematics and Jacobians, and solve inverse kinematics analytically and numerically. Read and use the manipulator equation, and check motions against torque limits. Build, tune and debug a PID controller, including anti-windup, and explain cascaded and impedance control.
