Combine the pieces into one script. Your 2-link arm follows a circle with its hand: inverse kinematics turns each point into joint targets, a PID controller (one per joint) drives simulated joints toward them, and the dynamics model from lesson 4 supplies gravity compensation so the controller only corrects errors. Plot the hand path against the desired circle and report the largest tracking error. If the path is a wobbly circle you have found a tuning problem; if it is a clean one, you are ready for the next module, where you will connect software pieces like these together with ROS 2. Start with The anatomy of a robot.

Beginner30 minBefore this:Python basics · High-school physics Picture a small delivery robot rolling down a corridor. A person steps out of a doorway. Within a fraction of a second the robot must notice them, decide to brake, and cut power to its wheels, all without browning out its own computer. Behind that one smooth stop sits a whole chain of parts: something that senses, something that thinks, something that moves, and something that feeds them all. This lesson gives you the map of that chain, so every later lesson has somewhere to attach. You will be able to Name the four subsystems of a robot (sensing, compute, actuation, power) and say what each one does. Distinguish proprioceptive from exteroceptive sensors and give two examples of each. Trace a signal around the sense-think-act loop and say where delay and noise enter. Estimate a rough power budget and data-rate budget for a small mobile robot.

Strip away the metal and a robot is one idea repeated: sense, think, act. It measures the world, decides what to do, pushes on the world, then measures again to see what happened. The world changes, so the loop never stops. Four physical subsystems make that loop real: Sensors turn the physical world into numbers. Compute turns numbers into decisions. Actuators turn decisions into forces. Power keeps the other three alive. Everything in robotics, from a toy line-follower to a humanoid, is a different answer to "which parts, and how are they wired together?" The loop is the robot A robot is not defined by its body. It is defined by a closed loop: measure, decide, act, repeat. A great body with a slow or noisy loop behaves badly. A modest body with a fast, clean loop can look magical.
documents.s: A robot is a loop, not a machine

documents.t: A sensora device that converts a physical quantity such as light, motion or force into an electrical signal never gives you "the truth". It gives you a number that is related to the truth, plus noise, plus delay. Sensors fall into two families, and the names come from the same Latin root as this course. Proprioceptive sensors measure the robot itself: how far a joint has turned, how fast a wheel spins, how much current a motor draws. This is the robot's inner sense of its own body, the thing the name Proprio points at. Exteroceptive sensors measure the outside world: a camera, a lidar, a microphone, a bump switch. Sensor Measures Family Typical rate Joint encoder Shaft angle Proprioceptive 1 kHz and up IMU (gyro + accelerometer) Angular rate, acceleration Proprioceptive 100 Hz to 1 kHz Motor current sense Torque (indirectly) Proprioceptive 1 kHz to 20 kHz Force/torque sensor Contact forces Proprioceptive (at the wrist) 100 Hz to 1 kHz Camera Light intensity (a grid of pixels) Exteroceptive 15 to 120 Hz Lidar Distance along many rays Exteroceptive 5 to 40 Hz Depth camera Distance per pixel Exteroceptive 15 to 90 Hz Two properties matter more than any datasheet headline: Rate: how many measurements per second. A fast controller needs fast feedback. Latency: how old the number already is when it reaches your code. A camera frame that was exposed 80 ms ago describes a world that has moved on. Note "Typical rate" figures are ballpark values to build intuition. Always read the datasheet of the actual part you buy.
documents.s: Sensors: how a robot knows things

documents.t: Robots usually have more than one computer, because different jobs have different demands. Microcontrollers (MCUs) run tight, fast, predictable loops: reading an encoder, closing a motor current loop at several kilohertz. They are simple, cheap and have no operating system getting in the way. Single-board computers and embedded GPUs (a Raspberry Pi class board, or an NVIDIA Jetson class module) run an operating system, ROS 2, perception and planning. Workstations or the cloud train big models and run heavy offline jobs. The key word is real-timebehaviour in which a result is guaranteed to arrive within a fixed time limit, not merely on average. A joint controller that is usually on time but occasionally 50 ms late can make an arm shake. That is why low-level control lives on MCUs or on a carefully configured real-time thread, while "slow thinking" such as route planning lives on the bigger computer. You will meet this split again in the ROS 2 module.

An actuatora device that converts energy, usually electrical, into mechanical motion or force is anything that makes the robot move. The common ones: Brushed DC motors: cheap and simple. Fine for wheels and toys. Brushless DC (BLDC) motors: efficient, long-lived, the standard choice for drones, gimbals and modern robot joints. Servo motors: a motor bundled with an encoder and a small controller so you command a position. Stepper motors: move in fixed angular steps, popular for 3D printers. Hydraulic and pneumatic actuators: fluids give huge force for their weight, but add pumps, hoses and leaks. Motors spin fast and weakly; robots usually need slow and strong. A gearbox trades speed for torque. A gear ratio of NNN multiplies torque by about NNN and divides speed by NNN, minus friction losses: τout≈N η τmotor,ωout=ωmotorN\tau_{\text{out}} \approx N\,\eta\,\tau_{\text{motor}}, \qquad \omega_{\text{out}} = \frac{\omega_{\text{motor}}}{N}τout​≈Nητmotor​,ωout​=Nωmotor​​ where η\etaη is the gearbox efficiency (a number below 1). Gearing has a catch: a high ratio makes the joint hard to back-drive, which is great for holding a load but poor for gentle contact with people. Many modern legged robots use low ratios on purpose, so they can feel the ground.
documents.s: Actuators: how a robot pushes back

documents.t: Batteries store energy (watt-hours); loads draw power (watts). Runtime is roughly their ratio: trun≈EbatteryPavgt_{\text{run}} \approx \frac{E_{\text{battery}}}{P_{\text{avg}}}trun​≈Pavg​Ebattery​​ Three habits will save you pain: Peak is not average. A motor accelerating a heavy arm can pull several times its idle current for a moment. Size wiring and the battery's maximum discharge rate for the peak. Separate noisy and quiet rails. Motors create electrical noise and voltage dips. Put them on a different regulator from your computer and sensors, or a motor surge will reboot the brain. Have an emergency stop. A hardware path that cuts motor power must not depend on software being alive. Warning Lithium batteries can start fires if shorted, over-discharged or punctured. Use a battery management system (BMS), fuse the main supply, and never charge unattended.
documents.s: Power: the quiet subsystem that limits everything

documents.t: Parts talk over buses, shared wires with agreed rules (a protocol). You will see these constantly: Bus Typical use Notes I²C, SPI Chips on one board (IMUs, small sensors) Short distance, simple UART / serial MCU to computer, GPS Easy, slow CAN / CAN FD Motor drivers, vehicles Robust against noise, multi-drop EtherCAT Fast joint networks in arms and humanoids Tight timing USB Cameras, lidar Convenient, shared bandwidth Ethernet Lidar, cameras, computers High bandwidth, long runs The bus must carry the data fast enough. A 640×480640 \times 480640×480 colour camera at 30 frames per second with 3 bytes per pixel produces about 640⋅480⋅3⋅30≈27.6640 \cdot 480 \cdot 3 \cdot 30 \approx 27.6640⋅480⋅3⋅30≈27.6 MB/s. That fills an old USB 2 link and is why compressed streams and hardware encoders exist.

Let us turn this into code. The script below builds a tiny budget for a mobile robot: average power, runtime, and raw sensor data rate. budget.py from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class Load: name: str watts: float # average draw duty: float = 1.0 # fraction of time it is on (0 to 1) @property def average(self) -> float: return self.watts * self.duty @dataclass class Stream: name: str bytes_per_sample: int rate_hz: float @property def megabytes_per_s(self) -> float: return self.bytes_per_sample * self.rate_hz / 1e6 loads = [ Load("drive motors", watts=60.0, duty=0.5), Load("compute (SBC + GPU)", watts=15.0), Load("lidar", watts=8.0), Load("camera", watts=2.5), Load("microcontroller + sensors", watts=1.5), ] streams = [ Stream("camera 640x480 RGB", 640 * 480 * 3, 30), Stream("lidar 1080 pts x 8 B", 1080 * 8, 10), Stream("IMU 6 floats", 6 * 4, 200), Stream("wheel encoders", 2 * 4, 1000), ] battery_wh = 100.0 usable = 0.8 # never plan to drain a battery to zero p_avg = sum(load.average for load in loads) print(f"Average power: {p_avg:.1f} W") print(f"Runtime: {battery_wh * usable / p_avg:.2f} h") total = 0.0 for s in streams: print(f"{s.name:<24} {s.megabytes_per_s:8.3f} MB/s") total += s.megabytes_per_s print(f"Total raw sensor data: {total:.2f} MB/s") Run it and you will see two lessons at once: the drive motors dominate the power budget, and the camera dominates the data budget. Real design is mostly noticing which single item dominates and attacking that.

Walk back through the loop and ask "what can go wrong here?" Sensing: noise (random jitter), bias (a steady offset), and latency. Compute: processing time, and scheduling jitter if the operating system pauses your code. Communication: bus delay, dropped messages. Actuation: the motor cannot change torque instantly, gears have backlash (a little free play), and limits clip your command. Add those delays up and you have the loop latency. As a rule of thumb, the feedback loop should be much faster than the thing it controls. That is the seed of the control lesson later in this module.
documents.s: Where delay and noise sneak into the loop

documents.t: You will turn the budget script into a design tool. Save the script as budget.py and run it with python budget.py. Note the average power and the largest data stream. Change the battery to 50 Wh and the drive-motor duty to 0.8. Predict the new runtime before you run it, then check your prediction. Add a second camera stream (a stereo pair) and a 3D lidar that produces 300,000 points per second at 16 bytes per point. Does your total still fit a gigabit Ethernet link (about 100 MB/s of useful throughput)? Add a Load called "emergency stop relay" with 0.5 W and write one sentence on why it must not be powered through the compute board. You know it worked when you can explain, in one sentence, which component limits your runtime and which limits your bandwidth.

Gear it downBeginner A motor produces 0.05 N·m at 6,000 rpm. A gearbox with ratio 50 and efficiency 0.8 sits on its shaft. What torque and speed come out? Show solutionHide solution Torque: 0.05×50×0.8=2.00.05 \times 50 \times 0.8 = 2.00.05×50×0.8=2.0 N·m. Speed: 6000/50=1206000 / 50 = 1206000/50=120 rpm. You traded 50 times less speed for about 40 times more torque (the missing 20 percent is lost to friction). Sort the sensorsBeginner Classify each as proprioceptive or exteroceptive: wheel encoder, lidar, motor current sensor, microphone, IMU in the torso, contact switch on a bumper. Show solutionHide solution Proprioceptive: wheel encoder, motor current sensor, IMU. Exteroceptive: lidar, microphone, bumper contact switch. (A contact switch touches the world, so it senses something outside the robot's own body.) Will it fit on the bus?Intermediate Your arm has 7 joints. Each joint sends 12 bytes of state at 1,000 Hz over a single CAN FD bus. How many megabits per second is that, and is it comfortable for a bus rated at 5 Mbit/s (ignoring protocol overhead)? Show solutionHide solution 7×12×1000=84,0007 \times 12 \times 1000 = 84{,}0007×12×1000=84,000 bytes/s, which is 0.6720.6720.672 Mbit/s. That is about 13 percent of 5 Mbit/s before overhead, so it fits, but real frames add headers, so leave generous margin and check the actual frame format.

1Which of these is a proprioceptive sensor? AA lidar scanning a roomBA camera watching a doorCA joint encoder measuring shaft angleDA microphone listening for a voice 2Why do robot designers often put low-level motor control on a microcontroller instead of the main computer? AMicrocontrollers are always faster than GPUsBThey run tight loops with predictable timing and no operating-system delaysCROS 2 cannot run on bigger computersDMicrocontrollers need no power 3A gearbox with ratio 20 and efficiency 0.9 is attached to a motor that makes 1 N·m. Roughly what torque comes out? A0.05 N·mB1 N·mC18 N·mD20 N·m 4Which statement about the sense-think-act loop is most accurate? AIt runs once at start-upBDelay and noise can enter at every stage, not just at the sensorCOnly sensors add delayDActuators respond instantly to commands 0 of 4 answered Takeaways A robot is a closed loop of sensing, compute, actuation and power; the body is only one part of it. Proprioceptive sensors measure the robot itself; exteroceptive sensors measure the world. Rate and latency matter as much as accuracy when you choose a sensor. Gearboxes trade speed for torque; power budgets must plan for peaks, not just averages. Split fast, predictable control (MCU) from slow, heavy thinking (main computer), and keep a hardware emergency stop. Do the arithmetic early: one component usually dominates both the power and the data budget. Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

ROS 2 documentation: the software side of connecting all these parts together. Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (Siegwart, Nourbakhsh, Scaramuzza): a classic textbook on sensors, locomotion and navigation. Modern Robotics (Lynch and Park): free book and video course; its early chapters match the next lessons. Next: Frames and rigid transforms

Intermediate45 minBefore this:Dynamics essentials · Python and NumPy · Basic calculus You command a robot arm to move to 1 radian. It overshoots to 1.2, swings back to 0.9, and wobbles for a few seconds before settling. Or worse, it never quite reaches 1 because of a stubborn gravity load. The motors are fine; the commands are just badly chosen. Control is the craft of choosing commands, many times per second, so the robot does what you asked and not something near it. You will be able to Explain open-loop versus closed-loop (feedback) control and why feedback wins in the real world. Write a PID controller and test it against a simulated DC motor. Describe what each of P, I and D does, tune them step by step, and read overshoot, settling time and steady-state error from a response. Add anti-windup and a filtered derivative, and say why each matters. Describe cascaded control and impedance control at a conceptual level.

An open-loop controller sends a command and hopes. "Run the motor at 6 V for 2 seconds" is open loop. It works only if the world is exactly as you assumed: no extra load, no friction change, a full battery. Real robots break those assumptions constantly. A closed-loop or feedback controlcontrol that measures the result and uses the error between the goal and the measurement to adjust the next command system measures what actually happened and corrects. The error is e(t)=r(t)−y(t)e(t) = r(t) - y(t)e(t)=r(t)−y(t) where rrr is the reference (the goal) and yyy is the measured output. The controller turns eee into a command uuu. Feedback has one big gift: it makes a system robust. Whatever disturbs the output, the error grows and the controller pushes back. It also has one big danger: a loop with too much correction or too much delay can start to oscillate, or even run away. Most of control engineering is balancing those two.

The most used controller in industry is almost embarrassingly simple. It combines three terms: u(t)=Kp e(t)+Ki∫0te(τ) dτ+Kd dedtu(t) = K_p\,e(t) + K_i\int_0^t e(\tau)\,d\tau + K_d\,\frac{de}{dt}u(t)=Kp​e(t)+Ki​∫0t​e(τ)dτ+Kd​dtde​ Each term has a personality. P (proportional) reacts to the error now. Big error, big push. Like a spring pulling you to the goal. Too little gives sluggishness and leaves a steady-state error under load; too much causes oscillation. I (integral) reacts to the error's history. A small error that lasts keeps adding up until the push is big enough to remove it. It eliminates steady-state error but can add overshoot and, as we will see, windup. D (derivative) reacts to how fast the error changes. It acts like a shock absorber: it predicts where you are heading and brakes early. It reduces overshoot but amplifies sensor noise. P is the spring, D is the damper, I is the patience Think of a mass on a spring with a damper. P is the spring stiffness, D is the damping, and I is a slowly growing force that wins against any constant disturbance, such as gravity or a heavy payload.

To practise safely we simulate a DC motor with a voltage input and shaft angle output. Electrically, the armature current is i=(V−Keω)/Ri = (V - K_e\omega)/Ri=(V−Ke​ω)/R, where KeωK_e\omegaKe​ω is the back-EMF (the motor acts as a generator that opposes the voltage). The torque is KtiK_t iKt​i, and the rotor obeys Jω˙=Kti−bω−τloadJ\dot\omega = K_t i - b\omega - \tau_{\text{load}}Jω˙=Kt​i−bω−τload​. The code below integrates this with a small time step. Then comes the controller, built the way real firmware builds it. Two practical touches are included from the start, and both are explained below the code: a filtered derivative on the measurement, and anti-windup by conditional integration. pid_motor.py import numpy as np class DCMotor: """A DC motor + gearbox lumped into a few parameters. Voltage in, shaft angle out.""" def __init__(self, J=0.01, b=0.1, Kt=0.05, R=1.0, Ke=0.05): self.J, self.b, self.Kt, self.R, self.Ke = J, b, Kt, R, Ke self.theta = 0.0 # shaft angle (rad) self.omega = 0.0 # shaft speed (rad/s) def step(self, volts, dt, load_torque=0.0): current = (volts - self.Ke * self.omega) / self.R torque = self.Kt * current - load_torque alpha = (torque - self.b * self.omega) / self.J self.omega += alpha * dt self.theta += self.omega * dt return self.theta class PID: def __init__(self, kp, ki, kd, out_limit=12.0, dt=0.001, anti_windup=True, tau_d=0.01): self.kp, self.ki, self.kd = kp, ki, kd self.limit = out_limit # the supply voltage: the actuator cannot do more self.dt = dt self.anti_windup = anti_windup self.tau_d = tau_d # derivative filter time constant (s) self.integral = 0.0 self.prev_meas = None self.d_filtered = 0.0 def update(self, setpoint, measurement): error = setpoint - measurement # Derivative on the MEASUREMENT (not the error) so a setpoint jump does not # cause a huge spike, then low-pass filtered to tame sensor noise. if self.prev_meas is None: self.prev_meas = measurement raw_d = -(measurement - self.prev_meas) / self.dt alpha = self.dt / (self.tau_d + self.dt) self.d_filtered += alpha * (raw_d - self.d_filtered) self.prev_meas = measurement unsaturated = self.kp * error + self.integral + self.kd * self.d_filtered output = float(np.clip(unsaturated, -self.limit, self.limit)) # Conditional integration: only keep adding to the integral if the output is # not saturated, or if the error is trying to pull the output back out of it. saturated = output != unsaturated if (not self.anti_windup) or (not saturated) or (error * unsaturated < 0): self.integral += self.ki * error * self.dt return output def run(pid, motor, setpoint=1.0, t_end=3.0, dt=0.001, load=0.0, load_time=1.5): """Simulate; apply a constant load torque after load_time. Returns the angle history.""" n = int(t_end / dt) history = np.zeros(n) for i in range(n): volts = pid.update(setpoint, motor.theta) extra = load if i * dt > load_time else 0.0 motor.step(volts, dt, load_torque=extra) history[i] = motor.theta return history def metrics(history, setpoint=1.0, dt=0.001): overshoot = max(0.0, (history.max() - setpoint) / setpoint * 100.0) outside = np.where(np.abs(history - setpoint) > 0.02 * setpoint)[0] settle = (outside[-1] + 1) * dt if len(outside) else 0.0 return overshoot, settle, abs(setpoint - history[-1]) if __name__ == "__main__": configs = { "P only": (20.0, 0.0, 0.0), "PD": (20.0, 0.0, 1.5), "PID": (20.0, 10.0, 1.5), } print(f"{'controller':<8} {'overshoot %':>12} {'settle (s)':>11} {'final error':>12}") for name, (kp, ki, kd) in configs.items(): history = run(PID(kp, ki, kd), DCMotor(), load=0.05) os_, settle, err = metrics(history) print(f"{name:<8} {os_:12.2f} {settle:11.3f} {err:12.4f}") Run it. A load of 0.05 N·m hits the motor at 1.5 s. Look at the final error column: with P or PD the motor ends up slightly short of the goal because the spring term needs a persistent error to produce the holding voltage. With the integral term the error is far smaller and still shrinking when the run ends (give it more time and it reaches zero). That is the integral's whole job.

There is theory for tuning (Ziegler-Nichols, loop shaping, model-based design), but a patient engineer with a plot can tune by hand using the personalities above. Start with Ki=Kd=0K_i = K_d = 0Ki​=Kd​=0. Raise KpK_pKp​ until the response is fast but overshoots a bit. Add KdK_dKd​ until the overshoot shrinks to acceptable levels. If the output gets jittery, lower KdK_dKd​ or raise the derivative filter's time constant. Add KiK_iKi​ slowly, just enough to remove the steady-state error in the time you can afford. Too much brings back overshoot. Test with disturbances, not just step moves: a load, a payload change, a bump. Read the response with three numbers: overshoot (how far past the goal), settling time (when it stays within a small band, often 2 percent), and steady-state error (what remains forever). Speed, smoothness and accuracy trade against each other, and the right balance depends on your robot. Pro tip Tune in the same control loop rate that you will deploy. A controller tuned at 1 kHz can go unstable at 100 Hz, because the delay between measuring and acting grew.

Real actuators saturate: a 12 V supply cannot give 40 V. While the output is stuck at its limit, the error stays large, and a naive integral term keeps accumulating, "winding up" a huge value. When the robot finally reaches the goal, the stored integral keeps pushing it past, causing big overshoot. Anti-windup stops that. Our code uses conditional integration: skip integrating while the output is saturated (unless the error would pull it back). Other methods include clamping the integral and "back-calculation". You can see the effect by commanding a large move: windup_demo.py from pid_motor import PID, DCMotor, run, metrics big_move = 30.0 # rad: the 12 V supply saturates for a long time for anti_windup in (False, True): history = run(PID(20.0, 60.0, 1.0, anti_windup=anti_windup), DCMotor(), setpoint=big_move, t_end=6.0) overshoot, _, final_error = metrics(history, setpoint=big_move) print(f"anti_windup={anti_windup!s:<5} overshoot {overshoot:5.1f} % final error {final_error:.3f} rad") Without anti-windup the motor overshoots by many percent. With it, the overshoot nearly vanishes.

Real joints rarely use one loop. They nest several, each faster than the one outside it: This is cascaded control. The inner current loop makes the motor behave like a clean torque source. The velocity loop above it makes speed follow its command. The position loop at the top makes the angle follow the goal. Each loop sees a simpler system below it, and the inner loops can reject disturbances (a sudden load) before they reach the outer one. The rule of thumb: each inner loop should be several times faster than the one it serves.
documents.s: Beyond a single loop: cascaded control

documents.t: Position control tries to reach a point no matter what. That is dangerous when the robot touches things: a stiff controller will push through a person's hand or a fragile object. Impedance control instead gives the hand the behaviour of a virtual spring and damper: F=K (xd−x)+D (x˙d−x˙)F = K\,(x_d - x) + D\,(\dot x_d - \dot x)F=K(xd​−x)+D(x˙d​−x˙) where KKK is the stiffness and DDD the damping. Using τ=JTF\tau = J^{\mathsf T}Fτ=JTF from the dynamics lesson, you can turn this hand force into joint torques. Low stiffness makes the robot soft and compliant; high stiffness makes it precise. Collaborative robots, legged robots, and almost any robot that must touch the world use some version of this idea.
documents.s: Impedance control: making a robot behave like a spring

documents.t: You will tune the controller and see what each term does. Save pid_motor.py and run it. Record overshoot, settling time and final error for each controller. Change PID(20, 10, 1.5) to a higher proportional gain, such as 50. What happens to overshoot and to the noise in the derivative term? (Print np.std(np.diff(history)) as a quick roughness measure.) Make the derivative unfiltered by setting tau_d=1e-6, and add measurement noise: replace motor.theta with motor.theta + np.random.normal(0, 0.002) inside run. What does the voltage output look like? Save windup_demo.py and confirm the effect of anti-windup. Try an integral gain of 100. Open question: lower the loop rate by calling the PID every 10 ms instead of every 1 ms. Does the same tuning still behave? You know it worked when you can predict, before running, whether a change to KpK_pKp​, KiK_iKi​ or KdK_dKd​ will make the response faster, smoother or more accurate, and the plots or metrics agree.

Spot the controllerBeginner A robot arm reaches its target but sags 3 degrees below it whenever it holds a heavy tool. Which PID term fixes that, and why? Show solutionHide solution The integral term. A constant disturbance (gravity on the tool) needs a constant holding torque. A P-only controller only produces that torque if a constant error remains. The integral accumulates the small error until the holding torque is supplied, driving the error to zero. Why measure, not error, in the D term?Intermediate When the operator suddenly changes the setpoint from 0 to 1, what happens to a derivative computed on the error, and why does the code differentiate the measurement instead? Show solutionHide solution The error jumps from 0 to 1 in a single step, so de/dtde/dtde/dt is enormous for one sample: a "derivative kick" that slams the actuator. The measurement does not jump (the motor has inertia), so differentiating it avoids the spike. In steady operation the two are the same except for sign, because e=r−ye = r - ye=r−y and the reference is constant between changes. Conditional integration by handAdvanced Describe in words what the code in update does with error * unsaturated < 0, and why that condition is needed. Show solutionHide solution When the output is saturated the integrator is normally frozen. But if the error has the opposite sign from the unsaturated output (for example, the output is stuck at +12 V but the error has gone negative because we overshot), then integrating would help pull the output out of saturation, so the code allows it. Without that exception the integrator could stay frozen while the robot overshoots, and the output would never come off its limit.

1Which statement best describes why feedback beats open-loop control on real robots? AFeedback needs no sensorsBFeedback measures the result and corrects errors from disturbances and modelling mistakesCOpen loop is always less accurate in simulationDFeedback makes the robot lighter 2Which PID term eliminates a steady-state error caused by a constant load? AProportionalBIntegralCDerivativeDNone of them 3What is integral windup? AThe integral term growing very large while the actuator is saturated, causing overshoot laterBA motor winding that overheatsCNoise in the derivative termDA sensor that stops updating 4What does impedance control make a robot behave like? AA rigid position sourceBA virtual spring and damper at the handCAn open-loop systemDA thermostat 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Feedback control measures the output and corrects the error, which is how robots cope with disturbances and unknowns. PID adds three behaviours: P is the spring, I removes steady-state error, D damps and predicts. Tune step by step (P, then D, then I) and test with disturbances, judging overshoot, settling time and steady-state error. Anti-windup, derivative on measurement and a filtered derivative are standard practice, not extras. Real joints nest fast inner loops (current, velocity) inside slower outer ones (position). Impedance control gives a robot a tunable spring and damper at the hand so that it can touch the world safely. Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

Modern Robotics, chapters 9 to 11: trajectory generation, motion control and force control, including impedance. Brian Douglas, Control Systems Lectures (YouTube): clear visual explanations of feedback and PID. Next: ROS 2 architecture and DDS

Intermediate40 minBefore this:Forward and inverse kinematics · Newton’s laws · NumPy A robot arm holds a 2 kg weight straight out. Nobody is moving it, yet the shoulder motor is working hard and getting warm. Now the arm swings fast and the elbow motor suddenly struggles even though the weight has not changed. Kinematics cannot explain either fact. Dynamics can: it connects the torques your motors produce to the motion you get, and it tells you which motor to buy. You will be able to Explain what rigid-body dynamics adds to kinematics and state Newton-Euler and Lagrange approaches in words. Read the manipulator equation M(q)q¨+C(q,q˙)q˙+g(q)=τM(q)\ddot q + C(q,\dot q)\dot q + g(q) = \tauM(q)q¨​+C(q,q˙​)q˙​+g(q)=τ term by term. Compute the mass matrix, Coriolis and gravity terms for a 2-link arm in NumPy. Use forward and inverse dynamics, and check a motion against joint torque limits.

Dynamicsthe study of how forces and torques cause motion, taking mass and inertia into account answers two practical questions. Inverse dynamics: given the motion I want (positions, velocities, accelerations), which joint torques do I need? Used for control, for sizing motors, and for checking a plan is feasible. Forward dynamics: given the torques I apply, how will the robot move? Used by every physics simulator, including the ones in the simulation module. Both come from one equation. Before we meet it, build the intuition for the forces that appear.

Newton's law for a body is F=maF = maF=ma. Its rotating twin, Euler's law, is τ=Iα\tau = I\alphaτ=Iα (torque equals rotational inertia times angular acceleration). The moment of inertiathe rotational analogue of mass: how hard it is to change an object’s spinning speed about a given axis III depends on both the mass and how far from the axis it sits. A long arm is much harder to spin than the same mass held close to the shoulder. The Newton-Euler method applies these two laws link by link. A forward pass starts at the base and works outward, computing each link's velocity and acceleration. A backward pass starts at the hand and works inward, computing the force and torque each joint must supply to produce that motion and carry the links beyond it. It is efficient, running in time proportional to the number of joints, and it is what most real-time dynamics libraries use. The Lagrange method reaches the same equations from energy. Write down the kinetic energy KKK and potential energy UUU, form L=K−UL = K - UL=K−U, and apply a derivative recipe. It gives neat symbolic equations for small arms, which is why we use it by hand here.

For any serial arm the result has the same shape: M(q) q¨+C(q,q˙) q˙+g(q)=τM(q)\,\ddot q + C(q,\dot q)\,\dot q + g(q) = \tauM(q)q¨​+C(q,q˙​)q˙​+g(q)=τ Each term has a meaning you can feel. M(q) q¨M(q)\,\ddot qM(q)q¨​: inertia. MMM is the mass matrixa symmetric, positive-definite matrix describing the arm’s effective inertia as seen at each joint, which depends on the arm’s posture. It changes with posture: an extended arm has more inertia about the shoulder than a folded one. C(q,q˙) q˙C(q,\dot q)\,\dot qC(q,q˙​)q˙​: velocity-dependent forces. Centrifugal forces (a spinning link wants to fly outward) and Coriolis forces (swinging one joint pushes on another). They grow with the square of speed. g(q)g(q)g(q): gravity. The torque needed just to hold the arm still. It depends on posture but not on speed. τ\tauτ: the joint torques your motors supply. (Real arms also have joint friction, which we leave out for clarity.) Gravity is often the biggest term For a slow arm, q¨\ddot qq¨​ and q˙\dot qq˙​ are small, so almost all the torque goes into holding the arm against gravity. That is why shoulder motors are the biggest, why brakes matter, and why a good controller always adds a gravity-compensation term g(q)g(q)g(q).

Take a planar arm moving in a vertical plane, with link masses m1m_1m1​, m2m_2m2​, lengths l1l_1l1​, l2l_2l2​, centres of mass at distances lc1l_{c1}lc1​, lc2l_{c2}lc2​ from each joint, and inertias I1I_1I1​, I2I_2I2​ about those centres. Joint angles are measured from the horizontal. Using the Lagrange method, the pieces are M(q)=[m11m12m12m22]M(q) = \begin{bmatrix} m_{11} & m_{12} \\ m_{12} & m_{22} \end{bmatrix}M(q)=[m11​m12​​m12​m22​​] with m11=m1lc12+m2(l12+lc22+2l1lc2cos⁡q2)+I1+I2m12=m2(lc22+l1lc2cos⁡q2)+I2m22=m2lc22+I2\begin{aligned} m_{11} &= m_1 l_{c1}^2 + m_2\bigl(l_1^2 + l_{c2}^2 + 2 l_1 l_{c2}\cos q_2\bigr) + I_1 + I_2 \\ m_{12} &= m_2\bigl(l_{c2}^2 + l_1 l_{c2}\cos q_2\bigr) + I_2 \\ m_{22} &= m_2 l_{c2}^2 + I_2 \end{aligned}m11​m12​m22​​=m1​lc12​+m2​(l12​+lc22​+2l1​lc2​cosq2​)+I1​+I2​=m2​(lc22​+l1​lc2​cosq2​)+I2​=m2​lc22​+I2​​ and, defining h=−m2l1lc2sin⁡q2h = -m_2 l_1 l_{c2}\sin q_2h=−m2​l1​lc2​sinq2​, C(q,q˙)=[hq˙2h(q˙1+q˙2)−hq˙10],g(q)=[(m1lc1+m2l1) gcos⁡q1+m2lc2 gcos⁡(q1+q2)m2lc2 gcos⁡(q1+q2)]C(q,\dot q) = \begin{bmatrix} h\dot q_2 & h(\dot q_1 + \dot q_2) \\ -h\dot q_1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad g(q) = \begin{bmatrix} (m_1 l_{c1} + m_2 l_1)\,g\cos q_1 + m_2 l_{c2}\,g\cos(q_1+q_2) \\ m_2 l_{c2}\,g\cos(q_1+q_2) \end{bmatrix}C(q,q˙​)=[hq˙​2​−hq˙​1​​h(q˙​1​+q˙​2​)0​],g(q)=[(m1​lc1​+m2​l1​)gcosq1​+m2​lc2​gcos(q1​+q2​)m2​lc2​gcos(q1​+q2​)​] Three observations. MMM is symmetric. Its off-diagonal term couples the joints: accelerating joint 2 needs torque at joint 1. And ggg is largest when the arm is horizontal (cos⁡0=1\cos 0 = 1cos0=1) and zero when it points straight up or down. dynamics.py import numpy as np m1, m2 = 2.0, 1.5 # link masses (kg) l1, l2 = 0.4, 0.3 # link lengths (m) lc1, lc2 = l1 / 2, l2 / 2 # centre of mass at the middle of each rod I1 = m1 * l1**2 / 12 # thin-rod inertia about the centre I2 = m2 * l2**2 / 12 G = 9.81 def mass_matrix(q): c2 = np.cos(q[1]) m11 = m1 * lc1**2 + m2 * (l1**2 + lc2**2 + 2 * l1 * lc2 * c2) + I1 + I2 m12 = m2 * (lc2**2 + l1 * lc2 * c2) + I2 m22 = m2 * lc2**2 + I2 return np.array([[m11, m12], [m12, m22]]) def coriolis(q, qd): h = -m2 * l1 * lc2 * np.sin(q[1]) return np.array([[h * qd[1], h * (qd[0] + qd[1])], [-h * qd[0], 0.0]]) def gravity(q): g1 = (m1 * lc1 + m2 * l1) * G * np.cos(q[0]) + m2 * lc2 * G * np.cos(q[0] + q[1]) g2 = m2 * lc2 * G * np.cos(q[0] + q[1]) return np.array([g1, g2]) def inverse_dynamics(q, qd, qdd): """Torques needed to produce acceleration qdd at state (q, qd).""" return mass_matrix(q) @ qdd + coriolis(q, qd) @ qd + gravity(q) def forward_dynamics(q, qd, tau): """Acceleration produced by torques tau at state (q, qd).""" return np.linalg.solve(mass_matrix(q), tau - coriolis(q, qd) @ qd - gravity(q)) if __name__ == "__main__": q = np.array([0.5, 0.8]) qd = np.array([1.0, -0.5]) qdd = np.array([2.0, 1.0]) tau = inverse_dynamics(q, qd, qdd) print("torques needed:", np.round(tau, 3), "N·m") print("forward dynamics recovers qdd:", np.allclose(forward_dynamics(q, qd, tau), qdd)) print("holding torque, arm horizontal:", np.round(gravity(np.array([0.0, 0.0])), 3), "N·m") print("mass matrix eigenvalues (all > 0):", np.round(np.linalg.eigvalsh(mass_matrix(q)), 4)) The round trip, inverse then forward dynamics, returning the same acceleration is a useful self-test for any dynamics code you write or import.

Because you now have g(q)g(q)g(q) and M(q)M(q)M(q), you can cancel the arm's own dynamics. Suppose a simple controller asks for a desired acceleration aaa (computed from position error, as in the next lesson). The computed-torque command is τ=M(q) a+C(q,q˙) q˙+g(q)\tau = M(q)\,a + C(q,\dot q)\,\dot q + g(q)τ=M(q)a+C(q,q˙​)q˙​+g(q) Plugging it into the manipulator equation gives q¨=a\ddot q = aq¨​=a: the nonlinear arm now behaves like a pile of simple, independent joints that obey whatever aaa you ask for. This is called feedback linearisation. It depends on a good model: wrong masses mean imperfect cancellation, which is one reason real controllers keep feedback on top.

Often you care about a force on the hand: pressing a sponge on a table, pushing a door. The Jacobian from the last lesson converts a hand force FFF into the joint torques that produce it: τ=J(q)TF\tau = J(q)^{\mathsf T} Fτ=J(q)TF This is the same Jacobian, transposed. It also explains a useful fact about singularities: in the direction the arm cannot move, a hand force needs almost no joint torque, because the stiff straight links carry the load. A stretched arm can brace hard, but it cannot move or sense gently in that direction. The relationship is also the basis of the impedance control you will meet at the end of this module.

Every motor and gearbox has a peak torque (short bursts) and a continuous torque (what it can supply indefinitely without overheating). Dynamics lets you check a motion against them before you run it. If the holding torque g(q)g(q)g(q) alone exceeds the continuous rating, the joint will overheat even when "standing still". Fast motions raise Cq˙C\dot qCq˙​ and Mq¨M\ddot qMq¨​. Doubling the speed of a swing roughly quadruples the Coriolis torque. A payload adds to the mass of the last link. Many arms specify torque-limited payload versus reach curves: carrying more at a longer reach demands more shoulder torque. A planner that ignores torque limits can produce a path that is geometrically perfect and physically impossible. Time-optimal trajectory methods, such as time-optimal path parameterisation, bake these limits into the speed profile for exactly this reason. Warning Never run a new, fast motion on a real arm without first checking it against the torque and speed limits, either in simulation or with a slow trial. A joint that saturates in the middle of a fast move can make the arm deviate from the planned path suddenly.
documents.s: Torque limits and what they mean

documents.t: You will size the motors for a motion. Save dynamics.py and run it. Confirm the round trip prints True. Write a function tau_for_trajectory that takes joint paths q(t)q(t)q(t) sampled at 100 Hz for 2 seconds, going from q=(0,0)q = (0, 0)q=(0,0) to q=(1.2,0.8)q = (1.2, 0.8)q=(1.2,0.8) with a smooth cubic profile q(t)=q0+(qf−q0)(3s2−2s3)q(t) = q_0 + (q_f - q_0)(3s^2 - 2s^3)q(t)=q0​+(qf​−q0​)(3s2−2s3) where s=t/2s = t/2s=t/2. Compute q˙\dot qq˙​ and q¨\ddot qq¨​ analytically or with np.gradient. For each sample, call inverse_dynamics, and print the peak absolute torque on each joint. Add a 1 kg payload by increasing m2 by 1.0 and re-running. How much did the peak shoulder torque rise? Pretend the shoulder motor's peak rating is 20 N·m. Does your motion respect it? If not, lengthen the motion time and re-check. You know it worked when the shoulder peak torque rises noticeably with the payload and drops when you slow the motion down.

Holding torqueBeginner A uniform rod of mass 2 kg and length 0.5 m is held horizontally by a motor at one end. What static torque is needed? Show solutionHide solution The weight acts at the centre, 0.25 m from the joint, so τ=mg l/2=2×9.81×0.25≈4.9\tau = m g\, l/2 = 2 \times 9.81 \times 0.25 \approx 4.9τ=mgl/2=2×9.81×0.25≈4.9 N·m. If the rod points straight up, the torque falls to zero (ignoring friction), because the weight line passes through the joint. Which term dominates?Intermediate Using dynamics.py, evaluate the three torque contributions separately at q=(0.5,0.8)q = (0.5, 0.8)q=(0.5,0.8) for q˙=(0.2,0.1)\dot q = (0.2, 0.1)q˙​=(0.2,0.1), q¨=(0.5,0.5)\ddot q = (0.5, 0.5)q¨​=(0.5,0.5), then again with q˙=(3,2)\dot q = (3, 2)q˙​=(3,2). Describe how the shares change. Show solutionHide solution Compute mass_matrix(q) @ qdd, coriolis(q, qd) @ qd and gravity(q) separately. At slow speed gravity dominates and the Coriolis term is tiny. At the faster speed the velocities are 15 to 20 times larger, and because the Coriolis term grows with velocity squared it becomes a couple of hundred times larger, while gravity stays unchanged. The lesson: gravity matters at rest and slow speed, velocity terms matter during fast motion. Why is M symmetric and positive definite?Advanced Give a physical reason that every eigenvalue of M(q)M(q)M(q) must be positive. Show solutionHide solution The kinetic energy of the arm is K=12q˙TM(q) q˙K = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot q^{\mathsf T} M(q)\,\dot qK=21​q˙​TM(q)q˙​. Any real motion of a body with mass has strictly positive kinetic energy, so q˙TMq˙>0\dot q^{\mathsf T}M\dot q > 0q˙​TMq˙​>0 for every nonzero q˙\dot qq˙​. That is the definition of positive definite. It also guarantees MMM is invertible, which is why forward dynamics can always solve for q¨\ddot qq¨​.

1In M(q) q̈ + C(q, q̇) q̇ + g(q) = τ, which term holds the arm still against gravity? AM(q) q̈BC(q, q̇) q̇Cg(q)Dτ is not related to holding 2What is inverse dynamics? AComputing motion from torquesBComputing the torques needed for a given motionCComputing hand pose from joint anglesDComputing joint angles from a hand pose 3Why does the mass matrix depend on the arm’s posture? ABecause mass changes as the arm movesBBecause inertia depends on how far masses are from each joint axisCBecause motors weigh more when hotDIt does not depend on posture 4A good reason to add g(q) to a controller’s output is to… AMake the arm fasterBCancel the arm’s own weight so feedback only handles errorsCReplace the sensorsDReduce the number of joints 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Dynamics links joint torques to motion; kinematics alone cannot say what a motor must supply. The manipulator equation has inertia, velocity-dependent, and gravity terms plus the applied torque. Inverse dynamics gives torques for a desired motion; forward dynamics gives motion from torques and powers simulators. Gravity is usually the largest torque for slow motions; velocity terms grow with speed squared. The mass matrix is symmetric and positive definite, and depends on posture. Check planned motions against continuous and peak torque limits before running them on hardware. Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

Modern Robotics, chapter 8 (dynamics of open chains): Lagrange and Newton-Euler in depth. Pinocchio documentation: rigid-body algorithms (RNEA, CRBA) that compute these terms for any robot. Featherstone, Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms: the standard reference for efficient dynamics. Next: Control and PID

Intermediate45 minBefore this:Frames and rigid transforms · NumPy · Basic calculus (derivatives) You tell a robot arm "put the gripper at the cup". The arm does not understand positions in space; its motors only understand joint angles. Turning a joint-angle recipe into a hand position is easy. Turning a desired hand position into a joint-angle recipe is the real work, and it is called inverse kinematics. Every pick-and-place, every humanoid footstep and every animated character relies on it. You will be able to Define forward kinematics, the Jacobian and inverse kinematics, and say how they relate. Compute forward kinematics for a 2-link planar arm and describe the idea behind DH and product-of-exponentials for 6-DOF arms. Derive and code the analytic inverse kinematics of a 2-link arm, including the two solutions. Build the Jacobian and use damped least squares to solve IK numerically in NumPy. Recognise singularities and explain why damping helps near them.

Kinematicsthe study of motion by geometry alone, ignoring the forces and masses that cause it asks only "where is everything?", never "what force is needed?". Two questions define the field: Forward kinematics (FK): given joint values qqq, where is the end effector (the hand or tool)? Always has exactly one answer. Inverse kinematics (IK): given a desired hand pose, which joint values qqq achieve it? May have zero, one, several or infinitely many answers. A degree of freedom (DOF)the number of independent motions a mechanism can make; for a serial arm it usually equals the number of joints is one independent way to move. A planar 2-link arm has 2 DOF. A typical industrial arm has 6, which is the minimum needed to place a hand at any position and orientation in 3D.

Two rigid links of lengths l1l_1l1​ and l2l_2l2​ rotate in a plane. Joint 1 turns link 1 by q1q_1q1​ from the xxx-axis. Joint 2 turns link 2 by q2q_2q2​ relative to link 1. The hand position is the sum of the two link vectors: x=l1cos⁡q1+l2cos⁡(q1+q2),y=l1sin⁡q1+l2sin⁡(q1+q2)x = l_1\cos q_1 + l_2\cos(q_1+q_2), \qquad y = l_1\sin q_1 + l_2\sin(q_1+q_2)x=l1​cosq1​+l2​cos(q1​+q2​),y=l1​sinq1​+l2​sin(q1​+q2​) This is forward kinematics. Notice the absolute angle of link 2 is q1+q2q_1 + q_2q1​+q2​: angles accumulate down the chain, exactly like composing transforms in the previous lesson.

For a general arm you chain one transform per joint: 0Tn(q)=0T1(q1) 1T2(q2)⋯n−1Tn(qn){}^{0}T_{n}(q) = {}^{0}T_{1}(q_1)\;{}^{1}T_{2}(q_2)\cdots{}^{n-1}T_{n}(q_n)0Tn​(q)=0T1​(q1​)1T2​(q2​)⋯n−1Tn​(qn​) Two systematic recipes describe each link: Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) parameters describe each joint with four numbers (link length, link twist, link offset, joint angle). It is compact and in textbooks everywhere, but the frame-placement rules are fiddly and there are several conventions. Product of exponentials (PoE) describes the robot in its home pose with one matrix MMM and each joint by a screw axis Si\mathcal{S}_iSi​ (a rotation axis plus a point on it): T(q)=e[S1]q1 e[S2]q2⋯e[Sn]qn MT(q) = e^{[\mathcal{S}_1]q_1}\,e^{[\mathcal{S}_2]q_2}\cdots e^{[\mathcal{S}_n]q_n}\,MT(q)=e[S1​]q1​e[S2​]q2​⋯e[Sn​]qn​M PoE needs only a single fixed base frame and no per-link frames, which is why many modern libraries prefer it. In practice you will rarely compute either by hand: a robot's URDF file (you will write one in the ROS 2 module) stores the joint geometry, and a library such as KDL, Pinocchio or MoveIt does the chain multiplication for you. What matters is that you understand what it is doing.
documents.s: For six joints: DH and product of exponentials

documents.t: Differentiating forward kinematics gives the Jacobianthe matrix of partial derivatives that maps joint velocities to end-effector velocity J(q)J(q)J(q): x˙=J(q) q˙\dot{x} = J(q)\,\dot{q}x˙=J(q)q˙​ For our 2-link arm, differentiate xxx and yyy with respect to q1q_1q1​ and q2q_2q2​: J(q)=[−l1sin⁡q1−l2sin⁡(q1+q2)−l2sin⁡(q1+q2)l1cos⁡q1+l2cos⁡(q1+q2)l2cos⁡(q1+q2)]J(q) = \begin{bmatrix} -l_1\sin q_1 - l_2\sin(q_1+q_2) & -l_2\sin(q_1+q_2) \\ l_1\cos q_1 + l_2\cos(q_1+q_2) & l_2\cos(q_1+q_2) \end{bmatrix}J(q)=[−l1​sinq1​−l2​sin(q1​+q2​)l1​cosq1​+l2​cos(q1​+q2​)​−l2​sin(q1​+q2​)l2​cos(q1​+q2​)​] The Jacobian is the workhorse of robotics. It converts speeds, it converts forces too (joint torques are τ=JTF\tau = J^{\mathsf T} Fτ=JTF, which you will meet again in the dynamics lesson), and it tells you when the arm is in trouble. The Jacobian is a local linear map Forward kinematics is curved and nonlinear. Near any one configuration, though, tiny joint changes produce tiny hand changes in a linear way: Δx≈J Δq\Delta x \approx J\,\Delta qΔx≈JΔq. Almost every IK method is built by repeatedly using this straight-line approximation to take small steps toward a goal.
documents.s: The Jacobian: how joint speeds become hand speeds

documents.t: For the planar arm, det⁡J=l1l2sin⁡q2\det J = l_1 l_2 \sin q_2detJ=l1​l2​sinq2​. When q2=0q_2 = 0q2​=0 (arm fully stretched) or q2=πq_2 = \piq2​=π (folded back), the determinant is zero and JJJ cannot be inverted. These are singularities. At a stretched arm the hand cannot move radially outward, no matter how the joints move, so a whole direction of motion is lost. Worse, asking for motion in that direction demands huge joint speeds. Singularities are why robots sometimes whip a joint violently when a path passes through full extension.
documents.s: Singularities: where the arm loses a direction

documents.t: For a target (x,y)(x, y)(x,y), use the law of cosines on the triangle formed by the two links. Let r2=x2+y2r^2 = x^2 + y^2r2=x2+y2. cos⁡q2=r2−l12−l222 l1l2\cos q_2 = \frac{r^2 - l_1^2 - l_2^2}{2\,l_1 l_2}cosq2​=2l1​l2​r2−l12​−l22​​ If the right-hand side is outside [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1], the target is out of reach. Otherwise sin⁡q2=±1−cos⁡2q2\sin q_2 = \pm\sqrt{1 - \cos^2 q_2}sinq2​=±1−cos2q2​​, and the two signs are the two solutions: the elbow bends one way or the other. Then q1=atan2⁡(y,x)−atan2⁡(l2sin⁡q2, l1+l2cos⁡q2)q_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x) - \operatorname{atan2}\bigl(l_2\sin q_2,\; l_1 + l_2\cos q_2\bigr)q1​=atan2(y,x)−atan2(l2​sinq2​,l1​+l2​cosq2​) Use atan2 everywhere, never plain atan; it keeps the correct quadrant. two_link.py import numpy as np L1, L2 = 0.4, 0.3 # link lengths in metres def fk(q): q1, q2 = q x = L1 * np.cos(q1) + L2 * np.cos(q1 + q2) y = L1 * np.sin(q1) + L2 * np.sin(q1 + q2) return np.array([x, y]) def jacobian(q): q1, q2 = q s1, c1 = np.sin(q1), np.cos(q1) s12, c12 = np.sin(q1 + q2), np.cos(q1 + q2) return np.array([ [-L1 * s1 - L2 * s12, -L2 * s12], [ L1 * c1 + L2 * c12, L2 * c12], ]) def ik_analytic(x, y, elbow_positive=True): """Both closed-form solutions; elbow_positive picks q2 > 0.""" r2 = x * x + y * y c2 = (r2 - L1**2 - L2**2) / (2 * L1 * L2) if abs(c2) > 1.0: raise ValueError("target is out of reach") s2 = np.sqrt(1.0 - c2 * c2) * (1.0 if elbow_positive else -1.0) q2 = np.arctan2(s2, c2) q1 = np.arctan2(y, x) - np.arctan2(L2 * s2, L1 + L2 * c2) return np.array([q1, q2]) if __name__ == "__main__": target = np.array([0.35, 0.25]) for positive in (True, False): q = ik_analytic(*target, elbow_positive=positive) print(f"q = {np.round(q, 4)} -> fk = {np.round(fk(q), 4)}") # check the Jacobian against a numerical derivative q = np.array([0.3, 0.8]) eps = 1e-6 J_num = np.column_stack([(fk(q + eps * e) - fk(q - eps * e)) / (2 * eps) for e in np.eye(2)]) print("Jacobian ok:", np.allclose(J_num, jacobian(q), atol=1e-6)) print("det J =", round(np.linalg.det(jacobian(q)), 5), " l1*l2*sin(q2) =", round(L1 * L2 * np.sin(q[1]), 5)) Run it: both solutions land the hand on (0.35,0.25)(0.35, 0.25)(0.35,0.25), one with the elbow bent each way. This is a real feature of IK, not a bug. A controller must pick one, usually the one closest to the current joint angles so the arm does not flip. Analytic IK is fast and exact, but only exists in closed form for special geometries. Many 6-DOF industrial arms are deliberately built with three wrist axes meeting at a point so that a closed form exists. For arbitrary arms, and for arms with more than 6 joints, we iterate.
documents.s: Analytic inverse kinematics for the 2-link arm

documents.t: Idea: stand at the current guess qqq, measure the error e=xtarget−fk(q)e = x_{\text{target}} - \text{fk}(q)e=xtarget​−fk(q), and use the Jacobian to find a joint step Δq\Delta qΔq with JΔq≈eJ\Delta q \approx eJΔq≈e. Then repeat. The naive step is Δq=J−1e\Delta q = J^{-1}eΔq=J−1e, or J+eJ^{+}eJ+e with a pseudo-inverse. Near a singularity J−1J^{-1}J−1 explodes. The fix is damped least squares (the Levenberg-Marquardt idea): minimise the error and the step size together, Δq=JT(JJT+λ2I)−1e\Delta q = J^{\mathsf T}\bigl(JJ^{\mathsf T} + \lambda^2 I\bigr)^{-1} eΔq=JT(JJT+λ2I)−1e The damping λ\lambdaλ is a small positive number. When JJJ is healthy, the damping barely matters. When JJJ is nearly singular, the damping caps the step, trading a little accuracy for a lot of stability. ik_dls.py import numpy as np from two_link import fk, jacobian def ik_dls(target, q0, damping=0.05, tol=1e-6, max_iter=200): """Damped least squares IK. Returns (q, iterations used).""" q = np.array(q0, dtype=float) for i in range(max_iter): err = target - fk(q) if np.linalg.norm(err) < tol: return q, i J = jacobian(q) # Solve (J J^T + lambda^2 I) y = err instead of forming an inverse. y = np.linalg.solve(J @ J.T + damping**2 * np.eye(J.shape[0]), err) q = q + J.T @ y return q, max_iter if __name__ == "__main__": target = np.array([0.35, 0.25]) q, n = ik_dls(target, q0=[0.1, 0.1]) print(f"reachable target: converged in {n} iterations, error {np.linalg.norm(target - fk(q)):.2e}") # Just past the arm's reach (l1 + l2 = 0.7): damping stops the joints from blowing up. far = np.array([0.75, 0.0]) q, n = ik_dls(far, q0=[0.1, 0.1]) print(f"unreachable target: used {n} iterations, joints stay finite: {np.round(q, 3)}") print("closest the hand gets:", np.round(fk(q), 3)) Two things to notice. The solver starts from a guess, so which solution you get depends on where you begin: start the elbow bent positive and you stay on that branch. And for an unreachable target the loop does not crash; it settles as close as the damping allows, which is exactly the graceful behaviour you want on real hardware. Info Real arms add joint limits and the orientation of the hand, so the Jacobian becomes 6×n6 \times n6×n and the error has six components. The loop is the same. Extra DOF (7-joint arms, humanoids) give a null space: motions of the joints that do not move the hand. You can use it to stay away from limits or obstacles.
documents.s: Numerical IK with damped least squares

documents.t: You will make the arm draw a circle with its hand and prove the IK works. Save two_link.py and ik_dls.py in one folder. Write a script that samples 60 points on a circle of radius 0.1 centred at (0.4,0.2)(0.4, 0.2)(0.4,0.2). For each point, solve IK with ik_dls, starting each solve from the previous solution (this keeps you on one elbow branch). For every solution, call fk and assert the position error is below 1e-4. Print the minimum and maximum ∣det⁡J∣|\det J|∣detJ∣ over the path. Is the arm ever close to singular? Optional: use matplotlib to plot the arm links for a few of the frames. You know it worked when all 60 assertions pass and the joint angles change smoothly from one point to the next, with no sudden flips.

Reach and workspaceBeginner For l1=0.4l_1 = 0.4l1​=0.4 and l2=0.3l_2 = 0.3l2​=0.3, what is the farthest the hand can reach, and what is the nearest it can get to the base? Show solutionHide solution Farthest: the arm fully stretched, l1+l2=0.7l_1 + l_2 = 0.7l1​+l2​=0.7 m. Nearest: the arm folded back on itself, ∣l1−l2∣=0.1|l_1 - l_2| = 0.1∣l1​−l2​∣=0.1 m. The reachable workspace is the ring between radii 0.1 m and 0.7 m (ignoring joint limits). Velocity of the handIntermediate At q=(0,π/2)q = (0, \pi/2)q=(0,π/2) with l1=0.4l_1 = 0.4l1​=0.4, l2=0.3l_2 = 0.3l2​=0.3, the joints move at q˙=(1,0)\dot q = (1, 0)q˙​=(1,0) rad/s. What is the hand velocity? Show solutionHide solution At q1=0q_1 = 0q1​=0, q2=π/2q_2 = \pi/2q2​=π/2: sin⁡q1=0\sin q_1 = 0sinq1​=0, cos⁡q1=1\cos q_1 = 1cosq1​=1, sin⁡(q1+q2)=1\sin(q_1+q_2) = 1sin(q1​+q2​)=1, cos⁡(q1+q2)=0\cos(q_1+q_2) = 0cos(q1​+q2​)=0. The first Jacobian column is (−l1⋅0−l2⋅1, l1⋅1+l2⋅0)=(−0.3,0.4)(-l_1\cdot 0 - l_2\cdot 1,\; l_1\cdot 1 + l_2 \cdot 0) = (-0.3, 0.4)(−l1​⋅0−l2​⋅1,l1​⋅1+l2​⋅0)=(−0.3,0.4). With q˙=(1,0)\dot q = (1, 0)q˙​=(1,0) the hand velocity is (−0.3,0.4)(-0.3, 0.4)(−0.3,0.4) m/s. The hand sweeps in a direction perpendicular to the line from the base to the hand, at speed 0.50.50.5 m/s (=== distance 0.5 m times 1 rad/s). Why does the damping term help?Advanced Explain in two or three sentences what happens to the DLS step as λ→0\lambda \to 0λ→0 and as λ→∞\lambda \to \inftyλ→∞. Show solutionHide solution As λ→0\lambda \to 0λ→0 the step becomes the pseudo-inverse step J+eJ^{+}eJ+e: exact but unstable near singularities. As λ→∞\lambda \to \inftyλ→∞ the term JJT+λ2IJJ^{\mathsf T} + \lambda^2 IJJT+λ2I is dominated by λ2I\lambda^2 Iλ2I, so the step shrinks toward JTe/λ2J^{\mathsf T}e/\lambda^2JTe/λ2: very small, safe, but slow (it becomes a scaled gradient step). A moderate λ\lambdaλ gives full-speed steps when healthy and small steps when singular.

1Which statement about forward and inverse kinematics is true? AFK can have several answers; IK always has oneBFK always has one answer; IK can have zero, one, or manyCBoth always have exactly one answerDIK does not need a robot model 2For the 2-link planar arm, when is the Jacobian singular? AWhen q1 = 0BWhen q2 = 0 or q2 = π (stretched or folded)CWhen the arm is at restDNever 3Why use atan2 rather than atan in IK formulas? AIt is fasterBIt returns degreesCIt keeps the correct quadrant using both signsDIt avoids using a square root 4What does the damping term in damped least squares do near a singularity? AIt increases the step sizeBIt removes the JacobianCIt limits the size of the joint step so the solver stays stableDIt makes the target reachable 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Forward kinematics maps joint values to a hand pose and always has one answer; inverse kinematics reverses it and may have none, several or infinitely many. DH and product-of-exponentials are two ways to describe a serial arm; libraries do the chain multiplication for you. The Jacobian maps joint velocities to hand velocity and is a local linear model of the arm. A 2-link arm has a closed-form IK with two elbow solutions, found with the law of cosines and atan2. Damped least squares solves IK numerically and stays stable near singularities. Singularities lose a direction of motion and demand huge joint speeds; plan paths to avoid them. Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

Intermediate40 minBefore this:Python and NumPy basics · Matrix multiplication · Trigonometry A camera on a robot's head sees a red cup 0.6 m ahead and 0.1 m to the left. The arm needs to grasp it, but the arm does not speak "camera". It speaks "shoulder". Somebody has to convert between the two, and if the conversion is wrong by a few degrees the gripper closes on thin air. This lesson is about that conversion: the single most used tool in all of robotics. If matrices still feel rusty, skim Linear algebra and transforms first. This lesson goes further and builds code you will reuse for the rest of the course. You will be able to Describe a pose (position plus orientation) of one coordinate frame relative to another. Build and apply rotation matrices and 4×4 homogeneous transforms in NumPy. Compose and invert transforms, and read the order of multiplication correctly. Explain why Euler angles can fail (gimbal lock) and convert between rotation matrices and quaternions. Use frame notation such as ATB{}^{A}T_{B}ATB​ without getting lost.

A framea coordinate system, with an origin point and three perpendicular axes, attached to a place or an object is a set of axes you measure from. The world has one. So does the robot's base, each link of its arm, and each sensor. A point has no meaning until you say which frame its coordinates are in: "(1, 0, 0)" in the base frame is a different spot from "(1, 0, 0)" in the camera frame. We write Ap{}^{A}pAp for "the point ppp, expressed in frame AAA", and ATB{}^{A}T_{B}ATB​ for "the pose of frame BBB expressed in frame AAA". Read the superscript as "in" and the subscript as "of": the transform of BBB, seen from AAA. This notation is worth the effort because errors become visible. If you multiply a point in BBB by ATB{}^{A}T_{B}ATB​, the matching letters cancel and you get a point in AAA: Ap=ATB Bp{}^{A}p = {}^{A}T_{B}\;{}^{B}pAp=ATB​Bp Letters should cancel When you chain transforms, write the frame letters and check that the inner ones match and cancel, like ATB BTC=ATC{}^{A}T_{B}\,{}^{B}T_{C} = {}^{A}T_{C}ATB​BTC​=ATC​. If they do not cancel, your code is wrong before you run it.

In 2D, rotating a point by angle θ\thetaθ is familiar. In 3D we use a 3×33 \times 33×3 rotation matrixa square matrix R with R transposed times R equal to identity and determinant +1; it rotates vectors without stretching them. The three basic rotations, about the xxx, yyy and zzz axes, are: Rz(θ)=[cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ0sin⁡θcos⁡θ0001]R_z(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}Rz​(θ)=​cosθsinθ0​−sinθcosθ0​001​​ and similarly for RxR_xRx​ and RyR_yRy​. Two properties make rotations pleasant: The inverse is the transpose: R−1=RTR^{-1} = R^{\mathsf T}R−1=RT. No matrix inversion needed. Order matters: rotating 90° about xxx then 90° about zzz is a different orientation from zzz then xxx. Try it with a book. Each column of RRR is where one axis of the rotated frame points, written in the parent frame. That gives a quick sanity check: the columns must be perpendicular unit vectors.

A pose has an orientation RRR and a position ppp. Applying it to a point xxx is Rx+pRx + pRx+p. That is not a pure matrix product, which is annoying. The trick is to add a fourth coordinate equal to 1 and pack both parts into a 4×44 \times 44×4 homogeneous transforma 4x4 matrix that combines a rotation and a translation so a rigid motion becomes a single matrix multiplication: T=[Rp0 0 01],[x′1]=T[x1]T = \begin{bmatrix} R & p \\ 0\;0\;0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = T \begin{bmatrix} x \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}T=[R000​p1​],[x′1​]=T[x1​] Now a rigid motion is one multiplication, and composition is just matrix multiplication. The inverse has a neat closed form that avoids a general matrix inverse: T−1=[RT−RTp0 0 01]T^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} R^{\mathsf T} & -R^{\mathsf T} p \\ 0\;0\;0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}T−1=[RT000​−RTp1​] Here is a small library. We will reuse it in the next lessons. transforms.py import numpy as np def rot_x(a): c, s = np.cos(a), np.sin(a) return np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, c, -s], [0, s, c]]) def rot_y(a): c, s = np.cos(a), np.sin(a) return np.array([[c, 0, s], [0, 1, 0], [-s, 0, c]]) def rot_z(a): c, s = np.cos(a), np.sin(a) return np.array([[c, -s, 0], [s, c, 0], [0, 0, 1]]) def make_T(R, p): """Pack a 3x3 rotation and a 3-vector into a 4x4 homogeneous transform.""" T = np.eye(4) T[:3, :3] = R T[:3, 3] = p return T def invert_T(T): """Closed-form inverse of a rigid transform (cheaper and more accurate than np.linalg.inv).""" R, p = T[:3, :3], T[:3, 3] Ti = np.eye(4) Ti[:3, :3] = R.T Ti[:3, 3] = -R.T @ p return Ti def apply_T(T, point): """Transform a 3D point (length-3 array) by a 4x4 transform.""" return (T @ np.append(point, 1.0))[:3] if __name__ == "__main__": # Camera sits 0.5 m above and 0.1 m forward of the robot base, tilted down 30 degrees. base_T_cam = make_T(rot_y(np.deg2rad(30)), [0.1, 0.0, 0.5]) cup_in_cam = np.array([0.6, 0.1, 0.0]) # cup as the camera sees it cup_in_base = apply_T(base_T_cam, cup_in_cam) # same cup, in the base frame print("cup in base frame:", np.round(cup_in_base, 3)) # Going back: the inverse transform undoes it. back = apply_T(invert_T(base_T_cam), cup_in_base) print("round trip ok:", np.allclose(back, cup_in_cam)) print("R is a rotation:", np.allclose(base_T_cam[:3, :3].T @ base_T_cam[:3, :3], np.eye(3)))
documents.s: Homogeneous transforms: rotation and translation in one matrix

documents.t: Suppose the world-to-base pose is WTB{}^{W}T_{B}WTB​ and the base-to-camera pose is BTC{}^{B}T_{C}BTC​. The camera's pose in the world is WTC=WTB BTC{}^{W}T_{C} = {}^{W}T_{B}\;{}^{B}T_{C}WTC​=WTB​BTC​ The letters cancel, so the order is right. Reading left to right, you move down the chain of frames from the world to the camera. A common bug is multiplying in the opposite order; the result is still a valid transform, just for a different robot than the one you built. There are two equivalent mental models, and being able to switch between them is a superpower: Intrinsic (body-fixed) view: each new rotation is about the current, already-moved axes. Multiply new transforms on the right. Extrinsic (fixed-frame) view: each new rotation is about the original, fixed axes. Multiply new transforms on the left. compose.py import numpy as np from transforms import rot_z, make_T, invert_T, apply_T # A robot standing at (2, 1) in the world, facing +y (yaw 90 degrees). world_T_base = make_T(rot_z(np.pi / 2), [2.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # A lidar 0.3 m in front of the base centre, same orientation. base_T_lidar = make_T(np.eye(3), [0.3, 0.0, 0.2]) world_T_lidar = world_T_base @ base_T_lidar # letters cancel: W.B then B.L print("lidar position in the world:", world_T_lidar[:3, 3]) # A wall point seen 4 m straight ahead of the lidar: hit_in_lidar = np.array([4.0, 0.0, 0.0]) print("hit in the world:", apply_T(world_T_lidar, hit_in_lidar)) # What is the base pose seen from the lidar? Invert and compose. lidar_T_base = invert_T(base_T_lidar) print(np.allclose(base_T_lidar @ lidar_T_base, np.eye(4))) Check the first print by hand: the base faces +y+y+y, so "0.3 m forward" moves the lidar to (2,1.3)(2, 1.3)(2,1.3) in the world. If you get (2.3,1)(2.3, 1)(2.3,1) you have the order or the rotation wrong.
documents.s: Composition and the order of multiplication

documents.t: The most intuitive way to describe an orientation is three angles: roll, pitch, yaw. These are Euler anglesthree successive rotations about chosen axes that together describe any 3D orientation. Humans like them; they are easy to read and plot. But they have two problems. Convention chaos. "Roll, pitch, yaw" can mean rotating about xxx, yyy, zzz in different orders, in fixed or moving axes. Two libraries can disagree about the same three numbers. ROS uses fixed-axis roll-pitch-yaw (about xxx, then yyy, then zzz of the fixed frame), which equals the matrix Rz(yaw) Ry(pitch) Rx(roll)R_z(\text{yaw})\,R_y(\text{pitch})\,R_x(\text{roll})Rz​(yaw)Ry​(pitch)Rx​(roll). Gimbal lock. At a pitch of 90°, two axes line up and you lose a degree of freedom. Different yaw/roll combinations give the same orientation, and the angles jump wildly near that point. Prove the lock to yourself: gimbal.py import numpy as np from transforms import rot_x, rot_y, rot_z pitch = np.pi / 2 A = rot_z(0.8) @ rot_y(pitch) @ rot_x(0.5) B = rot_z(0.3) @ rot_y(pitch) @ rot_x(0.0) print("different angles, same orientation:", np.allclose(A, B)) Only the difference "yaw minus roll" matters at the lock. One degree of freedom has vanished.
documents.s: Euler angles, and why they bite

documents.t: A unit quaterniona four-number representation of a 3D rotation, usually written (w, x, y, z), with unit length represents a rotation by an axis n^\hat{n}n^ and an angle θ\thetaθ: q=(cos⁡θ2, n^sin⁡θ2)=(w,x,y,z),w2+x2+y2+z2=1q = \left(\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2},\; \hat{n}\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = (w, x, y, z), \qquad w^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1q=(cos2θ​,n^sin2θ​)=(w,x,y,z),w2+x2+y2+z2=1 Advantages over Euler angles: no gimbal lock, smooth interpolation (slerp, spherical linear interpolation), and compact, cheap composition. Two quirks to remember: qqq and −q-q−q describe the same rotation, and ROS stores them in the order (x,y,z,w)(x, y, z, w)(x,y,z,w) while many math texts write (w,x,y,z)(w, x, y, z)(w,x,y,z). Always check the order. quaternions.py import numpy as np def quat_to_R(q): w, x, y, z = q / np.linalg.norm(q) return np.array([ [1 - 2*(y*y + z*z), 2*(x*y - z*w), 2*(x*z + y*w)], [2*(x*y + z*w), 1 - 2*(x*x + z*z), 2*(y*z - x*w)], [2*(x*z - y*w), 2*(y*z + x*w), 1 - 2*(x*x + y*y)], ]) def R_to_quat(R): tr = np.trace(R) if tr > 0: s = 2.0 * np.sqrt(tr + 1.0) w = 0.25 * s x = (R[2, 1] - R[1, 2]) / s y = (R[0, 2] - R[2, 0]) / s z = (R[1, 0] - R[0, 1]) / s else: i = int(np.argmax(np.diag(R))) j, k = (i + 1) % 3, (i + 2) % 3 s = 2.0 * np.sqrt(1.0 + R[i, i] - R[j, j] - R[k, k]) q = np.zeros(4) q[1 + i] = 0.25 * s q[0] = (R[k, j] - R[j, k]) / s q[1 + j] = (R[j, i] + R[i, j]) / s q[1 + k] = (R[k, i] + R[i, k]) / s w, x, y, z = q q = np.array([w, x, y, z]) return q if q[0] >= 0 else -q # pick the sign with w >= 0 def quat_mul(a, b): aw, ax, ay, az = a bw, bx, by, bz = b return np.array([ aw*bw - ax*bx - ay*by - az*bz, aw*bx + ax*bw + ay*bz - az*by, aw*by - ax*bz + ay*bw + az*bx, aw*bz + ax*by - ay*bx + az*bw, ]) def slerp(q0, q1, t): d = float(np.dot(q0, q1)) if d < 0.0: # take the short way round q1, d = -q1, -d if d > 0.9995: # nearly equal: plain lerp is fine q = q0 + t * (q1 - q0) return q / np.linalg.norm(q) theta = np.arccos(d) return (np.sin((1 - t) * theta) * q0 + np.sin(t * theta) * q1) / np.sin(theta) if __name__ == "__main__": from transforms import rot_x, rot_z R = rot_z(0.7) @ rot_x(1.1) q = R_to_quat(R) print("round trip:", np.allclose(quat_to_R(q), R)) qa, qb = R_to_quat(rot_z(0.5)), R_to_quat(rot_x(0.4)) print("composition matches:", np.allclose(quat_to_R(quat_mul(qa, qb)), rot_z(0.5) @ rot_x(0.4))) print("halfway to 90 degrees about z:", np.round(slerp(R_to_quat(np.eye(3)), R_to_quat(rot_z(np.pi / 2)), 0.5), 4)) In practice you will rarely write these by hand; libraries such as scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation and the ROS tf_transformations helpers do it for you. Writing it once is what lets you trust them. Pro tip Store and pass orientations as quaternions or rotation matrices. Use Euler angles only at the edges: to display a value to a human or to read a human-typed angle.

You will build a two-frame setup and verify it numerically. Save transforms.py and quaternions.py from this lesson in one folder. Create a world frame, a robot base at (1,2,0)(1, 2, 0)(1,2,0) with yaw 45°, and a camera on the base at (0.2,0,0.6)(0.2, 0, 0.6)(0.2,0,0.6) pitched down 20° (use rot_y(np.deg2rad(20))). Compute world_T_cam by multiplying the two transforms. Print the camera position. A detection arrives: a mug at (1.5,0,0)(1.5, 0, 0)(1.5,0,0) in the camera frame. Convert it to the world frame with apply_T. Convert it back with invert_T and check you recover (1.5,0,0)(1.5, 0, 0)(1.5,0,0) with np.allclose. Convert world_T_cam[:3, :3] to a quaternion and back, and confirm the matrix is unchanged. You know it worked when every round trip passes np.allclose and the camera sits above and slightly ahead of the base position, rotated 45° about the vertical axis.

Inverse by handIntermediate A frame BBB is at p=(2,0,0)p = (2, 0, 0)p=(2,0,0) with a 90° rotation about zzz relative to AAA. Where is the origin of AAA, as seen from BBB? Show solutionHide solution T−1T^{-1}T−1 has translation −RTp-R^{\mathsf T}p−RTp. With R=Rz(90°)R = R_z(90°)R=Rz​(90°), RT=Rz(−90°)R^{\mathsf T} = R_z(-90°)RT=Rz​(−90°), and Rz(−90°) (2,0,0)T=(0,−2,0)TR_z(-90°)\,(2,0,0)^{\mathsf T} = (0,-2,0)^{\mathsf T}Rz​(−90°)(2,0,0)T=(0,−2,0)T. So the origin of AAA is at −(0,−2,0)=(0,2,0)-(0,-2,0) = (0, 2, 0)−(0,−2,0)=(0,2,0) in frame BBB. Sanity check: BBB looks along its own xxx axis, which points along AAA's +y+y+y axis, so AAA lies off to BBB's left, which is +y+y+y in BBB. Correct. Is it still a rotation?Intermediate After many floating-point multiplications a rotation matrix can drift. Write a function that re-orthonormalizes a drifted 3×3 matrix using the SVD. Show solutionHide solution import numpy as np def nearest_rotation(M): U, _, Vt = np.linalg.svd(M) R = U @ Vt if np.linalg.det(R) < 0: # fix a reflection U[:, -1] *= -1 R = U @ Vt return R The SVD finds the closest orthogonal matrix to M; the determinant check flips the sign if the result is a mirror image rather than a true rotation. Spot the gimbal lockAdvanced At roll 0.2, pitch 90°, yaw 0.9, find another (roll, yaw) pair with the same pitch that gives the identical orientation under the RzRyRxR_z R_y R_xRz​Ry​Rx​ convention. Show solutionHide solution At pitch +90°+90°+90° only the difference yaw minus roll matters: here 0.9−0.2=0.70.9 - 0.2 = 0.70.9−0.2=0.7. Any pair with the same difference works, for example roll 0 and yaw 0.7, or roll 0.5 and yaw 1.2. Verify with rot_z(yaw) @ rot_y(np.pi/2) @ rot_x(roll) and np.allclose.

1In the expression W_T_B @ B_T_C, what is the result expressed as? AThe pose of W in CBThe pose of C in WCThe pose of B in CDA point in B 2What is the inverse of a rotation matrix R? AIts negativeBIts transposeCIts determinantDIts square 3What is gimbal lock? AA quaternion with length zeroBTwo Euler axes aligning so one degree of freedom is lostCA broken motor jointDA transform that cannot be inverted 4The quaternions q and −q describe… AOpposite rotationsBThe same rotationCRotations by half the angleDInvalid rotations 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Every coordinate needs a frame; write ATB{}^{A}T_{B}ATB​ and make the letters cancel when you chain transforms. A rotation matrix is orthonormal with an inverse equal to its transpose; order of rotations matters. A 4×4 homogeneous transform packs rotation and translation so composition becomes matrix multiplication. Invert rigid transforms in closed form: transpose the rotation and rotate the negated translation. Euler angles are readable but suffer from gimbal lock and convention confusion. Quaternions avoid gimbal lock and interpolate smoothly; watch for the (x, y, z, w) versus (w, x, y, z) ordering. Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

Hand-written planners and controllers are wonderful when you can describe the problem precisely. Folding a towel, picking an object you have never seen, or walking over rubble is much harder to write rules for. Robot learning replaces some of those rules with a model trained on data: either demonstrations from a person, or the robot's own trial and error. This module goes from a small neural-network refresher to the ideas behind today's robot policies. You will train a network on toy data, learn why copying an expert is trickier than it sounds, run reinforcement learning on a classic control task, see how thousands of simulated robots are trained in parallel, and look at the datasets that make large robot models possible.

Train and evaluate a small PyTorch model and spot overfitting. Explain behavior cloning, covariate shift and DAgger, and describe how ACT and Diffusion Policy produce actions. Define an MDP, returns and value functions, and run a policy-gradient agent on CartPole. Describe how massively parallel simulation, reward design, domain randomization and curricula fit together in Isaac Lab. Judge a robot dataset for quality, coverage and embodiment, and explain why cross-embodiment data matters.
