Teach something small. Pick a task in a simulator (CartPole is fine to start, a simulated arm reaching task is better) and solve it two ways: once with imitation from a scripted expert, once with reinforcement learning. Compare how much data or experience each needed, how well each handled starting positions it had not seen, and what broke first. A one-page write-up with two learning curves is the deliverable.

Advanced35 minBefore this:Imitation learning · A machine learning refresher for robotics Language models got good by reading a huge slice of the internet. Robots have no such free supply of data: every example of "arm picks up cup" has to be produced by a real machine and, usually, a real person. If you want robot models to improve the way language and vision models did, you must answer three questions. How do we collect robot data cheaply? How do we know it is any good? And can data from different robots be pooled? This lesson covers all three. You will be able to Compare the main ways of collecting robot demonstrations and their trade-offs. Audit a dataset for the problems that quietly ruin imitation learning. Describe what Open X-Embodiment is and why pooling data across robots is hard. Explain what "scaling" means for robot data, and what kind of diversity helps.

A robot dataset is a collection of episodes (also called trajectories): one attempt at a task from start to finish. Each episode is a time series. At every time step it typically holds: Observations: one or more camera images, joint positions and velocities, gripper state, sometimes force or tactile readings. Actions: what the robot was commanded to do (joint targets or end-effector deltas, plus the gripper command). Language instruction: a text label such as "put the red block in the bowl", increasingly common. Metadata: which robot, which task, success or failure, who collected it, the control rate, camera calibration. Common storage formats include RLDS (used for Open X-Embodiment) and the LeRobot dataset format on the Hugging Face Hub, both designed for episodes of synchronised multimodal data. Whatever the format, the lesson from the last chapter holds: treat the episode as the unit, and split train and validation sets by episode.

The dominant source of high-quality manipulation data today is teleoperation: a human drives the robot, and the system records observations and the commanded actions. Method How it works Strengths Weaknesses Leader-follower arms Human moves a lightweight "leader" arm, the robot copies it Natural, high-quality, direct joint actions (the ALOHA style) Needs matching hardware, operator skill VR or hand tracking Headset or camera tracks the operator’s hand, robot follows Flexible, works with many robots Latency, retargeting errors Spacemouse or gamepad Operator commands end-effector velocity Cheap and simple Slow, hard for fine dexterous tasks Handheld grippers Human holds a sensorised gripper to demonstrate, no robot needed Fast, scalable, no robot in the loop Needs careful design so data transfers to the robot Scripted or planner experts A program generates demonstrations in simulation Unlimited, cheap Behaviour limited to what you can script Autonomous policy with human takeover Policy runs, human intervenes on failure Targets exactly what the policy cannot do Needs a working policy first Handheld-gripper approaches such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) show a direction for scaling: take the robot out of the data-collection loop so that many people can record data in many places. Collect for the deployment, not for the demo The best dataset is not the biggest. It is the one that covers the variation your robot will meet: different object positions, lighting, backgrounds, clutter and starting states, plus the recoveries from mistakes. A thousand near-identical demonstrations teach less than two hundred varied ones.

Be consistent. If demonstrators grasp the same object in five different ways, a simple policy averages them (the multimodality problem from the last lesson). Agree on one strategy for a first dataset. Be smooth. Hesitations and corrections that look natural to a human confuse a policy. Decide whether to keep or trim them. Record at a steady rate and keep timestamps for every stream, so cameras and joint data line up. Log failures too, labelled as failures. They are useful for evaluation and for learning what to avoid. Write down everything: robot version, camera positions, calibration date, operator, software commit. You will need it when results change inexplicably.

Most disappointing imitation-learning results trace back to the data. Problems to hunt for: Dropped frames and desynchronisation. An image from 200 ms ago paired with the current action teaches the wrong association. Glitches. Sudden jumps from tracking loss or a bad calibration produce absurd action spikes. Idle segments. Long periods of no motion dominate the dataset and teach the policy to stay still. Label errors. Episodes marked successful that failed, or a wrong language instruction. Calibration drift. If the camera moves between sessions and nobody noticed, a policy trained on mixed sessions sees contradictory geometry. Narrow coverage. All demos begin from one start pose, so any other start is out of distribution. You can automate many of these checks. This script builds a small fake dataset, with a dropped-frames episode, a glitch and an idle tail planted in it, then audits each episode. audit_dataset.py import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(0) FPS = 30 def make_episode(n_steps=300, dropped_frames=0, jump=False, idle_tail=0): """Fake teleoperation episode: timestamps, 7-D actions (6 joints + gripper).""" t = np.arange(n_steps) / FPS actions = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.01, (n_steps, 7)), axis=0) actions[:, 6] = (np.sin(t) > 0).astype(float) # gripper open/closed if jump: actions[n_steps // 2:, :6] += 1.5 # a glitch: sudden 1.5 rad offset if idle_tail: actions[-idle_tail:] = actions[-idle_tail] # robot sits still at the end if dropped_frames: keep = np.sort(rng.choice(n_steps, n_steps - dropped_frames, replace=False)) t, actions = t[keep], actions[keep] return {"t": t, "actions": actions} episodes = [make_episode() for _ in range(8)] episodes.append(make_episode(dropped_frames=40)) episodes.append(make_episode(jump=True)) episodes.append(make_episode(idle_tail=150)) def audit(ep, max_dt=1.5 / FPS, max_jump=0.5, max_idle_frac=0.3): problems = [] dt = np.diff(ep["t"]) if dt.max() > max_dt: problems.append(f"timestamp gap of {dt.max() * 1000:.0f} ms (dropped frames)") step = np.abs(np.diff(ep["actions"][:, :6], axis=0)).max() if step > max_jump: problems.append(f"action jumps by {step:.2f} between steps") still = (np.abs(np.diff(ep["actions"][:, :6], axis=0)).sum(axis=1) < 1e-9).mean() if still > max_idle_frac: problems.append(f"robot idle for {still:.0%} of the episode") return problems for i, ep in enumerate(episodes): issues = audit(ep) print(f"episode {i}: {'ok' if not issues else '; '.join(issues)}") Run it. Episodes 0 to 7 should pass, and the last three should each report one problem. The exact size of the timestamp gap depends on your NumPy version’s random numbers, but it will be well above one frame period. On a real dataset you would add checks for image blur, camera exposure, calibration changes and success labels, and you would look at the data: watch a random sample of episodes as video. That step catches what no script will. Pro tip Before training anything, replay a few recorded action sequences on the robot or in simulation. If replaying the data does not reproduce the task, the policy trained from it never will.

For years every lab collected its own small dataset on its own robot. The Open X-Embodiment collaboration (2023) pooled datasets from many labs, covering many different robots, into a single shared collection in a common format. The paper, "Open X-Embodiment: Robotic Learning Datasets and RT-X Models", also trained RT-X models on the combined data, and reported that a single model trained on many robots’ data could do better on individual robots than models trained only on that robot’s own data, a form of positive transfer across embodiments. Later datasets such as DROID (a large, diverse set of real-world manipulation demonstrations collected in many locations) and BridgeData V2 follow the same trend: more environments, more objects, more operators.

Robots differ, and a model must cope with those differences: Action spaces. One robot is commanded in joint angles, another in end-effector deltas, another in velocities. Datasets often convert to a shared convention (for example normalised end-effector motion) and accept some loss of precision. Observation setups. Different cameras, viewpoints and resolutions. Kinematics and dynamics. A trajectory feasible for one arm may be impossible for another. Control rates and latencies. Dataset quality varies a lot between contributors, and the average quality of a pooled dataset can be lower than the best individual one. Cross-embodiment models usually take robot-specific details as input or handle them with small robot-specific heads, while sharing most of the network. The hope is that shared knowledge (what a "drawer" is, how to approach an object) transfers even if joint-level control does not. Note Large pretrained robot policies built on these datasets (vision-language-action models) appear in a later module. Specific model names and benchmark numbers change quickly, so check the current releases and papers rather than relying on figures from any single source.

In language models, bigger data and bigger networks reliably improved results. Robotics is still working out the equivalent. What practitioners see so far: Diversity beats repetition. More scenes, objects and operators help generalisation more than more demos of the same scene. Quality matters as much as quantity. Cleaning or filtering a dataset can improve a policy more than adding data. Pretraining helps. Starting from a model trained on internet-scale images and text, then fine-tuning on robot data, usually generalises better than training from scratch. Evaluation is the bottleneck. Testing a policy on a real robot is slow, and results depend on lighting, wear and operator. Careful, repeated trials matter. Simulation can supplement, not replace. Synthetic data is cheap and adds coverage, but real data anchors the policy. Good practice is to treat data as a product: version it, document it, track which dataset each policy was trained on, and keep a held-out set of tasks you never train on, so that you can tell generalisation from memorisation.

Save audit_dataset.py and run it. Confirm that exactly episodes 8, 9 and 10 report a problem. Add a check that flags episodes shorter than 100 steps or longer than 600 steps. Plant one such episode and confirm it is caught. Add a check for gripper behaviour: flag an episode in which the gripper never closes. Create a test episode for it. Choose a public robot dataset on the Hugging Face Hub (search for "lerobot" datasets), or a dataset from the Open X-Embodiment collection, and write down: the robot, the number of episodes, the action space, the control rate and the camera views. Success: a half-page note that would let a teammate decide whether the data suits their robot.

Plan a collectionBeginner You will train a policy to put cups on a shelf. List five sources of variation you would deliberately include in your demonstrations. Show solutionHide solution Examples: cup position and orientation, cup type and colour, shelf height and position, lighting (day and night), background clutter, different operators, and recovery cases such as a cup knocked over. Any five sensible sources of variation are acceptable. The key is covering what you expect at deployment. Why does pooled data sometimes hurt?Intermediate You merge a high-quality dataset from your own robot with a larger dataset from another lab and the policy gets worse on your robot. Give two possible reasons and one way to test each. Show solutionHide solution (1) The other dataset uses a different action convention, so the combined actions are inconsistent. Test by replaying converted actions on your robot or checking the action statistics. (2) The other dataset is lower quality or covers different tasks and dilutes yours. Test by training with only a fraction of it, or by weighting your own data more heavily, and compare results. Audit extensionAdvanced Describe a check that could detect a camera that moved between two collection sessions, without a calibration target in view. Show solutionHide solution Compare the first frame (or an average of the first frames) of each session using a feature such as the position of fixed landmarks (a table edge or a marker) or an image-similarity score. A large shift in a fixed landmark’s position between sessions means the camera moved. You can also compare the learned or detected pose of the robot base across sessions.

1Why record failures as well as successes? ATo make datasets biggerBThey are useful for evaluation and for learning what to avoid, if labelled correctlyCTo confuse the policyDFailures are never useful 2Which of these hurts imitation learning most when it slips into a dataset unnoticed? AConsistent timestampsBA camera frame paired with an action from 200 ms laterCMetadata fieldsDLanguage instructions 3What is a central challenge of cross-embodiment learning? ARobots all use the same actionsBDifferent robots have different action spaces, sensors and kinematicsCThere is too little codeDCameras are unnecessary 4Which statement about scaling robot data is best supported? ARepeating the same demonstration more times is always bestBDiversity of scenes, objects and operators often helps more than repetitionCQuality does not matter if you have enough dataDSimulation data can fully replace real data 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Robot data comes as episodes of synchronised observations and actions, plus metadata. Treat the episode as the unit. Teleoperation methods trade quality, cost and scalability. Collect data for the variation your robot will meet. Data quality problems (dropped frames, glitches, idle time, label and calibration errors) quietly ruin policies. Automate checks, and watch the videos. Open X-Embodiment pooled data across many robots and showed positive transfer. Differences in action spaces and sensors make this hard. Diversity, quality and pretraining matter at least as much as raw volume. Version your data and keep a held-out test set.

Khazatsky et al., "DROID: A Large-Scale In-The-Wild Robot Manipulation Dataset" (arxiv.org/abs/2403.12945). Chi et al., "Universal Manipulation Interface: In-The-Wild Robot Teaching Without In-The-Wild Robots" (arxiv.org/abs/2402.10329). Advanced45 minBefore this:A machine learning refresher for robotics · Control and PID · Deep learning for detection and segmentation Try writing the rules for folding a shirt or inserting a cable. Hundreds of tiny decisions depend on cloth shape and contact. Now imagine instead that you guide the robot through the task twenty times, and it learns from those examples. That is imitation learning, and it powers some of the most impressive manipulation demos of recent years. You will be able to Describe behavior cloning as supervised learning on demonstrations. Explain covariate shift and why small errors compound over time. Explain how DAgger gathers corrective data, and why it needs an expert on call. Describe, in concept, how Action Chunking with Transformers and Diffusion Policy output actions. Place LeRobot in a practical imitation-learning workflow.

A policyA mapping from what the robot observes to what it does πθ(a∣o)\pi_\theta(a \mid o)πθ​(a∣o) turns an observation ooo (camera images, joint positions) into an action aaa (joint targets, end-effector motion, gripper command). In behavior cloning (BC) you collect demonstrations from an expert, usually a human teleoperating the robot, and treat each step as a labelled example: observation in, action out. Then you train with ordinary supervised learning, exactly like the previous lesson: θ∗=arg⁡min⁡θ E(o,a)∼D[ ℓ(πθ(o),a)]\theta^* = \arg\min_\theta \; \mathbb{E}_{(o, a) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \, \ell\big(\pi_\theta(o), a\big) \right]θ∗=argθmin​E(o,a)∼D​[ℓ(πθ​(o),a)] where D\mathcal{D}D is the demonstration dataset and ℓ\ellℓ is something like squared error. No rewards, no trial and error on the robot, and it can work with a few dozen demonstrations for a focused task. That simplicity is why BC is the default starting point.

Here is the problem. During training, the policy sees states the expert visited. During deployment, the policy’s own tiny errors push it into states the expert never visited, where it has no training data and makes bigger errors, which push it further off. This mismatch between the training distribution of states and the deployment distribution is covariate shift. Think of learning to drive from videos of an expert. The expert never drifts toward the kerb, so the videos contain no examples of how to recover from drifting toward the kerb. The first time you drift for real, you are on your own. Formally, if the policy makes a mistake with probability ϵ\epsilonϵ per step on the expert’s states and a task lasts TTT steps, the expected total cost can grow like T2ϵT^2 \epsilonT2ϵ rather than TϵT \epsilonTϵ (Ross, Gordon and Bagnell, 2011). Errors compound. The longer the task, the worse the problem. Imitation fails at the edges of the data A cloned policy is only trustworthy on states resembling the demonstrations. Because the policy’s own mistakes move it away from those states, you need either demonstrations that include recovery, a way to collect them, or a model that tolerates drift. Most advances in imitation learning are different answers to this one problem. You can see this in a small experiment. The code below uses a toy system that drifts away from zero unless pushed back. A near-perfect expert stays in a narrow band, so all demonstrations cover a tiny range. We train a network on them, let the learner drive with some execution noise, and compare how wrong it is on demo states versus the states it actually visits. covariate_shift.py import numpy as np import torch from torch import nn torch.manual_seed(0) rng = np.random.default_rng(0) def expert(pos): return -float(np.clip(10.0 * pos, -1.0, 1.0)) # firm push back to 0, but it saturates at 1 def rollout(policy, start, steps=40, act_noise=0.0): """Unstable 1D system: left alone it drifts away from 0.""" pos, states = start, [] for _ in range(steps): states.append(pos) a = policy(pos) + act_noise * rng.standard_normal() pos = pos + 0.1 * (0.8 * pos + a) if abs(pos) > 3: break return states def fit(states, epochs=2000): X = torch.tensor(states, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1) Y = torch.tensor([expert(s) for s in states], dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1) net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 1)) opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-2) for _ in range(epochs): loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(net(X), Y) opt.zero_grad() loss.backward() opt.step() return net def as_policy(net): def policy(pos): with torch.no_grad(): return net(torch.tensor([[pos]], dtype=torch.float32)).item() return policy def mistake(net, states): """Average gap between the learner's action and what the expert would do, on these states.""" pol = as_policy(net) return float(np.mean([abs(pol(s) - expert(s)) for s in states])) # Demonstrations: the expert is nearly perfect, so it visits only a tiny band around 0. demo = [s for _ in range(30) for s in rollout(expert, rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1), act_noise=0.1)] net = fit(demo) print(f"demo states span {min(demo):+.2f} .. {max(demo):+.2f}") # Let the learner drive and look at the states IT visits. probe = lambda: [s for st in rng.uniform(-0.2, 0.2, 20) for s in rollout(as_policy(net), st, act_noise=0.8)] visited = probe() print(f"learner states span {min(visited):+.2f} .. {max(visited):+.2f}") print(f"mistake on demo states: {mistake(net, demo):.3f}") print(f"mistake on learner states: {mistake(net, visited):.3f} <- covariate shift") # DAgger: add the learner's own states, labelled by the expert, and retrain. data = list(demo) for it in range(3): data += probe() net = fit(data) print(f"DAgger round {it + 1}: mistake on the same learner states {mistake(net, visited):.3f}") Run it. You should see the learner’s states spread well beyond the demonstration band, the mistake on demo states near zero, and a clearly larger mistake on the states the learner visits. After a few DAgger rounds, the mistake on those same states falls. Exact numbers vary with your PyTorch version, but the pattern is the point.

DAgger (Dataset Aggregation) attacks covariate shift head on. The loop: Train a policy on the current dataset. Run the learner’s policy, and record the states it visits. Ask the expert what they would have done in each of those states. Add the new labelled states to the dataset and repeat. Now the training data contains the states the learner actually gets into, with the right corrections. DAgger’s error grows roughly like TϵT \epsilonTϵ rather than T2ϵT^2 \epsilonT2ϵ. The cost is that you need the expert on call, and labelling is not always natural. Labelling states a robot arm visited, after the fact, is awkward for a human. Practical variants include human-gated or interventional collection: the robot runs on its own, a person watches and takes over when it goes wrong, and those takeover segments are added to the dataset. Another cheap fix is noise injection during demonstrations: perturb the robot while the expert corrects it, so the data contains recovery behaviour.
documents.s: DAgger: asking the expert to correct you

documents.t: Two more problems appear on real robots. Multimodality. Suppose the expert sometimes goes left of an obstacle and sometimes right. A network trained with squared error learns the average, which drives straight into the obstacle. Policies need to represent several good answers. Compounding error in single steps. Predicting one action at a time at high frequency gives errors many chances to add up.
documents.s: Modern policies: predicting chunks and distributions

documents.t: ACTAction Chunking with Transformers: a policy that predicts a short sequence of future actions at once was introduced with the ALOHA low-cost bimanual robot system (Zhao et al., 2023). Instead of one action per step, the policy predicts a chunk of the next kkk actions from the current camera images and joint positions. The robot executes the chunk, then predicts the next. Chunking shortens the effective horizon: with k=100k = 100k=100, a 1000-step task needs only about ten decisions, so errors have fewer places to compound. ACT’s network is a transformer, trained as a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE), which lets it capture variation between demonstrations. At run time, overlapping predictions can be combined with temporal ensembling, averaging the predictions for the same moment, for smoother motion.

Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2023) borrows the idea behind image generators. It treats action sequences like an image to be generated. Starting from random noise, a network repeatedly denoises the sequence, conditioned on the current observation, until it becomes a plausible action sequence. Because sampling starts from random noise, different runs can land on different valid modes (left of the obstacle or right of it), which handles multimodality naturally. It also predicts chunks and executes them in a receding-horizon fashion. The cost is more computation per decision, since denoising takes several network passes. Idea Fixes Trade-off Behavior cloning Simplicity Compounding error, averages modes DAgger Covariate shift Needs expert labels on learner states Action chunking (ACT) Long horizons, jerky motion Less reactive within a chunk Diffusion Policy Multimodal behaviour More compute per action Note Newer imitation-learning models, including large pretrained vision-language-action policies, build on these same ingredients: demonstration data, chunked action outputs, and a generative head. Later lessons cover them. Check current releases for what is state of the art.

LeRobot is an open-source PyTorch library from Hugging Face that packages the practical parts of this workflow. It provides a standard dataset format that you can load and share through the Hugging Face Hub, implementations of policies including ACT and Diffusion Policy, training and evaluation scripts, and support for low-cost robot hardware and simulators. The typical flow is: teleoperate and record demonstrations into a dataset, train a policy on it, evaluate it on the robot or in simulation, then iterate by recording more data where it failed. Command names and options in LeRobot have changed between releases, so follow the README and documentation for the current version rather than copying commands from old posts. Pro tip Spend your effort on the demonstrations. Consistent, smooth, deliberate demonstrations of one way to do the task often beat twice as many sloppy, varied ones. Cover the variation you expect at deployment (object positions, lighting), and record recoveries.

Save covariate_shift.py and run it. Record the printed spans and mistakes. Increase the demonstration noise from act_noise=0.1 to 0.4 in the demo rollout. How do the demo span and the "mistake on learner states" change? Why? Change the learner’s act_noise from 0.8 to 0.0. Does the covariate-shift gap shrink? What does this tell you about when the problem matters? Increase the number of DAgger rounds to 6. Does the mistake keep falling, or does it plateau? Success looks like this: you can explain in two sentences why the mistake is near zero on demo states but larger on learner states.

Why does BC average?Beginner Half of your demonstrations pass an obstacle on the left and half on the right. A BC policy trained with squared error drives into the obstacle. Why? Show solutionHide solution Squared error is minimised by the mean of the targets. At the decision point, half the actions say "steer left" and half "steer right", and the average is "go straight", which is the one choice that is never right. Use a policy that can represent several modes, such as a diffusion policy or a mixture model, or make the demonstrations consistent. Pick the fixIntermediate Your policy works for 10 seconds, then drifts into positions it was never shown and fails. You can collect 100 more demonstrations or run an interventional data collection. Which do you choose, and what do you record? Show solutionHide solution Interventional collection. Run the policy, let it fail, and have a person take over at the moment it goes wrong and complete the task. Add those takeover segments, which include the recovery behaviour the original data lacked. 100 more clean demonstrations would mostly repeat states the policy already handles. Chunk length trade-offAdvanced You switch from predicting one action per step to chunks of 50 actions at 50 Hz. Name one benefit and one risk. Show solutionHide solution Benefit: fewer decisions per task, so less compounding error, and smoother motion. Risk: the robot runs open loop for up to a second within a chunk and cannot react to a sudden disturbance until the next prediction. Temporal ensembling or shorter executed chunks (predict 50, execute 10) trade some smoothness back for reactivity.

1What is covariate shift in imitation learning? AThe robot’s camera changes colourBThe states the policy visits at deployment differ from those in the training dataCThe expert changes over timeDThe loss function is wrong 2What does DAgger add to the dataset in each round? AMore random actionsBStates visited by the learner, labelled by the expertCOnly the expert’s original demonstrationsDSimulated noise only 3Why predict a chunk of actions at once, as ACT does? AIt uses less memoryBIt shortens the effective horizon so errors compound lessCIt removes the need for camerasDIt makes the expert unnecessary 4How does Diffusion Policy handle multiple valid ways to do a task? AIt averages themBIt starts denoising from random noise, so different samples can land on different modesCIt ignores demonstrationsDIt requires a reward function 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Behavior cloning turns demonstrations into supervised learning: observation in, action out. Covariate shift makes small errors compound, so cloned policies fail in states the demos never covered. DAgger and interventional collection add corrective data from the learner’s own states. ACT predicts chunks of actions, and Diffusion Policy generates action sequences by denoising, which handles multimodal demonstrations. LeRobot packages datasets, policies and tooling. Data quality and coverage matter more than policy choice.

Ross, Gordon and Bagnell, "A Reduction of Imitation Learning and Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning" (arxiv.org/abs/1011.0686), the DAgger paper. Zhao et al., "Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware" (arxiv.org/abs/2304.13705), the ACT paper. Chi et al., "Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion" (arxiv.org/abs/2303.04137). The LeRobot repository and documentation on huggingface.co and github.com/huggingface/lerobot. Next: Reinforcement learning

Intermediate40 minBefore this:Python for robotics · Calculus and optimization · Probability for robots Your robot’s arm has a quirk: the gearbox backlash means that when you command a joint angle, the real hand height is not quite what the textbook formula says. You could model that by hand, or you could record a few hundred measurements and let a small neural network learn the mapping. This is the basic move of robot learning: replace a formula you cannot write with a function fitted to data. You will be able to Explain supervised learning in terms of inputs, targets, a model and a loss. Describe how gradient descent trains a network and what a learning rate does. Recognise overfitting and use a validation set to catch it. Write and run a complete PyTorch training loop.
documents.s: A machine learning refresher for robotics

documents.t: In supervised learning you have examples of inputs xxx paired with the correct outputs yyy, and you want a function fθ(x)f_\theta(x)fθ​(x) that predicts yyy for inputs it has not seen. The θ\thetaθ stands for the model’s parameters, the numbers the training process adjusts. Robotics examples are everywhere: Input xxx Output yyy Task Camera image Object label Classification Camera image Grasp point Regression Joint angles and torques Next joint angles Dynamics model Image and robot state Next action Policy (imitation learning) When yyy is a category, we call it classification. When yyy is a number or a vector, it is regression. Both train the same way. A neural network is a flexible function built from layers: each layer multiplies by a matrix, adds a bias and passes the result through a non-linearity such as ReLU (max⁡(0,z)\max(0, z)max(0,z)). Stack a few layers and the network can approximate very complicated functions. The matrices and biases are θ\thetaθ.

To train, we need a number that says how wrong the model is. That number is the loss. For regression, the usual choice is the mean squared error: L(θ)=1N∑i=1N(fθ(xi)−yi)2L(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( f_\theta(x_i) - y_i \right)^2L(θ)=N1​i=1∑N​(fθ​(xi​)−yi​)2 For classification, the usual loss is cross-entropy, which punishes confident wrong answers heavily. Choosing the loss is choosing what "good" means. If you train a grasp predictor with a loss that treats all errors equally, it will not care that a 2 cm miss ruins a grasp while a 2 mm miss does not, unless you design the loss or the data to reflect that.

Training means finding θ\thetaθ that makes LLL small. The loss is a landscape over all the parameters, and the gradient ∇θL\nabla_\theta L∇θ​L points uphill. So we step downhill: θ←θ−η ∇θL\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \, \nabla_\theta Lθ←θ−η∇θ​L The step size η\etaη is the learning rate. Too small, and training crawls. Too large, and the loss bounces around or blows up. Frameworks compute gradients automatically by backpropagation, which applies the chain rule from the loss back through every layer. In practice you do not use the whole dataset for every step. Stochastic gradient descent uses a small random batch, which is faster and adds helpful noise. Adam is a popular optimizer that adapts step sizes for each parameter and is a good default. One pass through all the training data is an epoch. The training loop is always the same four steps Predict, compute the loss, backpropagate the gradient, update the parameters. Every neural network you will meet in robotics, from a tiny regressor to a giant vision-language-action model, trains by repeating these four steps on batches of data.

A model can memorise its training examples instead of learning the pattern. That is overfitting. It scores brilliantly on data it has seen and badly on new data, which is exactly what matters on a real robot. The standard defence is to split your data: Training set: used to update parameters. Validation set: held back and used only to measure performance and choose settings. Test set: touched once at the end for an honest final score. Watch the gap. If training loss keeps falling but validation loss stops improving or rises, you are overfitting. Remedies include more data (almost always the best), a smaller model, regularisation such as weight decay or dropout, data augmentation, and early stopping (stop when validation loss stops improving). Warning In robotics, leaking information between training and validation sets is easy and costly. If frames from the same demonstration appear in both, the model recognises the episode rather than learning the skill, and your validation score looks great while the real robot fails. Split by episode, not by frame.

Here is a runnable example. We pretend the true relation between a joint angle qqq and the hand height is sin⁡(q)\sin(q)sin(q), add measurement noise, and train a small network to recover it. train_toy.py import torch from torch import nn torch.manual_seed(0) # Toy task: predict hand height from a joint angle. The "true" relation is sin(q) plus noise. q = torch.rand(400, 1) * 3.0 # joint angle in [0, 3] rad y = torch.sin(q) + 0.05 * torch.randn_like(q) # noisy measured height perm = torch.randperm(400) train_idx, val_idx = perm[:300], perm[300:] x_train, y_train = q[train_idx], y[train_idx] x_val, y_val = q[val_idx], y[val_idx] model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 1)) loss_fn = nn.MSELoss() opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2) for epoch in range(301): model.train() pred = model(x_train) loss = loss_fn(pred, y_train) opt.zero_grad() loss.backward() opt.step() if epoch % 50 == 0: model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): val_loss = loss_fn(model(x_val), y_val) print(f"epoch {epoch:3d} train {loss.item():.4f} val {val_loss.item():.4f}") Install PyTorch from pytorch.org (the CPU version is plenty for this) and run it. Both losses should fall quickly and settle near the noise level (about 0.052=0.00250.05^2 = 0.00250.052=0.0025). Because the data are noisy, the loss cannot go to zero. A model that gets training loss far below the noise level is fitting the noise, which is overfitting. A few details that trip beginners: opt.zero_grad() clears the old gradients. PyTorch accumulates them by default. model.train() and model.eval() switch layers such as dropout on and off. They make no difference in this tiny model, but form a habit. torch.no_grad() skips gradient bookkeeping when you only want predictions. For real datasets, wrap your data in a Dataset and a DataLoader, which handles batching and shuffling. The loop gains an inner for batch in loader: and the rest is the same.

Robot data has quirks that ordinary benchmarks hide: Time matters. Consecutive frames are nearly identical, so a million frames may be a few hundred distinct situations. Split and count by episode. Data is expensive. Real robot hours are slow, so effective data use (augmentation, pretrained models) matters. Mistakes have physical cost. A prediction error of 5 degrees in a vision classifier is a footnote. The same in a joint command can break a gripper. The training data shapes behaviour. A model only knows the situations it was shown. This is the root of the covariate-shift problem in the next lesson. Pretraining is powerful. Starting from a model already trained on huge image or text datasets, then fine-tuning on your robot data, usually beats training from scratch.

Install PyTorch and save train_toy.py. Run it and note the final training and validation losses. Change lr to 1e-4, then 1.0. Describe what happens to the loss each time. Reduce the training set to 20 samples (perm[:20]) and make the network larger (64 units per layer). Train for 2000 epochs. Compare training and validation losses. Is it overfitting? Restore the data, then add weight_decay=1e-3 to the Adam optimizer. Does the gap between the two losses shrink? Success looks like this: you can explain, from the printed numbers, which run overfit and why.

Spot the problemBeginner Your training loss is 0.01 and your validation loss is 0.40. What is happening, and name two things you could try. Show solutionHide solution The model is overfitting: it fits the training data well but generalises poorly. Try more training data, a smaller model, weight decay or dropout, data augmentation, or stopping earlier. Split correctlyIntermediate You recorded 50 demonstrations of 200 frames each. You shuffle all 10,000 frames and use 80% for training and 20% for validation. Why is the validation score misleading, and how do you fix it? Show solutionHide solution Neighbouring frames from the same demonstration look almost identical, so the validation set contains near-copies of training frames. The score measures memorisation. Split by episode instead: for instance, train on 40 demonstrations and validate on the other 10. Add early stoppingIntermediate Modify the training loop to stop when the validation loss has not improved for 20 consecutive epochs, and keep the best parameters. Sketch the code. Show solutionHide solution Track best_val and best_state. After each epoch, compute the validation loss. If it is lower than best_val, update best_val, store copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()) and reset a counter to 0. Otherwise increment the counter, and break when it reaches 20. After the loop, call model.load_state_dict(best_state).

1What does the learning rate control? AHow many epochs to runBThe size of each parameter update stepCThe batch sizeDThe number of layers 2Training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises. This is: AUnderfittingBOverfittingCA bug in backpropagationDNormal and desirable 3Why split robot data by episode instead of by frame? AIt is fasterBFrames from one episode are nearly identical, so frame splits leak data into validationCPyTorch requires itDIt increases the dataset size 4What does opt.zero_grad() do in a PyTorch loop? AResets the model weights to zeroBClears accumulated gradients before the next backward passCStops trainingDSets the learning rate to zero 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Supervised learning fits a function from inputs to targets by minimising a loss on examples. Training repeats four steps: predict, compute loss, backpropagate, update parameters. The learning rate sets step size. Adam is a solid default optimizer. Overfitting shows up as a gap between training and validation loss. Fight it with more data first. In robotics, split by episode, expect expensive data, and prefer fine-tuning pretrained models when you can.

The official PyTorch tutorials at pytorch.org/tutorials, especially "Learn the Basics". Deep Learning by Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville (deeplearningbook.org), free online. Andrej Karpathy’s "A Recipe for Training Neural Networks" (karpathy.github.io), a practical checklist. Next: Imitation learning

Advanced45 minBefore this:A machine learning refresher for robotics · Probability for robots · Calculus and optimization A quadruped robot is asked to walk. Nobody can write down the correct joint torque for every instant, and no human can demonstrate the thousand-step recovery from a stumble. But it is easy to say what we want: move forward, stay upright, don’t waste energy. Reinforcement learning (RL) lets a robot discover its own behaviour from that kind of feedback, by trying things and seeing what scores well. You will be able to Define a Markov decision process, a policy, a return and a value function. Write the policy-gradient update and explain why it works. Run a policy-gradient agent on CartPole with Gymnasium and read its learning curve. Describe in plain words what PPO changes and why it is popular for robots.

An RL problem has an agent interacting with an environment in a loop. At each step the agent sees a state sts_tst​, picks an action ata_tat​, and the environment returns a reward rt+1r_{t+1}rt+1​ and a new state st+1s_{t+1}st+1​. This is formalised as a Markov decision processMarkov decision process: states, actions, transition probabilities, a reward function and a discount factor (MDP). The agent’s behaviour is its policy π(a∣s)\pi(a \mid s)π(a∣s): the probability of choosing action aaa in state sss. The goal is a policy that maximises the expected return, the total reward collected over time with later rewards discounted by γ∈[0,1)\gamma \in [0, 1)γ∈[0,1): Gt=rt+1+γ rt+2+γ2rt+3+⋯=∑k=0∞γk rt+k+1G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma\, r_{t+2} + \gamma^2 r_{t+3} + \dots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k \, r_{t+k+1}Gt​=rt+1​+γrt+2​+γ2rt+3​+⋯=k=0∑∞​γkrt+k+1​ Discounting says "a reward now is worth more than the same reward later" and keeps the sum finite. Values around 0.99 are typical. The Markov part means the state contains everything needed to predict what happens next, so the past does not matter beyond the current state. For a robot, "state" must therefore include velocities, not only positions, or the problem will not be Markov.

How good is it to be in a state? The state-value function is the expected return from state sss if you follow policy π\piπ: Vπ(s)=Eπ[Gt∣st=s]V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi \left[ G_t \mid s_t = s \right]Vπ(s)=Eπ​[Gt​∣st​=s] The action-value function Qπ(s,a)Q^\pi(s, a)Qπ(s,a) is the same, but for taking action aaa first and then following π\piπ. Their difference is the advantage: Aπ(s,a)=Qπ(s,a)−Vπ(s)A^\pi(s, a) = Q^\pi(s, a) - V^\pi(s)Aπ(s,a)=Qπ(s,a)−Vπ(s) The advantage tells you whether an action was better or worse than the policy’s average behaviour in that state. It will be the star of the policy-gradient method below. Values obey a self-consistency rule, the Bellman equation: the value of a state is the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state. Vπ(s)=Ea∼π, s′∼P[r+γ Vπ(s′)]V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi,\; s' \sim P} \left[ r + \gamma\, V^\pi(s') \right]Vπ(s)=Ea∼π,s′∼P​[r+γVπ(s′)] Value-based methods such as Q-learning and DQN use this recursion to learn values and act greedily on them. They work well for discrete actions. Robots usually have continuous actions (motor torques), where policy-gradient methods are the common choice.

Instead of learning values and deriving a policy, we can parameterise the policy directly, πθ(a∣s)\pi_\theta(a \mid s)πθ​(a∣s), with a neural network, and improve θ\thetaθ by gradient ascent on the expected return J(θ)J(\theta)J(θ). The policy gradient theorem gives a surprisingly simple estimate: ∇θJ(θ)=Eπθ[∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st) Gt]\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta} \left[ \sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \; G_t \right]∇θ​J(θ)=Eπθ​​[t∑​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)Gt​] Read it as: make the actions you took more likely, in proportion to how much return followed them. Good outcomes push up the probability of the actions that led to them, bad outcomes push them down. This is the REINFORCE algorithm. RL is trial, error and credit assignment The policy gradient reinforces whatever the agent just did, weighted by how well things went afterwards. The hard part is credit assignment: with long episodes and sparse reward it is unclear which of thousands of actions deserves the credit. Baselines, value functions and well-designed rewards all exist to make this signal less noisy. Raw returns are noisy: if every return is positive, REINFORCE pushes up every action a little. Subtracting a baseline (such as the average return or a learned V(s)V(s)V(s)) leaves the expected gradient unchanged but cuts the variance a lot. Using Gt−V(st)G_t - V(s_t)Gt​−V(st​), an estimate of the advantage, gives an actor-critic method: the policy is the actor and the learned value function is the critic.

CartPole is the "hello world" of RL: a cart with a hinged pole, where the agent pushes left or right and earns +1 for every step the pole stays up. The maximum episode length in CartPole-v1 is 500 steps. Install the dependencies: terminal pip install gymnasium torch REINFORCE (from scratch) PPO with stable-baselines3 cartpole_reinforce.py import gymnasium as gym import torch from torch import nn torch.manual_seed(0) env = gym.make("CartPole-v1") policy = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 2)) # logits for [left, right] opt = torch.optim.Adam(policy.parameters(), lr=1e-2) gamma = 0.99 def run_episode(): obs, _ = env.reset() log_probs, rewards = [], [] done = False while not done: logits = policy(torch.as_tensor(obs, dtype=torch.float32)) dist = torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=logits) action = dist.sample() obs, reward, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(action.item()) log_probs.append(dist.log_prob(action)) rewards.append(reward) done = terminated or truncated return log_probs, rewards def discounted_returns(rewards): returns, g = [], 0.0 for r in reversed(rewards): g = r + gamma * g returns.append(g) returns.reverse() return torch.tensor(returns) for episode in range(1, 301): log_probs, rewards = run_episode() returns = discounted_returns(rewards) returns = (returns - returns.mean()) / (returns.std() + 1e-8) # baseline and scaling loss = -(torch.stack(log_probs) * returns).sum() # gradient ascent on expected return opt.zero_grad() loss.backward() opt.step() if episode % 50 == 0: print(f"episode {episode:3d} length {len(rewards):3d}") terminal pip install stable-baselines3 cartpole_ppo.py from stable_baselines3 import PPO model = PPO("MlpPolicy", "CartPole-v1", verbose=1) model.learn(total_timesteps=50_000) env = model.get_env() obs = env.reset() for _ in range(500): action, _ = model.predict(obs, deterministic=True) obs, reward, done, info = env.step(action) if done[0]: obs = env.reset() Look at how the from-scratch version maps onto the maths. dist.log_prob(action) is log⁡πθ(at∣st)\log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)logπθ​(at​∣st​). returns is GtG_tGt​. Normalising the returns subtracts a baseline and scales them. The loss is the negative of the policy-gradient objective, since optimisers minimise. Run the first script and watch the episode lengths. The first few are short (the pole falls in 10–40 steps) and later ones climb towards 500. Learning is noisy and may swing between good and bad episodes. That is normal for REINFORCE, and it is why more stable algorithms exist. Because the agent samples actions, different seeds give different curves. Pro tip Always plot a learning curve over several random seeds before believing an RL result. A single lucky run can look like success. Also check what the reward actually encourages: RL optimises exactly what you wrote, not what you meant.

REINFORCE has a weakness: one big update can wreck the policy, and the data it just collected is useless for the next update because the policy has changed. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO, Schulman et al., 2017) stays popular for robotics because it makes updates more cautious and reuses data a little. The intuition: collect a batch of experience with the current policy. Then take several gradient steps on that batch, but clip how far the new policy’s action probabilities may move from the old ones. With the probability ratio ρt(θ)=πθ(at∣st) / πθold(at∣st)\rho_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \,/\, \pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_t \mid s_t)ρt​(θ)=πθ​(at​∣st​)/πθold​​(at​∣st​) and advantage estimate A^t\hat{A}_tA^t​, the objective is L(θ)=Et[min⁡ ⁣(ρtA^t, clip(ρt, 1−ε, 1+ε) A^t)]L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t \left[ \min\!\big( \rho_t \hat{A}_t, \;\; \mathrm{clip}(\rho_t,\, 1-\varepsilon,\, 1+\varepsilon)\, \hat{A}_t \big) \right]L(θ)=Et​[min(ρt​A^t​,clip(ρt​,1−ε,1+ε)A^t​)] If an action had positive advantage, the objective rewards making it more likely, but only up to a ratio of 1+ε1+\varepsilon1+ε (often 0.2). Beyond that, the clip removes the incentive. This acts like a guard rail: improve, but do not take a step so large that things collapse. PPO also uses a learned value function for advantages (typically Generalized Advantage Estimation) and runs many environments in parallel. PPO is on-policy: data is used for a few epochs and then thrown away, so it needs a lot of experience. That is fine in simulation, where you can generate millions of steps, and painful on a real robot. The next lesson is about exactly that. Warning Reward design is where many RL projects go wrong. Agents exploit loopholes: a robot rewarded for forward speed may learn to fall forward and slide. When training behaves strangely, inspect the behaviour in a video, not only the reward number.

Install Gymnasium and PyTorch. Run cartpole_reinforce.py and note when episode length first reaches 500. Remove the return normalisation line and rerun. What happens to learning speed and stability? Change gamma to 0.5. CartPole needs the agent to care about the future. Does it still learn? Run cartpole_ppo.py with stable-baselines3 and compare the sample efficiency and stability to your own implementation. Success looks like this: a plot or printed log showing episode length climbing to the 500-step cap, and a sentence on how it differed across two seeds.

Compute a returnBeginner An episode gives rewards 1, 1, 1, 0 and ends, with γ=0.9\gamma = 0.9γ=0.9. What is G0G_0G0​? Show solutionHide solution G0=1+0.9×1+0.92×1+0.93×0=1+0.9+0.81+0=2.71G_0 = 1 + 0.9 \times 1 + 0.9^2 \times 1 + 0.9^3 \times 0 = 1 + 0.9 + 0.81 + 0 = 2.71G0​=1+0.9×1+0.92×1+0.93×0=1+0.9+0.81+0=2.71. Why a baseline?Intermediate In a task where every reward is positive, why does vanilla REINFORCE learn slowly, and what does subtracting the mean return change? Show solutionHide solution With all-positive returns, every sampled action’s probability is pushed up, only by different amounts, so the useful signal (which actions were better) is buried in noise and the gradient estimates have high variance. Subtracting a baseline centres the returns, so above-average actions are pushed up and below-average ones are pushed down. The expected gradient is unchanged, but the variance is much lower. Spot the reward bugIntermediate A robot arm should place a block in a bin. You reward "negative distance between block and bin" at every step. The agent learns to push the block off the table and into the bin’s direction without placing it. What went wrong, and how might you fix it? Show solutionHide solution The reward only measures distance, so any motion that shrinks distance scores well, even if the block ends in a useless place. Add terms for the real goal (a large bonus for the block being inside the bin and at rest), penalise the block leaving the workspace, and shape reward in stages (reach, grasp, lift, place). Then watch rollouts to check that behaviour matches intent.

1What does the discount factor gamma do? ASets the learning rateBWeights later rewards less than immediate onesCChooses the actionDNormalises observations 2What does the policy gradient do, in words? AMakes actions more likely in proportion to the return that followedBMinimises prediction errorCCopies an expertDChooses the highest-value action 3Why subtract a baseline in policy gradients? ATo make the policy deterministicBTo reduce variance without changing the expected gradientCTo increase the discountDTo skip backpropagation 4What does PPO’s clipping do? ALimits how much the policy can change in one updateBClips the reward to zeroCLimits episode lengthDRemoves the need for a value function 0 of 4 answered Takeaways RL is an agent-environment loop. An MDP defines states, actions, transitions, rewards and a discount. The return is discounted total reward. Value functions VVV and QQQ predict it, and the advantage compares an action to the average. Policy gradients nudge the policy to make good actions more likely. Baselines and critics cut the variance. PPO clips policy updates to keep training stable and is a common choice for robot learning in simulation. Rewards define the behaviour you get, so test them by watching rollouts, and judge results across several seeds.

Advanced35 minBefore this:Reinforcement learning · Isaac Sim essentials · The sim-to-real gap Reinforcement learning needs millions of attempts. A real robot makes a few thousand falls before something breaks, and each fall costs time and money. A simulator can run thousands of robots at once, faster than real time, and a fall is free. This lesson shows how modern robot-learning pipelines use that advantage, using NVIDIA Isaac Lab as the worked example. You will be able to Explain why massively parallel GPU simulation changed robot reinforcement learning. Describe the main building blocks of an Isaac Lab task: observations, actions, rewards, terminations, events and curricula. Design a reward function with several terms and recognise common reward-design traps. Choose domain randomization parameters and a curriculum for a task. Info Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab change quickly. This lesson teaches the concepts and the structure of a task, not version-specific commands. Check the current Isaac Lab documentation at isaac-sim.github.io/IsaacLab for installation steps and the exact API of your release.
documents.s: Reinforcement learning in simulation with Isaac Lab

documents.t: Classical RL on a robot ran one simulation on the CPU and shuttled data between the simulator and the neural network. That became the bottleneck: the GPU that trains the network sat idle waiting for the CPU that simulates the physics. The breakthrough was to run thousands of copies of the environment at once, inside one GPU simulation, and keep all the data (states, observations, rewards) on the GPU as tensors. The policy network also runs on the GPU. Nothing crosses to the CPU each step. Work that once took days of wall-clock time can finish in a much shorter time. A well-known demonstration of this idea is "Learning to Walk in Minutes Using Massively Parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning" (Rudin et al., 2021), which trained legged-robot walking in minutes on a single GPU. Parallelism turns RL from rare luck into routine engineering With thousands of robots training together, each learning step sees a huge, varied batch of experience. You can afford to try many reward designs, many random seeds and many randomizations in a day. The limiting factor shifts from compute to the quality of your task design: rewards, randomization and terminations. Isaac Lab is NVIDIA’s open-source framework for robot learning on top of Isaac Sim. It grew out of earlier NVIDIA robot-learning projects and provides ready-made robots, sensors, tasks and integrations with common RL libraries. You write a task description, point an RL library at it, and training runs across thousands of environments in parallel.

Isaac Lab describes a task as a set of configuration pieces. In its manager-based style, each piece has a manager that you configure with terms. (There is also a more hands-on direct style where you write the step logic yourself as tensor code.) The usual pieces are: Piece Question it answers Example Scene What exists? Robot, ground plane, objects, sensors Observations What does the policy see? Joint positions and velocities, base orientation, last action, commanded velocity Actions What does the policy control? Target joint positions for a PD controller Rewards What counts as good? Track velocity, stay upright, save energy Terminations When does an episode end? Robot falls, time runs out Events What changes at reset or during the episode? Randomize friction, mass; apply random pushes Curriculum How does difficulty grow? Harder terrain as the robot succeeds Commands What goal is the policy given? Desired forward velocity Everything is vectorised: each term is a function that takes tensors with one row per environment and returns tensors with one row per environment. You do not write a loop over robots.

The policy should see what a real robot can sense, plus nothing it cannot. If you feed the policy the exact simulator contact forces and the robot has no such sensor, the policy will fail in the real world. Add realistic sensor noise to observations during training. Actions are usually target joint positions that a low-level PD controller tracks, rather than raw torques. That makes learning easier and behaviour smoother, and it matches how many real robots are driven. A popular trick is asymmetric actor-critic: the critic (used only in training) is allowed to see privileged simulator information, such as exact terrain height or friction, while the actor (the deployed policy) sees only what the real robot can sense. This speeds up learning without breaking deployment.

Rewards are a sum of weighted terms. For legged locomotion, a typical recipe is one or two terms that define the goal (track a commanded velocity) plus several small penalty terms that shape how the robot achieves it (smooth, efficient, upright). Here is a vectorised reward function in plain PyTorch. It is not Isaac Lab code, but it has the same shape as the terms you would write: tensors with a leading dimension for the number of environments. locomotion_reward.py import torch def locomotion_reward(base_lin_vel, cmd_vel, joint_torques, action, last_action, up_z, fell): """Every tensor has a leading dimension of num_envs, so thousands of robots are scored in one call.""" vel_err = torch.sum((cmd_vel - base_lin_vel[:, :2]) ** 2, dim=1) track = torch.exp(-vel_err / 0.25) # 1.0 when perfect, decays smoothly with error torque_penalty = torch.sum(joint_torques ** 2, dim=1) # discourage wasting energy jerk_penalty = torch.sum((action - last_action) ** 2, dim=1) # discourage twitchy actions return ( 1.0 * track - 1e-4 * torque_penalty - 0.01 * jerk_penalty + 0.2 * up_z # stay upright (1.0 = perfectly upright) - 5.0 * fell.float() # big penalty for falling over ) n = 4096 r = locomotion_reward( base_lin_vel=torch.randn(n, 3) * 0.3, cmd_vel=torch.full((n, 2), 0.5), joint_torques=torch.randn(n, 12), action=torch.randn(n, 12), last_action=torch.randn(n, 12), up_z=torch.rand(n), fell=torch.rand(n) < 0.02, ) print(r.shape, round(r.mean().item(), 3)) Run it: you get one reward per environment, from a single call that handles 4096 robots. The weights matter. The exp shaping gives a smooth, bounded reward that is largest at zero error, which tends to behave better than a raw negative error. Small penalties on torque and action change keep motions gentle, but if you make them too large the robot learns that standing still is the safest option.

Reward hacking. The agent finds a loophole. A robot paid for speed may fall forward. Watch rollouts, not only reward curves. Conflicting terms. Rewarding both "move fast" and "use very little energy" with similar weights gives an agent that does neither well. Tune one term at a time. Sparse reward. A reward that only appears on complete success (such as "block in bin") gives almost no signal early on. Add shaping terms (distance to block, grasp contact, lift height) but check they do not create a new loophole. Over-shaping. Many hand-tuned terms can lock the robot into your idea of the solution rather than a better one. No termination signals. Without early termination for falling, simulators waste time on robots that are already lying on the floor. Pro tip Add reward terms one at a time and log each term’s contribution separately. When training goes wrong, a per-term plot tells you which term dominates.

A policy trained in one perfect simulation will overfit to its quirks. Domain randomization deliberately varies the simulation across environments (and across resets), so the policy has to work in all of them. The real world then looks like just another variation. Things worth randomizing for a legged or manipulation robot: Physics: ground friction, restitution, link masses and centres of mass, payload mass. Actuators: motor strength, PD gains, joint friction and damping, and latency between command and effect. Sensing: observation noise, bias, dropped or delayed frames, camera pose and lighting for vision policies. Disturbances: random pushes, force impulses, uneven terrain. Choose ranges that bracket your best estimate of reality, wide enough to cover errors in your model but not so wide that the task becomes impossible. Randomizing everything massively can produce a cautious, slow policy that works everywhere and excels nowhere. Measure real parameters where you can (weigh the robot, measure latency) and centre your ranges there.

Throwing the hardest version of a task at a beginner policy can leave it with no reward signal at all. A curriculum starts easy and raises the difficulty as the policy improves. For a walking robot, terrain is a natural curriculum: start every robot on flat ground. When a robot successfully traverses its terrain, move it to a harder patch (slopes, steps, rough ground). If it fails badly, move it back to an easier one. Command ranges can grow similarly, from slow forward walking to faster, turning and sideways motion. Because thousands of robots train at once, different robots can be at different difficulty levels simultaneously. Curricula can be hand-designed or automatic. The key is a measurable progress signal (distance walked, success rate) that triggers promotion.

A trained policy is a small neural network. Export it, run it at the control rate on the robot’s computer, and check the following before trusting it: Observation order and scaling match training exactly. The action is applied the same way (same PD gains, same joint limits, same control rate). You have a safe stop and conservative limits for the first run. Expect a gap anyway. Compare simulation and hardware logs for the same command, find where they diverge, then adjust the randomization ranges, add the missing effect to the simulator, or both. This loop is covered in depth in the simulation module’s sim-to-real lesson.
documents.s: From training to a real robot

documents.t: Save locomotion_reward.py and run it. Confirm the output shape is (4096,). Add a term that penalises joint velocities above a threshold. Plot how the mean reward changes for random inputs. Write down a plan for a new task, "a robot arm slides a block to a target spot on a table". List: the observations (what a real robot can sense), the action space, four reward terms with signs and rough weights, two termination conditions. For the same task, list five parameters you would randomize with a sensible range for each, and a one-line curriculum plan. Optional, if you have an NVIDIA GPU: follow the current Isaac Lab installation guide and run one of its built-in training tasks. Success: reward curves climb across training and a playback shows the policy moving.

Why GPU tensors?Beginner Why does keeping observations and rewards on the GPU, instead of copying them to the CPU each step, speed up training so much? Show solutionHide solution The transfer between CPU and GPU, and the Python loop over environments, would dominate the time. Keeping states, observations, rewards and the policy on the GPU means every step is a batch tensor operation across thousands of environments with no round trips. Diagnose the lazy robotIntermediate Your walking policy learns to stand still. Name two likely reward-design causes and a fix for each. Show solutionHide solution (1) Penalty terms (torque, action rate) outweigh the velocity-tracking reward, so staying still is the best score. Reduce penalty weights or increase the tracking term. (2) The tracking reward is too sparse or too sharply peaked, so early policies get no gradient towards moving. Use a smoother shaping such as an exponential of the error, or start with a curriculum of easy commands. Randomization budgetAdvanced You randomize friction from 0.05 to 3.0, mass by plus or minus 80 percent and add 200 ms latency. The policy trains but moves timidly even on good ground. What is a likely cause, and how do you investigate? Show solutionHide solution The ranges are probably much wider than reality, so the policy optimises for the worst case in the set and becomes conservative. Narrow the ranges to plausible values (measure the real mass, friction on your floor and latency), then test which individual randomization hurts performance by turning them on one at a time.

1What made modern robot RL much faster? ASmaller neural networksBThousands of simulated robots running in parallel on the GPU with data kept as GPU tensorsCRemoving rewardsDTraining on real robots only 2Why use an asymmetric actor-critic? AThe critic may use privileged simulator information the real robot cannot sense, while the actor sees only deployable inputsBTo halve the network sizeCTo remove rewardsDTo disable randomization 3What is the purpose of domain randomization? AMaking the simulator fasterBForcing the policy to work across many variations so the real world looks like one more variationCAdding more reward termsDReducing GPU memory 4What does a terrain curriculum do? AStarts easy and promotes robots to harder terrain as they succeedBGives all robots the hardest terrain firstCRandomizes the rewardDStops training early 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Running thousands of environments in parallel on the GPU, with all data as tensors, makes robot RL fast enough to iterate on. An Isaac Lab task is built from a scene, observations, actions, rewards, terminations, events and a curriculum, all vectorised across environments. Rewards are weighted sums. Add terms one at a time, log each, and watch rollouts for hacking. Domain randomization makes policies robust, but ranges should bracket reality rather than ignore it. Curricula keep difficulty matched to progress. Always compare real-robot behaviour to simulation and iterate.

Almost every modern robot is a set of programs working together: one reads sensors, one plans, one controls motors, one watches for danger. ROS 2 (the Robot Operating System, version 2) is the open-source toolkit that lets those programs find each other, share data and be started, inspected and replayed in a consistent way. Learning it is the biggest single step from "I can code" to "I can build a robot system", and it is used in research labs and companies worldwide. This module teaches ROS 2 Jazzy Jalisco on Ubuntu 24.04, in Python. You start with how ROS 2 is put together, then write real packages: publishers, subscribers, services, actions, parameters and launch files. You describe a robot with URDF, keep track of its coordinate frames with TF2, and learn the debugging and recording tools that professionals use daily. Everything runs on your own machine and needs no hardware.

Explain the ROS 2 graph, DDS discovery, QoS and executors, and pick sensible QoS settings. Write, build and run Python packages with publishers, subscribers, services and clients. Use actions for long-running tasks, parameters for configuration, and launch files for whole systems. Describe a two-wheeled robot in xacro, publish its transform tree and view it in RViz. Debug a live system with the ros2 CLI and rqt, and record and replay data with rosbag2.
