AIt has exactly one parent, and there are no cyclesBIt has many parentsCIt has no parentDIt has a mesh attached 2Which standard frame is smooth over time but drifts, built from wheel odometry? AmapBodomCbase_linkDlaser 3What does robot_state_publisher need in order to publish the wheel transforms? AThe URDF in robot_description, and joint angles on /joint_statesBA cameraCGazeboDA map 4What is xacro for? ACompiling URDF to binaryBAdding properties, maths and macros to URDF, which it expands to plain URDFCRunning physicsDDrawing meshes 0 of 4 answered Takeaways TF2 stores a tree of coordinate frames with timestamps and answers "where is A relative to B" by chaining transforms. Use the standard frames map, odom, base_link, and give each frame exactly one parent. Broadcast moving transforms on /tf and fixed ones on /tf_static; look them up with a Buffer and TransformListener. URDF describes links and joints; xacro adds properties, maths and macros so you do not repeat yourself. robot_state_publisher turns the URDF and joint states into the TF tree automatically. Always validate with check_urdf, and inspect the tree with view_frames and RViz. Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

Real robots are slow, expensive and fragile. A bad line of code can snap a gripper, and a single experiment can take an afternoon of resetting the scene. Simulation turns all of that into a command you can run a thousand times in parallel, overnight, for free. Every serious robotics team, from a student club to a humanoid startup, develops in simulation first. This module teaches you to build and use those virtual worlds. You will write Gazebo worlds from scratch, spawn robots into them, give them cameras, lidar and an IMU, and bridge everything to ROS 2. You will also meet NVIDIA Isaac Sim, the GPU-based simulator used for synthetic data and robot learning, and then face the honest hard part: a robot that works in simulation often fails on the real floor. You will learn why, and what to do about it.

Explain what a physics engine does, where it cuts corners, and when to trust it. Write an SDF world, spawn a URDF robot into Gazebo Harmonic, and drive it from a ROS 2 topic. Add camera, depth, lidar and IMU sensors and bridge their data to ROS 2 with ros_gz_bridge. Describe the Isaac Sim stack (USD, Omniverse, PhysX, Replicator) and when you would choose it over Gazebo. Apply domain randomization and system identification to shrink the sim-to-real gap.

Build a small differential-drive robot world. Your project is one launch file that starts Gazebo Harmonic with your SDF world, spawns your robot, starts the ros_gz_bridge for /cmd_vel, /odom, /scan and /camera/image_raw, and opens RViz showing all of them. Then drive the robot with ros2 run teleop_twist_keyboard teleop_twist_keyboard and record a short bag. You will reuse this world in the motion and perception modules, so keep it tidy. Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right.

Intermediate40 minBefore this:ROS 2 nodes and topics · URDF basics · Linux terminal You have a URDF for your robot and a ROS 2 workspace, but no floor to drive on, no walls to bump into and no physics. Before you can test navigation or a grasp, you need a world and a way to drop your robot into it. Gazebo is the simulator the ROS community uses for exactly this, and in this lesson you will build a world from scratch and drive a robot around it. You will be able to Explain how Gazebo, SDF and URDF relate to each other. Write a Gazebo Harmonic world in SDF with physics, a ground, lights and obstacles. Spawn a URDF robot with ros_gz_sim and give it a differential-drive controller plugin. Launch everything from one ROS 2 launch file and drive the robot with a Twist command.

GazeboThe modern Gazebo simulator (formerly Ignition), a modular set of libraries for physics, rendering, sensors and a GUI is the simulator. We use the Harmonic release, which is the one that pairs with ROS 2 Jazzy. Its command line tool is gz, and you start a simulation with gz sim. SDFSimulation Description Format: Gazebo’s XML file format for worlds, models, lights, sensors and plugins is the file format Gazebo reads natively. A world is an SDF file describing everything: physics settings, lights, ground, and models. A model is a thing in the world (a robot, a table) made of links (rigid bodies) connected by joints. You already know URDF from ROS 2. URDF describes only a robot, and it has no way to describe worlds, lights or sensors in detail. Gazebo converts a URDF to SDF on the fly when you spawn it, and lets you add Gazebo-only extras inside <gazebo> tags. Gazebo has its own message system (called Gazebo Transport) that is separate from ROS 2. A bridge translates between the two. We will meet the bridge properly in the next lesson, but you will already use it here.
documents.s: The pieces and how they fit

documents.t: On Ubuntu 24.04 with ROS 2 Jazzy: terminal sudo apt install ros-jazzy-ros-gz gz sim shapes.sdf shapes.sdf is a demo world that ships with Gazebo. Press the play button at the bottom left of the window. If a box, sphere and cylinder fall and the physics runs, you are set. Quit with Ctrl+C in the terminal.

Create a folder proprio_sim/ and the following file. Read the comments: every block matters. proprio_world.sdf <?xml version="1.0"?> <sdf version="1.10"> <world name="proprio_world"> <!-- Physics: step 1 ms, try to run in real time --> <physics name="1ms" type="ignored"> <max_step_size>0.001</max_step_size> <real_time_factor>1.0</real_time_factor> </physics> <!-- Systems: Gazebo is built from plugins that you opt into --> <plugin filename="gz-sim-physics-system" name="gz::sim::systems::Physics"/> <plugin filename="gz-sim-user-commands-system" name="gz::sim::systems::UserCommands"/> <plugin filename="gz-sim-scene-broadcaster-system" name="gz::sim::systems::SceneBroadcaster"/> <plugin filename="gz-sim-sensors-system" name="gz::sim::systems::Sensors"> <render_engine>ogre2</render_engine> </plugin> <plugin filename="gz-sim-imu-system" name="gz::sim::systems::Imu"/> <light type="directional" name="sun"> <cast_shadows>true</cast_shadows> <pose>0 0 10 0 0 0</pose> <diffuse>0.9 0.9 0.9 1</diffuse> <specular>0.2 0.2 0.2 1</specular> <direction>-0.5 0.1 -0.9</direction> </light> <model name="ground_plane"> <static>true</static> <link name="link"> <collision name="collision"> <geometry><plane><normal>0 0 1</normal><size>100 100</size></plane></geometry> </collision> <visual name="visual"> <geometry><plane><normal>0 0 1</normal><size>100 100</size></plane></geometry> <material> <ambient>0.7 0.7 0.7 1</ambient> <diffuse>0.7 0.7 0.7 1</diffuse> </material> </visual> </link> </model> <!-- An obstacle: a static box 2 m in front of the origin --> <model name="box_obstacle"> <static>true</static> <pose>2 0 0.25 0 0 0</pose> <link name="link"> <collision name="collision"> <geometry><box><size>0.5 0.5 0.5</size></box></geometry> </collision> <visual name="visual"> <geometry><box><size>0.5 0.5 0.5</size></box></geometry> <material> <ambient>0.8 0.2 0.2 1</ambient> <diffuse>0.8 0.2 0.2 1</diffuse> </material> </visual> </link> </model> </world> </sdf> A few things to notice: Plugins are the engine. Physics, user commands from the GUI, the scene broadcaster (which feeds the GUI), and the sensors system are all separate plugins. If you forget one, that feature silently does not exist. Missing the Sensors plugin is the most common reason a simulated camera is blank. <pose> is x y z roll pitch yaw, in metres and radians, relative to the parent frame. <static>true</static> tells the engine this model never moves, which saves computation. Each link usually has two shapes: a <collision> (what physics sees, kept simple) and a <visual> (what you see). Run it: terminal gz sim -r proprio_world.sdf The -r flag starts the simulation running; without it the world starts paused. Worlds are built from opt-in systems Gazebo Harmonic has almost no built-in behaviour. Physics, sensors, controllers and the GUI link are all plugins listed in your world or robot file. When something does nothing, check that its plugin is loaded before you check anything else.

Here is a small two-wheeled robot as URDF. It has a body, two driven wheels and two caster balls, and one Gazebo plugin that turns cmd_vel messages into wheel motion. proprio_bot.urdf <?xml version="1.0"?> <robot name="proprio_bot"> <link name="base_link"> <inertial> <mass value="5.0"/> <inertia ixx="0.0302" iyy="0.0708" izz="0.0927" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyz="0"/> </inertial> <visual> <geometry><box size="0.4 0.25 0.1"/></geometry> <material name="blue"><color rgba="0.2 0.3 0.8 1"/></material> </visual> <collision> <geometry><box size="0.4 0.25 0.1"/></geometry> </collision> </link> <!-- Wheels: cylinders rotated so their axis points along the robot's y axis --> <link name="left_wheel"> <inertial> <mass value="0.5"/> <inertia ixx="0.001317" iyy="0.0025" izz="0.001317" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyz="0"/> </inertial> <visual> <origin rpy="1.5708 0 0"/> <geometry><cylinder radius="0.1" length="0.04"/></geometry> </visual> <collision> <origin rpy="1.5708 0 0"/> <geometry><cylinder radius="0.1" length="0.04"/></geometry> </collision> </link> <joint name="left_wheel_joint" type="continuous"> <parent link="base_link"/> <child link="left_wheel"/> <origin xyz="0 0.15 0"/> <axis xyz="0 1 0"/> </joint> <link name="right_wheel"> <inertial> <mass value="0.5"/> <inertia ixx="0.001317" iyy="0.0025" izz="0.001317" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyz="0"/> </inertial> <visual> <origin rpy="1.5708 0 0"/> <geometry><cylinder radius="0.1" length="0.04"/></geometry> </visual> <collision> <origin rpy="1.5708 0 0"/> <geometry><cylinder radius="0.1" length="0.04"/></geometry> </collision> </link> <joint name="right_wheel_joint" type="continuous"> <parent link="base_link"/> <child link="right_wheel"/> <origin xyz="0 -0.15 0"/> <axis xyz="0 1 0"/> </joint> <!-- Frictionless casters keep the body level --> <link name="caster_front"> <inertial> <mass value="0.1"/> <inertia ixx="0.0001" iyy="0.0001" izz="0.0001" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyz="0"/> </inertial> <collision><geometry><sphere radius="0.05"/></geometry></collision> <visual><geometry><sphere radius="0.05"/></geometry></visual> </link> <joint name="caster_front_joint" type="fixed"> <parent link="base_link"/> <child link="caster_front"/> <origin xyz="0.15 0 -0.05"/> </joint> <link name="caster_rear"> <inertial> <mass value="0.1"/> <inertia ixx="0.0001" iyy="0.0001" izz="0.0001" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyz="0"/> </inertial> <collision><geometry><sphere radius="0.05"/></geometry></collision> <visual><geometry><sphere radius="0.05"/></geometry></visual> </link> <joint name="caster_rear_joint" type="fixed"> <parent link="base_link"/> <child link="caster_rear"/> <origin xyz="-0.15 0 -0.05"/> </joint> <gazebo reference="caster_front"> <mu1>0.0</mu1><mu2>0.0</mu2> </gazebo> <gazebo reference="caster_rear"> <mu1>0.0</mu1><mu2>0.0</mu2> </gazebo> <gazebo> <plugin filename="gz-sim-diff-drive-system" name="gz::sim::systems::DiffDrive"> <left_joint>left_wheel_joint</left_joint> <right_joint>right_wheel_joint</right_joint> <wheel_separation>0.3</wheel_separation> <wheel_radius>0.1</wheel_radius> <odom_publish_frequency>30</odom_publish_frequency> <topic>cmd_vel</topic> <odom_topic>odom</odom_topic> <tf_topic>tf</tf_topic> <frame_id>odom</frame_id> <child_frame_id>base_link</child_frame_id> </plugin> <plugin filename="gz-sim-joint-state-publisher-system" name="gz::sim::systems::JointStatePublisher"/> </gazebo> </robot> Three details worth understanding: Inertia values must be present and plausible. A link with zero mass or zero inertia is a classic cause of robots that explode or sink through the floor. The numbers above come from the formulas for a box and a cylinder. Wheel axis. A URDF cylinder points along its local z axis. We rotate the shape by 90 degrees (rpy="1.5708 0 0") and spin the joint about y. Friction. mu1 and mu2 are friction coefficients that Gazebo carries over when converting to SDF. Casters should slide freely, so we set them to zero. The DiffDrive plugin listens on cmd_vel, converts the linear and angular velocity into left and right wheel speeds using the wheel separation bbb and radius rrr (vL,R=(v∓ωb/2)/rv_{L,R} = (v \mp \omega b/2)/rvL,R​=(v∓ωb/2)/r, the standard differential-drive kinematics; see Anatomy of a robot for the robot parts involved), and publishes odom and the odom to base_link transform.

With the world already running, you can spawn the robot from another terminal: terminal ros2 run ros_gz_sim create -file proprio_bot.urdf -name proprio_bot -z 0.12 -name is the model name inside Gazebo, and -z lifts it a little so the wheels do not start inside the floor. You can also spawn from a ROS parameter with -topic robot_description, which is what you do when a robot_state_publisher already holds the URDF. Now put it all in one launch file so that starting the whole thing is a single command. sim.launch.py import os from launch import LaunchDescription from launch.actions import IncludeLaunchDescription from launch.launch_description_sources import PythonLaunchDescriptionSource from launch_ros.actions import Node from launch_ros.substitutions import FindPackageShare HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)) def generate_launch_description(): gz_sim = IncludeLaunchDescription( PythonLaunchDescriptionSource( [FindPackageShare("ros_gz_sim"), "/launch/gz_sim.launch.py"] ), launch_arguments={"gz_args": f"-r {HERE}/proprio_world.sdf"}.items(), ) spawn = Node( package="ros_gz_sim", executable="create", arguments=[ "-file", f"{HERE}/proprio_bot.urdf", "-name", "proprio_bot", "-z", "0.12", ], output="screen", ) bridge = Node( package="ros_gz_bridge", executable="parameter_bridge", arguments=[ "/clock@rosgraph_msgs/msg/Clock[gz.msgs.Clock", "/cmd_vel@geometry_msgs/msg/Twist]gz.msgs.Twist", "/odom@nav_msgs/msg/Odometry[gz.msgs.Odometry", ], output="screen", ) return LaunchDescription([gz_sim, spawn, bridge]) Run it with ros2 launch ./sim.launch.py. The symbols [ and ] in the bridge arguments set the direction of travel; the next lesson explains them in detail. Pro tip Gazebo finds models referenced as model://name through the environment variable GZ_SIM_RESOURCE_PATH, a colon-separated list of folders. You can also pull ready-made models from Gazebo Fuel, the online model library, using an <include> with a <uri> that points at a Fuel model. Look up the exact model URL on the Fuel website rather than guessing it.

Create proprio_sim/ and save proprio_world.sdf, proprio_bot.urdf and sim.launch.py into it. Run ros2 launch ./sim.launch.py from inside the folder. The Gazebo window should open with the robot sitting on the ground, 2 m from the red box. In a second terminal, run ros2 topic list. You should see /clock, /cmd_vel and /odom. Drive forward: ros2 topic pub --rate 10 /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {x: 0.3}}". Watch ros2 topic echo /odom --field pose.pose.position and confirm x grows while the robot rolls toward the box, and stops when you press Ctrl+C on the publisher. It worked if the robot drives straight, hits the box and stops, and the x in odometry matches roughly what you see in the window.

Make a corridorBeginner Add two long thin static boxes to the world to form a corridor 1.2 m wide, starting 3 m from the robot. What do you change to place them? Show solutionHide solution Copy the box_obstacle model, rename each copy (model names must be unique), change the <size> to something like 4 0.1 0.5, and set <pose> so that their centres are at y = +0.65 and y = -0.65. The inner faces are then 1.2 m apart (0.65 minus half of the 0.1 thickness, times two). Debug a sinking robotIntermediate You spawn your robot at -z 0 and it tumbles and jitters. List three things to check. Show solutionHide solution (1) The wheels start inside the ground, so spawn higher. (2) Missing or tiny inertia values in a link. (3) Collision shapes that overlap each other inside the robot body, which makes the solver push them apart. Turn in placeIntermediate What Twist do you send to rotate on the spot at 1 rad/s, and what wheel speeds result with b=0.3b = 0.3b=0.3 m and r=0.1r = 0.1r=0.1 m? Show solutionHide solution Send linear x = 0 and angular z = 1.0. Then vL=−ωb/(2r)=−1.5v_L = -\omega b/(2r) = -1.5vL​=−ωb/(2r)=−1.5 rad/s and vR=+1.5v_R = +1.5vR​=+1.5 rad/s, so the wheels spin in opposite directions.

AThey are the same format with different file extensionsBURDF describes a robot only; SDF can describe whole worlds and Gazebo converts URDF to SDFCSDF is only for camerasDURDF replaces SDF in Gazebo Harmonic 2Your simulated camera shows a black image even though it is in the model. Which is a likely cause? AThe Sensors system plugin is missing from the worldBThe ground plane is staticCThe robot has two wheelsDThe world file ends with a newline 3What does the -r flag of gz sim do? ARecords a videoBStarts the simulation running instead of pausedCRestarts the world every minuteDRemoves the GUI 4Why do links have separate collision and visual geometry? AVisuals are for physics and collisions for renderingBTo let collisions be simple and fast while visuals can be detailedCBecause SDF forbids reusing shapesDIt is only a naming convention 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Gazebo Harmonic is the simulator; gz sim runs it; SDF describes worlds and models. A world file chooses the physics step and lists the system plugins you want. URDF robots are converted to SDF when spawned with ros_gz_sim create; Gazebo-only extras live in <gazebo> tags. Inertia, wheel axes and friction values are the usual sources of strange behaviour. The DiffDrive plugin turns cmd_vel into wheel motion and publishes odometry. One launch file should start the world, spawn the robot and start the bridge.

Gazebo Harmonic documentation: gazebosim.org/docs/harmonic SDF format reference: sdformat.org/spec ROS 2 and Gazebo integration (ros_gz): gazebosim.org/docs/harmonic/ros2_integration Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right. Next: Simulated sensors and ros_gz

Intermediate30 minBefore this:Gazebo worlds and robots · Simulated sensors and ros_gz Your vision team needs 200,000 labelled images of cluttered shelves, each with a different lighting setup, camera angle and set of boxes. A real photoshoot would take months. Gazebo could render the scenes, but the images would look flat and the labelling would be work you have to build yourself. This is the job Isaac Sim was made for: photorealistic scenes, automatic labels, and thousands of robots training in parallel on one GPU. You will be able to Describe what Isaac Sim is built from: Omniverse, USD, PhysX and RTX rendering. Explain what a USD stage, prim and layer are, and author a small USD scene in Python. Describe how Replicator produces labelled synthetic data with domain randomization. Explain how Isaac Sim talks to ROS 2, and decide when to pick Isaac Sim versus Gazebo. A note on versions Isaac Sim and its companion libraries change quickly. Menu names, extension names and Python APIs move between releases. This lesson teaches the stable ideas. For exact steps, always follow the documentation for the release you install, at docs.nvidia.com. We deliberately do not quote version numbers or menu paths here.

Isaac SimA robotics simulator from NVIDIA, built on the Omniverse platform, with GPU-accelerated physics (PhysX) and ray-traced rendering is a robot simulator that runs on NVIDIA GPUs. It sits on top of Omniverse, NVIDIA’s platform for building and connecting 3D applications. Four ingredients matter. USD (Universal Scene Description). The scene format. Everything, from the robot to the lighting, is a USD file. PhysX. The physics engine. It can simulate many environments on the GPU at the same time, which is what makes reinforcement learning at scale feasible. RTX rendering. Ray-traced graphics. Images look like photographs, with believable reflections, shadows and materials, which matters when you train a vision model on them. Python and extensions. You script scenes and experiments in Python, and add features through extensions.
documents.s: What it is, in one picture

documents.t: USDUniversal Scene Description: an open file format and library, originally from Pixar, for describing 3D scenes as a hierarchy of typed objects with properties describes a scene as a tree. The whole tree is a stage. Each node is a prim (short for primitive), such as a transform, a cube, a camera, a light or a robot. Prims have attributes (size, position, colour) and live at a path like /World/Box. USD files are built from layers, stacked on top of each other like transparent sheets. A base layer might hold the factory building; an upper layer moves one shelf. Because layers compose rather than overwrite, a team can share one robot file and each person can add their own changes without touching the original. Files come in a readable text form (.usda) and a compact binary form (.usdc), and .usd can be either. You can try this without installing Isaac Sim. The USD library is available on its own: terminal pip install usd-core make_scene.py from pxr import Gf, Usd, UsdGeom stage = Usd.Stage.CreateNew("scene.usda") UsdGeom.SetStageUpAxis(stage, UsdGeom.Tokens.z) UsdGeom.SetStageMetersPerUnit(stage, 1.0) world = UsdGeom.Xform.Define(stage, "/World") stage.SetDefaultPrim(world.GetPrim()) box = UsdGeom.Cube.Define(stage, "/World/Box") box.GetSizeAttr().Set(0.5) UsdGeom.XformCommonAPI(box).SetTranslate(Gf.Vec3d(2.0, 0.0, 0.25)) stage.GetRootLayer().Save() print(stage.GetRootLayer().ExportToString()) Run it and open the printed text. You will see a def Xform "World" containing a def Cube "Box" with size = 0.5 and a translate operation. This is exactly the same format Isaac Sim loads. It is the equivalent of the SDF world you wrote for Gazebo, but USD is also used by film studios, game engines and digital-twin tools, which is why robotics adopted it. USD is the one shared language In Isaac Sim, the robot, the world, the materials, the lights and even physics settings are all USD. Learn to read a .usda file and you can debug almost any problem in the simulator by looking at what the scene actually contains.

You rarely write robot USD by hand. Isaac Sim includes importers that convert a URDF (or MJCF, the format used by MuJoCo) into USD, creating articulations, joints, colliders and physics properties. It also ships with libraries of ready-made robots, props and environments that you can reference into your stage. After importing, check three things, the same ones that broke your Gazebo robot: mass and inertia, joint limits and drive settings (stiffness and damping for each joint), and collision shapes. A robot imported with the wrong joint drive gains will flop or vibrate.

Cameras in Isaac Sim are rendered by the RTX renderer, so you can get realistic reflections, motion blur and lens effects. Lidar can be simulated with ray tracing against the scene. Because the simulator knows the full truth of the scene, it can also give you annotators: extra outputs that come for free with each frame. 2D and 3D bounding boxes with class labels Semantic segmentation (a class for every pixel) and instance segmentation (an id for every object) Depth and surface normals Object poses ReplicatorNVIDIA’s Isaac Sim toolkit for generating synthetic data: it randomises scene properties and writes images with automatic labels is the Isaac Sim toolkit that automates this. You describe a scene, declare what should vary, and ask for N frames. The loop looks like this: That "randomise" step is called domain randomizationTraining on data where scene properties such as colours, lighting and positions are varied widely, so the model cannot rely on details that differ in the real world. If every simulated image has the same lighting, your detector may learn "boxes are the things lit from the left". If lighting, colours and clutter are random, the detector has to learn what a box really is. You will see this idea again in lesson five. Pro tip Randomise the things you do not know, and keep fixed the things you do. If your real cameras are always 1.5 m above the floor, do not randomise camera height over 0 to 5 m: you waste training capacity on views that never occur.

Isaac Sim includes a ROS 2 bridge: an extension that publishes simulated sensor data as standard ROS 2 messages and subscribes to ROS 2 commands. You configure which topics to publish using a visual graph system called OmniGraph, or through Python. Typical bridged data includes the clock, camera images and camera info, lidar scans or point clouds, TF, joint states and odometry, and the commands you send back are joint targets or cmd_vel. The result is the same as in Gazebo: your Nav2 or perception nodes run unmodified against a simulated robot. Separately from the simulator, NVIDIA publishes Isaac ROS, a set of GPU-accelerated ROS 2 packages (for example, for stereo depth and visual SLAM) that you can run on real hardware. Do not confuse the two: Isaac Sim is the world, Isaac ROS is software that runs on the robot. Isaac Sim also forms the base for Isaac Lab, a framework for robot learning that runs thousands of environments in parallel. You will use it in RL in simulation with Isaac Lab.

Question Gazebo Harmonic Isaac Sim Hardware needed Any reasonable laptop A recent NVIDIA RTX GPU (check the current requirements) Image realism Good enough for navigation Photorealistic ray-traced Synthetic data and labels You build it Built in (Replicator) Massive parallel RL Not its focus A core use case ROS 2 integration Native with ros_gz Via the ROS 2 bridge extension Learning curve Gentle, XML files Steeper, USD and extensions Cost and licensing Open source Free to use for many users, but check the current licence terms A sensible rule: start in Gazebo for navigation, control and integration work, and reach for Isaac Sim when you need photorealistic synthetic data, large-scale learning or a digital twin of a factory.
documents.s: Choosing between Gazebo and Isaac Sim

documents.t: Install the standalone USD library with pip install usd-core and run make_scene.py. Open scene.usda in a text editor. Add a second prim: a sphere of radius 0.2 at position (1.0, 1.0, 0.2), using UsdGeom.Sphere.Define. Print the file again and find it in the output. Write a plan (no code needed) for a synthetic dataset for your capstone idea: what objects, what randomisation (list at least five things that vary), what labels, and how many images. If you have an NVIDIA RTX machine, install Isaac Sim following the current NVIDIA documentation and load one of the bundled example robots. If you do not, read the "Getting started" section of the docs and note down the system requirements. You know it worked when your scene.usda contains both prims and you can explain, in your own words, what each layer of the Isaac Sim stack does.

Read a USD fileBeginner In the text output of make_scene.py, what is the full path of the cube prim, and what attribute holds its edge length? Show solutionHide solution The path is /World/Box and the attribute is size, set to 0.5. Its position comes from an xformOp:translate attribute. Design the randomisationIntermediate You are generating images to detect cardboard boxes on warehouse shelves with a camera mounted at a fixed height. List four properties to randomise and one to keep fixed. Show solutionHide solution Randomise: lighting direction and brightness, box textures and colours, box positions and counts, distractor objects, camera yaw and small pose changes. Keep fixed: the camera height and approximate pitch, since the real camera does not change them. Gazebo or Isaac?Intermediate For each project, pick a simulator and justify it: (a) testing a Nav2 configuration on a laptop, (b) training a quadruped to walk using 4,096 parallel environments, (c) producing a photorealistic dataset for a segmentation model. Show solutionHide solution (a) Gazebo: light, native ROS 2, geometry and lidar are enough. (b) Isaac Sim with Isaac Lab: GPU-parallel physics is designed for this. (c) Isaac Sim with Replicator: ray-traced images and automatic masks.

The ROS 2 bridge lets your ROS nodes run unchanged against Isaac Sim. Gazebo is lighter and ROS-native; Isaac Sim wins on realism, synthetic data and parallel learning. Advanced40 minBefore this:Why simulate · Simulated sensors and ros_gz · Basic probability (mean, standard deviation) · Python and NumPy Your walking policy runs for ten flawless minutes in simulation. You load it on the real robot, and it takes two steps and falls over. Nothing is "wrong" with the policy: the real motors are slower than the simulated ones, the floor is a bit slicker, and the camera image arrives 80 milliseconds late. This disagreement between the virtual and the real world is called the sim-to-real gapThe difference in behaviour between a robot controller or learned policy in simulation and on real hardware, caused by modelling errors and unmodelled effects, and managing it is half of modern robotics. You will be able to List the main sources of the sim-to-real gap: dynamics, actuators, sensors, latency and visuals. Fit a simulation model to real measurements with system identification. Use domain randomization to produce controllers that survive uncertainty, and see the effect in code. Add realistic noise and latency models to a simulation, and plan a safe ladder of tests from sim to hardware.

Think of the simulator as a guess about the world. Each part of that guess can be wrong. Source What the simulator assumes What reality does Rigid-body parameters Exact mass, centre of mass, inertia Cables, batteries and paint change them Contact and friction One friction coefficient, ideal contact Surfaces vary, wear, get dusty and wet Actuators Instant, perfect torque or position tracking Limited bandwidth, saturation, backlash, heating, voltage sag Sensors Clean, or lightly noisy Bias that drifts, dropouts, motion blur, lens dirt, rolling shutter Latency Zero or a fixed small delay Variable delays through drivers, networks and compute Visuals Clean render, perfect textures Glare, shadows, reflections, camera auto-exposure World Exactly as modelled People, clutter and surprises There are four broad strategies, and good teams use all of them together: Make the simulator more accurate (system identification). Make the controller robust to what is still wrong (domain randomization, robust control). Adapt on the real robot (online adaptation, fine-tuning with a small amount of real data). Make the real test safe (staged testing, limits and an emergency stop). You cannot make the simulator perfect, so make the controller tolerant The goal is not a flawless simulator. The goal is a controller that works across a whole range of plausible worlds that contains reality. That is the core of domain randomization.

System identificationEstimating the parameters of a mathematical model by fitting its output to measurements from the real system means measuring the real system and tuning simulator parameters until the simulation reproduces it. The mathematical form is simple. Given a model with parameters θ\thetaθ, input signals uku_kuk​ and measured outputs yky_kyk​, find θ^=arg⁡min⁡θ∑k∥yk−y^k(θ)∥2,\hat{\theta} = \arg\min_{\theta} \sum_{k} \left\| y_k - \hat{y}_k(\theta) \right\|^2 ,θ^=argθmin​k∑​∥yk​−y^​k​(θ)∥2, where y^k(θ)\hat{y}_k(\theta)y^​k​(θ) is what the simulator predicts. That is nonlinear least squares. A motor is a good first example. Apply a step of voltage and record the speed. A common model is first-order: τω˙=Ku−ω\tau \dot{\omega} = K u - \omegaτω˙=Ku−ω, with gain KKK (steady-state speed per volt) and time constant τ\tauτ (how quickly it responds). The code below fakes "real" measurements from known values, then recovers them. You can replace the fake data with a real logged step response. It needs pip install numpy scipy. sysid.py import numpy as np from scipy.optimize import least_squares def simulate(params, u, dt): gain, tau = params w = np.zeros_like(u) for k in range(1, len(u)): w[k] = w[k - 1] + dt * (gain * u[k - 1] - w[k - 1]) / tau return w rng = np.random.default_rng(0) dt = 0.01 t = np.arange(0.0, 3.0, dt) u = np.where(t > 0.5, 6.0, 0.0) true_params = (2.0, 0.25) measured = simulate(true_params, u, dt) + rng.normal(0.0, 0.05, t.shape) fit = least_squares( lambda p: simulate(p, u, dt) - measured, x0=[1.0, 0.1], bounds=([0.01, 0.01], [10.0, 2.0]), ) print("true params :", true_params) print("fitted : gain=%.3f tau=%.3f" % tuple(fit.x)) Run it. It prints fitted values very close to the true ones. In real life three rules make system identification work: Excite the system. Use inputs that move the robot through the range you care about; a robot that never moves tells you nothing. Fit what matters. Fit the parameters that change behaviour a lot (actuator lag, friction, mass), not everything. Validate on new data. Check the fitted model against a recording it was not fitted to, just like any machine-learning model. Typical quantities worth identifying: motor gain and time constant, joint friction and damping, link masses, ground friction, sensor noise standard deviations, and total latency from command to motion.

Even after system identification, parameters stay uncertain and some drift over time. Domain randomizationVarying simulator parameters (physics, sensors, visuals) randomly during development so the result works across many possible worlds, including the real one treats this honestly: instead of one simulator with fixed numbers, use many simulators with numbers drawn from plausible ranges. If ξ\xiξ is the vector of uncertain parameters with distribution p(ξ)p(\xi)p(ξ), you tune a controller or policy π\piπ to do well on average: max⁡π Eξ∼p(ξ)[J(π;ξ)],\max_{\pi} \; \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim p(\xi)} \left[ J(\pi ; \xi) \right] ,πmax​Eξ∼p(ξ)​[J(π;ξ)], where JJJ is the performance score (reward, or negative error). A policy that scores well across the whole range is unlikely to be surprised by the real values. What do you randomise? Dynamics: mass, friction, restitution, joint damping, motor strength. Actuators: gain error, delay, saturation. Sensors: noise level, bias, dropout, calibration error. Visuals (for camera inputs): lighting, textures, colours, camera pose, distractors, as in the Replicator workflow from the previous lesson. Disturbances: random pushes, payload changes. Here is a complete, runnable example. A cart is driven by a PD controller. In the "nominal" simulator, mass, friction and gain are exact and there is no delay. In the randomised one, they vary, and observations are delayed by 0 to 7 steps and are noisy. We pick the controller gains twice (once per simulator) and test both on a held-out randomised "reality". randomization_demo.py from collections import deque import numpy as np class CartEnv: """A 1D cart: m * x'' = f - c * x'. Parameters are re-drawn on every reset.""" def __init__(self, randomize: bool, seed: int = 0): self.randomize = randomize self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) self.dt = 0.01 def reset(self): r = self.rng if self.randomize: self.m = r.uniform(0.7, 1.5) # mass error self.c = r.uniform(0.0, 1.0) # friction error self.gain = r.uniform(0.8, 1.2) # actuator strength self.delay = int(r.integers(0, 8)) # sensor latency in steps self.noise = r.uniform(0.0, 0.01) # sensor noise std (m) else: self.m, self.c, self.gain, self.delay, self.noise = 1.0, 0.2, 1.0, 0, 0.0 self.x, self.v = 0.0, 0.0 self.buf = deque([(0.0, 0.0)] * (self.delay + 1), maxlen=self.delay + 1) return self._observe() def _observe(self): x_old, v_old = self.buf[0] if self.noise > 0: nx, nv = self.rng.normal(0.0, self.noise, 2) else: nx = nv = 0.0 return x_old + nx, v_old + nv def step(self, f): f = float(np.clip(f, -50.0, 50.0)) * self.gain a = (f - self.c * self.v) / self.m self.v += a * self.dt self.x += self.v * self.dt self.buf.append((self.x, self.v)) return self._observe() def run_episode(env, kp, kd, steps=400): """Return the integrated absolute error: lower is better.""" obs = env.reset() cost = 0.0 for _ in range(steps): x, v = obs obs = env.step(kp * (1.0 - x) - kd * v) cost += abs(1.0 - env.x) * env.dt if abs(env.x) > 50: # diverged: stop early with a big penalty return 50.0 return cost def score(env, kp, kd, episodes=100): return float(np.mean([run_episode(env, kp, kd) for _ in range(episodes)])) candidates = [(kp, 0.8 * 2 * np.sqrt(kp)) for kp in (20, 80, 300, 1000, 3000)] nominal_env = CartEnv(randomize=False) random_env = CartEnv(randomize=True, seed=1) reality = CartEnv(randomize=True, seed=999) # held-out "real world" best_nom = min(candidates, key=lambda g: score(nominal_env, *g, episodes=1)) best_dr = min(candidates, key=lambda g: score(random_env, *g)) for name, g in (("tuned on nominal sim", best_nom), ("tuned with randomisation", best_dr)): cost = score(reality, *g, episodes=300) print(f"{name:26s} kp={g[0]:5.0f} kd={g[1]:5.1f} cost in 'reality' = {cost:.3f}") Run it. The controller tuned only on the perfect simulator picks stiff, high gains, because with no delay a stiff controller looks best. In the delayed and noisy "reality" those gains oscillate. The controller tuned with randomisation picks gentler gains and scores far better on the held-out worlds (when we ran it, the cost was about three times lower). You have just seen the sim-to-real gap, and a cure, in 70 lines. Randomisation has a cost Randomise too little and the real world falls outside your range. Randomise too much and the task becomes impossible or the controller becomes timid and slow. Start with ranges you can justify from measurements, and widen them only when real tests demand it.
documents.s: Domain randomization: train for a range of worlds

documents.t: Two effects deserve their own models because they break so many controllers. Sensor noise. Real sensors are not just Gaussian. A better IMU model adds a slowly drifting bias, bk+1=bk+ηkb_{k+1} = b_k + \eta_kbk+1​=bk​+ηk​, to the white noise wkw_kwk​, so the reading is zk=xk+bk+wkz_k = x_k + b_k + w_kzk​=xk​+bk​+wk​. In Gazebo, noise blocks inside sensors (as in the previous lesson) give you the white-noise part; for biases, you can post-process in a bridge node or in your own wrapper. Latency. Every real loop has delay between sensing and acting: camera exposure, USB transfer, image processing, network hops, motor drivers. A feedback loop with a delay of TdT_dTd​ has extra phase lag of ωTd\omega T_dωTd​ at frequency ω\omegaω, which eats into its stability margin. That is why the delay in the cart example mattered so much. Measure the true end-to-end latency on your robot (for example, flash an LED on command and film it, or timestamp messages at each stage), then put that delay into your simulation as a buffer.
documents.s: Noise and latency are not optional

documents.t: Even good randomisation does not remove the need for careful real tests. Climb a ladder, never skipping a rung: Software in the loop: the real code against the simulator (what you have been doing). Hardware in the loop: the real controller computer or motor drivers, with the plant still simulated. This finds timing and driver problems. Real robot, restrained: on a stand or a tether, wheels or feet off the ground, with torque limits reduced. Real robot, free: with an emergency stop within reach, conservative limits, and a clear area. Log everything. When the real robot disagrees with the simulator, record the same signal in both and compare. That difference is the data that drives your next round of system identification.

Run sysid.py. Change the noise standard deviation from 0.05 to 0.5 and see how the fitted values degrade. Then lengthen the recording from 3 s to 10 s and see how they recover. Run randomization_demo.py and record the costs for both rows. In CartEnv, widen the randomised delay from integers(0, 8) to integers(0, 20) and re-run. What happens to the best randomised gains? Add a second uncertain parameter of your own choice, such as a random constant disturbance force, and re-run. You know it worked when you can explain why the randomised-tuned controller picks lower gains than the nominal-tuned one.

Which strategy?Beginner Your robot arm’s real joint lags behind the commanded position by about 60 ms, but in simulation it tracks instantly. Name the simplest first fix. Show solutionHide solution Identify the lag by recording a step response on the real joint, fit a first-order model (or a pure delay), and add it to the simulation as a dynamics model or a delay buffer. Then re-tune or retrain against the corrected simulator. Estimate latency stabilityIntermediate A feedback loop has a crossover frequency of 5 Hz and a total delay of 40 ms. How much extra phase lag does the delay add at crossover? Show solutionHide solution Phase lag in radians is ωTd=2π⋅5⋅0.04≈1.26\omega T_d = 2\pi \cdot 5 \cdot 0.04 \approx 1.26ωTd​=2π⋅5⋅0.04≈1.26 rad, which is about 72 degrees. That is large enough to remove most of a typical 60 degree phase margin, so the loop would be close to unstable. Design the rangesAdvanced You are training a policy for a robot that carries between 0 and 3 kg of payload on a floor you have measured to have a friction coefficient between 0.5 and 0.9. State the ranges you would randomise for payload and friction, and one parameter you would keep fixed. Show solutionHide solution Randomise payload uniformly from 0 to 3 kg (perhaps slightly wider, such as 0 to 3.5 kg, for margin) and friction from about 0.4 to 1.0. Keep the robot’s own link geometry fixed, since you know it from the CAD or measurements. Document the ranges and widen them only if real tests fail outside them.

1What is system identification? ANaming every part of a robotBFitting a simulation model’s parameters to real measurementsCRendering the robot in 3DDLogging in to the robot over SSH 2Why can a controller tuned on a perfect simulator oscillate on hardware? AHardware has no gravityBIt ignores delay, noise and parameter errors that real systems haveCSimulators always use smaller numbersDPython is slower on robots 3What does domain randomization optimise for? ABest performance in a single exact simulatorBGood average performance across many plausible worldsCThe smallest possible modelDFastest rendering 4In the testing ladder, which step comes right before running the robot freely? AWriting the paperBReal robot, restrained, with reduced limitsCDeleting the simulatorDSkipping hardware-in-the-loop 0 of 4 answered Takeaways The sim-to-real gap comes from imperfect dynamics, actuators, sensors, latency, visuals and the world itself. System identification fits simulator parameters to real data with least squares; validate on held-out data. Domain randomization trains for a range of worlds, so the controller tolerates the real one. Model noise (including bias) and latency explicitly; latency eats stability margin. Randomise what you are unsure about, not everything, and justify your ranges with measurements. Move from simulation to hardware in stages, logging both sides to keep improving the model.

Tobin et al., "Domain Randomization for Transferring Deep Neural Networks from Simulation to the Real World": arxiv.org/abs/1703.06907 Peng et al., "Sim-to-Real Transfer of Robotic Control with Dynamics Randomization": arxiv.org/abs/1710.06537 Gazebo documentation on sensor noise models: gazebosim.org/docs Stuck? Intermediate45 minBefore this:Gazebo worlds and robots · ROS 2 topics and QoS · TF2 basics Your robot now drives, but it is blind and deaf. It cannot tell a wall from open floor, and nothing you have learned about perception or navigation can be tested yet. In simulation, a sensor is just a few lines of XML on a link, and a bridge process that copies its messages into ROS 2. Once you do this, your simulated robot looks, to your ROS code, exactly like a real one. You will be able to Add camera, depth camera, lidar and IMU sensors to a robot with SDF sensor blocks. Read and write ros_gz_bridge argument syntax, including direction symbols and YAML configuration. Explain how noise models and update rates affect what your code sees. Visualise images, laser scans, point clouds and TF in RViz, with the right QoS and simulated time.
documents.s: Simulated sensors and the ros_gz bridge

documents.t: In Gazebo, a sensor is attached to a link, like a physical camera is bolted to a robot. The Sensors system plugin (which we already loaded in the world) renders the cameras and ray-casts the lidar every step according to the sensor’s <update_rate>, and publishes the result on a Gazebo Transport topic. Add each sensor to proprio_bot.urdf from the last lesson: a new link and a fixed joint to hold it, plus a <gazebo reference="..."> block that carries the sensor definition.
documents.s: A sensor is a link plus a recipe

documents.t: proprio_bot.urdf (add inside <robot>) <link name="camera_link"> <inertial> <mass value="0.05"/> <inertia ixx="1e-5" iyy="1e-5" izz="1e-5" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyz="0"/> </inertial> <visual><geometry><box size="0.03 0.06 0.03"/></geometry></visual> </link> <joint name="camera_joint" type="fixed"> <parent link="base_link"/> <child link="camera_link"/> <origin xyz="0.2 0 0.08"/> </joint> <gazebo reference="camera_link"> <sensor name="camera" type="camera"> <always_on>true</always_on> <update_rate>30</update_rate> <topic>camera/image_raw</topic> <gz_frame_id>camera_link</gz_frame_id> <camera> <horizontal_fov>1.047</horizontal_fov> <image> <width>640</width> <height>480</height> <format>R8G8B8</format> </image> <clip><near>0.1</near><far>20</far></clip> <noise> <type>gaussian</type> <mean>0.0</mean> <stddev>0.007</stddev> </noise> </camera> </sensor> </gazebo> Look at what each part controls. horizontal_fov is the field of view in radians (1.047 is about 60 degrees). width and height set the resolution, which with the field of view fixes the intrinsics you will study in the next module. clip sets the nearest and farthest distances that are rendered. The noise block adds Gaussian noise to each pixel, so your vision code does not get unrealistically clean images.

A depth camera has the same structure, with type="depth_camera" and a floating-point image format: proprio_bot.urdf (depth camera sensor block) <gazebo reference="camera_link"> <sensor name="depth" type="depth_camera"> <always_on>true</always_on> <update_rate>15</update_rate> <topic>depth_camera</topic> <gz_frame_id>camera_link</gz_frame_id> <camera> <horizontal_fov>1.047</horizontal_fov> <image> <width>320</width> <height>240</height> <format>R_FLOAT32</format> </image> <clip><near>0.2</near><far>8</far></clip> </camera> </sensor> </gazebo> It publishes a depth image and also a point cloud on a topic ending in /points. Use gz topic -l while the simulation runs to see the exact topic names your version creates.

A lidarLight detection and ranging: a sensor that measures distance by timing laser pulses; a 2D lidar sweeps one plane and returns a list of ranges in simulation is done by ray casting: Gazebo shoots virtual rays from the sensor and measures where each hits. proprio_bot.urdf (lidar) <link name="lidar_link"> <inertial> <mass value="0.1"/> <inertia ixx="1e-4" iyy="1e-4" izz="1e-4" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyz="0"/> </inertial> <visual><geometry><cylinder radius="0.04" length="0.05"/></geometry></visual> </link> <joint name="lidar_joint" type="fixed"> <parent link="base_link"/> <child link="lidar_link"/> <origin xyz="0 0 0.1"/> </joint> <gazebo reference="lidar_link"> <sensor name="lidar" type="gpu_lidar"> <always_on>true</always_on> <update_rate>10</update_rate> <topic>scan</topic> <gz_frame_id>lidar_link</gz_frame_id> <lidar> <scan> <horizontal> <samples>360</samples> <resolution>1</resolution> <min_angle>-3.14159</min_angle> <max_angle>3.14159</max_angle> </horizontal> </scan> <range><min>0.12</min><max>10.0</max><resolution>0.01</resolution></range> <noise> <type>gaussian</type> <mean>0.0</mean> <stddev>0.01</stddev> </noise> </lidar> </sensor> </gazebo> 360 samples over a full circle gives one ray per degree. Values returned for rays that hit nothing come back as infinity, and your code must handle that.

An IMUInertial measurement unit: a sensor that measures angular velocity with gyroscopes and linear acceleration with accelerometers reports angular velocity and linear acceleration. The Imu system plugin (also loaded in the world) drives it. proprio_bot.urdf (IMU) <gazebo reference="base_link"> <sensor name="imu" type="imu"> <always_on>true</always_on> <update_rate>100</update_rate> <topic>imu</topic> <gz_frame_id>base_link</gz_frame_id> <imu> <angular_velocity> <x><noise type="gaussian"><mean>0.0</mean><stddev>0.0002</stddev></noise></x> <y><noise type="gaussian"><mean>0.0</mean><stddev>0.0002</stddev></noise></y> <z><noise type="gaussian"><mean>0.0</mean><stddev>0.0002</stddev></noise></z> </angular_velocity> <linear_acceleration> <x><noise type="gaussian"><mean>0.0</mean><stddev>0.017</stddev></noise></x> <y><noise type="gaussian"><mean>0.0</mean><stddev>0.017</stddev></noise></y> <z><noise type="gaussian"><mean>0.0</mean><stddev>0.017</stddev></noise></z> </linear_acceleration> </imu> </sensor> </gazebo> Where noise values come from The numbers above are plausible, not magic. For a real robot you copy them from the sensor’s datasheet or measure them: record the sensor sitting still and compute the standard deviation. Honest noise in simulation is a big part of closing the sim-to-real gap, which is the topic of lesson five.

Gazebo’s sensor topics are not ROS 2 topics. ros_gz_bridge is a node that subscribes on one side and republishes on the other, converting message types. The command-line form is: TOPIC@ROS_TYPE@GZ_TYPE bidirectional TOPIC@ROS_TYPE[GZ_TYPE Gazebo to ROS 2 only TOPIC@ROS_TYPE]GZ_TYPE ROS 2 to Gazebo only Think of the bracket as an arrow head: [ points toward ROS (it "opens" on the Gazebo side) and ] points toward Gazebo. A simple way to remember it: sensors go out of Gazebo ([) and commands go in (]). Here is the full set for our robot: terminal ros2 run ros_gz_bridge parameter_bridge \ /clock@rosgraph_msgs/msg/Clock[gz.msgs.Clock \ /cmd_vel@geometry_msgs/msg/Twist]gz.msgs.Twist \ /odom@nav_msgs/msg/Odometry[gz.msgs.Odometry \ /tf@tf2_msgs/msg/TFMessage[gz.msgs.Pose_V \ /joint_states@sensor_msgs/msg/JointState[gz.msgs.Model \ /camera/image_raw@sensor_msgs/msg/Image[gz.msgs.Image \ /camera/camera_info@sensor_msgs/msg/CameraInfo[gz.msgs.CameraInfo \ /depth_camera/points@sensor_msgs/msg/PointCloud2[gz.msgs.PointCloudPacked \ /scan@sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan[gz.msgs.LaserScan \ /imu@sensor_msgs/msg/Imu[gz.msgs.IMU Sensor ROS 2 message Gazebo message Camera image sensor_msgs/msg/Image gz.msgs.Image Camera info sensor_msgs/msg/CameraInfo gz.msgs.CameraInfo Lidar sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan gz.msgs.LaserScan Point cloud sensor_msgs/msg/PointCloud2 gz.msgs.PointCloudPacked IMU sensor_msgs/msg/Imu gz.msgs.IMU Odometry nav_msgs/msg/Odometry gz.msgs.Odometry For more than a handful of topics, a YAML file is neater and easier to review: bridge.yaml - ros_topic_name: "scan" gz_topic_name: "scan" ros_type_name: "sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan" gz_type_name: "gz.msgs.LaserScan" direction: GZ_TO_ROS - ros_topic_name: "cmd_vel" gz_topic_name: "cmd_vel" ros_type_name: "geometry_msgs/msg/Twist" gz_type_name: "gz.msgs.Twist" direction: ROS_TO_GZ terminal ros2 run ros_gz_bridge parameter_bridge --ros-args -p config_file:=bridge.yaml Images are bulky. The ros_gz_image package offers an image bridge that publishes through ROS 2’s image transport, so compressed streams are possible: terminal ros2 run ros_gz_image image_bridge /camera/image_raw The bridge only carries what you list Nothing crosses the bridge by itself. If a topic does not appear in ROS 2, check three things in order: does the topic exist on the Gazebo side (gz topic -l), is it in your bridge arguments with the right type pair, and is the direction symbol the right way round.

Sensors need frames. Your lidar scan is "in the lidar_link frame", and Nav2 or SLAM must know where that frame sits relative to base_link. Run a robot_state_publisher with the URDF so that all the fixed-joint transforms exist, and make everything follow the simulator clock: terminal ros2 run robot_state_publisher robot_state_publisher \ --ros-args -p robot_description:="$(cat proprio_bot.urdf)" -p use_sim_time:=true The /tf bridged from Gazebo carries odom to base_link; robot_state_publisher adds base_link to camera_link and lidar_link. The frame id inside each sensor message must match a real TF frame, which is why we set gz_frame_id in each sensor block. Warning If RViz or Nav2 complain about "extrapolation into the future" or messages being dropped, the usual cause is a node not using simulated time. Pass use_sim_time:=true to every node, including RViz, and bridge /clock.

terminal rviz2 --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true Set Fixed Frame to odom. Then use Add to create displays: TF, LaserScan on /scan, Image on /camera/image_raw, PointCloud2 on /depth_camera/points. If a sensor display stays empty even though ros2 topic hz shows data, open the display’s Topic settings and change Reliability to Best Effort. Sensor topics normally use the "sensor data" QoS profile, and a display that asks for reliable delivery will not match it.
documents.s: Looking at the data in RViz

documents.t: Here is a node that prints the closest obstacle seen by the lidar. It is the first piece of a reactive "stop before the wall" behaviour. closest_obstacle.py import math import rclpy from rclpy.node import Node from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan class ClosestObstacle(Node): def __init__(self): super().__init__("closest_obstacle") self.create_subscription(LaserScan, "/scan", self.on_scan, qos_profile_sensor_data) def on_scan(self, msg: LaserScan): valid = [ (r, msg.angle_min + i * msg.angle_increment) for i, r in enumerate(msg.ranges) if math.isfinite(r) and msg.range_min <= r <= msg.range_max ] if not valid: self.get_logger().info("no returns") return r, angle = min(valid) self.get_logger().info(f"closest: {r:.2f} m at {math.degrees(angle):.0f} deg") def main(): rclpy.init() rclpy.spin(ClosestObstacle()) if __name__ == "__main__": main() Notice the two filters: infinite ranges (rays that hit nothing) and values outside range_min and range_max. Real lidars return both kinds of junk, and your code must treat them the same way.
documents.s: Reading sensors from your own node

documents.t: Add the camera, lidar and IMU blocks to proprio_bot.urdf. Keep the Sensors and Imu plugins in the world file. Extend sim.launch.py with the bridge arguments from this lesson and a robot_state_publisher node with use_sim_time set to true. Launch, then run ros2 topic hz /scan and ros2 topic hz /camera/image_raw. The rates should be close to 10 Hz and 30 Hz. Start rviz2 --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true, set Fixed Frame to odom, and add TF, LaserScan and Image displays. Drive toward the box with teleop_twist_keyboard and watch the scan points in front of the robot move closer. Run closest_obstacle.py and compare its printed distance with what RViz shows. You know it worked when the scan outlines the red box, the camera image shows it growing as you approach, and closest_obstacle.py prints a distance that shrinks.

Pick the arrowBeginner Write the bridge argument that sends /cmd_vel from ROS 2 into Gazebo only. Which bracket do you use, and why? Show solutionHide solution /cmd_vel@geometry_msgs/msg/Twist]gz.msgs.Twist. The ] means ROS 2 to Gazebo, and a velocity command is something ROS sends into the simulator. Narrow the viewIntermediate Change the lidar so it only scans the front 180 degrees with 180 samples. Which fields change, and what happens to the ranges array length? Show solutionHide solution Set min_angle to -1.5708 and max_angle to 1.5708 and samples to 180. The ranges array then has 180 entries, with angle_min and angle_max in the message set accordingly. Your code should always compute angles from angle_min and angle_increment, not from a hard-coded assumption. Why is my scan frame wrong?Intermediate RViz shows the lidar points rotated 90 degrees from where the wall is. Give two possible causes. Show solutionHide solution The lidar link is mounted with the wrong orientation in the URDF joint origin (a yaw error), or the frame_id in the scan message does not match the intended link so the TF lookup resolves to a different frame. Check the joint rpy and the sensor’s gz_frame_id.

1In the bridge syntax, which symbol sends data from Gazebo to ROS 2 only? A]B[C@ aloneD> 2A lidar ray that hits nothing within range appears as what in a LaserScan? AZeroBNegative oneCInfinityDThe maximum range as a finite number, always 3RViz shows nothing for /scan although the topic has data. Which setting is a likely culprit? AFixed Frame is blankBDisplay reliability does not match the sensor QoSCThe robot has too many wheelsDGazebo is in dark mode 4Why do you add noise to simulated sensors? ATo slow down the simulatorBBecause real sensors are noisy and your code should be tested against thatCBecause Gazebo cannot render clean imagesDNoise is required by SDF 0 of 4 answered Takeaways A Gazebo sensor is an SDF block attached to a link, driven by the Sensors or Imu system plugins. Update rate, field of view, resolution, range and noise are the settings that shape what your code receives. ros_gz_bridge copies listed topics between Gazebo and ROS 2; [ goes to ROS, ] goes to Gazebo, @ is both. Use a YAML file for larger bridges and ros_gz_image for efficient image streams. Frames and clocks must be right: publish TF, match frame_id, and set use_sim_time:=true everywhere. Handle infinite and out-of-range lidar values in your own code.

Gazebo sensors tutorial: gazebosim.org/docs/harmonic/sensors ROS 2 and Gazebo bridge documentation: gazebosim.org/docs/harmonic/ros2_integration RViz user guide on docs.ros.org: docs.ros.org Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right. Next: Isaac Sim essentials

Beginner30 minBefore this:Python basics · Basic calculus (derivative as a rate of change) Imagine you have written a walking controller for a 40 kg humanoid. The first time you run it on the real robot, it falls forward and cracks a hip actuator that costs more than your laptop. Now imagine you could have run the same controller ten thousand times, in parallel, overnight, with every failure costing you nothing. That is what simulation buys you, and it is why nearly every robot you have seen in a lab video was first a program in a virtual world. You will be able to List the four big reasons robotics teams simulate: cost, safety, data and parallelism. Describe how a physics engine advances the world one small timestep at a time. Show with code how a bad integrator or a large timestep quietly breaks a simulation. Name the main approximations in contact, friction and sensors, and say when not to trust a result.
documents.s: Why simulate: physics engines and their limits

documents.t: Cost. Hardware breaks, wears out and needs a person to reset it. A simulated robot respawns in milliseconds. You can also try robots that do not exist yet: a different arm length, a wheelbase that is 10 cm wider, a sensor you have not bought. Safety. Early controllers are wrong. A controller that sends a torque command with the wrong sign is a bug in simulation and a hazard on a real robot next to a person. Simulation is where you are allowed to be wrong. Data. Machine-learning models need huge amounts of labelled data. In simulation the labels are free: the simulator already knows where every object is, so it can output perfect bounding boxes, depth maps and segmentation masks with every frame. Parallelism. A real robot gives you one experiment at a time, in real time. A simulator can run faster than real time, and a GPU simulator can run thousands of copies of the world at once. This is what made modern reinforcement learning for robots practical (you will use it in the robot learning module). Note Simulation is not a replacement for the real robot. It is a filter: it lets you throw away the 95% of ideas that are obviously bad before they touch hardware. The last stretch always needs reality.

A physics engineSoftware that advances the state of simulated rigid or soft bodies through time by solving the laws of motion, handling collisions and contact forces does one job over and over. Given the current state of the world (positions and velocities of every body) and the forces on it, it computes the state a tiny moment later. That tiny moment is the timestepThe fixed slice of simulated time, in seconds, that the engine advances per step; typical values for robots are 1 ms to 10 ms, written Δt\Delta tΔt. Each loop has three ingredients: Dynamics. Newton’s second law, mx¨=Fm\ddot{x} = Fmx¨=F, for each body, extended to rotation and to bodies connected by joints (you met the equations in Dynamics essentials). Collision detection. Find which shapes overlap or touch. Simple shapes (boxes, spheres, cylinders) are fast. Detailed triangle meshes are slow, which is why robot models use a simple "collision" shape and a pretty "visual" one. Constraint solving. Contacts and joints are rules ("this foot cannot go through the floor", "this hinge only rotates around one axis"). The engine finds forces that satisfy those rules. Common engines you will meet: ODE, Bullet, DART (the engines Gazebo can use), MuJoCo (popular for learning research) and PhysX (used by NVIDIA Isaac Sim). They make different trade-offs between speed, accuracy and how they treat contact.
documents.s: What a physics engine actually does

documents.t: The simplest way to move forward in time is explicit Euler: use the current velocity to update position, and the current acceleration to update velocity, all based on the old state. A tiny change, semi-implicit Euler, updates velocity first and then uses the new velocity for the position. That one change makes a big difference for anything that oscillates, like a swinging leg or a spring. Let us see it. A pendulum of length LLL has θ¨=−gLsin⁡θ\ddot\theta = -\frac{g}{L}\sin\thetaθ¨=−Lg​sinθ and, per unit mass, energy E=12L2θ˙2+gL(1−cos⁡θ)E = \tfrac12 L^2\dot\theta^2 + gL(1-\cos\theta)E=21​L2θ˙2+gL(1−cosθ). In a perfect world that energy never changes. integrators.py import math G, L = 9.81, 1.0 def energy(theta: float, omega: float) -> float: """Total energy per unit mass of a pendulum.""" return 0.5 * L**2 * omega**2 + G * L * (1.0 - math.cos(theta)) def simulate(method: str, dt: float, seconds: float = 20.0) -> float: """Return the final energy divided by the initial energy (ideal answer: 1.0).""" theta, omega = 1.0, 0.0 e0 = energy(theta, omega) for _ in range(int(seconds / dt)): alpha = -(G / L) * math.sin(theta) if method == "explicit": theta, omega = theta + omega * dt, omega + alpha * dt elif method == "semi-implicit": omega = omega + alpha * dt theta = theta + omega * dt else: raise ValueError(method) return energy(theta, omega) / e0 for dt in (0.001, 0.01, 0.05): for method in ("explicit", "semi-implicit"): print(f"dt={dt:<5} {method:<14} energy ratio = {simulate(method, dt):.3f}") Run it. With explicit Euler the energy ratio climbs well above 1.0 as dt grows: the pendulum gains energy from nothing, and with a large enough step it swings higher and higher until the simulation "explodes". Semi-implicit Euler keeps the ratio close to 1.0 and wobbles around instead of drifting away. This is why most engines use a semi-implicit scheme. A simulator is a numerical approximation, not reality Every simulator has a timestep and a solver, and both introduce error. Smaller timesteps are more accurate but slower. If your robot behaves strangely, the first debugging question is always "does it still do this at half the timestep?"
documents.s: Time is chopped into steps, and that has consequences

documents.t: Knowing the limits is what separates someone who uses a simulator from someone who is fooled by one. Contact. Real contact is messy: surfaces deform, micro-slip, stick-slip friction. Engines model it with simplified rules, often a Coulomb friction coefficient and a bit of "softness". Feet on a floor and fingers on a cup are exactly where those simplifications bite. Friction and restitution values. The engine needs numbers for how slippery and bouncy surfaces are. You will usually guess them. A wheel that grips perfectly in simulation may slip on a real tile floor. Actuators. A simulated joint often obeys a perfect torque or position command. Real motors have limited bandwidth, backlash, heating and gearbox friction. Flexible and soft things. Cables, cloth, liquids, food and rubber are hard. Most robot simulators treat everything as rigid. Sensors. A simulated camera has no motion blur or lens dirt unless you add it. A simulated lidar sees a perfect surface unless you add noise. Determinism and time. Simulation time and wall-clock time are different things. ROS 2 nodes in simulation use use_sim_time:=true so that they follow the simulator’s clock, not your computer’s. Warning A controller that works with a 1 ms timestep and perfect friction may fail on hardware for reasons that have nothing to do with the controller. Never celebrate a result in simulation as if it were a result on the robot. Lesson five of this module is entirely about closing that gap.

You can always make a simulation more realistic, but it gets slower and harder to set up. The right question is "what is the cheapest simulation that still answers my question?". Testing a navigation stack needs correct geometry and lidar, but not accurate wheel physics. Training a walking policy needs accurate contact, but not pretty graphics. Generating images for a vision model needs rich graphics, but may not need physics at all.
documents.s: Fidelity is a budget, not a goal

documents.t: Save the code above as integrators.py and run python integrators.py. Write down the energy ratio for each row. Change the number of seconds to 60.0 and re-run. Notice which method drifts further as time passes. Add a third method named "rk4" (fourth-order Runge-Kutta, a more accurate integrator) or simply try dt = 0.0001 with explicit Euler. Compare cost (run time) against accuracy. Decide, from your numbers, the largest dt you would be willing to use for each method if you needed the energy ratio to stay between 0.99 and 1.01. You know it worked when you can explain, in one sentence, why the explicit method gains energy and the semi-implicit one does not.

Cost of accuracyBeginner Running 20 simulated seconds at dt = 0.001 takes 20,000 steps. How many steps does it take at dt = 0.01? If a step costs the same, how much faster is the coarser run? Show solutionHide solution At dt = 0.01 it takes 2,000 steps, which is 10 times fewer, so about 10 times faster. The price is accuracy: in the pendulum experiment, the larger step can make explicit Euler drift in energy. Pick the fidelityIntermediate For each task, say which parts of the simulator must be accurate: (a) testing a lidar-based obstacle-avoidance planner, (b) training a robot hand to grasp a mug, (c) generating 50,000 labelled photos of warehouse shelves for a detector. Show solutionHide solution (a) Geometry and lidar ray casting; wheel physics only roughly. (b) Contact and friction; also the object’s mass and shape. Graphics hardly matter. (c) Rendering quality and variation (lighting, textures, camera pose); physics can be nearly ignored. Spot the physics bugIntermediate A simulated robot arm jitters violently when it presses on a table, although a real one would press quietly. Name two simulator-side settings you would check first. Show solutionHide solution The timestep (too large for stiff contacts) and the contact parameters (stiffness and damping, or the solver iteration count). Collision geometry that is slightly overlapping at rest can also cause jitter.

1Why is simulation especially valuable for training machine-learning models? AIt makes the real robot lighterBLabels such as depth and object positions are free and perfectCIt removes the need for any real data everDIt guarantees the model works on hardware 2In the pendulum experiment, what happens to explicit Euler as the timestep grows? AEnergy stays exactly constantBEnergy is lost to frictionCEnergy drifts upward and can blow upDThe pendulum stops moving 3Which is a typical weak spot of rigid-body physics engines? AGravityBContact and friction modellingCAdding two vectorsDPrinting log messages 4What does use_sim_time:=true tell a ROS 2 node to do? ARun twice as fastBFollow the simulator’s clock instead of the wall clockCDisable all sensorsDUse the GPU 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Teams simulate for cost, safety, free labelled data and massive parallelism. A physics engine repeats one loop: detect collisions, solve constraints, integrate forward by a small timestep. Timestep and integrator choice change results; semi-implicit schemes are stable where explicit Euler drifts. Contact, friction, actuators and sensors are the usual places where simulation and reality disagree. Choose the cheapest simulation that still answers your question. Simulation filters out bad ideas; it does not prove an idea works on hardware.

Gazebo documentation and tutorials: gazebosim.org/docs MuJoCo documentation, for a clear view of how contact is modelled: mujoco.readthedocs.io ROS 2 documentation on simulated time: docs.ros.org Stuck? Ask Rivet, the course assistant, bottom-right. Next: Gazebo worlds and robots

Every robot project starts with the same three questions. How will I work on this? What tools do I need? And what is the whole thing actually made of? This module answers them, so that the rest of the course is about robots instead of about installation errors. You will meet the habits that make the course work, build a workstation that runs ROS 2 Jazzy and Gazebo Harmonic, and get a map of Physical AI: the sense, think, act loop and the stack of hardware and software that supports it. Nothing here is hard, but skipping it is expensive. A broken setup in Module 03 costs you an evening.

Study the course efficiently using labs, exercises, quizzes and the Rivet assistant. Run a full robotics workstation: Ubuntu 24.04, ROS 2 Jazzy, Gazebo Harmonic, a Python virtual environment and VS Code. Prove the install works by running a ROS 2 talker and listener. Draw the Physical AI stack from motors to foundation models and say what each layer does. Place any robotics topic you meet later on that map.

Beginner25 minBefore this:Curiosity · A computer with a terminal Imagine reading a whole book on swimming, then jumping into a pool. Most people who learn robotics from reading alone end up in the same place: they understand every sentence and still cannot make a robot arm move. The gap between understanding and doing is where robotics is learned. This course is built to close that gap from the first lesson. You will be able to Describe the seven parts of a Proprio lesson and what each one is for. Use retrieval practice and spaced review to remember what you learn. Create a project folder and git repository that will hold your work for the whole course. Use progress tracking and the Rivet assistant effectively. Estimate your weekly time and pick a pace.

Every lesson has the same parts in the same order. That is on purpose: you spend your attention on the robot, not on working out the page. Hook and objectives. A real situation, then a short list of what you will be able to do. Teaching. Intuition first, then the precise version. You will see diagrams, math and code. Hands-on lab. A small build with a numbered list of steps and a clear check. Exercises. Tasks with a hidden solution under each one. Quiz. Four multiple-choice questions with an explanation after each answer. Takeaways. The few things to carry forward. Go deeper. Official docs and papers for when you want more. You will also see small boxes in the text. A key idea box marks something you must not skip. Dotted words, such as proprioceptionProprioception is a body's sense of where its own parts are, without looking., show their definition when you hover or tap them. Tips, notes and warnings appear as coloured admonitions. Reading is not learning Your brain keeps what it has to work for. The labs, the exercises and the quizzes are not extras at the end of the lesson. They are the lesson. A page you only read fades within days; a page you used to build something stays.
Two techniques from learning research do most of the work, and both are free.
documents.s: How to remember what you learn

documents.t: Retrieval practice means pulling an answer out of your head instead of looking it up. When the quiz asks a question, commit to an answer before you reveal the explanation. Getting it wrong is fine and even useful: the correction sticks better than a fact you never tested. Do it on your own too. After a lesson, close the tab and write down, from memory, the three most important ideas. Then compare with the Takeaways.

Spaced review means revisiting material after a gap, such as one day, one week, then one month. Each time, remembering is a little harder, and that effort is what builds long-term memory. A simple routine: at the start of each study session, spend five minutes redoing one exercise from an earlier lesson without looking at the solution. Over a few weeks, the key ideas become automatic. The ten-minute rule When you are stuck, struggle for ten minutes before you look for help. Read the error message slowly, change one thing at a time, and write down what you tried. If you are still stuck, then ask. You will find that half of the problems solve themselves, and the other half become much easier to explain.

The three kinds of practice have different jobs. Part What it tests How long What to do if it fails Lab Can you build it? 20 to 40 min Re-read the steps, check the verification line, ask Rivet Exercise Can you apply it to a new case? 5 to 15 min each Read the solution, then redo it without looking tomorrow Quiz Did the idea land? 3 min Re-read the section the explanation points to Labs always end with a check: a command whose output you should see, or a number you should get. If the check does not pass, the lab is not finished. Do not move on with a half-working lab, because the next lesson builds on it.

At the bottom of each lesson you can mark it complete. The mark is stored in your browser and shows up as a tick next to the lesson in the sidebar. Nothing leaves your machine, and you do not need an account. If you switch browsers or clear site data, your ticks reset, so keep a copy of your real progress in the thing that matters: your git history of labs.

Rivet sits at the bottom-right of every page. It answers questions about the course, and it can see which lesson you are reading, so you can ask "why does this step need source?" without pasting context. Use it to: Re-explain an idea in different words or with a different example. Check your reasoning on an exercise after you have attempted it. Debug an error message by telling it what you ran and what you saw. Treat it like a patient teaching assistant, not an answer key. It can make mistakes, especially with version numbers, so confirm commands against the official docs linked under Go deeper.

So that everyone has the same experience, the course uses one set of tools. When a lesson says "run this", it was written for this stack. Piece Version Operating system Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Robot framework ROS 2 Jazzy Jalisco (LTS) Simulator Gazebo Harmonic with ros_gz Language Python 3.12 (C++ where it matters) Libraries PyTorch, OpenCV, Nav2, MoveIt 2 Other versions often work, but then you are on your own for the differences. Lesson 2 gets you onto this stack.

Count honestly. A typical lesson is 30 to 45 minutes of reading and the same again for the lab and exercises, so plan about 90 minutes per lesson. At that rate: 4 hours a week finishes in roughly nine months. It is a steady pace for someone with a job. 8 hours a week finishes in the suggested 16 weeks. 15 hours a week or more is a bootcamp pace. Go this way only if you have the time to do the labs properly. Short, regular sessions beat long, rare ones. Forty-five minutes on five days is better than a single five-hour Saturday.

You will create the project folder and the git repository that will hold your work for the whole course. You need a terminal. On Windows, use PowerShell for now; the next lesson moves you into Ubuntu. Open a terminal and create the folder: mkdir proprio-workspace, then cd proprio-workspace. Install Git if it is missing (see git-scm.com), then run git --version and note the version. Initialise the repository with git init. Create a file named README.md that says what the project is, for example "My work through the Proprio robotics course", and add a line with today's date. Create journal.md and write two sentences: why you are taking the course, and the first thing you hope to build. Stage and commit: git add . then git commit -m "Start Proprio workspace". If Git asks who you are, set it once with git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "you@example.com". Run git log --oneline. You should see one commit with your message. That is the check. Mark this lesson complete, then ask Rivet: "Give me a one-line summary of what retrieval practice is."

Plan your paceBeginner Decide how many hours per week you can really give the course, then work out how many weeks 52 lessons will take at 90 minutes each. Write the answer in your journal.md. Show solutionHide solution Total time is 52 lessons times 1.5 hours, which is 78 hours. At 6 hours a week that is 13 weeks, at 8 hours it is about 10 weeks, and at 4 hours it is about 20 weeks. Add time for the capstone and for review. A 16-week plan therefore needs around 6 to 8 hours a week once you include the capstone. Any honest number is a good answer, as long as you wrote it down. Spot the retrievalBeginner Which of these is retrieval practice: (a) re-reading the lesson, (b) highlighting key sentences, (c) closing the lesson and writing the three main ideas from memory, (d) watching a video about the same topic? Show solutionHide solution Only (c). Re-reading, highlighting and watching feel productive because the material looks familiar, but none of them forces you to produce the answer. Writing from memory does, and that effort is what strengthens recall. Design your review habitBeginner Write a spaced-review schedule for the lesson you just finished: on which days will you quickly redo one exercise, and what will you do if you cannot solve it? Show solutionHide solution One reasonable schedule is the next day, then 7 days later, then 30 days later. Each review is five minutes with the solution hidden. If you cannot solve it, read the solution, then try again the following day. Moving the next review closer after a failure is the whole trick: it tells your brain this matters.

The course uses one reference stack: Ubuntu 24.04, ROS 2 Jazzy, Gazebo Harmonic, Python 3.12. Progress ticks live in your browser, while your git history is your real record. Struggle for ten minutes first, then ask Rivet or a friend with specific details.
