Beginner30 minBefore this:How this course works A robot vacuum bumps into a chair leg, backs up, turns, and tries again. A warehouse arm lifts a box it has never seen before. A humanoid steps over a cable on the floor. These look like very different machines, but underneath they are all doing the same thing in the same loop. Once you see that loop and the layers around it, every robotics topic you meet later has a place to sit. You will be able to Define Physical AI and embodied intelligence in your own words. Describe the sense, think, act loop and give an example of each stage. Name the layers of the Physical AI stack and what each one does. Explain where humanoid robots fit and why they are hard. Match each Proprio module to a layer of the stack.

Most AI you have used lives on a screen. A chatbot takes text in and returns text. An image model takes a prompt and returns a picture. If it makes a mistake, you read the mistake and try again. Physical AIPhysical AI is artificial intelligence that perceives and acts in the real world through a body, such as a robot, a car or a drone. is AI with a body. It senses the world through cameras, microphones and touch, decides what to do, and acts through motors. The field is also called embodied intelligenceEmbodied intelligence is the idea that intelligence is shaped by having a body that senses and acts in an environment., because the body is part of how the intelligence works, not an accessory. The body changes everything about the problem: The world pushes back. Gravity, friction and collisions are not optional. A wrong move can break something. Sensing is noisy and incomplete. A camera sees one side of an object, lidar misses glass, and a wheel slips on wet floor. Time is hard. A balancing robot has a few milliseconds to react. A chatbot can think for seconds. Mistakes cost real things. You cannot press undo on a dropped plate. These constraints are why robotics took decades, and why the recent arrival of strong learned models is so exciting. Hard problems that were once hand-coded, such as recognising objects or understanding "bring me the red cup", are now solved well enough to try on real robots.

Every robot runs one loop, over and over, many times a second. Sense turns the world into numbers: camera pixels, lidar distances, joint angles, motor currents, the reading of an inertial sensor. Think turns numbers into a decision. This covers state estimation (where am I, what is around me), planning (what path or sequence of steps) and control (what torque this instant). Act turns the decision into motion: motors, grippers, wheels. The world then changes, partly because of the action, and the loop begins again. That feedback is the defining feature of robotics. A robot does not execute a plan blindly; it checks reality continuously and corrects. A robot is a feedback loop with a body If you remember one picture from this course, make it sense, think, act. Whenever a topic is confusing, ask: which part of the loop is this? A camera driver is sensing. A path planner is thinking. A motor controller is acting. The loop is the same whether the robot is a toy rover or a humanoid.

The loop does not run at one speed. A real robot nests several loops, fast on the inside and slow on the outside. Loop Typical rate Question it answers Motor control 1,000 Hz or more How much current to this motor right now? Balance and joint control 100 to 1,000 Hz Is the body staying upright? Perception 10 to 60 Hz What does the camera see? Motion planning 1 to 10 Hz What path avoids the obstacle? Task and language planning 0.1 to 1 Hz What should I do next to fulfil the request? Fast loops must be simple and reliable. Slow loops can be rich and flexible. A lot of robot design is deciding which loop a problem belongs in.

Think of the robot as layers, each built on the one below. Read it from the bottom. Hardware. Motors and gearboxes, sensors, batteries, the computer. Everything above has to respect what the hardware can physically do. Control. Software that makes joints and wheels do what you ask, using models of the robot's geometry (kinematics) and its forces (dynamics), plus feedback controllers such as PID. Middleware and tools. The plumbing that lets many programs share data: ROS 2 for messages, tf2 for coordinate frames, URDF for describing the robot, and simulators such as Gazebo for safe testing. Perception and state estimation. Turning raw sensor data into a usable picture: where objects are, where the robot is, and how sure it is. Planning. Deciding how to move: finding a collision-free path, driving to a room with Nav2, reaching and grasping with MoveIt 2. Skills and learning. Behaviours that are learned instead of hand-written, from demonstrations (imitation learning) or by trial and error (reinforcement learning). Foundation models. Large pre-trained models that understand language and images and can map them to actions. This is the newest layer, and the one moving fastest. The layers talk to each other. A foundation model might say "pick up the mug", a planner produces an arm trajectory, a controller tracks it, and sensors report whether it worked. Layers are not strict Modern research blurs the boundaries. A vision-language-action model may go straight from camera pixels and a sentence to motor commands, skipping several layers. You still need to understand the layers, because that is how you debug it and how you judge whether it is safe.

A humanoidA humanoid robot has a body shaped roughly like a person: a torso, two arms, two legs and a head. is not a different kind of intelligence. It is a robot that uses every layer of the stack at once, under tough conditions. Why build one at all? Our world, from stairs to door handles to tools, is designed for the human body. A humanoid could in principle work in it without the environment being rebuilt. The bet is that one general body plus a general brain can do many jobs. Why is it hard? Balance. A humanoid is a tall, narrow object standing on two small feet. It is unstable by design, and must keep correcting itself. Many joints. Dozens of joints that must move together: whole-body control is a large coordination problem. Contact. Walking and grasping are made of impacts and friction, which are hard to model. Hands. Human-like dexterity needs many small, strong, sensitive actuators. Safety. A falling humanoid is heavy and can hurt someone. That is why Module 08 sits late in the course. Balance, control, perception and learning all feed into it, and you should have them before you try the hardest robot.

Module Layer(s) it covers 00 · Start here Your workstation and this map 01 · Foundations The math, code and tools every layer uses 02 · Robot fundamentals Hardware understanding, control 03 · ROS 2 Middleware and tools 04 · Simulation Middleware and tools, testing every layer 05 · Perception Perception and state estimation 06 · Motion Planning 07 · Robot learning Skills and learning 08 · Humanoids All layers, applied to the hardest body 09 · Foundation models Foundation models and safety 10 · Capstone and career Integrating all layers on one project You can see the shape: the course climbs the stack, with foundations underneath and a capstone on top that uses it all.
documents.s: How the 11 modules map onto the stack

documents.t: You will make your own one-page map and check it against a running ROS 2 system. Use paper or any drawing tool. Draw the sense, think, act loop as three boxes with arrows, and add the world as a fourth box that closes the loop. Draw the seven stack layers as horizontal bars, with hardware at the bottom. Choose a robot you know, such as a robot vacuum, and write one real component beside each layer. For example: wheel motors (hardware), a PID speed loop (control), a bump sensor reading (perception). Mark which Proprio module teaches each layer, using the table above. Start the demo from the last lesson: ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker in one terminal and ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener in another. On your map, label the talker and the listener. Which stack layer is the message system between them? It is the middleware layer. Save the picture as map.png in your proprio-workspace repository, commit it, and write one sentence in journal.md about which layer you are most curious about. The check: every layer on your map has at least one real example, and you can say which layer ROS 2 belongs to without looking.

Classify the componentsBeginner Place each in the sense, think or act stage: a wheel encoder, a path planner, a gripper motor, a depth camera, an obstacle-avoidance decision, a PID controller sending voltage to a joint. Show solutionHide solution Sense: wheel encoder, depth camera. Think: path planner, obstacle-avoidance decision (and the PID computation itself). Act: gripper motor and the voltage that the controller sends. Notice the controller sits on the boundary between think and act. Boxes in a diagram are a guide, and real systems often blur them. Which loop is too slow?Beginner A teammate proposes running a language model to decide, on every control cycle at 1,000 Hz, whether to apply more torque to a leg joint. Using the loop table, explain why this is a poor design and where the model should run instead. Show solutionHide solution A language model takes tens or hundreds of milliseconds per answer, far slower than the 1 ms available at 1,000 Hz. It is also not reliable enough for a safety-critical loop. Joint torque belongs in a fast, simple, deterministic controller. The language model belongs in the slow task-planning loop, producing goals such as "walk to the door" that the faster layers then carry out. Trace a requestIntermediate A user says, "Bring me the water bottle." List, in order, which layers of the stack are involved from the sentence to the bottle in the user's hand. Show solutionHide solution Foundation models interpret the sentence and produce a task plan. Perception finds the bottle and the robot's position. Planning produces a path for the base and then an arm trajectory. Control tracks those trajectories and keeps the robot balanced, using hardware actuators. Sensors then confirm the grasp, and the loop repeats. Middleware, ROS 2, carries the messages between all of them throughout.

1What distinguishes Physical AI from a chatbot? AIt uses larger modelsBIt senses and acts in the real world through a bodyCIt never uses languageDIt runs only in simulation 2Which statement about the nested loops is correct? AEvery loop runs at the same rateBFast inner loops handle control, and slower outer loops handle planningCLanguage planning is the fastest loopDControl runs once per minute 3In the stack, which layer provides messaging between programs, coordinate frames and robot descriptions? AHardwareBMiddleware and toolsCFoundation modelsDSkills and learning 4Why are humanoids especially hard? AThey have no sensorsBThey are unstable, have many joints, and depend on contact and dexterous handsCThey cannot use ROS 2DThey do not need control 0 of 4 answered Takeaways Physical AI is AI with a body that senses the world and acts on it. Every robot runs a sense, think, act loop, and the feedback through the world is what makes it robotics. Real robots nest fast control loops inside slower planning loops. The stack runs from hardware to control, middleware, perception, planning, learning and foundation models. Humanoids use every layer under hard conditions, so they come late in the course. The 11 modules climb the stack, and the capstone uses it all together.

ROS 2 concepts overview: the official introduction to what ROS 2 provides. Gazebo documentation: where simulation sits in the toolchain. RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control: an early, widely cited paper on the foundation-model layer. Probabilistic Robotics (Thrun, Burgard, Fox): the classic textbook on the sensing and thinking half. Next: Python for robotics

Beginner45 minBefore this:A computer you can install software on · Comfort following written steps Nothing wastes a robotics beginner's time like a half-installed toolchain. Half the questions on robotics forums are not about robots at all: they are about a missing source line or a wrong Ubuntu version. In this lesson you build one clean workstation, once, and verify each layer before you add the next. You will be able to Choose between native Ubuntu 24.04, dual boot and WSL2, and set one up. Install ROS 2 Jazzy Jalisco from the official apt repository and source it in every shell. Install Gazebo Harmonic and check that it starts. Create a Python virtual environment that can see ROS 2 packages. Verify the whole stack with a ROS 2 talker and listener. Commands change Install steps are the most fragile part of any robotics course. The commands below follow the official ROS 2 Jazzy instructions at the time of writing. If any step fails, open the current page at docs.ros.org and follow it instead. When the docs and this page disagree, the docs win.

ROS 2 Jazzy is built for Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (the codename is Noble). Other operating systems work to varying degrees, but this course supports only one, so use it. You have three options. Native Ubuntu Dual boot WSL2 on Windows Best performance and simplest networking. Install Ubuntu 24.04 Desktop on a spare machine or a dedicated drive. Choose this if you have a spare laptop or want the smoothest simulation. Keep Windows and add Ubuntu on its own partition. Back up your data first, shrink the Windows partition from Disk Management, then install Ubuntu from a USB stick and choose "Install alongside". You get full speed and full GPU access, at the price of rebooting to switch. The easiest way in. Open PowerShell as administrator and run wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04, then restart and create your Linux user. Windows 11 includes WSLg, so graphical apps such as Gazebo and RViz open as normal windows. Expect slower simulation than native, and keep your project files inside the Linux file system (under ~) rather than under /mnt/c, which is much slower. Whichever you pick, finish with a terminal on Ubuntu 24.04. Check it: terminal lsb_release -a You should see Ubuntu 24.04 in the output. If you see another version, install the correct one before going on. Build in layers and test each layer A workstation is a stack: operating system, then ROS 2, then Gazebo, then your Python environment. After each layer you run a tiny command that proves the layer works. When something breaks later you will know which layer to blame.
Update the package list and install a few tools you will use everywhere. terminal sudo apt update sudo apt upgrade -y sudo apt install -y git curl wget build-essential python3-venv python3-pip

ROS 2ROS 2 (Robot Operating System 2) is a set of libraries and tools that lets the parts of a robot program talk to each other. is the middleware most robots run on. Each release has a name; Jazzy Jalisco is the long-term support (LTS) release for Ubuntu 24.04 and is supported until 2029. You install it from a package repository using apt.

ROS 2 needs a UTF-8 locale. Run these and check the last output shows UTF-8. terminal locale # check for UTF-8 sudo apt update && sudo apt install locales sudo locale-gen en_US en_US.UTF-8 sudo update-locale LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 LANG=en_US.UTF-8 export LANG=en_US.UTF-8 locale # verify settings
Some ROS dependencies live in Ubuntu's universe repository. terminal sudo apt install software-properties-common sudo add-apt-repository universe

The ROS project now publishes a small package, ros2-apt-source, that installs the repository and its signing key for you. The documented way is to fetch its latest release and install it: terminal sudo apt update && sudo apt install curl -y export ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/latest | grep -F "tag_name" | awk -F\" '{print $4}') curl -L -o /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb "https://github.com/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/download/${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}/ros2-apt-source_${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}.$(. /etc/os-release && echo ${UBUNTU_CODENAME:-${VERSION_CODENAME}})_all.deb" sudo dpkg -i /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb Note Older guides tell you to download a key with curl and write a ros2.list file by hand. The ros2-apt-source method replaces that. If the commands above fail because the project changed its process again, follow the current instructions at docs.ros.org.

terminal sudo apt update sudo apt upgrade -y sudo apt install -y ros-jazzy-desktop sudo apt install -y ros-dev-tools ros-jazzy-desktop includes the core libraries, RViz (a 3D viewer), demos and tutorials. ros-dev-tools adds colcon, the build tool you will use from Module 03.

ROS 2 installs into /opt/ros/jazzy. Your shell does not know about it until you source its setup script, which sets environment variables such as PATH and AMENT_PREFIX_PATH. terminal source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash echo "source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash" >> ~/.bashrc The second line adds the source command to ~/.bashrc, so every new terminal gets it automatically. Open a fresh terminal and test: terminal ros2 --help printenv | grep ROS You should see the ros2 command help and a line such as ROS_DISTRO=jazzy.

GazeboGazebo is a robot simulator: a physics engine plus sensors, a 3D world and a GUI. is the simulator you will use in Module 04. Gazebo Harmonic is the release paired with ROS 2 Jazzy, and the ros_gz packages connect the two. Installing the ROS integration pulls Harmonic with it: terminal sudo apt install -y ros-jazzy-ros-gz If you want Gazebo on its own, or the apt command cannot find the package, follow the Harmonic install page at gazebosim.org. Then check that it starts: terminal gz sim --version gz sim shapes.sdf The first command prints a version beginning with 8. The second opens a window with a few simple shapes; press the play button at the bottom-left to see them fall. Close the window when you have looked. If Gazebo is black or crashes on WSL2 Graphics drivers are the usual cause. Update your Windows GPU driver, run wsl --update from PowerShell, and then restart WSL with wsl --shutdown. If it still fails, ask Rivet with the exact error text, or try software rendering by running export LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 before gz sim.

Ubuntu 24.04 protects the system Python, so installing packages globally with pip fails with an "externally managed environment" error. The fix is a virtual environment, a private folder of packages for one project. Create it with --system-site-packages so it can still import ROS 2 Python libraries such as rclpy. terminal mkdir -p ~/venvs python3 -m venv --system-site-packages ~/venvs/proprio source ~/venvs/proprio/bin/activate python --version pip install --upgrade pip pip install numpy matplotlib scipy The version should be Python 3.12. Your prompt now starts with (proprio). Remember to activate it in a new terminal before running course Python code. To make it automatic, add source ~/venvs/proprio/bin/activate to the end of ~/.bashrc.

Ubuntu WSL2 Download the .deb from code.visualstudio.com, then install it with sudo apt install ./code_*.deb, or install the Snap with sudo snap install code --classic. Install VS Code on Windows, then add the WSL extension. From your Ubuntu terminal, run code . in a project folder and VS Code opens connected to Ubuntu. Add these extensions: Python, Pylance, and the Microsoft ROS extension. They give you completion, linting and ROS-aware tools.

Prove the stack works. You will run a ROS 2 talker that publishes messages and a listener that receives them, in two terminals. Open a terminal and confirm ROS is sourced: printenv ROS_DISTRO should print jazzy. In terminal 1, start the C++ talker: ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker. It prints lines such as Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' once a second. Open terminal 2 and start the Python listener: ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener. It prints I heard: [Hello World: 1] and keeps going. In a third terminal, list the topics with ros2 topic list. You should see /chatter. Show the live messages with ros2 topic echo /chatter, then stop with Ctrl+C in every terminal. Run ros2 doctor. It checks your install and prints warnings if something is off. A few harmless warnings are normal. In your proprio-workspace repository, create SETUP.md listing your OS version, ros2 --version or printenv ROS_DISTRO, and the output of gz sim --version. Commit it. The check: the listener is printing the talker's messages. A C++ program and a Python program just talked to each other through ROS 2, which is the whole idea of the framework.

Why source?Beginner Open a new terminal without your .bashrc line (or run bash --noprofile --norc) and type ros2 --help. What happens, and what does that tell you about the source step? Show solutionHide solution The shell reports ros2: command not found. Installing ROS 2 puts files in /opt/ros/jazzy, but your shell only knows about directories listed in PATH. Sourcing setup.bash adds the right directories and variables to the current shell. It does not change anything permanently, which is why you put it in .bashrc. Peek inside the topicBeginner While the talker runs, use ros2 topic info /chatter and ros2 topic hz /chatter. What message type does the topic carry, and how often does it publish? Show solutionHide solution The type is std_msgs/msg/String, and ros2 topic hz reports a rate close to 1 Hz because the demo publishes once per second. ros2 topic info also lists one publisher and one subscriber while the listener runs. Break it on purposeIntermediate Set a different domain ID in the listener terminal with export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7 and start the listener again while the talker (domain 0) is still running. What do you see, and why? Show solutionHide solution The listener receives nothing. ROS 2 nodes only discover each other when they share a domain ID, which is a number that separates independent robot networks on the same Wi-Fi. This is how teams share one lab without hearing each other. Set the same ID in both terminals, or unset it, and the messages return.
